sheet states *the screen cannot open a second account while the panel is up*, and inventing a
criterion row to hold a mark would be writing the sheet a claim its ticket never made. So **a net
for a premise has nothing on the sheet to mark**, and its citation goes inside the ☐ cell of the
claims it holds up, which is where a reader of that gap will look. The mark on the claims stays ☐,
with a date and the condition that would re-date it.

Two small instrument notes from the same afternoon. `listTable` in `users-screen.js` is
`table.first()`, and the editor draws two tables of its own, so a count taken through it reads 1 on
exactly the screen row 4 is about — the locator had to be scoped by the one column header the
accounts list carries. And a file-level `beforeEach` that signs in as a teacher makes an
administrator's row time out inside `signIn`, looking for a form the shell has already replaced;
the fix is a `test.describe` that owns the hook, with the module's helpers left outside it.

### What closed, and what did not

Sixteen of the nineteen claims now have a row — one on 2 October, three on 3 October, eleven
on 5 October and this one. The register in `57-pager.md` was recounted with
the instrument rather than adjusted — ☑ 498 · ⚙ 731 · ◐ 23 · ☐ 15, 1,267 rows in 39 sheets, where
5 October had recorded ☑ 499 · ⚙ 724 · ◐ 23 · ☐ 15 and 1,261. The difference belongs to #103 and
#195, which landed in between: *a hand-kept number in a file that grows every ticket is already
wrong*, and the only safe move is to run the counter, not to add and subtract from the old figure.
Criterion 4 therefore holds the ticket open on three claims, which is what it is for.

## #113 — the level the ticket proposed failed the ticket's own number, and the mark on top sank

#37's walk had ended with a sentence rather than a defect: *สีมันออกไปทางอ่อนไปหน่อย*, measured
that day as backgrounds 1.03 to 1.22 times the page's white. #113 turned it into two numbers — a
background at least 1.5 against white and text at least 4.5 on it — and proposed a level: *200*.

**The ticket's proposed level failed the ticket's own first number.** Tailwind's 200 measures 1.16
to 1.45 vsWhite, so four of the five bands would still have been under the line the same ticket
asked for. This is `#103`'s rule one step along: a ticket's cost line is a claim about the shape
its author pictured, and so is a ticket's *parameter*. 400 is the lowest uniform level where every
band passes both numbers — 1.51 to 2.77 against white, 5.06 to 5.84 for the text — and it was
chosen by measuring the ramp at each level rather than by reading the palette table, which is what
the ticket asked for in the words *วัดจากหน้าจอจริง ไม่ใช่จากตาราง Tailwind*. Band 1 reads at
`text-red-950` and not at 900 for the same reason and not as an exception: 900 on `bg-red-400` is
3.62, under AA. The criterion is the contrast number, not the digit on the token.

### What the re-walk found that the arithmetic could not

The ticket's sixth criterion is the expensive one — the walked rows of #37, #38, #42, #43 and #45
record *สิ่งที่ตาคนเห็นในวันนั้น*, and a palette change makes those records false. Re-walking them is
not bookkeeping; it is where this ticket earned its only finding.

Row 66 of `38` builds nine scores on the nine BR-20 edges and reads the colour and the `!` of each.
Re-walked on 10 October 2569, every edge fell in the band the arithmetic predicted — and the person
looking at it said *`!` จมไปกับพื้น*. **The mark's contrast had not failed; it was 5.84, which passes AA.**
What had failed was that the mark was the same colour as the figure beside it, so on a background
strong enough to carry both it read as part of the figure rather than as a second signal. A ratio
is a claim about a glyph against its background. It says nothing about whether the glyph is read
as a separate thing.

The repair is a colour the figure does not have. White is 2.77 on `bg-red-400` and would have
failed the contrast the ticket exists to raise, so the halo pays for it: `text-red-950` immediately
around every stroke is the contrast the eye actually reads a glyph against. A chip was built and
looked at on the same walk and read as a second control inside the cell, which is why the shipped
answer is a shadow.

**And the mark is drawn by four screens, not by the one the walk was on.** `LearningDetails`,
`ProgramLevelAllStudents` and `ProgramLevelIndividual` each wrote `<span className="ml-1
font-bold">!</span>` over a `BANDS` cell, so all three sank the same day and for one reason.
**The first count was three, and it was wrong** — a review found `ProgramLevelCompare` drawing
the same mark over the same cell from `passed === false` rather than from `flagged`, so a
census that looks for the flag's name cannot see it. The species is *a mark drawn over a
`BANDS` cell*; counting by the name is counting by what three of the four happen to call it,
which is #174's rule arriving one ticket later with the same shape. Sheet `44` carries no row
about colour or about the mark, so nothing on a sheet went false — which is why the fourth
screen was invisible to the re-walk as well as to the grep. Raising
a background is a change to everything drawn on it, and the census is the mark, not the screen. The
look moved to `FLAG` in `lib/bands.js`, where the file's own argument for `BANDS` already applies
— and the four uses stay four claims, because each screen's walk is what asserts its own.

### The walk step that refuted the fix's premise

The first draft of `FLAG`'s docstring said the shadow's colour was safe because *the figure is
flagged only where it is below the pass line, which is band 1*. Row 80 of the same sheet then asked
for `BAND_FLOORS` to be moved to `[0, 2.5, 3.5, 4.0, 4.8]` and the server restarted — a step
written three tickets earlier to prove the legend reads the rule rather than a copy in the browser.
With the floors moved, the mark came up on `bg-amber-400`, where a dark red halo is worth much less
than it is on red, **and the sentence written twenty minutes earlier was false.**

`38`'s own notes had said so since September, under the heading *ธงกับแถบเป็นเส้นเดียวกันโดยบังเอิญ*:
the flag follows `PASS` and the colour follows `BAND_FLOORS[1]`, two constants that are equal in
the delivered configuration and nothing makes them equal, which is [#110]. #141's rule is the
general one — a conclusion that is right for the wrong reason expires on the wrong day — and what
#113 adds is where such a premise gets caught: **a walk step written for another row can refute the
premise of the fix you made ten minutes ago, because its whole job is to move the thing your
premise assumed still.** The configuration is not one this installation ships, so the shadow was
kept after being looked at there; what changed is that the condition and its date are now written
in the docstring, beside the constant, rather than being a thing the author happened to know.
That paragraph did not survive the afternoon either, for a reason the next section is about.

### The fourth screen, and the premise that was false there without any condition

The mark is drawn by four screens and the first census found three, because three of them write
`flagged` and `ProgramLevelCompare` writes `passed === false`. That much is #174's rule arriving a
ticket later: count by the mechanism, which is *a mark drawn over a `BANDS` cell*.

What the walk of the fourth screen then found is one layer past that. `FLAG`'s docstring had just
been given a careful paragraph saying the dark red halo is safe because the mark lands on band 1,
with the condition — `BAND_FLOORS[1]` is written *as* `PASS` — and the date the condition was
checked. On the fourth screen that paragraph is not conditionally true, it is **false today**: the
mark is `passRate > OUTCOME_PASS_PERCENT`, a share of students, and the colour is `bandOf(mean)`.
A cohort with a mean of 3.9 and a pass rate of 55 per cent is an ordinary cohort, so the mark can
land on any of the five bands in the configuration this installation ships.

So **a condition written onto a premise is a claim about the population the premise was drawn
from** — the dating protects it against the future and says nothing about the sibling that was
already outside it. The paragraph was written in the same hour as the census that found the fourth
screen, and it generalised from the three; both mistakes have the same shape, which is why the
second one was invisible to the author of the first.

The seed contains no failing outcome, so the fourth screen draws no mark at all and there was
nothing to look at. The situation was built the way `38`'s row 80 builds its own — raise
`OUTCOME_PASS_PERCENT` to 95, restart the server, look, restore — which is the sheet's technique
borrowed for a different constant. The mark came up white-on-dark-red over `bg-yellow-400` and was
read as a separate signal, so nothing in the code changed; what changed is the sentence that said
why.

And the reason the screen was invisible to the re-walk is on its own sheet: `44` carries no row
about colour and no row about the mark. A re-walk driven by *which rows name a token* can only
reach the screens whose sheets say something about tokens, which is a census by the wrong property
one more time — the row that would have caught it is the row nobody wrote.

### What the re-walk did not change

Four of the documents the ticket's file list named carry these letters and are not this palette:
`42`'s row 76 and `45`'s rows 77 and 107 are a Y chip and a *ยังไม่มีคะแนน* badge, and `38`'s
row 105 is the unmeasured-outcome chip. *A ticket's file list is a grep somebody else ran*, and
matching every file on it answers half of *confirm before you change*. The rows that did move are
`37`:59, `38`:66, 67, 80, 104 and 196, `43`:67 and `45`:80 — each keeping its September record as
a record and gaining a dated one beside it, because a dated walk table says what one measurement
returned and not what the system is.

## #194 — the three marks #157 left out, and the control that refuted the reason for sweeping them

[#157](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/157) taught one mark of the four to the sixth
question and left the other three where it found them, which was not nowhere: it wrote the
deferral into `legends()`'s own docstring. That is the #119 shape — *a deferral written into prose
and not into the tracker is a decision nobody can find* — and this ticket exists because somebody
did find it, in the file, a month later.

### Criterion 1, and the row the ticket's own table had counted once

The ticket's table was 8 October's, at `f4da863`; re-measured at `75431b8` it reproduced exactly —
☑ four spellings over 39 defining sheets, biggest group 28; ⚙ eight, biggest 15; ☐ two, biggest
38; ◐ one, 38 sheets, which is #157's sentence untouched. What the table could not say is that the
sheet outside the biggest group for ☐ is also outside it for ☑: `15-programs.md` appears once in a
table whose rows are marks, and it was two of the thirty-six sheets to edit. The arithmetic the
four marks made reachable for the first time is exactly that — **one problem per sheet per mark**,
so summing the marks' counts and counting the sheets that differ at all give different numbers, and
`anchors_test.py` has one row whose only job is to be the place where they disagree.

### The agreed sentence is not the biggest group's

The temptation with a census of spellings is to let the plurality win, and here the plurality was
the silent one twice over: 28 sheets' ☑ sentence said nothing about which seam a walked row was
walked at, and 25 sheets' ⚙ sentence said nothing about the appearance half staying a person's.
Both meanings were already decided — `CLAUDE.md` §Marks on the sheets says *a row proved only at
the HTTP seam is ☑*, and §Two test seams says appearance stays a hand-walked row — so the sweep
took the two nine-and-one-sheet minorities that said so and wrote them into all thirty-nine. **A
census of wordings is evidence about the wordings; which wording is right is not in it.**

One clause is pinned by its text, `seam HTTP`, and it is pinned in `anchors_test.py` and not in
`legends()`, with the reason written beside it: the ⚙ sentence's appearance half is Thai, and a
fixture whose text the console cannot print is a fixture nobody proofreads. So the instrument
holds the agreement, one row holds the clause whose absence was the defect, and the rest is held by
the sheets, by this story and by `CLAUDE.md`.

### A reason that is true of one sheet reads exactly like a second definition

`15-programs.md` had written two of its own facts into its legend — that its ☑ rows were proved at
HTTP and recorded under *ผลการเดินด้วย curl*, and that its ☐ row is browser-only with no request to
check. Both are true, and to `legends()` they are indistinguishable from a sheet teaching the
vocabulary differently. They moved below the legend as a dated note, which is where a claim about
one sheet's rows belongs (#54's shape: the criteria say what the system is, a dated record says
what one measurement returned). The question cannot tell the two apart and now says so in its
docstring; a sheet that puts such a reason back inside its legend is reported as a second spelling,
which is the direction the error should fall in.

### The second counter was wrong, and the published instrument is what said so

Criterion 4 needed the gear rows selected, so a second walk over the tables was written for it —
and it answered 641 where the published figure is 731. Ninety rows, one per table: its header rule
read *the next line is a separator* as a prefix test that an empty line satisfies, so every table's
last row was counted as a header. The published counter had the rule right. **A counter that
disagrees with the instrument the figures came from is the counter's bug until it is proved
otherwise** — and the cheap way to prove it either way is to reconcile per sheet, where ninety
differences spread one-per-table over thirty-nine sheets name the shape immediately.

### Criterion 4: the read-back, and the control that refuted its premise

The population is 1,244 rows — the ☑, ⚙ and ☐ of the 1,267 marks, the 23 ◐ belonging
to the mark that names its own queue and to #157 — which nobody reads one by one, so the
selection was written down: every ⚙ row whose criterion or expectation names a drawn property, by a list of fourteen
words (colour, wording, menu, icon, order, position, spacing, bold, background, band, grey, size,
placeholder, font). That is 161 of 731, and the 65 on sheets whose legend had been silent about
appearance were read back by hand. None of them meant something else: the words were mentions
rather than claims — a menu *pressed* on the way to a screen, a banner whose *text* is asserted,
and more than once the criterion was *this is said in words and not by colour alone*, which is the
opposite of an appearance claim. Three rows on `38-learning-detail-heatmap.md` do assert colour at
the browser seam, and the colour was hand-walked twice (3 September and 10 October) in sibling ☑
rows two lines below, which those ⚙ rows do not mention. That is an observation about the record
and not a wrong mark - the marks are right and the walk happened - so it changed nothing here; it
is put to the owner as a question, because adding a cross-reference to three rows is the kind of
edit that moves a sheet's line numbers under the tickets that cite them, and a sheet's record is
not rewritten to tidy it.

The control is what made the half worth running. The fourteen sheets whose legend already carried
the appearance clause were read by the same selection, and the rate there is *higher* — 96 hits of
312 gear rows, against 65 of 419 where the clause was missing. **If the cause a census was built
around is real, the control group should be quieter; when it is louder, the cause was not the
cause.** The sheets' wording was never what decided how a row got marked, which is an argument for
the sweep being cheap bookkeeping and against the ticket's own expectation that this half would be
where the defects were.

### The other two marks, and the rows that were right while their legend was wrong

The first pass selected ⚙ rows only, which is one mark of the three the criterion names, and the ⚙
control result is evidence about ⚙ wording and transfers nowhere. The walked mark's defect shape is
the mirror image and lives on a different set of sheets: the nine whose own sentence said *เดินด้วย
มือจบแล้ว* — walked by hand — where a row proved only at the HTTP seam would be a row claiming a
person looked when nobody did. The twenty-eight silent sheets cannot hold that defect, because
silence licenses either proof and the agreed sentence says so; that is the written reason for
leaving their 323 walked rows out. On the eleven narrow sheets (the nine, plus `15`, whose own
sentence said its rows were HTTP-proved, and `47`, which already carried the agreed wording) there
are 176 walked rows, and **56 of them name a server proof with no hand walk** — every one saying
*พิสูจน์ที่ seam HTTP* or naming `backend/test/…` on its own face. So those rows had been telling
the truth their legend denied, and the defect was the sentence: a mark would have been the wrong
thing to change.

The ☐ rows are 14 in all, so they were read whole with no selection: each says *ยังไม่ได้ทดสอบ* with
either no caller able to make the request or a ticket number — `47` row 5 names
[#166](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/166), which is a ☐ pointing at a ticket and not a
gap in the sheet (#97's rule). Nothing to change there either.

### Criterion 5, and the figures that did not move

Each branch was broken on its own and the reds read, not merely counted: holding one mark again
(#157's shape) reddens 14 rows including the three written per mark; counting problems per spelling
instead of per sheet reddens exactly the one row written for that arithmetic; reporting a mark only
when it has more than one spelling reddens 13; and dropping the `seam HTTP` clause from one sheet's
legend reddens exactly the two rows that read the real store. Marks were not touched: ☑ 499 · ⚙ 731
· ◐ 23 · ☐ 14, the same 1,267 in 39 sheets that `anchors.py` prints. The ticket's own figures were
⚙ 726 and ☐ 15 on 8 October; the five gear rows arrived with #141, #113 and #195 since, and the ☐
is #103's row 5, walked since. Two sets of figures, said rather than hidden.

## #155 — the fixture the spec file said did not exist

[#81](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/81) had already carried half of
this ticket away, and its own spec file said so: a switch now navigates to the
first entry of the new grant's menu, the open screen unmounts, and the next one
asks for its data under the new hat. So the first move was to re-measure the
ticket, which is #66's rule and which paid again. **The ticket's table is dated
23 September 2569, six days before #81 landed, and two of its four rows now read
differently** — the URL does change, and the stale table is gone. Measured on
10 October 2569, the exact sequence it describes (`course-in-program`, committee
→ teacher) navigates to `/teacher/teacherDashboard`, draws none of the old
screen's rows, and asks `/api/program-subjects` nothing.

What is left is one case, and `81a`'s docstring had already named it: the switch
whose landing is the address the person is already standing on. `landingPath` is
keyed on `role_id` alone, so two grants of one role code at different scopes
share a landing; `navigate` then goes where the router already is, nothing
remounts, nothing is asked, and the table keeps the other scope's rows while the
picker and the server both say the new grant. It is two presses from anywhere:
the first switch lands you on the shared landing, and the second is stale.

### The sentence that said it could not be a row

`81a`'s docstring did not only name the residue. It said the residue could not
be measured, because **no seeded account has the shape** — one role code held
twice at two scopes. That sentence is true about the seed and says nothing about
the system: #12's grants route makes the shape at runtime, over HTTP, as
`admin@`. `155a` posts the second grant in `beforeAll` and deletes it in
`afterAll`, and the seed was never touched, so the question *may I grow the
seed* — which is the owner's — never had to be asked.

**A claim that a situation has no fixture is a claim about the seed. Ask whether
a route can build it at runtime before believing it**, and the sentence to
distrust is the one written in a spec file, because it reads like a measurement
and is usually a memory of one.

### The decision was the owner's, and it had two halves

`docs/06` §Out of Scope settles who answers a ticket like this, so what went to
the owner was a narrowed choice, measured rather than argued: re-read always, or
re-read only where the address does not change. The answer on 10 October 2569
was the second, which is why there are **two** rows and not one. Row 1 is the
re-read. Row 2 is the half that says *only there*: the screen a moving switch is
leaving is not re-read on its way out. Keying the outlet on the acting grant
alone — the cheaper-looking shape — remounts the screen being left, fires its
load under a hat that may not read it, and draws the refusal for as long as the
navigation takes to land. Row 2 is what refuses it, and `alwaysreread` is that
proposal made to run (#48).

The price was read off the mount points before choosing (#77): one `<Outlet />`
in `Mainpage.js` serves both route subtrees, so the fix is three small sites —
`RoleDropdown` decides, because it is the only place that knows both the landing
and where the router is standing; `Mainpage` holds the key; `Navbar` passes the
callback through — and not thirty-six pages.

### Three lessons met again, in the order they cost time

**#181.** Row 1's first red was replaced by its own teardown. The row ran out the
60-second timeout, Playwright closed the test context, and the `finally` that
revoked the grant threw *Target page, context or browser has been closed* over
the assertion that had actually failed. The repair is the one §#181 wrote: the
fixture moved to `beforeAll`/`afterAll` on a worker-scoped request context,
which outlives a timed-out row, and a cleanup that fails carries its own message
to a second `afterAll` instead of speaking over the row.

**#139.** `noreread` then killed row 1 at a `waitForResponse` timeout rather than
at its claim — a read of something a mutant stops from existing is a wait, not
an assertion. The expected list now comes from the server through
`page.request.get`, below the seam the row is about, and the mutant dies on
`.toEqual(owed)` with both lists printed.

**#107.** The fix split `navigate(landingPath(…) ?? '/main', { replace: true })`
into a `landing` constant and a `navigate(landing, …)`, which left #81's
`staysput` anchored on a line that no longer exists. `python mutation/anchors.py`
said so in seconds while the ticket was being finished, which is where it
belongs. Re-aimed, with the date and the reason written into the mutant file,
and then re-swept, because an anchor check says a mutant no longer applies and
only a sweep says it no longer proves anything.

### What the re-sweep found, which is a fact and not an argument

The re-aimed `staysput` still kills both of `81a`'s rows — and it kills `155a`
row 2 as well, leaving row 1 standing. That is not a defect in either row.
**Row 2's situation is #81's navigation**: a switch that *moves* is the thing
#81 built, so a mutant that takes the navigation away removes the situation row
2 is about, and the kill is the proof that row 2 really arrives there (#191's
framing, one ticket along). Row 1 stands because its landing equals its address,
which is the one case `staysput` cannot change. The sheet says this; nobody has
to re-derive it from the two files.

## #152 — the decision that was about the sentence, not about the line

#152 is a `question` ticket, so the first move is the measurement and the second
is the choice put to the owner. Both halves came back different from what the
ticket wrote.

### The population was counted by the screens, not by the mechanism

The ticket's first line says *the seven teacher screens* and its table has seven
rows, one line-number pair each. The mechanism it describes is narrower and
commoner than that: **a handler awaits something that cannot throw, and then
says it went right.** Counted that way — a census over `frontend/src/pages/`
that reads each file's locally defined `async`es, decides which of them swallow
(a `catch` that holds no `throw`, or no `throw` of its own and every async it
awaits is itself swallowing), and asks whether the success sentence is set
before or after such an await — the population is **twenty files, thirty-nine
sites**, of which **ten files and eighteen sites** set the sentence after.
Counting by *teacher screen* answers seven whatever the code says (#174).

Three of the ten are not on the ticket at all: `GradingWeights.js`,
`StudentGroups.js` and `SubjectStudents.js`, the last with two sites. And the
ticket's own note — *`remove` has the same shape, not measured* — was right:
seven of the eighteen are removals, and these rows are that measurement.

The census also lost a file between two passes, which is how a third reporting
channel was found. `RubricCriteria.js`'s `load` reports its failure with
`setRefusal` — screen state rather than an overwritable notice — and a census
written around `setNotice` and `report` cannot see it. That file is in the
BEFORE group not by order but by channel: it is the one place in the tree that
already does what the ticket's option 2 asks for.

### The escape clause was false for four of the eighteen

The ticket says the refusal survives only when another form was opened in the
meantime — the `showing.current === sent` guard, which is false when it was.
Read the three lines above each of the eighteen sites and **fourteen are guarded
and four are bare**: `GradingWeights.save`, `StudentGroups.after`,
`SubjectStudents.add` and `SubjectStudents.remove` have no such guard, so on
those four the escape clause never applied and the sentence always won. The four
sit on exactly the three screens the ticket never found, which is one
measurement read twice.

Two of the seven cited line pairs had also drifted, by five and six lines, and
both now point at the write rather than at the reload.

### *As today* was not one thing

The ticket's three options are **the refusal wins**, **both are said** and **as
today**. All three were already in the tree. Nine screens let the refusal win,
by order. `RubricCriteria.js` says both, by channel. Ten screens say the success
sentence over the refusal. So option 3 is not *change nothing*; it is *keep two
behaviours, ten to ten* — and that was the sentence the owner needed, because
the question being put to them was not whether to change the code but which of
two behaviours the system should have.

**A ticket's *as today* option is a claim that today is one thing. Count it like
any other of the ticket's numbers.**

### The decision, read literally, broke a closed ticket

The owner chose the refusal, and bringing the eighteen into line with the other
ten reads as one move: put the sentence above the reload, which is what the ten
BEFORE files do. Built that way it is a four-line diff per file and it passes
`152a` whole.

It also **fails fourteen rows of `149a`** — every card screen, on both the save
and the removal. #149's claim is that a reload keeps an open form, and its rows
assert that the banner of the earlier save is *not* on the screen once a later
form has been opened. A sentence set before the reload is set before the guard
can see where the person has moved to, so it lands over the new form. The
measurement took four minutes; the argument would have taken longer.

So the decision was implemented the other way up. `load` now reports whether it
drew — `return true` as the last statement of its `try`, `return false` as the
last of its `catch`, the `finally` returning nothing so it replaces neither
answer — and each of the eighteen handlers asks both questions: *did the reload
draw* and *is the screen still where it was*. Both tickets hold.

**An owner's decision is about what the person reads, not about the diff that
occurs to you first.** The cheapest implementation of a decision can break a
closed ticket, and which closed tickets it touches is a measurement: run their
suites against the obvious version before building it.

### The fix reached thirty-six mutants in eight files

Two lines changed at eighteen sites, and those two lines are what six other
mutation files were anchored on. `anchors.py` went from 0 problems to 36:
twenty-eight of `149`'s (six shared constants), `140`'s two enrolment mutants,
`25:addstaysonpage`, and `savenoreload` on `27`, `28`, `29`, `30` and `31`.
Thirty-one of them re-aim by making the same insertion the page files got, and
each mutant means exactly what it meant.

The other five do not. `savenoreload` **deletes** the awaited reload; re-aimed
by insertion it would leave `reloaded` undefined and every one of those screens
would throw on the next line — a mutant that stops the application, which is one
of the five ways to read a sweep and the one that proves nothing. Those five
substitute `const reloaded = true` instead: the same claim (nothing was
re-read) in code that still runs.

**When a fix puts a value where a call was, a mutant that deleted the call
cannot be re-aimed by insertion — substitute the value.** #140's rule one layer
along: a change to a function's signature reaches every mutant that writes a
call to it, and a change to what a call *returns* reaches every mutant that
removed one.

Two of those five also had a Thai sentence inside the anchor, there to make it
unique. The uniqueness was never the sentence's to provide — `const reloaded =
await load(…)` occurs once in each of those files, and the `setEditing(null)`
prefix separates the save from the removal — so the tuples were rewritten
without the Thai rather than with it retyped, which is the retyping that goes
wrong.

### What the re-sweep said

An anchor check says a mutant still applies; only a sweep says it still proves
anything (#107, #68). All thirty-three were re-measured, and thirty-two of them
landed exactly where their own record says: `27a` rows 4 and 8, `28a` and `29a`
rows 3 · 4 · 5, `30a` rows 3 and 5 — which is the figure `30`'s table already
carried from its 17 September re-sweep, not the older one above it — and all
twenty-eight of `149`'s each **failing 1 and passing 28** at its own screen's own
row, read from the names in the log rather than from the count.

The thirty-third is the one worth writing down. `31:savenoreload` used to fail
six rows: row 3, which is its claim, rows 2 and 4, which die at their own
reloads, and rows 5, 6 and 8, which its own table recorded as contamination —
the restores of rows 2–4 never reached the screen, so the file cleaned up
incompletely. Re-aimed by substitution it fails three. Nothing about the claim
moved: the mutant now *keeps* the reload call and only lies about its answer, so
the restores do reach the screen and the three bystanders are clean. **The
contamination was a property of the deletion, not of the claim** — so a mutant
re-aimed by substitution can be narrower than the one it replaces, and the
figure to compare it against is the row it was written for and not the total.

Four of the thirty-three came from a second run. `ContinuousImprovement.js`'s
four had no measurement on the first pass, for two reasons and neither of them a
verdict: one crashed the browser mid-run (`Target crashed`, then the worker
exited by itself) and three were cut off when the sweep was stopped. A red from a
crashed worker is not a red (#171 from the failing side), and what was measured
beside a stopped run is thrown away (#146) — so all four were run again the next
day from a fresh baseline of 29 of 29, and all four fail 1 and pass 28 at their
own rows.

Stopping the sweep taught one more thing. The harness restored cleanly, the ten
page files read exactly as the implementation left them, and `anchors.py` said
*problems 0* — then the same check two minutes later, after nothing but
documentation edits, reported three anchors of `ContinuousImprovement.js`
missing, and two minutes after that reported none again. The file was clean
throughout, by `git diff` and by counting each of the three anchors in it by
hand. Something left over from the killed run was still writing the tree.
**An instrument read just after a sweep is stopped can be reading a straggler's
write** — the processes the runner leaves behind outlive the runner, so clear the
ports, ask the machine what is still alive, and read the instrument twice.

### The second half: the two branches that moved the page instead of reading it

Both reviews of the first round pointed at the same six lines. `SubjectStudents`
has two paths where no `load` is called at all: `reload`, which asks for the
first page by moving `page`, and the removal of the last student on a page,
which steps back by moving it the other way. The read that follows is the
effect's, and nothing in the handler can await it — so the first round wrote
`return true` with a comment saying *nothing has refused anything in this
path*.

**That comment was a claim, and the thing it was wrong about was its own
subject.** What gets refused on that path is the read the path has just asked
for. The sentence is set synchronously, the move commits with it, and the
refusal arrives afterwards and replaces it: the person is told the enrolment
worked and then told the list could not be read, in that order, which is the
one sentence the owner's decision of 10 October says must not be said.

Measured per frame (#164), because *was it ever on the screen* has no other
answer: with the refusal answered at once the sentence was painted on **one
frame of thirty**; with the refusal held 300ms, on **nineteen of forty-seven**.
The fix hands the sentence over instead of saying it — a `waiting` ref that
`load` reads when it has drawn and `finally` always clears, so a read that was
refused, or that the screen has moved past, leaves no sentence behind.

The first probe of all this measured nothing at all, and said so convincingly:
zero frames of thirty, at every lateness. It was looking for
*เข้าชั้นเรียนแล้ว* and the screen writes *เข้าตอนเรียนแล้ว*. #171's rule from
the other side — **a locator for text the screen never writes reads empty on
the broken screen and on the fixed one**, so ten clean measurements of it mean
nothing. What saved it was reading the sentence out of the file rather than out
of my own memory of the file.

### The survivor that meant the row had read at the wrong moment

The three rows went in, passed, and then the sweep refused to agree:
`enrolmentmovedanyway` and `enrolmentmovedremovalanyway` — each of them the
pre-fix code exactly — **survived 21 of 21**.

They survived because the rows read at a settle point, which is what every
other row on this sheet does and what #50 asks for. At the settle point the
refusal has already **replaced** the success sentence, so the broken screen and
the fixed one say the same thing: the refusal, once. The claim is about a
sentence that exists only between two commits, and a read once it has settled
cannot hold it however carefully it is written.

So: **a survivor can mean the row read at the wrong moment, not that the claim
was never at risk.** That is a seventh reading, beside *never at risk*, *written
in two places*, *kills too much*, *a row that does not exist yet*, *the one the
sheet predicted*, and *a claim the harness cannot put at risk* — and the only
one of the seven where the row, not the mutant and not the code, is what is
wrong. The tell is that the mutant is a faithful copy of code a measurement has
already shown to misbehave: when the thing you measured by hand survives the
suite, the suite is reading somewhere the defect is not.

Rewritten as frame samplers, the two mutants die at `expect(seen.saying)` with
**19** and **18** painted frames — at the assertion that holds the claim, and
not at `onlyTheRefusal` below it, which both of them still pass.

### What the fixture had to build, and what the proof cost

The removal's branch needs a page above the first holding exactly one student,
and the seeded class list of fifty-odd cannot have one: the branch is in the
handler, not in the data. So the row trims the real answer — `students` cut to
one, `total`, `page` and `section` left as the server sent them — which is #96's
rule again, the fixture being the fix for a claim nothing else can reach.

The population is two sites and not twelve, and the census that says so is
worth writing down: `setPage(1)` as a way of asking for a read appears on eight
other screens — `Students`, `Offerings`, `Users`, `Programs`, `Subjects`,
`ProgramSubjects`, `Rubrics`, `Departments` — and every one of them is one of
the ten that set their sentence **before** reloading, so the refusal still
lands on top of it whichever branch runs. The shape is only a defect on the
screen whose handler consults an answer, which is the screen #152's own fix had
just created.

Keeping the removal's own `load` call out of `reload` was a decision about the
proof rather than about the code. Routing both through one call site would have
read better and would have merged `140:enrolmentreloadstalewins` and
`140:enrolmentremovestalewins` into one mutant that no row could tell apart —
#68's cost, paid in a place where nothing in the diff announces it.

And `onImported={reload}` had to be written out as `onImported={() => reload()}`
the moment `reload` took a parameter: **a caller passed by reference is
invisible to a grep for the call** (#68, #133), and `ImportPanel` calls it with
nothing. The first round's own note had counted three mutants unanchored by the
fix and not four, for exactly that reason — `onImported={reload}` had not been
touched that day, so the grep that found the others could not see it.


## #201 — the rule that had two halves because the loader had two dependencies

#201 was my own ticket, written on 11 October 2569 while closing #152, and like every
other ticket its *what is wrong* was a claim with a date on it. Measured before anything
was changed, it was wrong in two ways, and both were about the shape of the fix rather
than about whether there was a defect.

The defect was real. #151 had settled that **a read that fails keeps what the screen last
drew**, and its refusal is the banner above it; it landed on seven card screens by deleting
`setData(null)` from each `load`'s `catch`. The two screens that hold a *draft* were not
among them. `GradingWeights.load` said it outright — `setData(null)` **and** `setDraft([])`
— and `ActivityScores.load` said the rest of it through `recorded` (`if (!data) return {}`)
and the effect that writes `setDraft(recorded)`. One refusal wiped a whole class of typed
marks with no line in either file saying it would.

The first thing the ticket had wrong was arithmetic about decisions: it priced the weights
screen as two deletions, when the screen is drawn inside `{data && (` and every input reads
`draft`, so blanking either one takes the typed numbers with it. There is no middle shape to
choose between; it is one decision, which is also why the owner's question could be put as
one question.

The second was the more interesting one. The ticket said the second screen was *not a
deletion* — meaning the same fix, applied twice. But `ActivityScores.load` depends on
`activityId` as well as `sectionId`, and that changes what *keeping what was drawn* means.
A refused read there is one of two things: the re-read an import fires, which is the same
question and where keeping the grid keeps the marks typed beside it; and the read a move of
the picker asks for, which is a different question, where keeping the grid leaves the
previous Activity's rows under its own heading (`activity` is `data.activity`, not the
picker's option) while the picker reads the new one — #133's mismatch, arrived at through a
refusal instead of through a race. So: **a rule about keeping what was drawn is a claim
about what the drawing was an answer to.** On a loader with one dependency the two
coincide and the rule has one half. On a loader with two they come apart, and a fix written
as #151's was written is right in one case and builds #133's defect in the other.

That is a decision and not a measurement, so it went to the owner as two questions, with the
measurement under each. The answers, on 11 October 2569: the weights screen **keeps the
table and the numbers**; the marks screen **keeps it when the Activity is the same and
clears it when the picker moves**. The second is implemented with a ref that holds what
`data` is *of* rather than what was asked for — written where `setData` is and read in the
`catch` — and row 3 of `201a` is the net that says *only*, in #155's shape.

### The mutant that was a duplicate of another mutant by accident of a closure

Each data screen's row reads two things: *the rows are still there*, then *the typed value
is still in the field*. A mutant that blanks the screen dies at the first read, so the second
would never run — #151's own lesson, where `blanks` died at the visibility read and `blinks`
was what proved there was anything in the field. So two mutants per screen: one that blanks,
one that keeps the screen and throws the draft away.

The weights screen's second mutant, as first written, re-seeded the draft from `data`:

```js
setDraft(data ? data.weights.map(/* ... */) : [])
```

It reads as the obvious *keeps the table, loses the typed number* — and it is not a
measurement. `data` is not in `load`'s dependency list, so the `data` that line sees is the
one captured by the first render, which is `null`. The mutant therefore set the draft to
`[]`, which blanks the rows, and died at the **first** assertion: a duplicate of
`weightsblanks`, leaving `what was typed` as unrun as it had been before the mutant existed.
**A mutant that reads state from outside its function's dependency list measures the
closure, not the claim.**

Two things said so, and neither of them was the kill count — which read `1 failed, 2 passed`,
exactly as the table predicted. The first was the webpack lint line sitting in the run's own
log, naming the missing dependency. The second was that the assertion the row died at was not
the assertion the table written *before* the sweep had named for it. That is what the table is
for: a sweep's number answers *did something go red*, and only the assertion's name answers
*did the claim go red*. The replacement is a functional updater,
`setDraft(rows => rows.map(row => ({ ...row, weight: '' })))`, which reads the live draft and
depends on nothing: `1 failed, 2 passed (18.8 s)`, at `what was typed`.

### What the fix moved

The five mutants, swept one at a time against a baseline of `201a` **3 of 3 (18.9 s)**, each
failed exactly one row at its own named assertion: `weightsblanks` at *the scheme the screen
last drew* (19.2 s), `weightsforgetsthenumbers` at *what was typed* (18.8 s), `scoresblanks`
at *the grid the screen last drew* (18.5 s), `scoresforgetsthedraft` at *the mark typed
before the import* (18.9 s), and `scoreskeepsanyway` — the declined option made to run
(#48) — at *the grid of the Activity left behind* (18.2 s).

Then `python mutation/anchors.py` reported **problems 2**, which is #140 arriving on
schedule: the fix had moved two older mutants' anchors. `30:swallowrefusal` was cut out of
the two blanking lines that #201 deleted (its siblings on `28` `29` `31` `32` had been
re-aimed by #151 in September, for the same reason, which is why this screen was the one
left); and `133:scoresstalewins` removed an `isCurrent()` guard that is now a block, because
the ref is written beside `setData`. Both were re-aimed and **re-swept**, because an anchor
check says a mutant still applies and only a sweep says it still proves anything (#107,
#68): `133:scoresstalewins` **1 of 7 (45.9 s)** at `133a:398`, and `30:swallowrefusal`
**1 of 10 (53.9 s)** at row 10, each matching what its own sheet had recorded.

And one claim of mine in the new mutation file was wrong on the way past. Its docstring said
the paths do not overlap with `151`'s, which is true, and then used that to say the sweep was
safe — when what matters is whether *any* other file holds these paths. Nine do: `30` `111`
`122` `133` `141-superseded` and `152` hold the weights screen, and `34` `133`
`141-superseded` `141-the-guard` and `179` hold the marks screen, two of them both.
The rule was never about the ticket next door; it is **compare `FILES`** (#85, #87, #125),
and the comparison has to be against the whole directory.

## #200 — the instrument that measured the hand walk's scope as well as the code

#152 found its eighteen sites by walking every `await` in `frontend/src` by hand, because
neither census here can see the property: `superseded-answers.js` asks whether a drawing is
guarded, and `label-codes.js` asks about a label. #200 is that walk made into an instrument
that fails — `frontend/scripts/swallowed-refusals.js`, built on `superseded-answers.js`'s
architecture, down to the babel walk, the exported `examine`, the marker with a reason and a
ticket, and the hard exit 2 when `@babel/parser` is not there to be required.

Its question is three claims in sequence, each read from the code rather than from a list of
screens: does this function say a **success** sentence; does it `await` a function declared
in the same file whose `catch` does not rethrow; and is the answer of that call **read** —
directly in an `if`, or through a name bound to it. A function that says nothing but a
refusal is not in the family. A loader that reports by throwing is not either, because the
handler's own `catch` sees that refusal. And a `setNotice` whose argument it cannot classify
is reported as a problem of its own rather than dropped, so the shape that arrives next
cannot arrive unseen (#126).

**The first run was the measurement, and it was not about the code #152 changed.** 37
functions say a success sentence around a swallowing loader; 17 read the answer; **20 do
not**, in ten admin page files — `Departments` `Offerings` `Plos` `Programs`
`ProgramSubjects` `RubricCriteria` `Rubrics` `Students` `Subjects` `Users`, almost all of
them `save` and `confirmRemoval` in pairs, with `Offerings.runCopy` and `Users.toggle`
beside them. Two were measured by hand before any of this was believed: `Users.load` and
`Programs.load` catch, say their own refusal and return `undefined`, and both screens'
handlers say *saved* and then `await load(…)` reading nothing. They are #152's defect to the
letter, on the screens #152 scoped out.

So the lesson is about the relationship between the walk and the instrument, not about
either one: **a census written to replace a hand walk measures the walk's scope as well as
the code.** The hand walk counted what it was about to fix; the instrument counts the
property, and the difference between the two numbers is what the earlier ticket chose not to
do. That difference had been invisible for a day, in prose, in a closed ticket — and it is
now #203.

Which settled what #200 could close with. The ticket asked for the new file to be added to
`CENSUSES`, and `npm run census` is a gate, so wiring it in while 20 real sites are red
would have turned the gate red for everybody. Marking those sites would have written twenty
claims nobody holds. The owner chose the third way on 11 October 2569 — commit the
instrument unwired, open #203 for the twenty, and let #203 do the wiring as its last step,
which is in #203's task list and not only in its prose (#119, #89, #125).

**The before-and-after reading was identical at first, and that was the tell.** A script run
over `git show <rev>:<file>` reported *answer read 16 · unread 21* at both `fe0b3ee` and
`fe0b3ee^`, for a commit whose own `--stat` lists all ten files. Node's `execSync` on Windows
goes through `cmd.exe`, where `^` is the escape character, so `fe0b3ee^` had been quietly
read as `fe0b3ee` and the two runs were one run. Resolved to the SHA, `e15bef9` gives **0 of
37 read**, which is the instrument red on the whole corpus before #152 and the thing #141's
rule asks for: it has been seen to fail on real sites, not only on its own fixtures. The
shape to keep is that two readings agreeing to the digit are a reason to check that two
different things were read, and the cheapest check is `git rev-parse` on both.

One number of #152's does not appear in this census: it says eighteen sites and the
instrument sees seventeen. The eighteenth is `SubjectStudents`' deferral, where the handler
hands the sentence to `waiting.current` for the loader to say, so the handler says nothing
and is not in the population at all. The census's own fixtures hold that shape, along with
its three blind spots as claims rather than as prose: a loader arriving as a parameter has no
declaration to read, a `catch` inside a nested function counts as the loader's own, and one
setter's name is all it reads — so the run prints every other `set…` name in the tree that
looks like a notice and was not read, by name, for a new spelling to show up as a new word.
Today those are `setAlert` `setError` `setErrorMessage`. 20 fixtures, and `npm run census:test`
goes from 32 to 52.

## #202 — the question #146 asked in one handler, and the nine anchors that asking it again moved

#146 gave `save` the question *is the screen still where it was when I was sent*, thirteen
screens ask it there, and nothing asked it anywhere else. #202 is the rest of the file: a
removal, a status switch and a term copy each ended with a success sentence set
unconditionally after an `await`, so an answer arriving on a screen the person had moved on
from put *ลบ…เรียบร้อยแล้ว* over a form about something else — in the one place on the screen
where a sentence reads as being about what is in front of it.

**The ticket's figures were a claim, and the replacement for them was a claim about the
counter.** The ticket said 22 sentences did not ask the question and 20 did, in 13 files
each, counted with a throwaway script it did not commit. A second throwaway counter — every
`error: false` with an `await` above it in the same crudely cut function, guarded if a ref
comparison or #152's flag opens a block around it — says **41 sentences, 23 asking and 18
bare in 10 files** before the fix, and **34 asking and 7 bare** after: eleven sites moved,
which is the number the ticket's two shapes add up to.

What is left is where the instrument has to be read rather than believed, and reading it is
what found the second half of the ticket. Four of the bare sentences are the `save` of a
screen that closes ยกเลิก while saving, so nothing can take the screen while the write is
out: structurally unreachable today, and they get a dated note naming the condition that
would re-date them rather than a guard no row and no mutant could reach (#97). One is
`Offerings.onSection`, decided on 1 October 2569 and documented on itself — its sentence is
about the write the person asked for and not about the panel they are now looking at.

**And the counter was wrong about four sites, both ways round.** It reads the eight lines
above a sentence, so `if (await reload(said))`, which sits *below* it, read as bare; and
`const reloaded = await load(() => onScreen.current === load)`, which sits directly above,
read as a ref comparison when it is #152's flag. Asked of the code instead — every consumer
of that flag, and whether it asks the ref as well — the answer is four: `SubjectStudents.add`,
`SubjectStudents.remove`, `GradingWeights.save` and `StudentGroups.after`. So fifteen
sentences moved and not eleven.

And the instrument is no better after the fix than before it: it prints **33 asking, 2 on the
flag and 6 bare**, because the guard this ticket adds sits *below* the sentence at two of the
four sites and on the sentence's own line at a third — the eight-line window above is the one
place it cannot be. The figure that means anything is read against the code: **35 of the 41
decided by a ref comparison, 6 not**. A census is evidence about the property it counted
(#174), including the census written to replace somebody else's census; what it cannot see is
published beside what it says (#123), and here the misreadings point in opposite directions,
which is why its total looked plausible either way.

**There is a third misreading, and it is the one that decides a site's fate.** At
`ActivityScores.save` the line above the sentence is
`if (onScreen.current === asked) setData(answer)` - a one-line `if` that encloses nothing but
itself - so the counter filed the site under *asking* while the sentence has no guard at all.
That site is the sixth exception, and its written reason is `Offerings.onSection`'s with
#133's date on it rather than this ticket's. The instrument written to audit the instrument
read it the same way round for one run: `.*\)$` matches any line ending in a close paren, so
the patch meant to keep flagging a one-liner swallowed it instead. A census is evidence about
the pattern it typed, whoever typed it (#174).

**And the instrument found two sites the hand counts could not have found.** Committed with
this ticket as `frontend/scripts/sentences-after-a-move.js` - the population is every success
sentence after an `await` in `src`, and the question is asked of the **enclosure** rather than
of a window of lines - it answers **43 sentences, 35 enclosed, 8 marked**. The two beyond the
hand count's 41 are `GrantsPanel.add` and `GrantsPanel.remove`, which no window could have
reached either: both hand counters read `pages/` only. A census written to replace a hand walk
measures the walk's scope as well as the code (#200), and the scope is the half nobody
publishes. `GrantsPanel` is also the pair #141 found for the same reason one family along.

The eight marked sites are the four `save` handlers whose form replaces the table, plus
`Offerings.onSection`, `ActivityScores.save` and the two `GrantsPanel` handlers - the last
three carrying #133's decision, that the notice is about the write the person ordered rather
than about the panel in front of them. That is the doctrine the owner reversed for the eleven,
which is a question and not a task: the reasons are written down with their dates, and the
marker is what makes each one a claim an instrument counts (#93).

Its own fixtures pass either way, so the run that matters is the one against the tree with a
real guard taken out (#124, #141): removing `SubjectStudents.add`'s guard moved the report to
**enclosed 34, problems 1**, naming that line.

### The way in that belongs to another ticket

Nine of the eleven are a `confirmRemoval`, and the obvious objection is that while
`ConfirmDialog` is open there is no form to press anything from. There is: the table
underneath is still live. The overlay is `fixed inset-0` and traps nothing — no focus trap,
no `inert`, no `aria-hidden` — and the dialog does not even take focus when it opens, so
focus is still on the `ลบ` that opened it and every control of the table is still in the tab
order. A mouse click is eaten by the overlay; **Enter is not**. The row presses the add
button with `focus()` and `Enter`, which is the faithful half, and the expectation that the
control *is* focused before the key is sent is what says so.

That hole is #204, and it is a way in that exists because of a defect — so the two rows that
use it are written with the sentence #67 asks for: they expire the day #204 closes, and must
be re-aimed or left as nets that say they are nets. The same screen's second way in, the one
beside a live list, is `Users.toggle` and `Offerings.runCopy`, and it waits on nobody.

### The screens that had no ref at all

Four of the nine — programme learning outcomes, rubrics, rubric criteria, programme subjects
— never had `showing`, because #146 counted the screens whose `save` could be superseded and
those four close ยกเลิก while saving. The ref arrives with #202, for `confirmRemoval` alone,
and it brings **two claims, not one**: that the ref exists and is read, and that every control
that opens something writes it. `202:plosnorefatadd` is the second of those — it takes
`showing.current = {}` out of the add button, leaving the guard to compare `null === null`
and speak over the form that was just opened. Without it the sheet would be claiming a
mechanism one of whose halves nothing measures.

### The nine anchors the guard moved, the tenth its repair moved, and the new rule

`python mutation/anchors.py` reported **nine problems** in three closed tickets' files the
moment the guard landed, and in two different shapes:

* `139:{plos,pairs,rubrics,criteria}addkeepsask` found **0 sites** — the add buttons of those
  four screens gained a line, and the anchor was the old block. Re-aimed by putting
  `showing.current = {}` on both sides, which is the shape departments already had.
* `140:userstogglestalewins` found **0 sites** — `toggle`'s sentence went inside a block, so
  the line above the reload became `}` rather than `})`. `save` has the same pair; what tells
  them apart is the tail, `toggle` having no `finally`.
* `146:{departments,programs,subjects,users}closewins` found **2 sites each** — and this is
  the one worth writing down. **A guard copied from a closed ticket's guard makes that
  ticket's anchor ambiguous**: same question, same spelling, same indentation, same file. The
  harness refuses an anchor that matches twice, which is the design working rather than a
  problem; the repair is the line *above* the question, the one that says what the handler
  did before asking — `setEditing(null)` for the save that closes a form, `setRemoving(null)`
  for the removal that has no form to close. A Thai sentence inside the block is not what made
  such an anchor unique and comes out rather than being retyped (#152).

And then a **tenth**, which the guard did not move: the repair above was made by appending
`setEditing(null)` to a constant four mutants share, and `146:studentsclosewins` quotes that
same constant although `Students.js` was not touched by this ticket at all. It lost its anchor
to the repair and got a constant of its own, `setAdding(false)`, that screen closing its add
form rather than an edit. **A repair of a shared anchor constant re-aims every mutant that
quoted it**, in files the diff does not mention — the same species as #140's rule about a
signature reaching every mutant that writes a call, one layer in: here what changed was not
code at all but the quotation of it. Nothing reported this one, because by the time
`anchors.py` was run next the repair had already been made; it is in the diff and not in the
instrument's output, which is the only reason it was nearly shipped unswept.

Re-anchoring is not proof: *an anchor check tells you a mutant no longer applies; only a
sweep tells you it no longer proves anything* (#107, #68). All ten were swept again.

### What the sweep said

Swept on 11 October 2569, one mutant at a time over the whole of `202a` — baseline **6 of
6**:

- `202:departmentssaysanyway` **failed 2**, both of the departments rows
- `202:departmentssaysnothing` **failed 1**, the positive row alone
- `202:plossaysanyway` **failed 2**, both of the outcome rows
- `202:plosnorefatadd` **failed 1**, the negative row alone — the positive row cannot see
  it, nothing having taken the screen there for the guard to be wrong about
- `202:userssaysanyway` **failed 2**, both of the account rows

Each died at its own row's named assertion — *the removal's sentence*, *the suspension's
sentence*, or the sentence failing to be drawn at all — and not at a timeout.

And the nine re-aimed ones, each against the file it belongs to — baselines `139a` **46
of 46**, `140a` **32 of 32**, `146a` **49 of 49**:

- `139:plosaddkeepsask` `139:pairsaddkeepsask` `139:rubricsaddkeepsask`
  `139:criteriaaddkeepsask` **failed 1 each**, the row each was written for (*เพิ่ม… pressed
  while a … is out stays the add form*)
- `140:userstogglestalewins` **failed 1**, *the list a … reloads does not land on the page
  the pager has left*
- `146:departmentsclosewins` `146:programsclosewins` `146:subjectsclosewins` **failed 3
  each**, and `146:usersclosewins` **failed 2**

Those last four are the numbers their own sheets recorded on 20 September, row for row,
which is what re-anchoring was supposed to preserve and the only thing that shows it did.

And one shape of the five is worth keeping. `202:departmentssaysanyway` and its two siblings
replace `showing.current === sent` with `showing.current !== null` — the guard that remembers
*is a form open* instead of *which form* — and on a removal that **kills both rows of the
screen at once**: the row where a form took the screen now hears the sentence, and the row
where nothing did hears nothing, because `showing.current` is still `null` there. That is two
reachability claims and not one claim counted twice (#191). `202:departmentssaysnothing`,
which captures a fresh `{}` instead of reading the ref, is what separates them: it kills the
positive row alone. One screen carries that separation and the other two do not, which is
#68's price paid on purpose and said on the sheet.

### The second half — the four sentences that rode on a flag about the read

The first round closed on the eleven sites the counter called bare, and the review of it asked
one question of the two it had excused: does `if (await reload(said))` ask #146's question?
It does not. `load` ends its `try` with `return true` whatever `isCurrent()` says, so its
answer means *the read was not refused* and never *it drew* — which is exactly what #152 built
it to mean, a refusal being the thing it was written to let win. A sentence put behind it is
guarded against a refusal and not against a person who has moved.

**The way in needed no second defect.** `Pager` takes no `busy`: it disables its two ends and
nothing else (`frontend/src/components/Pager.js`), so ถัดไป is pressable for as long as a write
is out, and pressing it changes `page`, which rebuilds `load`, which makes `isCurrent()` false
for the reload already in flight. Nothing is drawn — #140's guard holds — and the sentence is
said anyway, over the rows of a page it is about neither of. #199 had found this by reading the
code on the same day and filed it as adjacent work; the four rows written here are the
measurement on the screen, and `await expect(next(page)).toBeEnabled()` inside them is the
premise rather than a nicety: it is the assertion that would fail first the day #199 is closed
by disabling the pager, which is what tells a later reader these negatives have expired (#67).

**Which of #199's three options, and what each would have cost.** Disabling the pager during
`busy` changes what the screen disables, which #142 settled as an owner's question and not a
defect, and it closes this one way in and no other. Making `load` return `isCurrent()` is the
shape `docs/lessons.md` §#152 recommends for exactly this collision — *make the awaited loader
report whether it drew, so both tickets hold* — and here it would have changed what that flag
means in ten files and put `mutation/152-the-refusal-wins.py`, `140-superseded-handler-reload.py`
and `25-section-enrolment.py` up for a re-sweep: a rule is read against the case it was written
for, and that one was written where the two questions had nowhere else to live. The third is
#146's question asked at the call site with the ref this screen already keeps — `onScreen`,
which #140 put there — and it costs two lines per site and no change to any flag's meaning.

**What I wrote beside that, that it costs no other file's mutants, was wrong, and
`anchors.py` said so the moment the guard landed.** The lines option 3 edits are the lines
those same three closed tickets' mutants quote, so six of them — `140:enrolmentremovestalewins`,
`152:{weightssaveanyway, groupsafteranyway, enrolmentaddanyway, enrolmentremovalanyway}` and
`25:addstaysonpage` — found 0 matches and had to be re-aimed and re-swept, their claims
unchanged. What survives of the distinction between the two options is narrower than the
sentence I chose on: option 2 changes what a flag **means** in ten files, option 3 changes the
**text** at four sites. A cost line is a claim about the shape its author pictured (#77), and
this one was my own, written about my own fix, in the paragraph that decided which option got
built — which is the half of #77's rule that is hardest to apply to yourself.

The eleven sites of the first half ask the same question with `showing`;
these four ask it with `onScreen`, because what supersedes them is not a form taking the screen
but the read being of something else.

`StudentGroups` is the one that needed thought: every write there ends in one `after`, which is
where the sentence is said, and by the time `after` runs the jump has already moved the ref. So
`after` takes `sent` as a parameter and its two callers read the ref before the write leaves —
*assert the precondition where it is used, not where it is set* (#51) read from the other end.
The counter beside the sentence, which the history panel reads, stays unguarded (#131).

Two of the four are proved, and the sheets say which two. `GradingWeights` and `StudentGroups`
are superseded by the section jump instead, which no row walks — their own `onScreen` comments
have said so since #133 — so they carry the guard, a dated sentence saying nothing proves it
here, and #68's price paid on purpose. **A deferral written into prose and not onto the sheet is
a decision nobody can find** (#119, #125).

**The sweep, fourteen runs.** Five clean baselines first, one per spec the sweep touches —
`202a` 10 of 10, `146a` 49 of 49, `140a` 32 of 32, `152a` 21 of 21, `25a` 15 of 15 — then nine
mutants, each read by the **name** of the row that died and the assertion it died at, never by
the count:

* `202:enrolmentaddsaysanyway` 1 of 10, at *says nothing over the page the pager moved to while
  the enrolment was out*, dying at that row's own `the enrolment's sentence` expecting 0; and
  `202:enrolmentremovesaysanyway` 1 of 10 at its twin, dying at `the removal's sentence`. Both
  positives passed under both mutants, which is what says the mutant removed a claim rather than
  stopping the application (#97).
* `146:studentsclosewins`, the tenth anchor, 1 of 49 at *a save that lands after the form was
  opened again leaves what was typed where it was* (`Students.js`), dying at `the form opened
  again` — the figure sheet `17` recorded on 20 September, reproduced after the re-aim.
* The six the guard moved, each at its own row: `140:enrolmentremovestalewins` 1 of 32,
  `152:weightssaveanyway` 1 of 21, `152:groupsafteranyway` 1 of 21,
  `152:enrolmentremovalanyway` 1 of 21, `25:addstaysonpage` 1 of 15.
* **And one that killed two**: `152:enrolmentaddanyway`, 2 of 21. The second row is *an enrolment
  from another page says the refusal of the first page and not that it enrolled*, which #152's
  own second half added in `c67392e` yesterday and never swept this mutant against — so sheet
  `25`'s **ล้ม 1 ผ่าน 17** was a figure about an eighteen-row spec, and the mutant proves one more
  claim than the sheet credits it with. *A kill count is a claim about the fixtures as much as
  about the code* (#48) with the other half added: **a count expires when the spec grows a row the
  mutant can reach**, and nothing reports that — the anchor was fine, the code was untouched, and
  only re-running it says so. Recorded as a dated line beside the old one rather than over it
  (#54).

## #112 — the cap one of two screens enforced, and the reason beside it that was false

`RadarChart` exports `MAX_AXES = 10`. `StudentResults.js` sliced to it and
`SectionResults.js` did not, so one component answered ten outcomes on #37 and
every outcome on #36. The seed holds nine, so nothing on either screen reached
it; #37's own review found it and the ticket was filed rather than fixed,
because capping #36 makes row 1 of its sheet — *the axes are every CLO of the
Offering* — false, and `36a` row 1 asserted exactly that. **Changing the
criteria of a closed ticket from inside an open one is the wrong shape**, which
is `docs/06` §Out of Scope and is why #112 states three questions instead of a
task.

### One of the three questions had already been answered

Question 2 was *if it caps, which ten?* — the first ten in the endpoint's order,
which the ticket says is `clo_number` sorted as text, so any cap inherits #96's
ordering defect and the two should be decided together. #96 closed on 9
September: `backend/lib/cloOrder.js` is the fragment ten sites in eight route
files now share, and the eleven read `CLO-1..CLO-11`. So the question expired
before the ticket was taken, and what expired it is written in a file the
ticket does not mention. *A ticket's diagnosis is a claim from the day it was
written* (#66, #111, #55, #155), and here one third of the decision the ticket
asked for was no longer anybody's to make.

### The reason written beside the constant, measured

`MAX_AXES`'s own docstring said what decides ten: *they sit on a ring of 154 and
grow outwards, and past ten they start meeting one another at the top and bottom
of the circle where the angle between two axes is narrowest.* That is a rule
about layout, and a rule about layout is checked with numbers (#111, #122,
#103). Asked of Chromium's `getBBox()` over the component's own geometry and its
own font stack: **0 overlapping pairs at every axis count from 8 to 24.** The
tightest clearance is 23.6px at fifteen axes, 9.4px at twenty, 3.7px at
twenty-four; the widest label is 33.5px across and 14.0px tall.

A first pass estimated the widths in Python and said the same thing, which is
why it was then asked of the browser: *a fallback that reimplements a library is
a claim about that library's answer* (#165), and a character's width is the
library's answer.

So the cap is right and its stated mechanism is false — *a conclusion that is
right for the wrong reason expires on the wrong day* (#141), met a second time
and from the other side: nothing the docstring predicted was ever going to fail,
because the number it defends is defensible for a different reason. What is left
of the reason is the density of the polygons laid over one another: four years on
#36, a Section average and four students on #37. The owner chose to keep ten and
correct the sentence, so `MAX_AXES` now carries the measurement with its date and
says in as many words that ten is a decision and not a measurement.
`mutation/37-student-results.py` repeated the refuted claim beside
`nocaponhowmanyaxes` and sheet 37's note repeated it as *a Subject with fifteen
would be a smear* — **the sentence to grep is the sentence, not only the figure**
(#130), and this one had three copies.

### The first cut of the fix took the whole screen away

#37's shape is a slice at the call site: `drawnClos`, axes and values from it,
and a sentence under the chart when `data.clos.length > MAX_AXES`. Copied to #36
— the Thai sentence moved as bytes rather than being retyped, which is the only
way to be sure two screens say the same thing — the screen drew **nothing at
all**: eleven `tbody tr` expected, zero resolved.

`series` is what the **table** reads its cells out of. Eleven rows against ten
values is `one.values[10]`, which is `undefined` and not `null`, so the
blank-or-score ternary takes the score branch and `undefined.toFixed(2)` throws
during render. *A guard written for one caller is a claim about every caller*
(#68, #133) one step along: **a value narrowed for one consumer is narrowed for
every consumer, and the one you did not think about is the one named after
something else.** The repair is to name the two things apart — `columns`, one per
year with a value per outcome of the Offering, which the table takes whole, and
`series`, the same list capped to ten, which the chart takes. One list, two
readers, the cap applied on the way into the drawing.

### The survivor that meant the row had read the wrong element

Three mutants went in. `nocaponsectionaxes` and `sectioncapnotsaid` killed what
they were written for. `seriesnotcappedtotheaxes` — the values uncapped while
the axes stay at ten — **survived 8 of 8**, and the row written for it had been
built on a reader made for exactly that mutant.

The reader asked every marker how far it was from the axis its own title names.
But `RadarChart` draws a marker at `pointAt(index, count, value)` with `count`
from `axes.length`, and draws the **line** through
`pointAt(index, values.length, ...)`. A marker is on its axis whatever length
the series is; only `pathOf` reads `values.length`. So eleven values on ten axes
leaves every marker, every radius, every title and every table cell right, and
draws the line at eleven-fold angles through none of them — and the instrument
written to catch it was measuring the half of the drawing the defect cannot
reach.

**That is an eighth reading of a survivor: the row read the wrong element.** It
is the twin of #152's *the row read at the wrong moment* — both are the row's
fault rather than the mutant's or the code's — and the tell is the same shape
from the other direction: there the hand measurement had already shown the
defect and the suite read where it was not; here the mutant is the defect
exactly and the reader was pointed at the element that cannot carry it. When a
survivor is a faithful copy of the thing you mean to catch, ask **which element
the claim lives on** before asking whether the claim was at risk.

`pathErrorsOf` replaces it: the `d` of each series' path, each vertex against
the nearest marker of the same series, the whole of it one sentence — *the line
passes through its own markers*. `pathOf` writes its vertices to one decimal
place, so a coordinate can be out by 0.05 and a vertex by `hypot(0.05, 0.05)`
= 0.071 with the drawing exactly right; the row asserts 0.2, and the stray an
uncapped series draws is whole pixels. The mutant then dies at that assertion,
named for the series it moved, and row 7 stands under it: *a row that pins today's value and a row that says
the screen reads the rule are two claims* (#145), and here the two rows are the
axis count and the line's own geometry, which no one mutant can fail together.

### What the sweep said

Base `36a` 8 of 8, 12 October 2569.

* `nocaponsectionaxes` 2 of 8, at row 7's and row 8's `axes.length` - the two new
  ones, *a Subject with more than ten outcomes* and *a previous year ticked onto a
  capped chart*, which is what their numbers mean and all a number can lose. One mutant,
  two rows, and no narrower mutant exists: both rows count the axes, so what
  each adds is that its own way in arrives there (#191).
* `seriesnotcappedtotheaxes` 1 of 8, at row 8's *the line should pass through its
  own markers*, naming the comparison year's label in the failure.
* `sectioncapnotsaid` 1 of 8, at row 7's `toBeVisible()` on the sentence.
* `tickedyearneverreachesthechart` 2 of 8 — **re-aimed by #112**. It quoted the
  whole `const series = […]` literal, which the fix rewrote into two lists, so
  it now takes the one the chart reads: `columns.slice(0, 1)`. *A change to what
  a call returns reaches every mutant that quoted it* (#140, #152). It kills row
  2 as before and row 8 as well, which is new and true: row 8 says both lines are
  there. The sheet's older table credits it with row 2 alone, which is the sweep
  it was written at and stays as the record, with the re-aiming noted beside it.

## #203 — the twenty rows that passed against the defect, and the screen that had nowhere to say it

#152 settled what the system does when a write succeeds and the list re-read is
refused: **the refusal wins**, decided by the owner on 10 October 2569. #152
carried that to eighteen sites in ten ผู้สอน files. `swallowed-refusals.js` —
the census #200 built out of that walk and committed unwired, because wiring it
would have turned `npm run census` red for everybody — counted the rest:
**twenty sites in ten administration files**, still 20 of 37 when re-measured on
12 October before anything was written, which is the one thing a ticket's own
list of sites is for (*a ticket's diagnosis is a claim from the day it was
written*).

The fix is #152's shape letter for letter: `load` answers whether it drew
(`return true` at the end of its `try`, `false` in its `catch`) and the handler
reads that answer before saying its own sentence. The flag says *the read was
not refused* and never *the screen is still the one that asked* — that second
question is #202's, asked by the caller with its own clause, and the two are two
clauses on purpose (#202).

### Nineteen of twenty rows passed against the code they were written for

Every one of the twenty sites says its sentence **above** the reload, so the
refusal that lands next *replaces* it. At any settle point the banner reads the
refusal and nothing else — on the broken screen exactly as on the fixed one.
Written as a single read at the settle point the handler ends with, **nineteen
of the twenty rows passed against the unfixed code**, before a mutant existed.

This is the seventh reading of a survivor (*a survivor can mean the row read at
the wrong moment*), which #152 paid for with two mutants that were faithful
copies of a measured defect and survived 21 of 21. #203 got the same finding for
nothing, because the rows were run against the defect first. That is the cheap
instrument and it generalises: **a new row is run against the unfixed code
before any mutant is written, and a row that passes there is measuring
nothing.** A sweep answers the same question four hours later and one mutant at
a time.

The rows then read `document.body.innerText` on every
`requestAnimationFrame` — `watchForTheSentence` and `neverSaid`, moved out of
`152a` into `e2e/support/frame-sampler.js` so both files share one sampler. That
move costs the proof nothing: no row's claim lives in the sampler, so it is an
instrument and not an assertion (#171's note on shared fixtures, and #68's price
is not paid). And each row asserts the refusal **is** on the screen at the end,
because a sampler looking for a sentence the screen never writes answers *never*
at every lateness, broken or fixed (#171).

### The screen that had nowhere to say it

Eighteen mutants, one per site, each `const reloaded = (await load(…)) || true`:
the reload still happens and is still refused, and what the mutant removes is
the *reading of its answer*, which is exactly what the ticket added. Eighteen
killed one row each, and in every case the row of their own site.

Two survived **0 of 22**: `rubriccriteriasaveanyway` and
`rubriccriteriaremovalanyway`. The mechanism is in the component and not in the
harness. `RubricCriteria`'s `load` does not put a banner over the table when the
list is refused — the whole screen is about one Rubric, so a refusal about that
Rubric is the *state of the screen*: it sets `refusal`, and the component then
returns a card carrying that sentence and a link back instead of the table and
its `<Notice>`. The sentence the handler sets after a refused reload has nowhere
to draw, before the ticket and after it, and the only way off the card unmounts
the screen.

So this is **the ninth reading of a sweep**: a survivor can mean the defect is
unreachable because the screen answers a refused read by *replacing the surface
