the sentence would be drawn on*. It is #47's sixth reading one step further —
#47's state was unreachable at the seam and reachable for a person; this one is
unreachable for anybody. The two mutants came out, and the two rows stay as nets
that say they are nets, with the condition that would re-date them written
beside them: the day that screen starts drawing a banner over its table instead,
the claim becomes reachable and those two mutants are the ones to write back.

The rows had to change as well, and that is the part worth keeping: a row that
says only *I never saw the sentence* passes on that screen for the wrong reason.
Each now also asserts the **mechanism** — that the refusal card and its way back
are what is in front of the person. *A red is not a measurement until the same
read has been seen green* (#171) has a twin here: **a green is not a measurement
until something is known to be able to make it red**, and on a screen where
nothing can, the row says so on its face.

The code change was kept on that screen anyway. Ten files now read their
loader's answer the same way, which is one shape to remember rather than nine
and an exception, and the guard is already there the day the loader changes. The
sheet carries why no mutant holds it.

### The half the census cannot see

Eight of the twenty handlers have no reload of their own to read: they **move
the page** instead — six removals that step back off a page they have emptied,
`Students.save` and `Offerings.runCopy` asking for page one. The read is the
*effect's*, so the handler has nothing to await and the sentence is handed to a
`waiting` ref for `load` to say once it has drawn, which is #152's shape on
`SubjectStudents.js`. The census cannot see any of it: it looks for a sentence
said after an awaited loader, and on this branch no loader is awaited.

That half is held by a **pair** of rows on the register, where 173 seeded
students make page two free: one says the handover happens at all, the other
that a refusal still wins across it. The pair is the point. With only the
negative row, deleting the line in `load` that says the waiting sentence would
have broken nothing — *before trusting a new assertion, break the thing it is
about* (#124), and `studentsdrewunsaid` is that break made permanent. The other
seven ways in are the same code, so what each would add is only that its own way
in arrives there (#191); the sheets say *ยังไม่ได้ทดสอบ* with the date and the
condition rather than borrowing the register's mark.

### Twenty-eight mutants of six closed tickets moved, and none of them says so

Adding a line to a block re-aims every mutant whose anchor quoted that block
whole (#121, #202). The ticket moved **twenty-eight**: sixteen of #140, five of
#146, three of #202, one each of #133, #21, #23 and #68. Two needed #152's other
rule — when a fix puts a value where a call was, a mutant that *deleted* the
call is re-aimed by **substituting the value**, because deleting the line now
leaves `reloaded` undefined, which stops the sentence as well as the read and
proves neither. And #146's four screens share two constants, so both were
redefined rather than split: *the repair of a shared constant re-aims every
mutant that quotes it, and the diff reads as whitespace* (#202).

`python mutation/anchors.py` was run while the change was being made rather than
at the end, and said `problems 0` — on 955 mutants and 976 anchors by the
close, three of the mutants being ones the re-sweep below made it necessary to
write. That is all it
can say: an anchor check tells you a mutant still grips, only a sweep tells you
it still proves anything (#107, #68), so all twenty-eight were re-swept against
their own suites — with the spec files named in full, because a test-file
argument is matched as a substring and `21a` would otherwise run `121a`, `68a`
`168a` (#154, #158).

The re-sweep paid for itself twice, and both times the thing it caught was
invisible to every other instrument.

**A guard that is split shrinks every mutant that quoted it whole.** #146's
`<screen>closewins` deletes the line that closes a form a later edit reopened,
and that line used to sit inside the block that also carried the save's
sentence, so one mutant failed **three** rows on Departments, Programs and
Subjects: two about the form and a third — `a save that lands while the next row
is being read says nothing` — about the sentence. #203 gave the sentence its own
`if`. The mutant still grips, still means what its sheet says it means, and now
fails **two**: the third row has no mutant under it at all. `anchors.py` cannot
see this, because the anchor is exact and the code it quotes is untouched; the
diff cannot, because the shrink is in a block the diff only adds a line to; and
nothing goes red, because the row still passes. Only re-running the mutant says
it. The repair is a mutant per screen aimed at the line that now carries the
claim — `146:<screen>savesaysanyway`, each
of which fails **3 of 49** — which is the same move as *a mutant that survives
where its own file predicted a kill has found a row that does not exist yet*
(#118), read from the other end: a row that exists and has quietly stopped being
proved. Three rows and not one, because the two form rows end with an assertion
that the earlier save's banner is not on the screen: what the new mutant proves
is read off **which assertion** died, not off the count (#201) — `closewins`
kills those two at the form, this one at the banner, and the third row at the
only claim it makes.

**A re-aim is faithful when it preserves the mistake, not when it finds the
line.** The first re-aim of #202's three `<screen>saysanyway` mutants moved them
onto the line #203 had written and dropped the whole clause, which reads like
the convention the same file already uses for its post-#152 mutants
(`enrolmentaddsaysanyway`). It is a different mutant. `showing.current !== null`
is a guard that remembers *is a form open* instead of *which form*, so it speaks
over the form that took the screen **and** stays silent where nothing did, and
it fails both of each screen's rows. No clause at all speaks always, so the
positive row — `says what it did when nothing took the screen` — passes, and on
sheets `19` and `11` that positive row cites this very mutant. Two more ⚙ rows
would have been left with nothing under them, by the fix for the problem one
paragraph up. What caught it was the drop from two kills to one read against the
sheet's own **description** of the mutant, which is a claim about what the mutant
means and not only about where it points. Mutating the comparison instead of the
line keeps that sentence true and kills both rows: **2 of 10** on each of the
three screens, against the 2 of 6 their sheets record from 11 October, which is
the same two rows measured with that day's suite.

## #205 — the sentence that was handed over, and the two guards that were asking about different things

#152 gave the ผู้สอน screens a ref: a handler that moves the page instead of
re-reading it cannot await the read, so it writes its sentence into
`waiting.current` and `load` says it once it has drawn. #203 carried the same
shape to ten administration files. #205 is about the shape itself, and both
halves of it were wrong.

The ticket named one of them. Measuring found two, which is #148/#149's rule —
**two mechanisms for one symptom are measured as a grid, not argued as a
choice** — and the second was the one that decided what the fix had to be.

### Mechanism A: the read that was superseded threw away a sentence handed over after it left

`load`'s `finally` read

```js
} finally {
  if (isCurrent()) {
    setLoading(false)
  }
  waiting.current = null
}
```

The clearing sat **outside** `isCurrent()`. A read the screen had already
replaced still landed, and on its way out it emptied the ref — including of a
sentence written into it *after* that read was sent. The person added a student
successfully and heard nothing at all.

That is #202's family read from the other end. #202 asked *is the screen still
the one that asked* around the **saying**; nothing asked it around the
**clearing**, and a clearing is a write about the same state.

### Mechanism B: a move that causes no read, and a sentence that is said later over another list

`reload` was `useCallback(async said => { … }, [page, load])`, so the `page` it
compared against was the one its render closed over. A handler that leaves page
2 while the write is out, meets a person who has walked back to page 1, and then
calls `setPage(1)`, sets the page to the value it already has: **React causes no
read.** The sentence stays in the ref.

My written prediction for that row was that the sentence is never said. The row
measured **1**, not 0: the ref outlives the handler, so the sentence is said by
the person's **next** read — over a list it is not about. This is #137 one layer
along (*what nothing measures, nothing cleans*): **a stranded sentence is not a
lost sentence; somebody else says it.** It was the assertion that said so, not
the reasoning, which is the argument for writing a prediction down as an
`expect` rather than keeping it in your head.

### The ticket's own reason for it not hurting yet was #179's shape, written by me

On 12 October I had written beside this ref that no row could reach the clause,
because the confirm button is `disabled={busy}`. That is **#179 exactly** — *a
reason that names a way in has named a way in, not the population* — and the
population here is eight screens whose `Pager` is **not** disabled while a write
is out, which this screen's own `add` had measured eleven days earlier as #199's
open owner question. The person who wrote the reason was the person who had just
measured the thing beside it (#113's twin).

### The fix, and the round of it that failed

The owner chose two layers of four: the ref holds what the sentence is **of**,
and the handler reads the live page rather than the one its render closed over.

```js
const readOf = (sectionId, page) => `${sectionId}:${page}`
```

one per screen, at module level, its parameters being that loader's own
dependency list minus the callbacks — which is #185's key rule (*a guard that
pairs an answer with what it was asked for has to name what identifies the
request*) applied to a sentence instead of to an answer. `load` computes its own
`key` first, says the sentence only when `waiting.current.of === key`, and clears
the ref **inside** `if (isCurrent())`.

The first round gave the by-hand branch the sentence to say itself, and row 2
stayed red at exactly the assertion it had been red at before. The reason is the
finding of this ticket: **two guards that both ask *is this still current* can be
asking about different things.** #202's `sent` is a *loader*, and a loader
belongs to a page; the sentence belongs to an *enrolment*, which does not. The
person had moved, so `onScreen.current === sent` was false and #202's guard
refused the sentence correctly — refusing a sentence that was about something
still on the screen. Ask what the claim is **of** before choosing who says it.
So both branches hand over, and `load`'s key decides. The three "back to page
one" sites (`25`, `17`, `23`) then carry one rule instead of two.

### What was not rebuilt, and why

The cleaner shape — *the handler never says anything; `load` says everything* —
would have deleted the lines five of #202's and #203's mutants quote. That is
#152's lesson from the other side (*the cheapest implementation of an owner's
decision can break a closed ticket*), so the minimum faithful change was built
instead: eleven mutants re-aimed, none deleted, and the six-screen shared
constants in `203-…py` left untouched by giving the two screens that changed
their own constants (#202's tenth re-aim lesson — a constant several mutants
share, edited to disambiguate them, moves every mutant that quoted it).

### Instruments

`npx prettier --check` fails on **all eight** of these files at HEAD, so it is
not a gate here; #189 recorded two such files and the number is eight. The
question it can still answer is whether prettier disagrees with the lines the
diff **adds**, which is answered by diffing prettier's own output before and
after. It did not.

The run of the three new rows, and of every suite afterwards, was watched with a
`grep -qE "passed|failed"` which matched the **test title**
`151a-failed-reload-keeps-the-list` and announced a 778-row suite finished at
row 308. A filter for a summary line is anchored at the start of it:
`^  [0-9]+ (passed|failed)`.

And the two new Thai rows shipped mojibaked through a heredoc, which ate the
backslash of `ร` so the Thai was already Thai before `unicode_escape` saw
it and was encoded twice. The memory rule for that is written down (*write edit
scripts to a file, not a heredoc*); what caught it was the codepoint scan, not
reading it.

### The three rows, and the one that needed the other two to exist

`205a` holds three rows, each built where the mechanisms are visible and each
run against the unfixed code before its mutant was written (#203). Rows 1 and 2
were red there — mechanism A and mechanism B. Row 3, the one that says *a read
of another list clears the sentence without saying it over that list*, was
**green** on the broken code, because the half it holds did not exist yet: the
sentence was indeed said over the wrong list that day, by mechanism B, and not
by a read the screen still wanted. Its mutant (`saysanyread`, which drops the
key comparison) is what puts it at risk, and it kills that row and no other.

Each of the three kills exactly one row, each a different one, each at its own
row's own assertion and not at a precondition or a timeout. The numbers are on
`docs/acceptance/25-section-enrolment.md`.

### Eleven mutants re-aimed, and the one sheet that needed no note

The fix changes code five sheets' mutants quote, so eleven were re-aimed and
each re-swept against its own file, whole, with that file's own clean baseline
first: `140a` 32 of 32, `152a` 21 of 21, `203a` 22 of 22, `68a` 3 of 3, `144a`
10 of 10. All eleven kill what their sheets say they kill — `140:…reloadstalewins`
its **two** rows, because `reload` is the one call site with two callers, and the
other ten one row each, every one at its own row's own assertion.

Two of them changed what they *mean*, which is the thing a kill count cannot
say. `203:studentssaveanyway` and `203:offeringscopyanyway` were
`(await load(...)) || true`: the branch read the answer and the mutant deleted
the reading. That branch no longer reads the answer at all — it hands the
sentence over — so the shape that preserves the mistake is *say the sentence
here, after the await*, which says it whatever the read answered. The sheets'
12 October paragraphs describe the old shape and stay as the dated records they
are (#54); the new meaning is written beside them with today's date.

One figure looked like a shrink and was not. Sheet `57` records
`140:studentssavestalewins` killing **2**, because a `144a` filter row presses
the same call site; swept against `140a` alone it kills 1. Measured against
`144a` as well it kills one there too — two rows across two files, which is what
the sentence meant. **A kill count carries the set it was measured on**, and a
re-measurement with a smaller set is not a finding (#154/#158).

And sheet `44` needed no note at all, though a grep for the eleven names put it
on the list. Its `staleclearsloading` is **#129's** mutant in
`mutation/129-stale-report.py`, aimed at `ProgramLevelCompare.js`; the one this
ticket re-aimed is #68's, aimed at `Students.js`. Same name, two files, and the
harness keys a mutant inside its own file — #185's collision, met from the
reading end: **a grep for a mutant's name finds the sheets of every ticket that
chose that name.** Ask the mutation file which target it carries before writing
on a sheet.

### The coordinate the fix had, and the row it did not have

Both review axes, separately, pointed at the same hunk: the by-hand branch asks
`onPage.current` for the page and then writes the key out of the render's
closure — `readOf(1, program)` — while the filter `<select>` carries no
`disabled` and does `setPage(1); setProgram(…)`. Move the filter while the save
is out and the handover names a read nobody is going to make.

My first reading of that was *a regression I introduced*, and measuring it says
both reviews and that reading were right about the behaviour and wrong about
what it is. At `HEAD` the sentence **is** said there — `load`'s
`return true` answers *not refused* whether or not `isCurrent()` held, and the
form ref the guard compares is untouched by a filter — so the banner reads 1 over
the moved filter's list. With the fix it reads 0. The row that measures it was
red before and green after, which is the only thing that separates the two
readings.

And the new behaviour is **the decision, not a defect**: the sentence belongs to
the read it was handed to, which is row 3's claim in the other half of the key.
*A read of this list is of a page and of a filter* — the same page of a
different programme is a different list — so what the owner settled for the page
coordinate settles the filter coordinate by the same sentence. What was missing
was not a fix but a **row**: nothing in the suite said so, and a behaviour no row
holds is an accident waiting to be refactored away. `205a` row 4 holds it, with
`205:keyforgetsthefilter` — `readOf` dropping its second parameter — to put it at
risk.

Two rules come out of that, and the first is about reviews. **A review finding
can be right about the behaviour and wrong about its name**: *regression*,
*intended consequence* and *untested claim* are three different things about one
diff, and only a row run on both sides of the change tells them apart. The
second is the repo's own, met from a new side: the question *is this still what
was asked for* has as many coordinates as the loader has dependencies (#140),
so a key written from one of them answers for one of them. `readOf`'s parameter
list is that census, which is why it is the loader's dependency list minus the
callbacks — and why the row that proves it has to move a **filter**, not a page.

## #108 — the ceiling one screen enforced, and the number the other screen could move

`activity_clo_mapping.score` is `ROUND(score_number * weight / 100, 2)`, written
by the Activity editor (#33) and read by the marks grid (#34) as the ceiling a
cell may not exceed, and by the attainment report (#38) as the denominator it
divides by. #34 guards it twice — `markOverClo` per outcome, `markOverActivity`
for the whole — and #33 could move it under marks already entered, because its
own guard stops at *removal*: `markedCloLeaving` refuses a CLO row leaving an
Activity people have been marked under, and says nothing about the row that
stays while the base beneath it changes. The editor's header had said so since
the ticket was written, and deferred the decision.

### Measured before anything was proposed

The ticket's *what is wrong* is a claim from the day it was written, so both of
its halves were measured at the seam first, with a throwaway test file that was
deleted afterwards. Both were true, and worse than the ticket's wording: `PUT
score_number: 1` was answered **200** and left **114** of the seeded marks above
their own share; `PUT weight: 1` on one row was answered **200** and left **57**;
and `cloAssessment.earnedOf` then read `earned 49.02 / available 1` for one
student on one outcome — 4,902% of an outcome, on a screen whose whole job is to
report attainment. So the state #34's two guards exist to prevent was reachable
from a screen two menu items away, which is what made this a defect rather than
an asymmetry.

That measurement also handed over the fixture (#117). The seeded `สอบกลางภาค`
carries three outcomes whose top mark sits within a hair of its share — 33.82 of
34.00, 32.95 and 32.91 of 33.00 — so one step either way separates a save that
must be refused from one that must go through. A fixture built big would have
proved much less.

### The decision was not mine, and it had three answers

`docs/06` §Out of Scope settles who answers a question a ticket contains, and
this one says so itself: *deciding what a changed denominator should do is a
product decision about marks*. So the three options were priced and put to the
owner — refuse every edit once marks exist, like `markedCloLeaving`; refuse only
where a recorded mark would be left above its new share; or rescale the recorded
marks. The owner chose the middle one on 13 October 2569.

The order of the gates then followed from #60: the new guard goes **last** in the
handler, after `refuseSave` and `markedCloLeaving`, because that is where it is
reached by exactly the saves that used to succeed silently. And the share is
computed in the same statement shape `save` writes, so the ceiling a person is
refused against cannot drift from the ceiling they would have been given by a
rounding step taken in another language. One comparison serves both of #34's
ceilings: a share cannot exceed the full mark, so a mark inside its share is
inside the whole by construction.

### The row that makes the other two rows mean anything

A guard of the shape *refuse only where X* is wrong in two directions — it can
let through a save that should be refused, and it can refuse a save that should
go through — and the two refusal rows cannot fail in the second direction at all.
The third row is the one that can: *an edit that leaves every recorded mark
inside its share still saves*. That is #48's rule met again (a criterion answered
*no* needs a row as much as one answered *yes*), and the mutant that holds it is
#48's other rule: the **declined** option made to run. `refuseseverymarkedrow`
is option one of the ticket, implemented as `WHERE s.score IS NOT NULL`, and it
is the only thing that turns *we chose otherwise* from a sentence on a sheet into
a claim the suite holds.

All three rows were run against the unfixed route before any mutant was written
(#203). The two refusal rows went red; the third passed on its own and failed in
the full file, because on the unfixed code the first two rows' saves **succeed**
and move the seed — the contamination being the defect itself. The restore
therefore went into the `finally` of all three rows and was written in SQL below
the seam, not as a second `PUT`: a cleanup that goes through the code under test
cannot land while a mutant is applied (#181). The first draft of that restore
used one parameter as both `int` and `numeric`, which Postgres refuses as
`inconsistent types deduced for parameter $3` — and because it threw in a
`finally`, the sweep's first run reported the *restore* rather than the row,
which is #181's other half arriving uninvited.

### What the sweep said that I did not know before running it

Three mutants, each against the whole backend suite rather than the one file,
since the code is in a route other files call — so *does it kill too much* is
asked in the same run (#45). Baseline **820 of 820** (25.4s).

`basecanmove` (`WHERE false`, which is the pre-#108 behaviour exactly) killed
**2 of 820** — the two refusal rows and nothing else. `namestheotherend` (order
from the far end) killed **1**, the full-mark row only, which is the half of that
row claiming *which* outcome the sentence names.

`refuseseverymarkedrow` killed **2**, and only one of them was the row it was
written for. It also killed the *weight* row, through the count in the sentence
rather than through the refusal: refusing every marked row counts all 57 marks
where the real guard counts only those above the new share. And it **survived**
the full-mark row, for the reason #117 gives: at half the full mark the new share
is 17.00 and all 57 marks are above it, so *every mark* and *every mark above the
share* are the same number there and the sentence is identical. A mutant that
swaps one implementation for another is invisible wherever the two agree — and
the place they disagreed was the row whose new share was 32.00.

## #206 — the step back that was made from a page nobody was on, and the row whose arithmetic hid half the fix

#205 gave the handed-over sentence a key, so that the read which draws the list
says it and a read of anything else does not. Seven removals wrote that key as
`readOf(page - 1, …)` out of the `page` their render closed over, while the move
itself was `setPage(current => current - 1)`, made from the page the pager is on.
For somebody standing still the two are one number. For anybody who moved while
the removal was out they are two, and the sentence is then keyed for a read
nobody is going to make — so it is **never said**, which is a different failure
from #205's *said over another list*, and the person is carried off the page they
moved to as well.

### The claim was measured before the code was touched

The ticket's *what is wrong* is a claim from the day it was written, so the
measurement came first, at the browser seam on the real screen with a throwaway
spec that was deleted afterwards. The pager under the dialog's overlay is
**enabled and focusable** while the removal is out; after the answer landed the
pages asked for were **2 then 1**, the success banner was said **zero** times,
and the person was carried from page 2 to page 1. A second press of *ก่อนหน้า*
asked the server for `page=0`, which `backend/lib/paging.js` floors to one — so
nothing is wrong on that side, and the whole defect is in front of it.

The way in needs no race at all. `ConfirmDialog` draws a `fixed inset-0` overlay
and traps no focus (#204), and `Pager` takes no `busy` (#199), so the pager's own
buttons are reachable by keyboard for as long as the write is out. That is #179's
rule being useful rather than cautionary: the ticket named a window, and the
population of ways in was larger than the window. The expiry condition is written
down beside the rows — the day either of those tickets closes is the day to
measure this way in again — because a blocker's own expiry condition is a claim
about which way in its author had in mind (#81, #141).

### The fix is #205's ref one layer along

`onScreen` answers *which read*; `onPage` answers *from which page*, and is
written by an effect keyed on `page`. The step back then happens only while
`onPage.current === page`, which is only while the pager is still on the page
that lost its last row. When the person has moved, nothing moves: the sentence is
keyed for the read of the list in front of them, and that list's own loader reads
and says it — the shape #205 arrived at for the branch whose move would cause no
read.

Three things were deliberately left byte-identical so that other tickets' anchors
stayed exact: the three handover lines in `SubjectStudents.js`, which
`152:enrolmentmovedremovalanyway` quotes whole; the `const stepBack = …` lines on
the departments and programmes screens, which `57:deptstay` and `57:progstay`
quote; and, on `Offerings.js`, the new loader was named `reader` rather than
`drawing`, because a one-line anchor is matched as a substring (#154) and eight
spaces of indentation are found inside ten — `anchors.py` reported exactly that,
two sites each for a mutant of #140 and one of #203, the first time the obvious
name was used.

### The survivor that found the row's arithmetic

The first draft of the row pressed *ก่อนหน้า* once. Two of the three mutants
killed what they were aimed at; `206:sentenceofthepagetheyleft` — the key written
from the closure page, which is a faithful copy of exactly half the defect —
**survived 1 of 1**. At one press the page the handler closed over is the last
one, so `readOf(page - 1)` names the page the person moved to: the key is right
by accident, and the half of the fix it is about is invisible.

That is #117's rule and #154's from the other side. Both are written about the
mutant — a substitution is invisible wherever the two values agree, so build the
fixture where they disagree — and here what made them agree was the **row's own
step count**, not the data. Two presses put the destination at `pages - 2` and
the stale key at `pages - 1`, which is the point where the two differ; the mutant
then dies at *the banner of the removal* with `element(s) not found`, which is
the ticket's sentence in the harness's words. Where a fix has two halves, the
number of steps a row takes is part of its claim.

The other two mutants say which half each row holds. `movecanbeofanypage` is the
pre-#206 behaviour exactly and kills row 1 at *the page the handler read*;
`nostepbackatall` is the guard made too strict and kills row 2, which is #48's
row the fix must not touch — a guard of the shape *only while X* is wrong in two
directions, and `57a` row 3 had asserted the step back for a year without ever
reading the sentence.

### The re-sweep found nothing, which is also a measurement

Wrapping three unchanged lines in a narrower branch changes no anchor and no
character, and `anchors.py` said `problems 0` over 966 mutants. But an anchor
check cannot say what a mutant still proves (#107, #68, #203), so the three
mutants whose code now sits inside the narrower branch were swept again against
their own whole files: `57:deptstay` still kills row 3 after 5 passes,
`57:progstay` still kills row 4 after 7, and `152:enrolmentmovedremovalanyway`
still kills its one row of 21. The branch narrowed around them, but their rows
are rows about somebody standing still, which is the branch that was kept.

Sheet 25's dated note *สิ่งที่กุญแจแยกไม่ออก (13 ต.ค. 2569)*, written the day
before, is closed by the ticket and says so beside itself rather than being
deleted. Its own site is fixed and has no row: a step back needs a last page
holding one **removable** row, and the seed's three sections hold 57, 56 and 60
enrolments whose highest codes all carry marks, which `enrolmentHasScores`
refuses. That is a seed change, so it is the owner's to decide (`docs/06`
§Out of Scope), and the condition that would expire the line is a seed with such
a section in it.

### What the review found that the sweep could not

Two axes read the change against the ticket and against the repo's own rules,
and four of their findings were real. The one that cost a mutant: a ⚙ means the
cited mutants cover the row **whole**, and row 2's banner assertion — the half
`57a` row 3 had never read, which is the entire reason that row exists — was put
at risk by nothing, because `nostepbackatall` dies at the page assertion above
it and the other two mutants leave row 2 standing. `206:stationarysentencelost`
is aimed at the line that holds that claim today, which is #203's and #205's code
and not this ticket's (#193), and it kills row 2 at the banner while `57a`,
`203a` and `202a` stay green at 41 of 41.

The other three are written on sheet 14 rather than fixed, because they are not
mine to settle. The ticket asked for the key and this fix also suppresses the
page move, which is a change to what the person reads and therefore a question
under `docs/06` §Out of Scope — priced both ways beside the rows. The ticket's
own table lists `SubjectStudents.js` as a key defect, and that site's key already
agreed with its own move, so there the change is the behaviour half alone (#54:
a ticket's supporting identifiers are a claim like its numbers). And the new
branch carries the same mechanism one layer along — a second move while its
awaited read is out leaves the sentence keyed for nobody — which is the direction
#205 chose rather than a new defect, dated with the condition that would expire
it: a sentence keyed by *what it is of* instead of by a page.


## #88 — the rule the field states while it is being chosen, and the two claims that sat behind another assertion

The validity window was walked on 21 August 2569 and the row *a window the wrong
way round* passed: a start of 29/08 with an end of 28/08 is refused by
`validateUser`, and if that comparison were ever flipped the table's own CHECK
constraint is behind it, which `mutation/125-validity-era.py` records. What
nothing did was say the rule while the dates were being chosen. Measured before
anything was changed, as a ticket's *what is wrong* always is: the two
`type="date"` inputs carried `className`, `value` and `onChange` and no bound at
all, so the browser's picker offered every day in both fields.

The fix is two attributes - `min={draft.valid_from || undefined}` on the later
field, `max={draft.valid_until || undefined}` on the earlier - and the ticket's
own sentence about them is the important one: **an addition and not a
replacement**. Neither server-side guard moves, because a rule a form enforces
alone is a rule with a way around it (ADR-0002).

`|| undefined` rather than `''` is the second claim and not a detail. The
server's rule is `from && until && from > until`, so an end with no start is an
open window the system accepts, and a field that bounded itself anyway would
refuse it - the other direction of a *refuse only where X* guard (#48, #108).

### The rule does not generalise to the other pair of date fields

`frontend/src` holds exactly four `type="date"` inputs, in two pairs: this one
and `components/activity/ActivityForm.js`'s `announcement_date` and
`deadline_date`. The second pair looks like the same shape and is not.
`readActivity` in `backend/routes/activities.js` never compares the two, so
there is **no rule to mirror** there: binding them would be a rule the screen
invented, which is the opposite of what this ticket did. A ticket that
generalises across screens has usually generalised the symptom (#122), and the
question that tells the two apart is whether the server has an ordering rule at
all - not whether the fields look alike.

### A claim written below another claim is proved by nothing

The five mutants were written for five claims, and the first sweep put three of
them behind a red row that was red for another reason. A row reports the
**first** assertion that fails and stops, so with `nolowerbound` applied row 1
died at *the min equals the start* and never reached the two `validity` reads
below it; with `lowerboundwhenthereisnone` it died at *there is nothing to bound*
and never reached *clearing the start takes the bound away*. Those three claims
would have been marked ⚙ on the strength of a kill that happened above them.

This is the `mode: 'serial'` rule one layer down - a serial file reports the
first dying row and skips the rest (#67) - and the repair is the same: measure
each claim on its own. Rows 4 and 5 were split out during the sweep, and the
sixth mutant (`theupperboundexcludesit`) was written because the first
off-by-one leaves `max` alone, so the one-day window asserted on the *start*
field still had nothing to be read against. Where the mutants die is what
decides how a spec's claims are divided into rows.

### A bound on the field changes who answers the person

Measured on 14 October 2569, after the fix: the form has no `noValidate` and
`required` fields of its own, so Chromium's constraint validation is live. With
the start at 29/08/2026 and 28/08/2026 typed into the end field, that field's
`checkValidity()` is false and its `validationMessage` reads *Value must be
29/08/2026 or later.* - so **the form is never submitted**, and the server's own
sentence, *ช่วงเวลาใช้งานไม่ถูกต้อง วันสิ้นสุดต้องไม่มาก่อนวันเริ่มต้น*, is no
longer reachable from this screen. It is still reached at the API and through
the import, and both guards are untouched; what changed is the path a person
takes to it.

Two things follow. The walked row that recorded that sentence **expires the day
the fix lands** - a survey of the store has a date on it, and a successful fix is
what expires one (#50, #85). And the wording a person now reads is the browser's,
in the browser's language rather than the screen's Thai, which is a question for
the owner and not a diff to choose: *the UI is reproduced as-is; any proposal to
change it is raised as a question* (`docs/06` §Out of Scope). The three options
are priced on sheet `11` beside the measurement - keep it, add `noValidate` and
give the Thai sentence back at the cost of the browser's `required` checks for
the whole form, or write a third copy of the rule on the screen - and the ticket
asked for `min`/`max` in as many words, so the attributes went in and the
consequence was written down rather than traded away.

## #207 — the rows the step back counted, and the probe that dated the defect beside it

#206 gave the step back the page the pager is on and wrote its second half into
prose. #207 is that half, filed as a ticket for the reason #206 itself existed:
a deferral written into prose and not into the tracker is a decision nobody can
find. The line it is about sits directly above #206's: `const stepBack = page >
1 && data.departments.length === 1`, where the count comes from the `data` the
render closed over. Two claims on neighbouring lines in one handler — which page
the person is standing on, and how many rows are in front of them — and the
second had nothing under it.

The ticket said so itself: **this claim has not been measured**, measure before
fixing, and if it cannot be reached say *structurally unreachable, with the
number*. So the first work was a measurement, and the ticket's own guess about
where to take it was wrong.

### A ticket's population of ways in is a claim like its numbers

The ticket proposed filters, because a filter changes the list without changing
the page. Every filter on all four filtered screens calls `setPage(1)`, so a
filter change *is* a page move and takes the branch #206 wrote — the one that
moves nobody. The import panel's `onImported` is the same, and where it does not
move (`page === 1`) the `page > 1` above the count is false. A second removal and
a save are both shut by `disabled={busy}` (#142). What is left is the shape the
ticket had not named: a read that lands while the removal is out **and leaves the
pager where it started**, which is the pager's own two presses — *ก่อนหน้า* then
*ถัดไป* — reachable because `Pager` takes no `busy` (#199) and `ConfirmDialog`
traps no focus (#204). The same way in as #206, with the same expiry date, and a
way in that *changes nothing about what was asked for* while changing what the
answer is of: the rule #199's story already wrote, met from the other side.

The row count also has to change meanwhile, which no control on the screen can
do, so the rows use a second actor on the browser's own cookie (`12a`): one
`page.request.delete` for the first row, two `page.request.post`s for the second.

Measured that way on 14 October 2569, against the unfixed code and before any
mutant was written (#203), the ticket's claim is **true in both directions**: the
handler that counted two rows asked for page 3 where the live list wanted 2, and
the handler that counted one asked for page 2 where the live list wanted 3. Not
aged, and not unreachable.

### The ticket's identifiers were two-thirds right

Its table named `data.subjects.length` for `ProgramSubjects`, which counts
`data.program_subjects`, and left the leading `!deactivated` off three of the
seven sites. The `deactivated` flag comes from the DELETE's **answer**, not from
a filter, so it is not a stale read and the fix leaves it alone — but the list
name is what a patch script matches on, and a ticket's supporting identifiers are
a claim like its numbers (#54).

### The fix, and why not a functional updater

A ref beside #206's `onPage`, written by an effect keyed on `data` and read where
the count was: `onPage` answers *where the person is standing*, `onRows` answers
*what is in front of them*. `setData(current => …)` does see the live value, which
is how #201 read live state — but it sees it in a later task, and this decision is
made here, in the handler, before anything is set. All seven screens take the
ref; `Departments.js` carries the reasons and the other six point at it, which is
this tree's convention for a ref many panels repeat. `SubjectStudents.js` reads
`data ? data.students.length : 0`, because that screen's `data` is `null` before
the first read and after a refused one — no rows, a state in which no handler can
read the ref at all, since a page with nothing on it has no row to remove.

### A live read is not the fix, and only the clean suite said so

The first round read `onRows.current` unconditionally. Its own two rows went
green, its three mutants each killed what they were aimed at, `57a` passed whole
— and in the full suite **`206a` row 1 was red**: *a removal says its sentence on
the page the person moved to, and leaves them there*, `Expected "1" Received
"3"`. A person who has moved two pages back leaves the live list a full page of
ten, so `stepBack` became false, the removal stopped stepping back at all, and
fell into the third branch. The sweep could not see it, because a sweep measures
the rows the mutant breaks and this was a row **the fix** broke (#83); 44.9
minutes of suite bought the one line that mattered, and the second round threw
the whole measurement away and ran it again.

What the count has to be is not *the live count* but **the count of the page the
removal was sent from**, which the live ref answers only while the pager is still
on that page. Once the person has moved, the render's own count is the only
reading of the page they left that exists. So the line is a **choice** and not a
read:

```js
const stepBack =
  page > 1 && (onPage.current === page ? onRows.current : data.departments.length) === 1
```

Which is #185's key one step along again: having asked *which answer is this of*,
the question here is *which page is this count of*. The guard #206 wrote on the
line below is untouched, so its anchors do not move — and the two halves of this
line get a mutant each, in opposite directions, so they are not two places
holding one opinion (#97).

### The third round: a key, not a position

The review's Spec axis and its Standards axis both landed on the same hunk, and
measured, they were right: `onPage.current === page` asks *is the pager where
this handler was sent from*, which is not the question the count needs answering.
Between the pager's press and the answer landing, `onPage.current` has already
moved to the new page while `onRows.current` still holds the **old** page's rows,
so for one window the condition is false and the line falls back to the closure
count — but it is also false in the window where the ref is the right reading and
the closure's is stale. One position cannot tell those two apart. A throwaway row
written to the window showed the second case live: the ref was of the page the
removal was sent from, the comparison said no, and the stale closure count
decided the move.

What identifies a count is not where the pager is but **what the count is of**,
which is #185's key written for a reading instead of for an answer. So the ref
carries the read's own coordinates and the line splits in two:

```js
const liveCountIsOfThisPage = onRows.current.of === readOf(page)
const lostItsLastRow =
  page > 1 &&
  (liveCountIsOfThisPage ? onRows.current.rows : data.departments.length) === 1
const stepBack = lostItsLastRow && liveCountIsOfThisPage
```

Two questions, two readings. *Did this page lose its last row* may be answered by
the stale closure count, because all it decides is which loader reads — the worst
it can do is read the same page twice. *May anybody be moved on this* may not:
moving on a count that belongs to another page carries a person off a page that
has filled up again, which is exactly the answer #206 calls the worse one. So the
`else if` below reads `lostItsLastRow` and the move reads `stepBack`, and #206's
own `if (stepBack && onPage.current === page)` is untouched for the third round
running — which is what chose this shape over putting a third clause inside it.

Each screen's key is the read's whole coordinate set and not the page alone:
`readOf(page, department)` on `Subjects`, `readOf(page, program, year, semester)`
on `Offerings`, `readOf(sectionId, page)` on `SubjectStudents`. A key that named
only the page would answer *this page's count* about a different department's
page 2.

The three row-3 failures that followed were each a measurement rather than an
argument, and each a premise of the row rather than a defect: `Pager` draws
`shown ?? page`, the page the **answer** describes, so inside the window the line
reads the page before and the premise has to come from the held request; `load`
raises `loading` before it asks, so what is in the table inside the window is the
placeholder and not the previous page's rows; and the two codes a row imported to
sit above the others sorted below everything the file already had. A row's own
premises are claims like a ticket's.

### The mutant that separates two rows written for one line

Five mutants, all on `Departments`. `closurerowcount` is the diagnosed code made
to run (#115) and kills all three rows, each at its own assertion and in its own
direction; `alwaysthelivecount` is **this ticket's own first round** made to run,
and it kills `206a` row 1 and nothing else — the only thing that turns *we got
this wrong once* from a sentence into a claim the suite holds, which is #48's
rule about a declined option with the ticket's author in the dock.
`trustthestalecount` is the **second** round made to run — `const stepBack =
lostItsLastRow`, which is the shape the review refuted — and it kills row 3 and
nothing else of the fourteen, which is the row written for that window saying so
on its own. Two rounds of this ticket are therefore mutants rather than
paragraphs. The other two are what make the pair of rows worth having:
`refnevermoves` freezes the ref at the first render's count, so nothing ever steps
back, and kills row 1 while row 2 passes; `refalwaysone` has the ref say *one row*
whatever is drawn, the other direction a *refuse only where X* guard is wrong in
(#48), and kills row 2 while row 1 and all nine rows of `57a` pass. The control
is the one that says the two rows are two claims rather than one claim read twice.

`refnevermoves` also kills `57a` row 3 after 5 passes — the same row, the same
line, as `57:deptstay` — and `206a` row 2, which it could not have reached before
this ticket: that row is the person who did not move, so only once the line reads
the ref at all does freezing the ref break it. One mutant, three rows, three
specs: three reachability claims and not one counted three times (#191). Which is
the other half of the sweep: `deptstay` and
`progstay` quote the `const stepBack` line whole, so this ticket re-aimed both by
substituting the new text and keeping the mistake they make (`const stepBack =
false`), ran `anchors.py` while changing rather than at closing time (#202), and
re-swept. Their figures on `57a` are unchanged — and `deptstay`'s figure expired
anyway, because `207a` is a spec that did not exist when it was counted and
`const stepBack = false` reaches its first row. Nothing reports that: the anchor
is exact, the code untouched, the diff only adds a file. Only running it says so.
Swept against `206a` as well this round, it kills that file's first row too —
which was already true the day #206 closed, `const stepBack = false` killing
every row about a step back however the count is reached; no round before this
one had swept it against that file. The sheet's cited line numbers had aged too — 202 and 264 read 215 and 277 today,
`57a` having grown thirteen lines elsewhere (#173).

### The probe that dated the defect the rows walked into

Row 2 would not settle. Its read is made with the `load` the handler closed over,
which the pager's two presses replaced, so #140's guard throws the answer away —
and `load` raises `loading` before it asks and lowers it only `if (isCurrent())`,
so a read that is superseded from the start leaves the table on its placeholder
until something else reads. The row was repaired by taking the sentence as its
settle point and reading the page off the pager's line, with the mechanism, the
date and *this is not this row's claim* written beside it.

That is branch three of `confirmRemoval` reloading with the closure's `load` where
branch two already uses `onScreen.current`, and it had nothing to do with the
count. **A defect this change caused and one it walked into are different
sentences** (#103), and the way to tell them apart is a probe built where the two
codes agree: a last page of three rows with one removed takes branch three before
and after the fix, because the count does not change. Green at `HEAD` and green
with the fix — so it is the second sentence, it has a ticket of its own, and the
probe was deleted, being an instrument and not a claim of this sheet.

The probe's first version measured nothing. It asked whether the removed row was
*still drawn*, and read 0 — because a screen stuck on its loading placeholder has
no rows on it at all, so the count answers the same whether the screen redrew
correctly or drew nothing ever again. A count of rows cannot tell a stale list
from no list, which is #164's blind sampler one species along, and the repair was
to ask the placeholder by name and then ask it again two seconds later.

### The split that left a neighbour's mutant with nothing to kill

`206:movecanbeofanypage` removes #206's comparison, and until this ticket it
killed `206a` row 1. Swept again after the third round it **survived 14 of 14**.
Nothing was wrong with it: in that row's situation the person has come down two
pages, so the list in front of them is of another page and `liveCountIsOfThisPage`
is false as well. Two conditions false at once, and a mutant that removes one of
them cannot make the move happen — which is #97 read from the other side, and
#203's rule exactly: a fix that splits a guard shrinks every mutant that quoted
the block whole, the anchor stays exact, the diff only adds a line, and no
instrument says a word. Only re-running it says so.

The repair is a row, not a mutant. `206a` gained a third row — *a removal moves
nobody while the page the pager asked for has not landed* — which measures #206's
claim **inside** the window this ticket opened: one press of *ก่อนหน้า* with that
page's list held at the route, so the list on the screen is still of the page the
removal was sent from, this ticket's key matches, and the only thing left
forbidding the move is #206's own comparison. `movecanbeofanypage` kills it
(`Expected "2" Received "1"`) and every one of this ticket's five mutants passes
it, which is what makes it #206's claim and not this one's.

### The direction the client cannot read at all

In the forward window — the rows arriving while the removal is out — the count of
the page the removal was sent from is available to no reading on the client. The
live ref is of another page by then, and the closure's count predates the second
actor's writes. So the step back does not happen where it should, and no
rearrangement of these two readings fixes it: it needs a read of a page nobody is
looking at. Written down as a ticket rather than argued, because a
deferral written into prose and not into the tracker is a decision nobody can
find (#119) — which is the sentence this whole ticket came from. It is **#209**,
filed on 14 October 2569 and wired `#209 ← #207`; the branch-three defect this
ticket walked into is **#208**, wired to nobody, because a defect walked into is
not the half another ticket left behind.

### And the handoff's own claim about the tracker was one too

Three handoffs in a row carried *the blockers for #206 and #207 are not wired,
and `gh` cannot wire them — it has to be done from the issue's web page*. Asked
rather than argued, the API answered on the first call: one `POST` to
`issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by` with the blocker's **database id**, which
is what `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` had documented all along. The edge went in
and the summary confirmed it. A handoff's statement about what a tool cannot do is
a claim with a date on it exactly like a ticket's numbers (#66, #111) — and this
one had been copied forward twice without being measured once, which is the same
species as a hand-kept figure in a file that grows every ticket. The copy to fix
is the live one; the two superseded handoffs are dated records and keep their
wording (#54).

The summary is also two numbers rather than one: `blocked_by` counts the **open**
blockers, which is the frontier's gate, while `total_blocked_by` counts the edges.
A retrospective edge between two closed tickets therefore reads `0` and `1`, and a
frontier query that read the second would never offer anything.

And both of those live under `issue_dependencies_summary`, not at the top of the
issue payload, so a `--jq` asked one level too high answers `null` in every field —
which reads exactly like *there is no edge* rather than like *you asked the wrong
question*. The answer that cannot be mistaken is the collection itself:
`issues/206/dependencies/blocked_by` returned `[{205, closed}]` and
`issues/205/dependencies/blocking` returned `[{206, closed}]` from the one `POST`,
which is also the measurement that says an edge is wired from the blocked side only
and never from both. The chain is #205 → #206 → #207, which is the order the three
tickets' own bodies describe.

## #199 — the pager that stayed live while the write was out, and the two windows a press could land in

[#199](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/199) says the enrolment screen's
`Pager` is clickable while that screen's own write is out, so a person can move
the page under a read that is already on its way, and asks for `busy` to reach
the control. Its *What is wrong* was read first (`CLAUDE.md`), and most of it had
expired.

### The diagnosis was aged by five hours

The ticket was opened on 11 October 2569 at 11:35 Bangkok and says this screen has
no superseded-answer guard at all, citing lines 107, 192 and 219. `0a884b0` — #202,
option 3 — landed the same evening and put
`if (reloaded && onScreen.current === sent) setNotice(said)` into both handlers.
By the morning the ticket was taken the guard was at lines 266 and 318, proved by
four rows of `202a` and two mutants. So the sentence the ticket wanted protected
was already protected, and what was left of the ticket was the control: the guard
decides whether to *speak*, and the pager decides what the screen is *of*.

### The probe, and the prediction it refuted

Four orderings, pressed by hand through a throwaway spec and then deleted (#207's
rule: a probe is an instrument, not a claim of any sheet):

| what was out | press | what the person got |
|---|---|---|
| the enrolment `POST` | *ถัดไป* | pulled back to page 1 **and told** |
| the enrolment's reload | *ถัดไป* | pulled back to page 1, **silent** |
| a removal, dialog open | *ถัดไป* with the mouse | the press never lands — the overlay eats it |
| a removal, dialog closed | *ถัดไป* | **silent** |

Two things came out of it that reading the code had not given. The first is that
the way in under the dialog is a **keyboard** way in and not a mouse one: the
overlay's `bg-black/50` intercepts pointer events, so that half of the population
lives entirely on #204's untrapped focus, which is the condition to write beside
it. The second is that my own prediction was wrong — I had read the two loaders
and expected a stuck `กำลังโหลด…`, and the measurement says never, in all four
orderings, because the superseded read raises `loading` before the current read
lowers it. A prediction from reading code is a claim with the same standing as the
ticket's.

### What makes it a defect rather than a preference

One handler, one person, one action, and whether they are told depends on which of
two invisible windows their press landed in. That is #52 — *anything written for
timing must not be able to decide anything* — met in the product rather than in a
fixture: both of the two behaviours are defensible, and the thing that is wrong is
that the system holds both and the clock picks. So the question for the owner is
not *which sentence* but *which single behaviour*, and every option that removes
the fork is an answer.

Three were priced. **A**: make the silent window speak, which inverts `202a`'s two
negative rows and strands #202's two mutants. **B**: give this screen's `Pager`
`disabled` while `busy`, which closes both windows by removing the press. **C**:
leave it, which leaves #52 breached. B is the only one that makes no closed ticket
wrong, and the owner took it on 15 October 2569.

### A fix that disables a control is a change to every row that presses it

The price was measured before building, over the seven files that touch the
enrolment screen or the pager: **4 failed / 91 passed**. `202a:389` and `202a:414`
were predicted — by `202a` itself, whose own comment says the two negatives use the
pager to move the screen. The other two, `205a:76` and `205a:146`, were not: my hand
estimate had been *two rows*, and it was counting the rows that are **about** the
pager. `205a` presses *ถัดไป* to arrange a superseded read — the control as an
**instrument**, not as a claim — and a row like that is invisible to an estimate
made by asking what the fix is about. The census to run before such a fix is the
**press**: grep the specs for the control, not for the claim.

### Where the four rows went

`202a`'s two negatives needed a way in that survives B. The handler speaks only
after `reload` returns `true`, which happens only on the page-one branch, so what
is left is a move that is not a page move: the **section jump**, which #141 had
already built a walk for. That walk came out into `e2e/support/section-jump.js`
(#171: a fixture a second file needs is shared, because no row's claim lives in
it), gained an `intoTheListedSectionScreen`, and both rows now say *says nothing
over the Section the jump moved to while the enrolment was out*. Ten of ten.

`205a` row 1 moved its superseding press to **before** the write, which is where
the claim always was — a read superseded when it *lands*. Row 2 had nowhere left
to stand at all, and became a net: it asserts both buttons enabled before the
write and disabled while it is out, then that the handover from page two still
says its sentence on page one. The mutant that row used to hold,
`205:alwaysmoves`, came out of `mutation/205-the-sentence-names-its-read.py` with a
dated section saying why. It needs a page move while a write of that screen's is
out, and the census of the ten sentence-handover sites says this was the only one
drawing a live pager beside a submittable form — the other two forms replace their
list, and the seven removals put a dialog over it. So after B it is unreachable
**for a person**, not merely at the seam: #47's sixth reading of a survivor one
step on, which is where #203's ninth already stands. What would put it back is
written beside it: #204's keyboard hole closed the other way, or any screen that
draws a live pager beside an open form.

### The re-aim that preserves the mistake

`57:prevalive` and `57:nextalive` quoted `disabled={page <= 1}` and
`disabled={page >= pages}`, which B rewrote. Each was re-aimed to drop **its own
half** and leave `busy` standing, because the mistake those two are about is the
**end rule** speaking never. Substituting `false` would have matched the file's
convention and been a different mutant — no rule at all — which 199a's rows would
also kill, and the sheet's sentence about what `prevalive` means would have stopped
being true of it (#203). `busy` is written first in both `||`s for exactly that
reason: so each half can be dropped on its own.

### What is still open

`Pager` is drawn at eleven call sites and B reached one; the prop defaults to
`false`, so the other ten are unchanged by construction. Whether each of them has
a sentence behind a read is the same question again, ten times, and it is its own
ticket rather than a deferral in prose (#119, #125). Two of the ten are already
known not to need it: `Students.js` draws `adding ? <StudentForm/> : <list +
Pager>`, so its pager is not on the screen while its write is out, and the
administration screens' pagers sit under the confirmation overlay — which is the
mouse half of the probe's third row, and expires with #204.

## #208 — the third branch's dead loader, and the census that went blind while staying green

#207's own record had written this one down as a draft: the third branch of
`confirmRemoval` read the list again with the `load` the handler closed over,
where the second branch had used `onScreen.current` since #205. When the pager
has moved and come back while the `DELETE` is out, that `load` is not the
screen's loader any more, so its `isCurrent()` is false **before the request
leaves** — the answer is thrown away by #140's guard and the removed row stays
drawn, and `load`, which raises `setLoading(true)` before asking but lowers it
only when `isCurrent()`, leaves the placeholder up with nothing to take it down.

### The ticket's numbers, and what the measurement made of them

The ticket counted **33 sites in 18 files** on 14 October and said so as the
scope of the *shape*. Measured on the day of the fix the shape has **59 call
sites in 19 files**, because the ticket had counted one spelling
(`const reloaded = await load(...)`) and the population is *calls of the loader
that read the list again* — which includes the calls whose answer nobody reads
and the ones inside a `try`. Underneath them are **64** declarations of
`const <name> = onScreen.current`: 59 that are called (`drawing` 58, `reader` 1,
renamed so a mutant's anchor stays unambiguous — #154) and **5 named `sent` that
are never called at all**, because `sent` is #202's key, which holds the loader
to *compare* with and not to call. Two shapes, one ref, counted apart.

### The reachability table, measured by who writes the dependency

The ticket's first criterion asked which sites a way in reaches, with a number
for the unreachable. The thing that decides it is not what the screen draws
(#174) but **who writes `load`'s dependency list**, since the loader in the ref
is replaced exactly when one of those changes, and there are two kinds of
writer:

- a setter the screen itself calls — `setPage`, `setProgram`, `setYear`,
  `setSemester`, `setDepartment`, `setFilters`: **38 sites in 9 files**, and
  those nine are exactly the nine that draw a `<Pager>`
- the route, through `useParams`: **21 sites in 10 files**

**Structurally unreachable: 0.** That number is not an argument either. #141
measured that the browser's own history list travels any number of entries in
one move, so two addresses of one route shape are always one move apart however
many screens sit between them — including two `rubricId` addresses with the
`Rubrics` list in the middle, which is the one case that looked exempt.

`report` appears in five of those dependency lists and is **not** a way in: it is
the error-reporting `useCallback`, not state any control writes. A dependency
list is a list of names, so reading it as a list of ways in is the same mistake
as reading a ticket's identifiers as a schema (#54).

The site a person meets without doing anything strange is `toggle` on `Users.js`:
the status switch asks nothing first (#86), so there is no dialog and no overlay,
and the pager, three filters and search box are ordinary mouse clicks while
`PUT /api/users/:id/status` is out. Neither #204 nor #210 reaches it. That is
also what lets its row claim something the departments screen cannot: `load`
there is keyed on `[filters, page]` and the search box writes `filters` on every
keystroke, so the stale loader asks a **question** the screen has replaced, and
the request says which outright (`?q=`), where on the departments screen both
loaders ask for the same page and only the drawing tells them apart.

**That paragraph is dated 15 October 2569 and #86 expired it the next day** —
the switch asks first now, so the overlay is on the screen while the write is
out and this screen's way in is the same shape as the other administration
screens: the keyboard, from under the overlay, resting on #204 after all. The
row still passes because `fill()` focuses the search box rather than clicking
it, which is a way in the tool has and a person does not (#47); what the row
claims is unchanged, and only the sentence about who can reach it is not.

### The two mechanisms as a grid

Measured rather than chosen between (#148, #149): fixing the read alone removes
both, because no caller can then hand `load` a guard that is already false — **0
of 59** — which makes the stuck placeholder structurally unreachable rather than
guarded, and so it has no mutant. Fixing the placeholder alone removes the
placeholder and leaves the table drawing the old list, which still holds the
removed row. The third row of the grid is what was measured on the screen on 14
October: both.

**And the grid's own population is a claim, which the spec review found over-
stated.** *Structurally unreachable* here means *through the nineteen loaders a
ref holds* — the 0 of 59 is a count of those callers. A screen whose ref holds a
**coordinate** instead holds no loader anywhere, so it is outside the population
and outside the instrument (#141, from the instrument's side this time: a census
whose population is *the calls that read a ref-held loader* cannot find the call
whose ref holds something else). Read on 15 October 2569: **4 such sites, 3 of
them a real gap** — `Plos.js:271,304,331`, whose `load` is keyed
`[program, report]` and raises `setLoading(true)` before asking but lowers it
only `if (isCurrent())`, so the curriculum filter moved while a write is out
leaves the placeholder up, which is this ticket's mechanism 2 alive;
`ActivityScores.js:555` is not, that `load` never touching `setLoading`. That
reading is **from the code and not from a row**, so it has the standing of a
ticket's own diagnosis (#199) and is owed a ticket rather than a sentence here
(#119, #125) — filed as #211 the same day, carrying all three options rather than one. The lesson is the shape: a number quoted as *structurally
unreachable* carries the population it was counted over, and the sentence has to
carry it too.

### A census can be blinded by somebody else's fix, and stay green

This census, `swallowed-refusals.js`, classifies a loader by its **declaration**.
A name bound to a ref is no declaration, so the moment every handler called
`drawing(...)` instead of `load(...)` the script answered *2 sites, 2 read* over
a tree it had answered **35 of 35** about the day before — **and `problems 0`,
exit 0, the gate green**. What said so was the count. Nothing else could: an
instrument that has stopped seeing its population reports a clean sweep of what
is left, and a gate is read for its exit code.

Following the ref did not restore 35. It found **42 loaders awaited, 35 read and
7 nobody had ever seen** — the `lostItsLastRow` branch of the removal on seven
screens, which hands its sentence to `waiting` by key and says nothing itself,
written by #205 and #207 and invisible to this script from the day they landed
(#141: a census whose population is *the calls that name a declaration* cannot
find the call that names none). The reason was in each of their comments all
along, in prose rather than in the syntax the instrument reads (#93), so all
seven were marked rather than changed.

**And the two figures in that docstring were settled with a worktree rather than
an argument** (#141): the script as it stood answers **37 of 37** at `89b66f6`,
its own commit of 12 October, and **35 of 35** at `607fa9f`, the last commit
before this ticket — both right for their day, two sites having stopped saying a
sentence of their own in between. Run at that same 14 October commit, the
ref-following version answers *sentences 35 · awaiting 42 · read 35 · problems
7*, which is the measurement that the seven were there and unseen for two days.

### The instrument the fix is worth, and what it cannot measure

`frontend/scripts/dead-loaders.js` is the fifth census. Its population is the
names a file declares as a function **and** assigns into some `<ref>.current`,
and it reads every call of one: inside a hook whose dependency array names it is
its own effect and not a site; a callee bound to `<ref>.current` is fresh, and
the guard is checked to name the **same** local, both ways round; a callee that
is the declaration is **stale** and needs `// dead-loader: <why> (#NNN)`. Clean:
*files read 137 · loaders 19 · own effect 19 · live off the ref 59 · marked 0 ·
problems 0*.

Proved by breaking real sites and not by its own fixtures (#141, #200):
`confirmRemoval` on `Departments` and `toggle` on `Users` put back to `load` give
`problems 2` with file and line, exit 1; a guard made to name a different local
in `Programs` gives the mismatch message, exit 1. Its sixteen fixtures take
`npm run census:test` from 71 to **87**.

What it cannot measure is written in it: it finds loaders **by the ref**, so a
guard whose ref holds a *coordinate* rather than the loader is invisible —
`Plos.js` writes `onScreen.current = program` and `ActivityScores.js` writes
`= activityId`, and whether that matters there depends on what those loaders
depend on; it says nothing about whether a site is reachable; it cannot see
frames; it does not ask whether the answer is read or the drawing guarded, which
are the other two censuses' questions; a loader passed in as a parameter has no
declaration to read; and a ref assignment it cannot classify is a problem rather
than a pass (#123 — a tool that cannot say what it did not look at).

### A hundred and one re-aimed mutants, and the two instruments that triaged them

The fix changes what callers write, so it reaches **101 mutants in 14 files** —
140 (28 of 31), 149 (28 of 43), 152 (17 of 21), 203 (14 of 20), 146 (3 of 45),
25 (2), 202 (2), 16, 21, and 27/28/29/30/31 one each, all `savenoreload`.
Sweeping all 101 was estimated at about seven hours, which is not proportionate
to the question they raise, and an anchor check cannot answer it (#107, #68). So
two instruments over the catalogue, neither of them a sweep:

- **an equivalence proof**: undo the re-aim on both halves of every mutant —
  delete each `const <name> = onScreen.current` line from the replacement,
  rename the callee back — and compare byte for byte with `HEAD`. **101 moved,
  100 certified identical, 1 not certified.** Its job is to say which mutants
  need the sweep, not to replace it.
- **a question asked of all 1,003 edits**: which replacements use `drawing` or
  `reader` without declaring it. Six flagged, five of them false positives whose
  declaration sits above the anchor, and one real.

The real one was `25:importstaysonpage`, whose replacement is the one-liner
`onImported={() => drawing(…)}` while the line declaring `drawing` is *inside*
the block the fix wrote — a mutant that stops the application and proves nothing
(#152 one step along), and invisible to `anchors.py`, whose anchor is still
exact. Repaired to a block and swept: `25a` **1 red, 14 passed, 59.1s**, the red
being row 7 alone, exactly what #25's file claims.

**Then two of the certified ones were swept anyway, to price the proof.**
`140:departmentsremovestalewins` → 1 red, 31 passed, 2.9m, matching #140's claim
of 1 of 31. `203:userstoggleanyway` → 1 red, 21 passed, 1.4m, the red being the
`Users.js` row its sheet names. Both exact — which is the only thing that makes
the equivalence proof worth anything, and it cost eight minutes against seven
hours.

One finding came free with it: `203a` has **22 rows** today, so its sheet's
*kills 1 of 21* is a figure about a smaller suite. The row that grew passes on
both sides, so the kill count never moved and the denominator did, and nothing
reports that (#202).

## #211 — the loader a coordinate ref cannot hold, and the question one line down

#208 gave nineteen page files one shape: a handler reads the loader **live** out
of the ref it is kept in, so what it reads again is a read of the page and the
filters the screen is on now. Its population was therefore *calls that reach the
loader through a ref*, and the screens that guard with a **coordinate** held no
loader anywhere — invisible to the ticket, and invisible to the census it left
behind (#141's species: a census whose population is *the things that carry X*
cannot find the thing that carries no X). #208 read those screens from the code
on the day it closed rather than leaving the sentence general, and filed what it
found as this ticket.

### A comparison and a choice are two uses of one ref

`onScreen.current === program` answers *is the filter still where it was when I
was sent* exactly, and it answers it for ever: `load` is rebuilt if and only if
`program` changes, `report` being stable. So every row resting on that
comparison — `133a`'s row 2 and row 7 — kept its claim word for word through
this fix, and the sweep says so (`133:ploshandlerstalewins`, re-aimed with its
`() => true` intact, still fails exactly its own row).

What a coordinate cannot do is **hand the handler a loader**. The question one
line down from *is this still current* is *which reader should do the reading*,
and a value cannot answer it, so the three handlers went on calling the `load`
they closed over. The guard was right and the caller was wrong, which is the
hardest pair to see on one line: the handler asked the correct question of the
wrong reader. That reader then refused itself — which is what #133 asks of a
superseded answer — and the placeholder it had raised stayed up, because
`load` raises `setLoading(true)` before asking and the only code that lowers it
is its own `finally`, inside `if (isCurrent())`. A success sentence over a table
reading *กำลังโหลด…* for ever.

### The stale loader has to be the *last* reader, which is what the row is for

The first draft of the mechanism was wrong in a way no reasoning caught and one
fixture did: *move the filter while the handler's request is out* is not enough.
Moving it replaces `load`, and the effect keyed on `load` reads the new
curriculum immediately and lowers the placeholder when that answer lands. The
stale read arriving afterwards is refused and takes nothing down — exactly what
#133 asks for.

The defect needs the stale loader to be **called** after the live read has
settled, and that is what a handler does: it reads again when its own request
comes back. So both rows hold the handler's request at the route, move the
filter while it is out, wait for the new list to be *drawn*, and only then let
the handler's answer go. The order is the claim.

### The way in a full-screen overlay leaves

`Plos.js`'s own docblock said *the dialog behind ลบ never covers the filter at
all*. #199 had measured the opposite four tickets earlier: `ConfirmDialog` is
`fixed inset-0 bg-black/50`, and it eats the click. The way in survives the
correction, which is why the row exists at all — #204 has measured that the same
dialog traps no focus, so a focused `<select>` answers ArrowDown, and the row
says in its own comment that this half expires the day #204 lands. The other
half needs nothing: a refused แก้ไข draws no form, so while that read is out the
filter is an ordinary mouse click, and `save` is unreachable for this mechanism
altogether — not because the form covers the filter, which the review of this
ticket caught the same day as false (`setEditing(null)` runs *before* the awaited
reload, which is what `133a`'s row 7 comment measured), but because the clearing
and the call are one tick: there is no moment in which the filter is on screen
with that loader not yet called. A conclusion right for the wrong reason expires
on the wrong day, and this one had the right reason written beside it. A
ticket that names an overlay has named a *pointer*, not the population of ways
in (#179's shape, met at the keyboard).

### The third kill nobody asked for

The four mutants the fix re-aimed were swept against the seven files that reach
`Plos.js` rather than against one each, and `202:plossaysanyway` — untouched in
substance, `showing.current !== null` where the code says `=== sent` — came back
**3 failed, 120 passed, 8 did not run** where its sheet recorded *2 of 10*. The
third is `19a:232`, the ordinary path: nothing takes the screen, so
`showing.current` and `sent` are both `null`, the real guard passes by
`null === null` and the mutant's `!== null` does not, and the sentence *ปิดการ
ใช้งานแทนการลบ* is never said. One mutant, wrong in both directions — speaking
over another screen, and silent on its own. The old figure was never wrong: it
was a figure about `202a` alone, and a wider set expires a count for a mutant
nobody edited (#202's rule, from the other end — there a spec gained a row, here
a sweep gained a file). `19a` runs `serial`, so the eight rows behind the red
did not run and are not passes (#67).

### The figure that was right and the sentence that was short

#208's blind-spot note said *4 call sites, and 3 of them are a real gap*, naming
two coordinate-ref screens. The figure is right — it counts call sites — and the
sentence is short by one: a third file holds a coordinate ref,
`components/users/GrantsPanel.js`, whose ref holds the `user.user_id` the panel
is of. It contributes **no call site at all**: its `add` and `remove` draw the
write's own answer under that coordinate, and its three guards are already a ☐
row of `docs/acceptance/12-role-grants.md` with a date and #141 on them. Count
by the mechanism and the census is right; read its sentence as a count of
screens and it is wrong. That is #174 from the reader's side.

### The census as the fix's own witness

Criterion 4 asked whether `dead-loaders.js` should grow a second population for
a ref that holds a coordinate. The answer is **no**, written into its docstring
with the date and with what would re-date it — a screen whose ref holds a
coordinate *and* whose loader raises `loading` without asking. The reason is
that the two remaining members are measured (`ActivityScores.js:555`, whose
`load` never touches `setLoading`; `GrantsPanel.js`, with nothing to count), so
the rule could only fire on a screen that does not exist yet, and it would have
to ask a different question to fire at all: not *which loader does this call
reach* but *is the coordinate this ref holds the loader's dependency set*, which
means re-deriving the `useCallback` deps and comparing.

What the answer rests on is a reading the instrument itself publishes. Before
the fix it counted **19 loaders · 19 own-effect reads · 59 live off the ref**;
after it, **20 · 20 · 62 · marked 0 · problems 0**. The three sites did not have
to be excused with a marker: they joined the population. An instrument that
counts the thing rather than the rows is also the cheapest proof that a fix
landed where it said it would (#58's rule, used forwards).

### What the review found, and the mutant the mechanism's two halves need

Three of the review's findings were real, and the one that mattered is #88's
rule arriving from a direction it had not come from before. Both ⚙ rows named
the stuck placeholder in *what must be seen* — it is the mechanism this ticket
exists to fix — and both mutants die at the row's **first** assertion, the
curriculum the handler read again. So the placeholder claim sat under another
claim and was proved by nothing, with the row red, the mutant credited and the
sheet reading modestly.

What makes that fixable rather than a split is that the defect has two halves
and a mutant can carry one each. The two first mutants are the whole mistake:
a stale **reader**, which asks for the curriculum the screen has left, so the
