first assertion goes red and nothing below it is read. The claim the sheet
needed proved is the other half: a live reader with the **guard** still written
against the loader it closed over — `await drawing(() => onScreen.current ===
load)`. That one asks for the right curriculum (the first assertion passes),
refuses its own drawing (the list on the screen is still the filter's own, so
that assertion passes too) and never reaches `setLoading(false)`, so it dies in
`settled` on *กำลังโหลด…* — which is the placeholder claim itself, said by the
helper that reads it. One line of difference, and the claim that had nothing
under it has a mutant whose first dying assertion is exactly it.

That is #97's *one crafted value per link of a guard*, read at the level of a
mechanism rather than a clause: a fix that closes two mechanisms at one site
needs a mutant per mechanism, and a mutant per **site** is what a criterion
asking for *a mutant per fixed site* will get you if you read it as arithmetic.

The second finding is `docs/lessons.md`'s own rule about a conclusion right for
the wrong reason, in three copies written the same hour — this file, the sheet
and the census's docstring all said `save` cannot reach the second mechanism
*because the form replaces the table for the whole of the write*. It does not:
`setEditing(null)` runs before the awaited reload, which is the sentence
`133a`'s row 7 comment has carried since #133, and which this ticket quoted as
its own reachability evidence five paragraphs earlier. The true reason was
sitting beside the false one in two of the three copies, which is why nothing
it predicted was wrong yet.

The third is smaller and the same species as #119's: option 2 of the ticket was
declined in my head and nowhere in the tree. A declined option that is not
written down is a decision nobody can find, and the mutant it would deserve
(#48) cannot be written for a decision that does not exist on paper. It is now
a dated section of the sheet, with what would expire it: a caller that sends a
loader out with no live read following it, where nobody raises a second
placeholder and the asymmetry inside `load` is a gap by itself.

## #49 — the menu that was hiding three screens, and the row that passed its clean run

The ticket was an owner's question and said so: *this needs the owner of the requirement, not an
implementer. Once the set is decided the implementation is a few lines.* Both halves were true, and
the second one was true for a reason the ticket did not give.

### What the placeholder was a claim about

`ExtAssessor.js` held one invented entry and said in its own docstring that it was a placeholder,
so the shape everybody had in mind was *this role can reach one screen and the set is unknown*. The
measurement says otherwise. All nine `/program-results/*` routes are guarded by one constant —
`READERS = ['PROG_MANAGER', 'EXT_ASSESSOR']`, `backend/routes/programResults.js` — and have been
since #42; `frontend/` has no per-role route guard at all, only `ProtectedRoute`, and `menus.js`'s
own docblock says so: hiding an entry is not what stops anybody, the route refuses them. So the
one-entry menu was **hiding** three screens rather than refusing them, and a typed address reached
all four. The implementation was a few lines because there was no guard to change — not because the
decision was small.

That is worth stating as a rule, because the price of the ticket was read off the placeholder:
**a placeholder menu is a claim about the menu, not about the routes.** Ask what the guard already
admits before pricing an owner's question about reach, since the answer decides whether what is
being asked for is a widening or only a drawing. Here it also decided which options were cheap: the
four screens share one constant, so *all four* and *none* were the only shapes that did not require
splitting it, and three of the four options put to the owner would have been more code than the one
they chose.

### A criterion that already held, and what was still owed

The fourth criterion — every screen the set excludes is refused server-side, with a test — was
already true in substance. A census of every route in the tree on 16 October 2569 found 161 routes,
9 naming this role (all of `programResults.js`) and 29 carrying no role guard at all, of which the
session-only ones are `auth/*`, `health`, the six `me.js` routes and the evidence file; everything
else resolved to a constant with no assessor in it. None of that is a test, and *already true* is
not *proved*: what was owed was the row, not a fix. The refusal table in `shell.test.js` is eleven
families, one route each because what a family shares is the constant its routes read, and it
carries the census's date and the three things the census cannot see — a guard that names the role
indirectly, a handler that widens its own answer below `requireRole`, and any route added after
that date. Two of the eleven rows have mutants: the declined option made to run (#48) at `plos.js`,
one of the shapes put to the owner having been *the reports plus the curriculum documents*, and the
same question asked of the other half of the tree at `/api/users`. The other nine are reachability
claims nothing can presently break, and the file says so rather than leaving the table looking
proved.

### The row that passed its clean run

Row 3 of `49a` read the roll with `expect(await rollRows(page).count()).toBeGreaterThan(0)`. The
row arrives by pressing the menu, so nothing in front of that read waits for the roll: `showIntake`
returns the moment the picker holds the year the screen opened on, and the pickers are a different
request from the roll. It is #132's rule — a helper that waits for the response has not waited for
the drawing — except that here no helper waited for anything.

It passed the clean run. Then it failed under **all four** of this ticket's mutants, including the
two aimed at other entries, and that pattern is the whole diagnosis: a mutant that points
`programLevelAllStudents` at a sibling's address cannot reach the roll, so a row that dies under it
is a claim about the row. **A bystander row that dies under every mutant is a flaky row, and the
sweep is the load test that says so** — four more samples of a row whose clean run was one. Read
from the other side it is the twin of the readings a survivor gets (#152's wrong moment, #112's
wrong element): a **kill that is not one**, where what is wrong is neither the mutant nor the code
but whether the row read at a moment at all.

The repair is a retrying read of the first row rather than a counted one, and the proof that it is
a repair is the re-sweep: four mutants, one red row each, the three bystanders green every time,
and each path mutant dying at its own `toHaveURL` with both addresses named — which is why `49a`
asserts the URL instead of waiting for it (#139, #160).

### Two rows where the sheet had one

`docs/acceptance/10-application-shell.md`'s criterion-2 exception row named two things: the set and
its appearance. #66's rule splits it. The set is ⚙ — `49a` row 1 compares the drawn menu against
labels written in the spec rather than against `MENUS`, which is the distinction sheet 10's own
first row makes about the user menu, and `assessormenuiscommittee` hands the role the committee's
whole menu so that every entry the other rows press is still there and only the set claim fails.
The appearance is ☐, and it is ☐ having been walked: the 3 September 2569 walk is kept inside the
row as a dated record (#54), and what it recorded — one entry, leading to a screen that did not
exist yet — is not the menu that is drawn now. A row can go back to ☐ because there is something
new to look at (#105).

### The press that closed the group it was opening

`arriveAt` in the first draft of `49a` pressed the group header and then the entry, which is what
the committee's four sibling rows did until #212 (`42a:83`, `43a:90`, `44a:132`, `45a:123` — the
four still resolve to the arrival, which is now the paragraph saying why there is one press).
A probe measured
what the press does: `SidebarItem.js` opens **every** group with a `sub` on arrival
(`setOpenMenu(menu.filter(item => item.sub).map(item => item.key))` for every non-TEACHER role) and
`Sidebar.js`'s `handleToggleSubmenu` **toggles**, while the entries render only while
`isMenuOpen` — before the press, five entries and the compare link visible; after it, one entry and
no compare link. So the press closes the group, unmounts the entries, and the click that follows
lands only by beating React's re-render — eight frames of it, counted on #212, which
also says what happens to a press that arrives after them.

**A press that arranges a precondition is a claim about the state on arrival** — #77's rule met in
a shell rather than in a grant: ask what is true before arranging anything, because a toggle pressed
on a thing that is already open is the undoing of the state the row needs. The press came out of
`49a` and out of the `42a` row this ticket wrote, with the measurement in the comment. The four
sibling rows are the committee's, written before this was measured, and they passed by winning
that race; rewriting them was not this ticket's to do, so they got a ticket — which is the deferral
going into the tracker and not into prose (#119, #125). That ticket is #212, and it counted the
race at eight frames before taking the press out (17 October 2569).

### What the review axes found, and why each was a mutant question

Three of the six verified findings were about the proof rather than the code, and all three are
already rules met again. The first was a mutant written at `plos.js`'s `MAINTAINERS` constant, which
guards the POST, PUT and DELETE as well as the GETs: as written it granted this role **write** on
the PLOs, which is not the read-only option the owner declined, and would have killed
`plos.test.js`'s write-refusal rows that no sheet credits it with. It was re-aimed at the one
`router.get('/plos')` line (#97, #123). The second is the other side of the same sentence:
*read-only* is **two** claims, and a mutant on a GET cannot put the second at risk, so `OWN-01`'s
clause earned a row that posts an empty body and a seventh mutant at `router.post('/plos')`. The
third was the kill scope of `assessormenuiscommittee`, which was assumed to be one row and measured
as two — `49a` row 1 and `52a` row 2, the committee's menu moving the landing out from under the
row that aged a window on a report. Both sheets carry it, dated, with sheet `10` as its home (#123).

And the sheet that was recounted was already wrong before this ticket touched it: at `4bb25b8`
sheet `10`'s table held 21 ⚙ of 28 rows while its own count sentence said *20 ⚙ … รวม 27 แถว*. A
hand-kept number in a file that grows every ticket is already wrong (#119), and the correction is a
figure counted from the mark column plus a dated paragraph saying the sentence had drifted — not a
silent overwrite, because which of the two was right on which day is the thing a later reader needs.

And one instrument answered back. The run recipe in the mutation file was wrapped across two lines
with a shell continuation, and `anchors.py`'s command check reported `NOT A REGEX ... -> '\'`: it
reads a recipe's **arguments**, so the backslash read as a test file. A recipe written inside a file
an instrument walks is a marker written for an instrument, and it has to be in a syntax the
instrument reads (#93) — one line, however long. Unwrapped, the check reads 86 arguments and
`problems 0`.

## #86 — the box the delivered screen had, and the way in it moved

The ticket was filed on 21 August 2569 while walking criterion 3 of #11, *suspend without
deleting*: one press and the account was suspended, with nothing asked. Criterion 3 never asked for
a dialog, so the walk did not fail, and the ticket was opened as a question for the owner of the
requirement rather than as a defect — correctly, by `docs/06` §Out of Scope. It offered two options:
use the existing `ConfirmDialog`, naming the account, or do nothing and rely on the change being
reversible.

### What changed the question into a job

`DEEP-QA-FRONTEND/src/pages/UserMangement/UserTable.js` already had the box. It holds
`statusModal`, a `Switch` in the *สถานะ* column, a `confirmStatus` that awaits the write and *then*
closes the modal — the same order the rebuild's nine other confirmations use — and a
`StatusConfirmModal` whose heading is *ยืนยันการเปลี่ยนสถานะ* and whose buttons are
*ยืนยันการเปลี่ยน* and *ยกเลิก*. The rebuild drew a text button beside *แก้ไข* and dropped the
question.

So the ticket was a regression wearing an `enhancement` label, and the question the owner was being
asked had already narrowed: not *shall we add a confirmation* but *which of the delivered words can
the shared component still say*. That is the rule worth keeping — **an owner's question about a
missing control is answered by the delivered UI before it is answered by the owner.** The pricing in
the ticket, and in my own first reading of it, came from the rebuilt screen alone.

Two of the delivered words survive verbatim: the heading and the confirm label. The message does
not. It read *ต้องการ* + *เปิด/ปิดการใช้งาน* + *การใช้งานบัญชีของ* + the name, which says
*การใช้งาน* twice and colours the verb — one is a duplication and the other is a **drawing**, and a
shared `ConfirmDialog` that takes a string can do neither. The repair is to say so out loud rather
than to approximate it: the message is this screen's own sentence, naming the account by code then
name like the nine siblings, and the suspend direction carries the consequence clause
*…จะถูกปฏิเสธทุกคำขอตั้งแต่คำขอถัดไป…*, which is not advertising — `11c` row 3 measured it at
`sessionAdmission` in August. The reactivating direction has no such clause, because there is
nothing to warn about.

The direction itself lives in one place, `suspends(user)`, read by the button's verb, the question
and the write (#97), and the dialog is rendered outside the form/table ternary so that closing the
form cannot unmount the question. One `busy` serves both halves, which is a measurement and not a
guess (#142): the form and the table are the two sides of one ternary, and *แก้ไข* on this screen
reads nothing from the server.

### What a restored control reaches

Seventeen presses in six closed tickets' spec files went through the switch. Converting them is
ordinary work; what is not ordinary is the second rule the ticket taught. **A fix that puts a dialog
in front of a control re-dates every other ticket's claim about how that control is reached.** The
rows keep their claims and their marks — `fill()` focuses the search box rather than clicking it,
which is a way in the tool has and a person does not (#47) — but four places had written, in prose,
that this switch asks nothing, that there is no overlay, and that its way in therefore does not wait
on #204: §#202 and §#208 of `docs/acceptance/11-user-accounts.md`, the mutant table of
`mutation/208-a-read-with-a-loader-the-screen-replaced.py`, and the #208 story in this file. Each is
dated rather than deleted (#54). Grep the sentences, not only the presses.

### The brace below the `catch`

Four mutants of closed tickets anchor on this handler's `catch`, which is what tells it apart from
the `save` above it. The fix adds `setSwitching(null)` as the first line of that `catch`, so all four
were re-aimed by insertion — the mutated line unchanged, the meaning unchanged (#140, #152, #203).

`anchors.py`, run **while** making the change (#202), found the one that was wrong: the fix also
turned the handler's closing `}` into `} finally {`, and `208:usersstaleloader`'s anchor quoted that
brace. An anchor that ends one line too low matches nothing, which the instrument says in seconds —
and the *replacement* half of that mutant had the same stale line, which no instrument asks about at
all; only the sweep does. The repair ends both halves at `report(error)`.

The patch script that re-aimed the four was written as a heredoc the first time, and the shell ate
the backslashes in its `\n`s, so it matched nothing and said nothing. The repair for that is older
than this ticket and is in the memory file: write edit scripts to a file.

### The sweep, and the assertion's name

Nine mutants, one at a time against `tests/86a` — baseline 5 of 5, at 28.9 s for the
first seven and 22.0 s for the two the review asked for:
`presswriteswithoutasking` (the diagnosed pre-#86 code made to run, #115) failed 3 and passed 2;
`wrongtitle` 3 and 2; `namesnobody` 2 and 3; `cancelwrites`, `alwayssuspends`, `alwaysrestores` and
`asksthewrongdirection` 1 and 4 each. The two direction mutants are built where the two values
disagree and not where they coincide (#154), and a mutant that closes the box altogether
(`open={false}`) was deliberately not written: it reddens all five rows and two of them would die at
a **wait** rather than at an assertion (#139).

The last two came from the review reading that table with #88 in hand. `alwaysrestores` and
`alwayssuspends` kill rows 3 and 5 at their **first** assertion, the sentence, so the claims
written under it — the box closed, the status cell, the button’s other verb — were never read
on those runs: the row is red, the mutant is credited, and three claims are proved by nothing.
`doesnotclose` (the success path keeps the box open; the `catch` still closes it) failed 2 and
passed 3, both rows at *the question, closed by its own answer*, and `togglenoreload` failed 2
and passed 3, both at *the row’s own status cell*. The second is #152’s rule read forwards:
deleting the reload leaves `reloaded` undefined, which kills the row at the **sentence** — a
duplicate of a mutant already there — so the value is substituted (`Boolean(drawing)`) rather
than the call removed.

What is left is the button’s verb on rows 1, 3 and 5. It is read off `suspends(user)` over the
same reloaded list as the status cell, so no mutant at that site can tell the two apart (#191),
and the honest move is the one #119 asks for: write down which claims the mutants reach and
date it, rather than letting three ⚙ marks read as whole.

One number was right and one sentence was wrong. `presswriteswithoutasking` kills row 1 at *writes
made before anybody answered*, not at the stored status on the line below, and the mutant file's
table — written before the sweep — had named the stored status. #201's rule arrived from the other
side here: the table written before the sweep is what the dying assertion's **name** is read
against, and it is worth correcting even when the kill count is exactly what was predicted.

### The re-sweep

The four re-aimed mutants were run again, each against its own spec file, because an anchor check
says a mutant still bites and only a sweep says what it still proves (#107, #68). All four kill
exactly the row they were written for, and nothing else:

- `140:userstogglestalewins` — failed 1, passed 31 of `140a`, at *the list ... reloads does not
  land on the page the pager has left*
- `202:userssaysanyway` — failed 2, passed 8 of `202a`, at both of the switch's rows
- `203:userstoggleanyway` — failed 1, passed 21 of `203a`, at *a suspension whose reload is refused
  says the refusal and not that it suspended*
- `208:usersstaleloader` — failed 1, passed 1 of `208a`, at *the question the handler asked again*

The denominators are today's, not the ones recorded beside those mutants in their own sheets: a
test-file argument is matched as a substring and every spec file has grown since (#154, #158).

## #212 — the eight frames the four rows were winning

### What the ticket got right, and the two things it had wrong

The claim was that four committee rows (`42a` `43a` `44a` `45a`) arrange their arrival by pressing
the **group header** in the menu and then the entry, that the press *closes* a group which is
already open, and that the rows therefore pass by winning a race rather than by arranging
anything. All of that held. Two supporting details did not, which is the ordinary reading of
*a ticket's supporting identifiers are a claim like its numbers* (#54):

- the mechanism's files are `frontend/src/components/SidebarItem.js` and `Sidebar.js`, not
  `components/SidebarItem/SidebarItem.js` — that directory exists and holds the menu **config**
  (`ProgManager.js` and its five siblings), which is a different thing from the component;
- the race is not against React's re-render alone. The sub-list leaves inside an
  `AnimatePresence` exit, so the entry stays in the document, visible and clickable, for a
  window the exit's duration decides.

### The probe, and what the margin was

#49's probe measured the **assessor's** shell. These four rows are the committee's, and the two
roles reach the same branch of the arrival effect by **reading** the code — which is not the same
as by measurement (#111's species: a claim nobody has put a number on). So the probe was built
again for `PROG_MANAGER`, run on `HEAD`, and deleted (#207):

```
PROBE arrival   {"links":12,"entry":1,"visible":true}
PROBE frames    {"samples":40,"firstFrameWithNoEntry":9, ...}
PROBE second    {"landed":"locator.click: Timeout 3000ms exceeded.","url":".../main/rubrics"}
```

Eight frames. Sampled per frame rather than after a wait, because *was it still there* is a
question about frames (#164). After the ninth the same press cannot land at all — it times out on
the locator, and the shell is still on the menu's first screen. So the four rows were not passing
*in spite of* the press; they were passing inside a window of about eight frames that nothing in
the suite, the sheets or the mutants mentions, and a slower machine or a longer exit would have
turned four green rows red for a reason none of their names would have explained.

**An arrangement that destroys what it arranged can still pass, and then it is measuring the
animation.** #77's rule from the other side — there, arranging a state the system had already
reached made a row *hang*; here it makes the row *pass*, which is worse, because a hang is a
report and a pass is a silence.

### The fix, and what it cost

Six lines out, seven in: each arrival keeps the entry's press and gains the paragraph saying what
the group header does and when it was measured, so the next row written here does not put the
press back (#96 — write it on the row). Then the ordinary price of touching four closed tickets'
spec files:

- the four mutants that hold those arrival rows were re-run, one at a time against their own spec
  file, because an anchor check says a mutant still bites and only a sweep says what it still
  proves (#107, #68). `42:committeemenumisleads` failed 1 passed 5, `43:menumisleads` failed 1
  passed 4, `44:comparemenumisleads` failed 1 passed 8, `45:individualmenumisleads` failed 1
  passed 6 — each killing its own sheet's row 1 at `waitForURL`, exactly as its sheet records, so
  no figure in the four tables moved;
- every line number cited **below** one of those arrivals moved by +6, in two files that say the
  same thing (`docs/lessons.md` §#174 and `e2e/README.md`): `43a:125`/`:128` → `:131`/`:134`,
  `43a:155`/`:167` → `:161`/`:173`, `45a:189`/`:203` → `:195`/`:209`. *A citation by line number
  ages the day anything above it grows* (#173), and this is the cheap half of that rule — the
  expensive half is that nothing reports it, since `anchors.py` reads citations **by name**. Two
  files, not three: `docs/handoff/2026-09-29-…` cites `43a:125` and `44a:240` and keeps them,
  being a dated record of what one measurement returned (#54);
- `42a`'s own comment beside the assessor's single press said *the committee's rows above press
  twice because they were written before that was measured*. True when #49 wrote it and false
  twenty minutes into this ticket: a claim written in prose expires like a number (#130).
  **And the copy that was missed is in the file this ticket was not changing** — `49a`'s
  `arriveAt` carries the same sentence about *the four sibling rows that press twice*, found by
  the review's spec axis and not by the grep that found the first one, because that grep was
  for the press and this is a sentence about the press. Its twin is in §#49 of this file, two
  lines below a sentence that had already been dated: a diff proofreads what it touches (#154).

### What is left

The group header's own behaviour — that pressing it closes a group and pressing it again reopens
it — is still proved by nothing. No row presses it on purpose, and the four that pressed it by
accident have stopped. That is a claim about the menu rather than about these four reports, so it
belongs to whichever sheet owns the shell — `docs/acceptance/10-application-shell.md` — and it
is [#214](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/214), opened the same day with the eight-frame
measurement and three options in it. Written in a story and not in the tracker it would have been
a decision nobody can find (#119, #89, #125), which is the half of this ticket that was owed after
the code was right: both review axes named it, and the answer to both was a number rather than a
paragraph.

## #90 — the word the delivered screen never said, and the rule it would have been

The ticket was filed against the scope field of the account screens: it offers
*name (code)* and nothing else, so which **kind** of thing a grant is confined to — a faculty,
a department or a programme — has to be inferred from how many digits the code has. Three of
its claims were measured before any of them was used. The endpoint did not need teaching:
`GET /api/users/grantable` has answered `kind` beside every entry all along, so the half the
ticket priced first had expired (#77). The seed holds **two** pairs of a department and a
programme under the same Thai name, not the one the ticket named. And the rule the ticket wrote
down — two digits is a department, four is a programme — cannot cover the faculty at all:
`CONTEXT.md` §Scope codes it `ENG` precisely so that it cannot collide with a numbered
department, and a field that is sometimes digits and sometimes letters is not a field a reader
counts.

### What the delivered screen answered, and what it did not

#86's rule says to ask the delivered UI before asking the owner, and the answer here is that
`DEEP-QA-FRONTEND` draws `{scope.nameTH}` bare — no kind word, and no code either. So the
wording is not a control the rebuild dropped, and nothing about it was already decided.

What the delivered screen *did* have was a different mechanism: its lists were keyed by role, so
the person choosing a scope was never offered two kinds of thing at once. The protection was
structural, and the ambiguity could not arise. The rebuild offers one mixed list, fed by the
server's own `assignable`, which is a divergence taken on purpose — and #90 is the price of it.
That reframes the ticket: it is not a cosmetic request, and it is not a regression either.

It also rules out the cheapest-looking fix. Filtering the list by the role being granted would
restore the delivered *mechanism*, but as a rule living in the UI that the server's grant list
does not hold — two places holding one opinion, which is a claim neither of them can be shown
to hold (#97), against a decision that says authority is derived server-side and nowhere else
(ADR-0002). Restoring a delivered mechanism can be a **new rule** rather than a restoration.

### The owner's answer, and the condition that was one case short

Four options were priced and the owner chose the word: the entry reads
*kind · name (code)*. Not `<optgroup>`, not role-filtering, not leaving it. The grant confined
to nothing carries **no** kind word, because its own label already names the whole of the
organisation and a word in front would say that twice; and a kind the map has never heard of reads
exactly the way every entry read before #90, rather than drawing `undefined`.

That condition was drawn from one case while a sibling was already outside it, which is #113 met
in my own code rather than in a ticket's. This organisation's faculty is named
`คณะวิศวกรรมศาสตร์`, so the screen drew *คณะ · คณะวิศวกรรมศาสตร์ (ENG)* — the very defect the
unconfined grant had been spared. Dating the condition protects it against the future and says
nothing about a sibling already outside it. Both wordings are defensible (every entry prefixed
scans down one column; dropping the duplicate means no entry says a word twice), so it went to
the owner, who answered *คณะวิศวกรรมศาสตร์* — drop it. The rule in the code then stopped being *the
unconfined grant has no word* and became **no word in front of a label that already says it**,
which covers both cases in one sentence. The sheet's row 3 had meanwhile written an expected
string the screen never writes, which a hand-walker would have hunted for (#118).

The wording of the unconfined entry — it still shows its sentinel in brackets — was raised
separately rather than changed on the way past (`docs/06` §Out of Scope).

### The rows, the row #88 made, and the row a blind mutant made

Every row was run against the unfixed code before its mutant was written, which is the cheap half
of #203: on the first round three went red at the assertion they were written for, and the fourth
would have passed, because what it claims is an **absence** that the broken screen also has. That
is the row to be most careful with, and it is the one the control mutant exists for.

The fourth row exists at all because of #88. A single row reading the central administrator's
list would have asserted the faculty's word and the unconfined entry's silence one below the
other, and a mutant reports the first assertion it kills — so the claim underneath would have
been proved by nothing while the row went red and the mutant was credited. Splitting it cost one
`openAt` and bought two claims that can fail apart.

The fifth row exists because the owner's second answer made a mutant blind. With the no-duplicate
rule, `nofaculty` — which drops `faculty` from the map — produces, for the seeded faculty, the
same string as suppressing the word deliberately: the two implementations agree there, so the
mutant proves nothing at row 3 (#117). The fix is the **row**, not deleting the mutant (#118), and
the fixture is built where the two disagree: a faculty whose name does *not* begin with its kind
word. A claim that no fixture can build that is a claim about the seed (#155) — this one is built
by writing to the database, as `133a` and `139a` read from it, and putting the name back in
`finally`, below the seam the row measures (#181, #134); the run's own `leftovers` report confirms
the `faculty` table did not move (#132). The map keeps its `faculty` entry because the entry is
the rule and the seed is one instance of it.

### The mutants, and the survivor I wrote myself

`nokind` is the diagnosed code made to run (#115): the label as it read before this ticket. It
kills rows 1, 2 and 5 and **leaves rows 3 and 4 standing**, on purpose — both of those claim an
**absence** of a kind word, which is true of the pre-#90 label too. They are its controls, and
that is what tells a row pinning today's value apart from a row reading the rule (#145). It
carries two edits, because the pre-#90 label had no map at all and leaving `KINDS` declared and
unreferenced is a warning react-scripts turns into a failed compile under `CI=true` — a mutant
that stops the application rather than failing a row (#101). `swapsthewords` gives the two
colliding kinds each other's word and kills rows 1 and 2. `nofaculty` kills row 5 alone.
`saysthekindtwice` drops the `startsWith` condition, which is the wording the owner declined made
to run (#48), and kills row 3 alone; row 5 passes under it, the renamed faculty being owed its
word either way. `namestheunconfined` gives the unconfined grant a word and kills row 4 alone.

`swapsthewords` **survived 5 of 5** on the first sweep, which is the survivor to distrust most,
because the sheet had predicted the kill (#51). It was not the code and not the row: the script I
used to regenerate the mutants swapped the two key-value *pairs* instead of the two words, which
only reorders the map. Two instruments said nothing. `anchors.py` answered problems 0 before and
after, correctly — the anchor had not moved, and an anchor check never says a mutant has stopped
proving anything (#107, #68). And my own assertion that the map's line occurred three times
passed, because all three occurrences were the same wrong text: a count is evidence about the
pattern typed, not about the claim wanted (#83), and the way to have caught it was to assert what
the built string must *say* — that the words had moved and the keys had not — which is what the
repair asserts now.

The reason the text was wrong at all is worth its own line. I read the map's line out of the
mutation file rather than out of `GrantPicker.js`, and in the mutation file that line lives inside
a Python string literal, so what came back ended `}\n",` — a quoted copy carries its quoting.
Reading rather than retyping is right (#118); the file to read from is the one the mutant edits.

Three other sites draw a scope with no kind word — the grants panel's own list of held grants,
the accounts table, and the role dropdown — and the unconfined entry still shows its sentinel in
brackets. They are [#215](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/215) and
[#216](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/216), opened the same day, because the blast
radius is an order of magnitude apart from one `<option>` list: those are places a person
**reads**, not places a person **decides**, and a deferral written in a story and not in the
tracker is a decision nobody can find (#119, #89, #125).

## #214 — the toggle nothing had ever pressed on purpose, and the negative read that can fail

#212 took a press out of four rows and left a hole behind it. The four committee arrivals had been
pressing the menu's group header believing the group arrived shut; it arrives **open** for every
role but the teacher, so the press was closing it, and what carried them to the entry underneath
was the eight frames `AnimatePresence` leaves the list in the document for. Taking the press out
was right, and it left `handleToggleSubmenu` proved by nothing at all: not one row in the suite
pressed a group header any more. #212 wrote that down as a ticket rather than as a paragraph
(#119, #89, #125), and this is that ticket.

The proof is a grid of three mutants against two rows, so that each row dies at **its own**
assertion (#88). `alwaysopen` makes the toggle add the key and never remove it — a menu that
opens and cannot close — and kills both rows: row 1 at its own claim, row 2 at the same line used
as its *precondition*. Two rows dying under one mutant in shared code is two **reachability**
claims and not one claim counted twice (#191), and row 2's own claim has its own mutant:
`neverreopens` removes the key and never adds it, kills row 2 alone, and **leaves row 1
standing**, which is what makes row 2 something other than a copy of row 1. The third,
`arrivesclosed`, empties the arrival effect, and it is the premise both rows rest on: without it
a shell that arrived shut would pass both, and row 1 — named for a press that closes — would be
measuring a press that opens.

### A retrying negative that can fail

Row 1 reads `toHaveCount(0)`, which in this suite is usually the assertion that cannot fail: a
retrying negative against an element that removes itself passes however broken the screen is
(#50). It can fail here, and the condition is worth writing down, because #50 is written as a
flat prohibition and this is the case outside it: **nothing removes this entry by itself.** The
only thing that takes the sub-list out of the document is the press under test, so the wait has
something to wait out, and `alwaysopen` is the evidence rather than the argument — it leaves the
entry in the document for ever and the read spends its whole timeout saying so. The question to
ask of a retrying negative is not *is it retrying* but *who else removes this element*.

The same eight frames then decide how row 2 is written. Its claim is that a second press brings
the group back, and pressed at a settle point straight after the first press it would read an
entry the exit animation had not finished removing — passing on a shell that never reopened
anything. So the close is read to completion first, which is #164's rule met from the other side:
there the question was *was it ever on the screen* and the answer was a sample per frame; here the
question is *has it gone yet* and the answer is to read the thing the row is about at the moment
it is about, not at the first convenient one.

### The window itself has no mutant, and the chevron has no seam

The eight frames belong to `AnimatePresence`, not to `handleToggleSubmenu`: all three mutants
leave the window exactly as it is, and `alwaysopen` never starts an exit at all. So the measured
window is a dated paragraph on `docs/acceptance/10` carrying #212's own probe figures — lifted,
not re-measured, because the frame count is a property of this machine — and not a row nothing can
fail (#47, #203).

The chevron is the other half of the same reckoning. It rotates when the group opens, which is
appearance, and no seam speaks for it; #214 did not touch the code that draws it. That is a ☐ row
on criterion 2 waiting on a **person** and on no ticket (#157), written rather than left unsaid,
because a sheet that records only what its ticket proved is a sheet whose silences are
indistinguishable from coverage.

`arrivesclosed` lives in `SidebarItem.js`, which four tickets now hold, so its reach outside this
sheet was measured rather than guessed (#123): five rows red over `49a` and `105a` — all four of
`49a`, whose arrivals click a sub-entry, and row 2 of `105a` — with **row 1 of `105a` standing**,
which names the teacher branch as a different line the mutant never touches. The mechanism is
*any row that reads or presses a sub-entry on a non-teacher menu*, which is not a list of files.
And the census that says which tickets share that file answered four where `mutation/README.md`'s
own bullet still said two: that bullet had been two tickets stale since #105, found by running the
script instead of reading the list (#85, #87, #125).

### What the review round found, and both of its findings were about the sheet

Neither axis found anything wrong with the spec or the mutants; both found the **documentation**
overclaiming, in two different ways, and both were right.

The spec axis read the two ⚙ cells and noticed each states **two** claims where only the first is
behind a mutant. Row 1's cell ends *and the header is still there to press again*; row 2's ends
*and the entry reaches its screen*. Both of those assertions exist and run — and both sit *below*
the line every mutant kills, so during a sweep they are never read: the row is red, the mutant is
credited, and the claim under the red line is proved by nothing. That is #88 exactly, met from the
sheet's side rather than the spec's, and the thing worth keeping is **how** it happens: a cell is
written in one breath, as a sentence about what the row does, while a mutant kills one assertion.
The repair was to say in each cell which half the mark covers and which half is a net, and to write
down what a mutant for the other half would have to break — for the header, nothing in
`handleToggleSubmenu` can take it away, which is nearer *structurally unreachable* than *untested*
(#102); for the navigation, a mutant on `to={subPath}` would disable every menu-driven move in the
suite, which is a mutant that kills too much (#45). Not moving the mark was deliberate: each row's
**first** claim is killed by its own mutant, which is what ⚙ says.

The standards axis counted the mark column and found the sheet's own summary sentence stale for
the **fifth** time: *22 ⚙ · 6 ☑ · 1 ◐ · 1 ☐, 30 rows* against a table now holding 24 ⚙ · 6 ☑ ·
1 ◐ · 2 ☐ and 33 rows. The figures were the smaller harm. The sentence also said *the one
remaining ☐ is the appearance of the four-entry menu*, and prose like that steers the walk queue —
it hid the ☐ row this very ticket had just added. #154's rule is that correcting one hand-kept
figure finds the one you are looking at, and this round proved its other half too: twenty lines
below the summary, *the seam has taken twenty-two rows* was stale in the same breath, and I had
re-read the summary without re-reading that. The paragraph above both of them has been recording
its own staleness since #111; what it still has no instrument for is the count itself — `anchors.py`
reads every sheet's mark column already (and is what counted this one, via `_cells` and
`_mark_column` rather than a second reader — #141, #174), but nothing asks a sheet whether its own
summary sentence matches its own table.

## #213 — the claim that was also the locator, and the mutant that had to be wrong on one side

#86 closed on 16 October 2569 with two debts written into its own sheet, which is the shape #119
asks for: a deferral written into prose and not into the tracker is a decision nobody can find.
The first debt was three ⚙ rows whose last assertion no mutant reached — the verb on the row's own
button, in rows 1, 3 and 5. The second was the dialog's appearance, which the browser seam cannot
answer at all. #213 is both, and it asked a real question about the first: *is this provable, and
if it is not, say why and downgrade the three marks.* It offered three unmeasured possibilities, of
which only the third lowered the marks: separate the two reads first and then place the mutant,
build a moment where the verb and the status cell genuinely disagree, or measure, find it cannot be
done, write why, and bring the three marks down to what is actually proved. The first round of this
write-up said *all three ended in the mark coming down*, which is the ticket's own failure mode
repeated in the file that diagnoses it — a claim copied until each copy looks checked.

**The ticket's reason was measured first, and it was false.** The sheet and the mutation file both
said the verb reads `suspends(user)` *on the same row the status cell reads*, so no mutant at that
site could separate the two claims (#191). The status cell reads `STATUS[user.status]?.label ??
user.status`; the button reads `{suspends(user) ? 'ระงับ' : 'เปิดใช้งาน'}`. Two expressions, two
sites, one field between them — and a mutant at either one separates them by construction. This is
`CLAUDE.md`'s first rule met again: a ticket's *What is wrong* is a claim from the day it was
written. What makes this one worth the telling is that the claim had been written three times — in
the issue, in the sheet and in the mutation file's own debt paragraph — and each copy made the next
one look checked.

**What was actually in the way is a different sentence, and it names the fix.** The press finds the
control *by the verb the claim is about*: `statusButton` in `e2e/support/users-screen.js` is
`getByRole('button', { name: label, exact: true })`, and `startStatusChange` passes the verb the
row expects. So a mutant that swaps the verb on both sides leaves every row with nothing to click,
and all five die in the locator at the timeout rather than at a claim (#139) — which is the same
reason #86 never wrote `open={false}`. The mutant that proves the claim therefore has to be **wrong
on one side only**: right on the side the row presses, wrong on the side the row reads. That is the
fourth option, and it is the answer — *yes, provable, at the button's own site, and without
separating the two reads first*. A ticket that asks *is this provable* is answered by a
measurement, and the measurement here was three mutants and a clean run.

- `pressflipstherow` — the press flips the row's control in the screen's own state with nothing
  written (an optimistic draw, written with a functional updater so the mutant measures the live
  state and not the first render's closure, #201). Row 1 dies at *the row, still offering the same
  change*, its own last assertion; 1 failed, 4 passed, and 44 of 44 outside the sheet.
  (The two verb mutants report 39 against that same population of 44, not a smaller one: a
  `mode: 'serial'` file skips its remaining rows after a red, and both runs print *5 did not run* —
  #67, read beside #154's rule about reading two figures side by side.)
- `alwaysoffersuspend` — the button offers *ระงับ* in both states. Row 3 dies at *the control, now
  offering the way back*, its own last assertion; 3 failed, 2 passed.
- `alwaysofferrestore` — its mirror. Row 5 dies at *the control, back to the change it offered
  before*; 4 failed, 1 passed.

**The eight other deaths are what the ticket paid for.** Under a one-sided mutant the rows that
arrive on the wrong side have nothing to press, so they die at a timeout: eight of them across the
two sweeps. A death at a wait is not a claim (#139), so `arrive()` gained one line — *the change
the row arrives offering* — read **before** the press. After it, every one of those eight deaths is
at a named assertion, and the rule the verb follows is a claim of all five rows in both directions
rather than an arrangement none of them states. The row that could not be proved and the deaths
that could not be read were the same mechanism seen from two ends.

**And once it is a claim, every row owes the citation** — which is what the standards review caught
in the first round of the sheet. If the arrival read is an assertion of each row, then the mutant
that kills a row *there* holds a claim of that row, so rows 1, 2 and 3 cite `alwaysofferrestore`
beside whatever else holds them and rows 4 and 5 cite `alwaysoffersuspend`: one mutant, several
reachability claims, not one claim counted twice (#191). Citing it only on the row whose *last*
assertion it kills would have left the mutation file's own kill column naming rows the sheet does
not — the second of the four ways to read a kills column, found in the file written the same day.

**The nine older mutants were not re-swept, and the argument is written down rather than assumed.**
A spec that gains a row a mutant can reach expires that mutant's count and nothing reports it
(#202) — but the new line runs *before* the press, and all nine act at the press or after it:
`presswriteswithoutasking` at the press, `wrongtitle` `namesnobody` `asksthewrongdirection` with
the box open, `cancelwrites` at *ยกเลิก*, `alwayssuspends` `alwaysrestores` `doesnotclose`
`togglenoreload` inside `confirmSwitch`. None of them changes what the new line can see, and the
clean 5 of 5 says the line is not red by itself. The condition that expires this reasoning is a
mutant of this sheet that touches how a row is drawn before the press.

**The out-of-sheet sweep found the claim already held one sheet over, as an instrument.** The
mutants live in `Users.js`, one screen, but the button is pressed from six files, so the sweep went
outside the sheet as well (#123 — a mutant's sheet is one of the places it kills, not the list).
`alwaysoffersuspend` failed 3 of 39, `alwaysofferrestore` 6 of 39; most of those deaths are at a
**press** in `11c` `13a` `202a` `203a`, which is an arrangement, but two are assertions and both
are in `208a`: *the row the answer carried, drawn* and *the account is live before the press*. That
is #83 from the other side — the tell that a claim has an owner you have not found can be a row in
another ticket's spec. The verb was not unheld before today; it was held as `208a`'s instrument,
which is exactly why the claim still belongs on this sheet and not there. `84a` is immune, its
locator being `/ระงับ|เปิดใช้งาน/`: it asks whether the button is dead, not what it says.

**Auditing the whole table against the definition found two more claims nobody had read.** ⚙ means
a mutant killed that row's own assertion *and* the cited assertions cover the row whole, so the
audit was the whole table and not the three rows the ticket named. Row 2 has `cancelwrites` dying
**above** one uncovered claim and **below** another — *the question, dismissed* above, *a sentence
about something that did not happen* below. That is #88's rule twice in one row, and both halves
got a mutant of their own in this ticket rather than a line of prose, because leaving them is the
species of debt #213 exists to close. Fourteen mutants now, where the ticket's scope was three.

**Part 2 is four ☐ rows, and the ticket asked for ◐ or ☑ *as far as can be walked*.** What landed is
the rows, written so they can be walked; what is owed is the walk, which needs a person in front of
the screen, so #213 does not close on this half yet and the four ☐ rows are the queue the walk comes
off. Saying *four ☐ rows is the whole of what it asked for* — as the first round of this section
did — is the same overclaim as a ⚙ that was never earned, one mark along. The appearance of a shared
`ConfirmDialog` — the red confirm in both directions, the box's size and position over the row it
names, where the consequence sentence breaks, and whether one sentence is enough to tell the two
directions apart — is hand-walked by definition, and each row is written in `ConfirmDialog`'s own
tokens rather than in eye-words, so a walker can check what they see against what the code says.
#105's line from the other side: a row can gain a walkable half the day a ticket lands, and here
the ticket's product *is* the walkable half. The rows carry the condition that #204 lands first, in
which case the focus half walks in the same pass.

**No application code changed in this ticket.** A proof gap is not a defect, and the fix for a mark
that overclaims is the mutant it was missing or the mark coming down — not an edit to the screen.

**Then the walk happened the same evening, and the two questions turned out to be one question.**
Two rows came back ☑ from the DOM of the real screen: the box is 384px of `max-w-sm` centred on the
viewport at 569–953, which lands over the middle of the `teach02` row it names (353–1474 × 303–359),
leaving the code and the name to its left and the status and buttons to its right, both unreadable
under a measured `blur(4px)` — so what tells the walker which row this is about is the sentence
inside the box, which names the account, and the criterion's *can a person confirm without
remembering which row they pressed* is answered yes by the wording and not by the geometry. The
consequence sentence takes four lines with no newline character in it, breaking after
*ภัทรา* · *ใช่หรือไม่* · *ถัดไป*, all three the author's own spaces, with `glued`'s 131 word
joiners holding every other boundary shut and `break-words` never firing. The other two rows are ◐, and reading them side by
side is what the walk added to the ticket: the title, both labels and both class strings are
identical to the letter in the two directions, so **the red button says *careful* and does not say
*which way*, and the only thing that says which way is one sentence**. Rows 1 and 4 are therefore
not two preferences to settle but one question with two halves, and it is the owner's
(`docs/06` §Out of Scope) — so it was asked rather than answered. The owner answered both the
same evening: **keep it as it is**, the red button in both directions and one sentence to tell
them apart, which takes the two rows to ☑ and finishes part 2. The declined-proposal rule
(#48) does not follow here, because what was decided is an **appearance** — a colour and a
wording — which this repo walks by hand rather than asserting at the browser seam, so what
guards the decision against an accidental change is the walked row itself and not a mutant.

**And proofreading the rendered diff caught two marks that had come back as a Thai letter — in my
own committed prose.** `◐ หรือ ☑` had been written to the sheet as `ส หรือ ส`, and `ครึ่ง` as `ครี่ง`,
by a patch script in the review round whose text had been through a cp874 round trip; the sentence
still read as Thai prose, which is why it survived a round of review and a commit. A scan of every
file the commit touched for a lone `ส` between spaces and for that one misspelling found exactly
one line, and §#165's own lone `ส` as the true positive it should — that line is *about* the
letter, and citing it by its story rather than by its line number is #173. The lesson that was
already written (proofread Thai by rendering the diff) is not a lesson about new prose: it is a lesson about **every** line a script rewrites, and the mark
characters are the ones to read first, being the only characters on these sheets that a Thai
codepage has no room for.

## #114 — the option the ticket said to look at first, which could not change anything

#114 was opened on 4 September 2569 during #37's own hand walk and waited six weeks. The symptom
was still true on the day it was taken: at `innerWidth` 1396 with the left menu open — the state
anybody opening the screen meets — every legend row beside the radar chart ran to three lines,
five rows drawn as fifteen. Nothing was lost, nothing overflowed, the page did not scroll
sideways; the ticket's own word for what was wrong was **รุงรัง**, which is why it was filed
rather than fixed in place. It offered three options and left the choice open, which `docs/06`
§Out of Scope makes the owner's. What it also left open, without saying so, was whether any of
the three works.

**A ticket's proposed options are claims like its numbers, and the cheapest one to check is the
option against the ticket's own acceptance condition.** Option 3 was *`xl` instead of `lg`*,
annotated as the one to look at by eye first because it changes the layout most people see. The
served CSS has `xl` = 1280px and criterion 1 is written at `innerWidth` 1396, which is past it:
at the width the ticket judges by, option 3 changes nothing at all. The option the ticket pointed
at first was the option that could not pass its own first criterion — and finding that out took
one grep of the served stylesheet, not a measurement session. It is #152's *as today* one layer
out: there the claim is about today, here about a proposed fix, and both are settled by reading
the ticket's own criterion back against them.

**Then the stated cause was not the cause, and the real symptom was the one the ticket did not
mention.** The ticket said *the chart reserves 448px and the legend gets the remainder*. Measured,
the chart never had 448 with the menu open: the card is the narrow half of
`lg:grid-cols-[20rem_minmax(0,1fr)]`, whose other column is the 320px picker, so chart and legend
shared 578px and the `<ul>` sat at its min-content **188px, identically at 1024 and at 1396**. The
side that could shrink was therefore the chart, not the legend: **366px at 1396, 122px at 1152,
0px at 1024**. *Nothing is lost* was true of the text and false of the picture — and the ticket's
options 1 (`whitespace-nowrap`) and 2 (`min-w-[18rem]`) both make that worse, to 84 and 22 at
1152, because both buy room for the words out of the chart. Only dropping the side-by-side layout
gives the space back, which is how a fourth option came to be the one on the table.

**And the delivered screen had already answered the half the owner was being asked.** #86's rule
again: `DEEP-QA-FRONTEND`'s version of this screen drew the legend **above** the chart at full
width, Chart.js's own `legend: { position: 'top' }`, so stacking it is a restoration and not an
invention. What was genuinely the owner's was *above* or *below* — asked with four screenshots
(today, option 1, below, above) and answered *below* on 17 October 2569.

**The ticket's reason for being unprovable was a claim too, and wrong in the ordinary way
(#141).** Criterion 4 said the row is walked by eye because the matter is purely one of
appearance and no seam can prove it instead. But what criterion 1 asks is *how many lines does a
row run to at this width*, which is a number a browser reads: a row's height over its
`line-height`. `114a` is the first spec in the suite to set a viewport **wider** than the project
default, which `98a` had already done from the narrow end. What stayed with the hand was the word
รุงรัง, and only that.

**The row claims one line where the criterion says at most two, on purpose.** Option 1 also gets
two lines, so a row asserting *at most two* would survive the mutant that makes the declined
option run, and the owner's decision would have nothing holding it (#48). The sweep is what shows
the stricter claim is the real one rather than a flourish: `beside` (the code before the fix,
#115) kills row 1 at `[2,2,2,3,2]` and `nowrapbeside` kills the same row at `[1,2,2,2,2]`, and
two different arrays are the evidence that the row is about *one* and not about *two*.
`minwidthbeside` leaves row 1 standing, because option 2 really does give one line — which is
what makes the row about the legend's **position** the one carrying the decision whole, rather
than a second copy of row 1.

**The layout is copied into two screens and not shared between them, so criterion 3 is a claim
and not a by-product.** `besidesection` puts the old layout back in `SectionResults.js` alone and
kills exactly one row. What it then measured was something the sheet had only been inferring from
the length of the words: it dies at the **position** assertion *after* that row's line-count
assertion has passed, so #36's legend was one line even beside the chart. The ticket's symptom was
never reachable on that screen, and what the fix buys it is the chart's own width instead. A
sentence about a sibling screen that reads like an inference is often one mutant away from being
a measurement — and the row holding it belongs on that screen's own sheet, not in this one's
prose (#50, #97).

**The review round found three things, and two of them are this file's own rules.** First, the JSX
comment: the fix is one class per file, so the comment explaining it was pasted into both — and
in `SectionResults.js` every figure in it (the picker grid, 578, 366, 0) belongs to a grid that
file does not have. #83's *a rule borrowed whole borrows its defect too*, in the shape a copied
layout invites, except that here the copy is prose, which is what a later ticket quotes. The
repair is a comment that says only what is true of its own file and points at #37's sheet for the
numbers. Second, the mutation file's docstring said `beside` killed row 1 at `[2,2,3,3,3]` where
the sheet said `[2,2,2,3,2]` — two documents written the same hour contradicting each other
(#154) on the very figure that carries the row-1-versus-option-1 argument. No sweep log had been
kept, so it was settled by running the mutant again and reading it rather than by picking: the
sheet was right. Third, `mutation/README.md` had the catalogue row and the corrected total but not
the shared-files collision bullet its own rule asks for, and #145's bullet — which had claimed
no file beside those three touches `SectionResults.js` — had been expired by this very ticket.
The census answers 71 → 72.

**One review finding was wrong, and what told them apart was the precedent rather than the
argument.** The spec axis read criterion 2's ☑ as claiming a person had looked on 17 October;
the standards axis read the same cell as correctly marked with its reason written in it.
`docs/acceptance/47-profile-photo.md`'s net row settles it — a row whose mutant survives is ☑
with the reason in the cell — so what was owed was the seam and the dates, not a changed mark.
About one finding a round being wrong is the rate this repo has measured before, which is the
argument for grepping a finding before editing on it.

**And a row added in review expires a mutant nobody edited.** Row 4 gained a row-count
precondition and a width assertion, which is #202's shape from the spec's side: the anchor is
still exact, the code untouched, nothing goes red, and only re-running says what the mutant now
proves. Hence two sweeps in one day — and the figures on the sheet are the second one's.

## #128 — the value that could not travel, and the fourth option

#128 was the question #89 wrote down and did not answer: should the refusal an account meets
before its window opens name the start date? The ticket said so itself — *item 1 is a question,
not work* — and listed three things that could be done about it: let the URL carry the date,
close with no diff, or tell the person at the doors that have a body and not at the one that
does not. The answer the owner gave was none of the three.

**The measurement did not change the answer; it changed the question.** All three of the ticket's
mechanical claims held: both keys are in `GOOGLE_REFUSAL_REASONS`, the Google refusal travels as
`/login?error=<reason>` with no body, `Login.js` keeps its own copy of the words keyed by the
reason alone, and `refuse()` hands `REFUSALS[reason]` to `JSON.stringify`, which is #125's shape
exactly. One figure had aged the way a ticket's figures do — the function-valued refusals the
ticket counted at 22 on 9 September were 24 — and that one decided nothing. The claim that did
decide something was the ticket's own asymmetry: *the doors that have a body* against *the door
that does not*, written as though it were one against one. There are **three** doors. The
password door answers with a body, `endAccess` in `backend/auth/authorise.js` answers `403` with
a body, and the Google door redirects. Two against one, and the option the ticket priced as the
cheap compromise was the one that would have left the same state of the same account saying
different things at two doors out of three — which is #66 in the shape of a refusal.

Measuring that is what made a fourth option visible, and it is not in the ticket: **where the
value cannot travel, what can travel is the way to get the value.** The date cannot cross a
redirect without going into a query string, into the browser's history and into every proxy log
on the way; the *sentence naming whom to ask* crosses as part of the words, at every door, with
no parameter and no composition on the screen — which is also what keeps `50a`'s sixth row
(*the screen does not invent a sentence*) true. The owner was asked with four options and took
that one, then chose the wording: the #89 sentence whole, with a clause appended.

The state was measured as reachable before any of that, because an unreachable state makes the
question hypothetical. Nothing in `backend/routes/users.js` restricts a validity window to the
external assessor role, and `admit` is the same function on both paths, so a `@kmitl` account
that signs in with Google only and carries a future `valid_from` reads this sentence at the door
with no body. The comment in `Login.js` that called the assessor *the only person who meets it*
is therefore a claim about the seed and not about the rules, and it was dated rather than
deleted (#130, #54). So was the paragraph in `refusals.js` explaining why neither sentence names
the date: every line of it still holds, and what changed is that one of the two sentences grew a
second clause.

**The fixture was already there.** `users.test.js` had a row building the not-started end by
creating an account with `valid_from: day(10)`, asserting the whole value and then the word
*อีกครั้ง* — waiting, which is #89's whole axis. The new claim went under it as a
third assertion with a name, and the ordering is the point: run against the unfixed code (#203)
it was the only thing that went red, and under the mutant that puts #89's sentence back it is
the assertion that dies, the two above it passing. A claim written below another claim is proved
by nothing when the one above dies first (#88); here the one above cannot, because the mutant
edits the same table the equality reads.

Two places hold the sentence, so there are two mutants (#97). `serversaysonlywait` is the
diagnosed code made to run (#115) and the declined options' own world (#48): it still refuses,
still says to wait, and says nothing about whom to ask. It killed one test in the whole backend
suite, at the named assertion. `screenkeepstheoldsentence` is the server fixed and the copy
forgotten — #111's shape — and it killed exactly row 1 of `50a`, the row that loops every key
against the backend's own `REFUSALS`. Nothing new was owed to `50`'s sheet but a mutant: the
claim *both doors say the same words* was already there, and a mutant is what makes it fail.

**The wording reached a mutant's anchor.** `89:screenmissesthenewend` is anchored on the
sentence itself in `Login.js`, so appending a clause re-aimed it (#140). The anchor was read out
of the file rather than retyped (#90), `anchors.py` said exact — and that is not a sweep (#107,
#68), so it was swept again: one row, the same row, 13 green. Reading `FILES` across the
catalogue to write this sheet's do-not-sweep-together list then found that #89's own list had
been missing `52-access-ended.py` since #52 took `Login.js`, which is the species of expiry
`mutation/README.md` keeps a section for: a list is dated by the day it was written and expires
by a file somewhere else (#154, #85).

Finally, a ticket's own appendix is a claim too. #128's §รูปแบบวันที่ asked for the date in
**พ.ศ.** if it were shown. The only place this pair of values is shown to anybody is the
*ช่วงเวลาใช้งาน* column in `Users.js`, which is ISO **ค.ศ.**, and `frontend/src` has no
Buddhist-era formatter at all — no `543` anywhere. The two readers are different people, so that
would have been a question for the owner rather than a defect; the answer made it moot, and it
is written down because it was the ticket's argument, not because it was decided.

**Both review axes found something no sweep could have.** The new assertion read only the first
words of the clause — *whom to ask* — under a name that claims the whole of it, and
`serversaysonlywait` could never say so, because it deletes the clause entire: a sentence that
appended only *or contact the staff* would have passed a row called *the not-started refusal
names a way to ask for the start date*. Check what an assertion says, not that one exists (#96,
#40); the name is the claim to hold it to, and the clause is now read whole.

The second finding was the ticket's **first** option, *let the URL carry the date*. The owner
declined all three and #48 says the declined option is the mutant to write; this one cannot be
written, and the reason is a measurement rather than a preference. `refuseToBrowser` builds one
URL for every reason, and the only row that reads a `location` exactly is driven by
`googleUnavailable` — so a mutant appending a date for *every* reason dies on a row about a
different refusal, which is a kill at the wrong claim (#125). A mutant faithful to the option,
appending only for `validityNotStarted`, survives everything, because that refusal is asserted at
the function seam, where no URL exists. #101's third category, not its second: untested, with the
condition that would change it written beside it.

And the census written to produce the do-not-sweep list answered a third question nobody asked
it. The figure the file carried from the day before — 71 shared paths, 9 threes — disagrees with
the instrument **at that same commit**, which says 72 and 10: #114's own sheet holds two shared
paths, and the hand count was taken before its sheet existed. A hand-kept figure in a file that
grows every ticket is already wrong (#119), and which of the two numbers is wrong is settled by
running the instrument at the commit the figure was written at (#141), not by argument. The same
read found the lists in `66`'s and `85`'s own headers short by three sheets each, the same species
as #89's missing `52` and for the same reason — a list expires by a file somewhere else.

## #204 — the question that announces itself, and the half that costs eleven rows

#204 was an accessibility ticket with a question inside it. `ConfirmDialog` has drawn a
`fixed inset-0 z-[9998] bg-black/50 backdrop-blur-sm` cover since #14 and contains nothing: no
`role="dialog"`, no `aria-modal`, no accessible name or description, no focus moved into the box,
no trap, no `inert`, no `aria-hidden` and no Escape. A mouse cannot reach the table underneath,
because the cover takes the click; a keyboard can, because nothing stops it. The ticket said the
decision was not the rebuild's (`docs/06` §Out of Scope) and offered three ways: trap and announce
in the component, all twenty sites at once; leave it as today with a dated reason; or disable the
table's controls while the box is open, which #142 had already answered.

**Three of the ticket's own claims were answered by measuring them.** The count was *19 call sites
in 18 files* and is **20 in 19**: #86 added the accounts screen's status switch on 16 ตุลาคม 2569,
which asks `switching ? asks(switching) : ''`, and `Offerings.js` has held two sites — in two
mutually exclusive returns — since `8fe0b6d`. The ticket's instruction to measure *which screens
have live controls underneath, because some replace the table with a form* rests on two states
being one state, and they are never the same state: no screen's dialog flag (`removing`,
`removingGroup`, `switching`, `opening`) is the flag that swaps the list for a form (`editing`,
`opening`), and `{removing ? (` choosing JSX occurs **0 times** in the tree. So the exemption the
ticket expected exempts nothing, and the work it asked for did not reduce the population by one.
And the delivered UI — which decides whether *leave it as today* means a regression or a
divergence (#86, #90) — contains nothing either: 25 hand-rolled `fixed inset-0` covers, no
`<Dialog>` or `<Modal>`, no trap, no Escape, and four `autoFocus` attributes, all on form fields
rather than on a box. Option 2 is therefore *as delivered*, and #204 is an enhancement.

**The measurement made a fourth option visible, and it was about the fix rather than about the
value** — #128's move one family along. Option 1 is two fixes with very different prices:

- The half that **announces** — `role`, `aria-modal`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, the
  focus moved into the box on open, Escape as a way out — costs **no row**. Every row in the suite
  that reaches a control under the cover gets there with `focus()` or `fill()`, and both move focus
  from wherever it was, so moving it into the box leaves all of them standing. Ten files, 71 rows,
  all green after the fix.
- The half that **contains** — a focus trap, `inert` or `aria-hidden` on the rest of the screen —
  is the one that removes reach, and it costs **10 rows in 5 files** plus a sweep of the 22 mutants
  those files hold.

`aria-modal="true"` is what makes that split worth stating precisely rather than as *announcement
against containment*: it asks a screen reader to read nothing outside the box, so for somebody
listening the way in is **already closed**, while a sighted keyboard user's tab order is untouched.
The deferred half is containment for the second kind of reader, not containment as such. The owner
was asked with four options and took the split, so `204a` holds five rows for the half that landed
and one row — a net — for the half that did not, with the deferred proposal made to run as its
mutant (#48), and the deferral written into the tracker rather than into prose (#119, #125).

**A sweep over serial specs cannot price a change that lands on several rows of one group.** The
`trapsfocus` mutant was run over the six files the price names and came back *8 failed, 12 passed* —
which looks like a census of eleven being wrong by three, and is not that either. Six rows never
ran: four of the five files configure `mode: 'serial'`, which stops a group at its first red (#67),
and the skipped rows are exactly the later rows of the groups whose first row the mutant killed. So
a one-sweep kill count is a **lower bound** on a price, and what turns it into a price is running
each skipped row on its own under the same mutant — #67 read as a statement about a price rather
than about a kill count.

Run that way the six split **three red, three green**, and the price is **ten rows in five files**,
not eleven: `202a` 3, `206a` 2, `207a` 3, `208a` 1, `211a` 1. The three the census was wrong about
are wrong in two different ways, and both are #174 from the losing side — a census is evidence
about the property it counted. `208a`'s accounts row reaches its search box with `fill()` and its
own comment says the way in is this ticket's; a trap does not close it, because `fill()` sets the
value and does not need focus to stay where it put it, so *presses a control under the cover* and
*writes into a control under the cover* are two mechanisms and only the first one is priced here.
`206a`'s second row and `211a`'s second row press nothing under the cover at all: one shares a
helper with a row that does, the other shares only the file, and reachability through a helper is
not the property the price is about.

Three wrong out of eleven leaves eight, and the measurement found ten, so the same census missed
two rows as well — and that is the other side of one mistake rather than a second one. A census
that finds the rows reaching a mechanism *through a helper it has identified* is blind to the rows
that reach it inline, which is where both the false positives and the misses come from: by its own
per-file counts (`206a` 2 named, 1 of them red; `211a` 1 named, green) the two it never named are
one row of `206a` and one of `211a`. The census found the population to measure; only the mutant
found the price, and a census figure is not even wrong in one direction.

**The fix moved an anchor nobody was looking at.** `aria-describedby={messageId}` made the
paragraph's attributes wrap onto their own lines, and `118:nobreakwords` had quoted the whole
`<p ...>` tag as a single line, so `anchors.py` answered `0 matches` — the fix adds an attribute,
the class it is about is untouched, and nothing else in the file notices. Re-aimed on the class
attribute alone, which is unique in the file, and preserving the mistake rather than widening it
(#203): `break-words` comes off and nothing else does.

What #204 leaves open is written down in three places rather than in one: the containment half is
#217, `SessionExpiredDialog` is the same shape with one call site in `App.js` and is
outside what #204 asked, and `focus:outline-none` on the box is an appearance claim that no row at
this seam can read — so it is a ☐ on the sheet and a question for a person, not a ⚙.

## #217 — the ten rows a trap was going to cost, and the way in that was left

#217 is the half #204 deferred: a focus trap, or `inert` on the rest of the screen. Its first
closing criterion was not a fix but a sentence — *the owner answers, and the answer is recorded on
the sheet with a date* — and its third option, the trap with the rest of the screen marked, said in
the ticket itself that it could not be chosen without a number that did not exist.

**So both halves were priced before the question was put**, with a probe built where it and `HEAD`
take the same branch, run on both sides and then deleted (#207), and against the whole suite rather
than against one sweep (#67). The trap alone reddens **11 rows** — the ten in five files and `204a`'s
own net — and **nothing else of the 823 rows the suite then held** (824 once row 7 below was
written, which is the denominator the figure was measured against and not a correction of it). The
trap with `inert` and `aria-hidden` reddens **14**, and
the three it adds are a different species: one row of `199a` reads `toBeDisabled()` on ถัดไป, one of
`86a` reads `toBeVisible()` on a row's ระงับ, one of `208a` reads its search box. Their claims stay
true; `getByRole` simply stops seeing what is `aria-hidden`, so they would need **rescoping**, which
is a different repair from a re-aim. The owner took the cheaper half: contain the focus, leave the
rest of the screen in the accessibility tree, and let `aria-modal` go on saying the same thing to
anybody listening.

**The ten rows were not the price of the fix; they were the price of one way in, and another way in
was standing there.** Every one of them needs the same situation — a write out, and the screen moved
on while it is out — and every one of them had arranged it by reaching *through* the cover with the
keyboard, which is the hole the ticket closes. What a person has instead is the box's own ยกเลิก: it
is inside the box where the cover cannot eat the click, it is not disabled while `busy` — the
component's rule is that its two ways out answer alike — and dismissing the question cancels nothing
that has already left the browser. The `DELETE` is still in flight, and its handler still says its
sentence and reads the list again. So the repair was ten one-line re-aims and not ten nets: dismiss
the question, then press the control with an ordinary mouse click, which is the way in needing no
second defect at all.

That is the rule the ticket pays for: **the price of closing a way in is the rows that arrange their
situation through it, and that price is paid in re-aims wherever a person has another way to the same
situation.** A row left as a net is what it costs when they do not (#47's sixth reading, #203's
ninth), and the two are told apart by asking what the person can still do, not by asking what the row
used to press.

**A mistake preserved, not a line found.** Each re-aim keeps the defect exactly as the sheet
describes it (#203): the write is out, the screen is somewhere else, the sentence lands on what the
person moved to. `211a`'s filter went from `focus()` and ArrowDown to `selectOption`, which is what
its own sibling row — the refused `แก้ไข`, with no overlay anywhere near it — had been doing all
along, so the file now says the same thing twice in one voice.

**The dismissal is an instrument, so it is shared and it is built on nothing any row claims.** Five
files need it, and no row's claim lives in getting out of a box, which is what makes it shared rather
than copied (#171). It waits for the box with `panel()` — the class — and not with
`getByRole('dialog')`: the role is a claim of `204a`'s own rows, and a locator five files share
would have turned it into their premise instead (#85, #111). The first draft did use the role, which
would have made `204:norole` redden five files it has nothing to do with.

**And the mutant changed sides.** `trapsfocus` was the deferred proposal made to run (#48), the only
mutant in its file that killed other files' rows, and that was the point of it: while it ran, *we
deferred the containment* was a claim the suite held rather than a sentence on a sheet. The day the
proposal was accepted it became `notrap` — the diagnosed code made to run (#115) — and its kills
moved home: *2 failed, 25 passed* over the six files, the two being `204a`'s own rows 6 and 7. That
the five files are green on **both** sides is the claim the sweep was for; it does not follow from
their passing once (#48 read from the kill-count side).

**`204a` row 6 turned round and brought a seventh with it.** The net became the containment, and it
is two rows because a trap fails two ways and a claim written below another claim is proved by
nothing (#88): the control outside may keep the focus, or it may lose it and still receive the keys.
Row 6 reads the focus after `focus()` — with the control read first, so that it cannot pass on an
empty screen (#164) — and row 7 presses Enter on it and reads the question, behind one round trip so
that the renderer has had its turn (#170). Both were run against the code before the fix and both
were red.

**A spec that gains rows expires the figures of mutants nobody touched** (#202), so the four
