`204` mutants that were not re-aimed were swept again: `norole`, `notmodal`, `noname` and
`nodescription` each still kill their own row, and *1 failed, 5 passed* is now *1 failed, 6 passed* —
the kill count unmoved, the denominator moved. `nofocusonopen` and `noescape` likewise, which also
says the two new rows are outside both mutants' reach: neither the focus moved in on open nor the
Escape handler is what holds the containment up.

**The ticket's second closing criterion was the 22 mutants those five files hold, and re-swept one
at a time they all still kill the rows their records name** — nothing survived, nothing else
reddened. Four readings came out of running them rather than out of the totals. A single-file run's
denominator is not the figure a record published (`211a` alone is 4 of 4 where its sheet says
129/130), so the comparison is *which rows died*, not *how many passed*. A `serial` file's
*ไม่ได้รัน* is a skip and not a survivor (#67). `207:alwaysthelivecount` failing all three `207a`
rows is what its own record predicts, the code being shared (#123, #191). And the one record whose
row name matches no row in its spec — `208:usersstaleloader` — is a **citation** defect and not a
measurement defect: the mutant still kills that spec's second row, which the same sheet says
elsewhere in words, and `anchors.py` cannot ask the question because it reads the `` `file:needle` ``
shape only and an italic name in prose is documented as what it does not look at (#173).

**And the trigger fired undated in 313 lines across 58 files.** Every sheet, spec docblock and page
comment that said *nothing contains the focus* or *Enter from under the cover* was a claim with
today's date on it (#130, #86), and the census found a larger population than either review axis
listed: nine page comments in `frontend/src/pages/`, six spec docblocks, a support helper, two
mutation files and three sheets. They are **dated, not deleted** (#54) — and what dates them is the
sentence beside the one you came for, because the same paragraph usually carries the way in *and*
the expiry condition it was written under.

## #141 (the instrument, again) — the shape #202 wrote and the census stopped seeing

#141's first closing criterion is *measure the list again first*, and since 1 October 2569 the thing
that measures it has been an instrument in the repository rather than a hand census. So the criterion
now has a second half nobody wrote down: **the instrument is a claim too, and the way to ask it is to
run it at the commit the last figure was written at.** Run at HEAD it answered `drawing the answer 60
· guarded 55 · marked 5 · problems 0`; run at `af357d0`, the commit the 8 October record was written
at, it answered `63 · 57 · 6`. Three sites had left the population with `problems 0` on both runs —
**the count is the tell, not the exit code** (#208), and which three is answered by diffing the
*lists*, never by subtracting the totals.

The cause was another ticket's fix spreading. #202 and #203 rewrote ten administration screens into a
shape that builds the sentence first, hands it to the loader, and draws it after — `const said = {…
student.full_name_th}` and then `setNotice(said)` — so the name the setter reads is not the name the
answer was bound to. `drawsTheAnswer` followed one hop, so an **unguarded** site written that way was
not reported as bare: it was not reported at all. That is the one answer a census of this kind must
never give, and it is #208's rule met a second time, from the other side: there an instrument went
blind because the spelling it classified by changed; here because the *distance* between the answer
and the drawing grew by one binding.

**Proved with four snippets through `examine`, then repaired, then broken on purpose.** Following
names to a fixed point over declarators brings the tree to `68 · 63 · 5 · problems 0` — eight sites
nobody had ever seen, all eight guarded, none of them in #141's own nineteen claims (those are
written in the one-hop shape, which is why the blindness never hid one). An instrument is not
believed because its own fixtures pass, so every one of the eight had its file's `.current` reads
replaced and every new site read **BARE** afterwards. The first attempt at that break aimed at the
*spelling* of the comparison and four of the eight files did not move, their guards being written
`showing.current === sent` and `onRows.current.of === readOf(page)` — *a break by spelling is
evidence about the spelling* (#111), one layer along from the grep it was written for.

**And a marker can outlive the gap it documented, which turns it into an exemption.** #202 rewrote
`SubjectStudents.add`'s marker on 11 October to begin `superseded-answer: guarded.` — a marker whose
own first word says it is not needed — and while the site was invisible nothing read it either way.
With the site visible again the guard answers and the marker is never reached; but with the guard
broken the census read `marked` rather than `BARE`, so the marker was standing there waiting for the
day the guard goes. The prefix came out, prose intact and **line-count neutral**, because this ticket
had to revert exactly that kind of rewrite on 5 October when six lines per file aged every citation
below it. *A marker written for an instrument has to be in a syntax the instrument reads* (#93) has a
twin: a marker that says the site is guarded is a claim the guard already makes, and the instrument
reads it only on the day it would do harm.

The three claims the ticket is still open for did not move. `GrantsPanel.load`, `.add` and `.remove`
are reached through a prop, `Users.js` writes `setEditing` to `null` at both of the two sites that
can run while the editor is up, and `users` has no `:id` for an address to carry — so 5 October's
asymmetric way in cannot reach them either. Criterion 3 says no row is ticked from reading code, so
the sentence that closes them is held by `141c`, run again today: **4 passed of 4**, row 4 green.
Criterion 4 keeps the ticket open.

**Then the review asked the question the repair had not: does the following count every identifier
on the right-hand side?** It did, and *a rule that is too loose fails the other way* (#174) had two
shapes here. `const { message } = await send(body)` followed by `const said = { message: 'done' }`
read as **a site with no flag**, because `message` as an object *key* was counted as a read of the
answer; `const { rows } = await listRows(id)` with `const count = other.rows` read the same way off
a member property name. Both are sites where nothing of the answer reaches the screen at all. So
`identifiersIn` now skips non-computed, non-shorthand keys and non-computed property names
(`isAName`; shorthand still taints, key and value being one node) — and the thing that says the
narrowing was not bought with blindness is that the tree reads `68 · 63 · 5 · problems 0`, every
figure unchanged: no real site was being counted through a key or a dot. The loud direction needs no
fixture, so the fixture went on the quiet one, which is the whole of why there are now 91 rows and
not 90.

**And a fix to an instrument ages the sentence that documents its rule.** The header of
`superseded-answers.js` promised, in its numbered contract, exactly the one-hop rule the repair had
just proved wrong, which is *a claim written in prose expires like a number* (#130) with the number
and the prose in the same file — and the dated measurement written into the new docstring published
`63 → 60` as the reading of a tree that reads 68, which is #54's split for a figure three paragraphs
from the code it is about. What the contract owes a later reader is the rule as it now stands, plus
what the following cannot say: it is scope- and order-blind, since the walk is over the whole of
`fn.body`, and it answers *a guard is there* and never *the guard is right* — the sites #207 and
#211 repaired were guarded by this question throughout.

**And then the ticket was closed on a count of the wrong population.** The owner's decision was to
move the remainder to a ticket whose title is true (#220) and close this one, and the comment
announcing it said *thirteen sites got rows*. Measured against the register's own tables it is
**fifteen** — four in `141a` and eleven in `141b` — and what is left is **one** site of the sixteen
carrying **three claims**, sheet `12`'s `load`, `add` and `remove`. The thirteen was real but
belonged to another population: the 5 October table's *another thirteen sites*, meaning the ones
whose **line numbers had not moved** that day. *A census is evidence about the property it counted*
(#174) read on a sentence instead of on a script, and the tell was reading the published text back
rather than the draft — the draft had been proofread for Thai and for codepoints, which is a
different question from whether its arithmetic is about the thing it names. Both the comment and
the new ticket were corrected in place, and the register now says which population each count is
of, because the two numbers go on living side by side in one sheet.

## #218 — the waiter that took delivery of a sibling's answer, and the route the ticket named

The red row of the 18 October full suite was `141a`'s *evidence the back button has left behind*, and
#218 wrote down a mechanism for it: `waitForActivities` filters answers with `API`, which is a
**prefix**, so the `/evidence` answer passes it and `untilActivitiesDrawn` reads `activities.length`
off a body that has no `activities`. The shape of that diagnosis is right and **the route it names is
not** — that row awaits the evidence answer *by identity* on the line before `upToParent`, so the
answer nobody is waiting for is `GET /activities/:activityId`, which has exactly one caller in the
application: `DEEPER_NAMES.activity` in `Mainpage.js`, resolving the breadcrumb, with
`{ activity: … }` for a body. The
ticket's own first criterion says that if the mechanism does not match the diagnosis the ticket closes
with a different fix and not by anchoring the regex; the mechanism matched the *species* and the fix
is the anchor, so what the criterion bought was the measurement, which named a different route and a
different screen's read.

Its other half had aged. The criterion exists because the failure text was believed lost to an
overwritten `test-results/`; the 18 October handoff had recorded it all along —
`TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length')` at
`untilActivitiesDrawn`'s first clause —
which is *a ticket's What is wrong is a claim from the day it was written* met on the evidence rather
than on the defect.

**The window had to be opened by hand, because nothing green says it is shut.** The full suite of
19 October was 824 passed, 0 red, this row among them, and running the first eighteen files in suite
order (161 passed, 11.3 minutes) was green too — with a probe inside the waiter reporting that it had
been pending three times and that what arrived in the window was the list on all three. So the window
is real and that day nobody walked into it. #207's instrument then opened it on purpose: hold the
breadcrumb's answer until the row releases it, and let the list's answer arrive behind it. Unfixed,
red at `untilActivitiesDrawn`'s first clause with the full suite's own message; fixed, green.
Built where the two
codes agree, run on both sides, deleted.

**A matcher two questions share cannot be narrowed for one of them.** The obvious fix is to anchor
`API`, and `API` is handed to `gate`, `waitForReload` and `page.route` by `CARD_SCREENS` in five spec
files whose question is *any request this screen makes* — writes among them. So the repair is a
**second** matcher beside the first, `isActivitiesList`, and the loose one keeps its callers plus a
reason with a date on it (#131): of the routes under the prefix, one POST and one PUT are reachable
from the screens those write waiters run on, measured 19 October against `backend/routes/`.

**Then the same shape elsewhere, counted by the mechanism and not by the name** (#174). The
population is *one waiter and one method: how many routes the server really mounts can satisfy it* —
161 routes against the 76 `waitForResponse` calls in `e2e/support`, 31 of them reads. It found
`clos-screen.js` accepting four GET routes with the identical defect, **never reported by anybody**,
and `program-subjects-screen.js`'s `openEditor` accepting four, on a screen that asks the catalogue
route as the form is typed into — so a search's answer can be handed to the editor's read. `weights`
had been repaired before this ticket with `endsWith('/weights')`, which is correct and unreadable to
an instrument, and became `isWeightsList` for that reason alone: *a reader that knows one spelling is
the reader that stops seeing its population* (#141).

Which it duly was, about itself. The first version recognised an inline regex by a leading `/^` and
so reported `evidence-screen.js` as something it could not resolve; walking back from `.test(` to the
opening slash sees a tail anchor as well. The census gives **three answers and not two** (#159) —
counted, exact by construction (`pathname ===` cannot accept two routes), and *could not ask* — and
the third is asserted by name and by count, because an instrument that quietly skips what it cannot
read is the one that prints `problems 0` over the sites it has stopped seeing (#208, #123). Then
**break a real site before believing it** (#124): the `$` came off `isActivitiesList` and four of the
six rows went red with the census printing all five routes; `plan-screen.js`'s waiter was made
unreadable and the census went red naming that file. Both restored from a copy — never with
`git checkout --` — and 48 of 48 again.

It lives at the third seam, `e2e/support/*.test.js` under `npm run test:support`, 42 rows to 48,
which is where it belongs twice over: these are claims about an instrument and not about the product,
so no sheet row rests on them, and at the browser seam the window has to be opened by hand to be seen
at all. What it cannot say is written beside it: it reads only `e2e/support` and not waiters written
inside a spec, it answers about **routes** and never about whether a waiter is fenced by `openAt`
(#160), which is the other half of this mechanism, and it compares against paths `router.<method>`
writes as plain strings, so a path assembled from a variable is invisible to it.

**Then the review read the record back, and three of its four findings were about the record rather
than the code.** The section that closes by saying a citation goes by file name *because a citation
by line number ages the day anything above it grows* had cited `activities-screen.js:69` three times
— and that citation was **already stale inside its own diff**, the thirty lines of new docstring
above the assertion having moved it to :99 before anything shipped. #173 is not a rule about other
people's sheets: it is about the paragraph you are writing, which is the one place a line number
looks safe because you have just read it. All of them now name a string that can be found —
`untilActivitiesDrawn`'s first clause, `DEEPER_NAMES.activity` in `Mainpage.js`, `32a`'s way in
through the menu — and the fifth caller the survey had enumerated short, `saveActivity`'s reload,
went in beside `removeActivity`'s. (The review also said `Mainpage.js:130` was off by one; read, it
was right, which is the one finding a round that is wrong — *verify before acting* — and the
citation went by name anyway.)

**And one finding was about the instrument going deaf in exactly the files it names.** The *could not
ask* group was a `Set` of **file names**, asserted against three of them, so a second unresolvable
waiter added to any of those three left the set identical, the two other counts untouched and the
gate green — the comment promising *named so that a new one is a red and not a silence* failing on
precisely the three modules most likely to grow one. It is now a count per file, and the proof is the
third break: a second unreadable waiter in `plos-screen.js` reds the row at `{"plos-screen.js":2}`.
The same reading turned the other two floors into equalities, because `counted >= 9` cannot see a
waiter that has slid from *counted* into *exact* — *a floor hides what has moved*, and the printed
groups are what the next person reads, never the total (#208).

## #210 — the blocker that was supposed to close the way in, and the fork that had already gone

#210 asks whether the six other administration screens have the two windows #199 measured, and
offers three options. Two of them are claims about **today**, and both were wrong by the time the
ticket was taken.

**Option 2 — *let #204 answer: if focus is trapped the keyboard cannot reach the pager and the way in
disappears on all six screens* — is refuted by the fix it was waiting for.** #217 landed the trap on
18 October; measured on 19 October, the pager is still live under the cover. The reason is in the
same dialog: ยกเลิก is not disabled while `busy`, so pressing it puts the question away while the
`DELETE` it confirmed is still in flight, and the pager is then an ordinary mouse press away — no
keyboard in the way in at all. This is #217's own lesson read from the other side: the price of
closing a way in is paid only where the person has no second way to the same situation, and here
they have one. It is also #141 and #179 again — **a blocker's expiry condition names the way in its
author had in mind**, and #210's blocker named the keyboard.

**Option 1's price is a claim about today too, and the seed answers it.** #57's end rule disables
both buttons on a one-page list, so the window needs a second page before anything can be pressed.
Of the six screens, exactly one — `Rubrics`, at 11 rows — has one in today's seed; the other five
read *หน้า 1 จาก 1*. So *send `busy` to all six* changes the behaviour of one screen today and is a
guard against growth on the other five, which is a different sentence from the one the ticket priced.

**And the defect the ticket inherited is not a fork any more.** #199 was a #52 — one person, one
action, and whether they hear the sentence decided by which invisible window the press landed in.
Measured across five orderings (press while the `DELETE` is out, press while the reload is out, the
step-back branch that hands the sentence on by key, and an unpressed twin on each screen), the sentence was
**said every time**, because #205 keyed it to the read that draws what it is about and #206 and #207
made the step-back read the page the command was sent from. What is left is one behaviour rather than
two: the sentence is drawn over the list of the page the person moved to, which the removal is not
about. `showing` holds *what is open on this screen* — a form or editor token — and not the list's
coordinate, so moving a page does not write it and #202's guard has nothing to compare; that is #205's
*two guards that both ask is this still current can be asking about different things*. Whether that
wording is wrong is `docs/06` §Out of Scope, so the ticket's question changed shape: not *which of
three fixes* but *is a sentence over the wrong list acceptable*, with the fork it was filed about gone.

**The rows wait on the answer, because option 1 is what deletes them.** A row that holds *the
sentence is said over the page the person moved to* arranges its situation by pressing the pager under
the cover, which is exactly the press option 1 makes impossible; written now, each would be rewritten
the day the owner says yes as a row that reads *the button is disabled*. What does **not** depend on
the answer — the way in is still open after #217 — `207a` already holds as a row, and is cited rather
than written twice (#171). The measurement itself was a probe, built on both sides, run, and deleted
(#207).

### What option 1 cost, once the owner answered

The owner's answer on 19 October was **option 1**, and the fix is one line at six call sites:
every one of the six screens already computes `const busy = writing || reading` for its own
form, so `busy={busy}` on the `<Pager>` is all of it. The whole of the ticket's cost is
somewhere else.

**The price of closing a way in is paid in mutants as well as in rows.** #217 priced a trap at
ten rows in five files and paid ten one-line re-aims, because the person had a second way to the
same situation. Here the census by mechanism — *rows that press the pager on one of the six
screens*, not *rows that mention the pager* — found four spec files, and three of them re-aimed
the same way: `206a` rows 1 and 3, `208a` row 1 and `140a`'s Offerings row all arrange their
situation through *something that re-reads the list while a write is out*, and the import panel
still does that (it keeps its own flag). What it does differently is ask for **page one**, which
is a move; and for three of those four rows a move is as good as a press. `140a`'s row was using
the pager as an instrument rather than as a claim, so it moved to the year filter instead.

The fourth file had nowhere to go. `207a`'s three rows need a read that lands while the removal
is out **and leaves the pager where it started**, and after option 1 the only control that reads
the list at all moves the person. So the three rows became one net asserting the mechanism (#203,
#47) — and **the four mutants whose only killers those rows were came out with them**. Nothing
reports that. `anchors.py` says the anchors are exact, because they are; the code the mutants
edit is untouched; the difference is in another file entirely. Only re-running them says it
(#107, #68), which is what the re-sweep did: `closurerowcount`, `trustthestalecount`,
`refalwaysone` and `alwaysthelivecount` survived all fifteen rows between them, and
`refnevermoves` kept two killers and stayed.

**The fourth of those four is the tenth reading of a survivor, met in the clearest shape yet.**
`alwaysthelivecount` was written against `206a`'s first row, not against `207a`, so the first
pass of this work listed it as staying — its killer was not one of the three rows being
withdrawn. The re-sweep an hour later found it surviving that row too, and the mechanism is
#206's own: the remaining way in is the import panel, whose read the row **holds at the route**,
so `data.departments.length` in the closure and `onRows.current.rows` in the ref are reading the
same drawn list and are the same number. A mutant that swaps one for the other is invisible
wherever the two agree, and closing the pager is what made them agree. The sheet's prediction
written before the sweep is what caught it (#201): the row it named did not go red.

### Two figures in a record I wrote the same hour

The withdrawal said the four were measured *16 rows each*. The files it names add up to
3 + 1 + 9 + 2 = 15, and the sweep's own output directory had no `208a` run for
`alwaysthelivecount` at all — so one of the four had thirteen. Both are species this file keeps
writing down (#119's hand-kept number, #173's figure published by a second counter instead of by
the instrument), and what is worth adding is where the answer was: **the directory of sweep
output is the record of which runs exist**, and it was sitting there while the sentence was
written from memory. The missing run was taken before the correction — the mutant put back into
`MUTANTS` for one run and taken out again, with `git diff` to say the file came back — and it
survived there too, so the corrected figure is 15 of 15 and measured rather than inferred. Then
the figure had a third copy, in the catalogue row written the same hour, which only grepping the
number found (#96, #130, #154).

### And the spec's own filename made a closed sheet's citations ambiguous

`210a-the-pager-while-a-write-is-out-on-the-administration-screens.spec.js` holds the string
`10a`. `anchors.py` resolves a citation's token as a **substring**, because that is what
Playwright's own file argument does (#154, #158), so the hour the file landed, sheet 10's sixteen
citations named two files and the instrument said so — thirteen of them, the other three being
inside code fences, which it counts and does not read. The repair is the spelling
`21-rubrics.md` has used since `121a` collided with `21a`: the whole stem, `10a-shell.spec.js:`.
Worth writing down only as the shape — **a new spec file is a change to every sheet whose
citation token is a substring of its name**, and the ticket number is where the collision comes
from, so it is predictable the moment the file is named.

And it reaches further than the citations: `mutation/README.md` carries a measured **37 tokens the
two resolution rules answer differently**, and `10a` joined that set the hour this file landed,
having matched one file under both rules before. So a figure in a document nobody was editing went
stale — #48's rule (*a kill count is a claim about the fixtures as much as about the code*) with
a filename in place of a fixture. What is interesting is what it costs to put right: the figure is
**dated and not corrected**, because a hand count of one definition of that population — the short
token of each of the 107 spec files — gives 24 at this commit, so 37 counts something else, and
nothing prints it. #141 says to run the instrument at the commit the figure was written at; where
there is no instrument, the honest repair is a note saying which way the number moved and that the
**population** is the thing missing, rather than a new number with the same problem.

### A row that goes red before the fix can still hold an assertion that cannot fail

Each of `210a`'s four rows read two buttons: `ถัดไป` disabled while the removal was out, and
`ก่อนหน้า` disabled beside it. Every row went red against the unfixed screens, which is the
check #203 bought for free and the thing a new row is supposed to be measured by — and it
licensed nothing about the second line. The rows stand on **page one**, because what the fixture
builds is a second page rather than a move onto a middle one, and `Pager` writes
`disabled={busy || page <= 1}`: at page one `ก่อนหน้า` is disabled by #57's end rule whatever the
flag says. The red came from the line above it every time.

This is #88's rule met on a clean run instead of under a mutant — *a claim written below another
claim is proved by nothing* — and the reading that generalises is that **a row is red or green,
while an assertion is proved or not**: the row's verdict is the verdict of its first failing
line, and nothing about the rest. What found it was the Standards and Spec axes reading the two
reads against `Pager`'s own expressions, which is the same question #171 asks about a locator
asked about an end rule. The half that was really at risk stayed, the other came out, and the
sheet says where the component's `ก่อนหน้า` half is held instead: `199a` reads it on page two
with the premise read above it, and `207a`'s net reads it on the **last** page of the department
screen, where the two halves swap roles — there `ถัดไป` is the end rule and `ก่อนหน้า` is the
claim. Three files, each proving the half its own page can put at risk.


## #209 — the expiry condition that was refuted by the species, not by the way in

#209 wrote its own expiry condition the way #81 asks: *if #199 and #204 close the way in, this ticket
cannot be reached either.* Both landed — #217 trapped the dialog on 18 October, #210 sent `busy` to
all six administration pagers on 19 October — and #210's own lesson says a blocker landing is not the
way in closing, so the first move was to measure rather than to read the paragraph. The paragraph was
right about the way in. The ticket was still reachable.

**A probe reached the defect with no race at all.** No pager, no cover, no held answer, no key
mismatch: a second actor writing the page the person is looking at, on the browser's own cookie,
**before** they press ยืนยัน. Two readings on `Departments`. A last page drawn with two rows, one of
them removed by the other actor, then the person removes the other: the screen stays on a page that
no longer exists and draws *หน้า 3 จาก 2* over *ยังไม่มีภาควิชาในระบบ*. A last page drawn with one
row, another row added to it by the other actor, then the person removes the drawn one: the screen
steps back off a page that still has a row on it, which is #206's worse answer. This is #179 one
layer out — **a ticket that names a race has named a window, not the population of ways in** — but
told about an *expiry condition* rather than about a diagnosis: the condition dates the way in its
author had in mind, and the symptom's species can outlive it. A reload does not clear this one, so it
is the version a person meets.

**And the mechanism is new. In both readings the key matched.** `onRows.current.of === readOf(page)`
held, so the handler read the live count and the live count was still wrong — because
***live* means the count of the list that is drawn, not the count of the page.** Every rule this
repo has written about that ref is about *which page the value is of* (#201, #185, #207); none of
them says the value can be of the right page and false, which is what a second writer makes it. A
key that matches says the reading is of the right question, not that it is still the answer.

**The fourth option was invisible until the handler's branches were counted.** The ticket priced its
alternative — *re-read the page they are on and let the server say how many pages there are* — as an
extra read, and priced the cheaper shape — *let the `DELETE` answer carry the remaining count* — as a
change to seven routes' contracts. Both prices are of a shape nobody checked (#77). Every branch of
the handler already re-reads the page the person is on, and that answer already carries `total`:
reading 1 is the proof, the screen holding `total 20` in hand while drawing *หน้า 3 จาก 2*. So the
server already says how many pages there are, and the option the ticket called an extra request adds
none in the common case. The other option reads cheaper than it is, and the branch is where the
difference lives: `rubrics` answers 200 with a body every time, and `programs`, `subjects` and
`program-subjects` answer 200 with `deactivated: true` — but only on the branch that switches a row

**The census that priced the rest was blind twice, a layer apart.** Asking for a `204` within six
lines of the deleted path answered 0 for six of the seven families: the backend tests spell the path

**The four mutants #210 withdrew stayed withdrawn, and for a different reason than the one written

**What the phase delivers is a question, not a fix.** Item 2 of the ticket is the owner's

**And the measurement found a symptom beside its own, which is a debt until it is filed.** The pager

### Phase B — the owner answered ก, and four mutants took four tries to be worth anything

The answer moved the decision off the client entirely: `load` reads the page the person is on, takes
`total` out of the answer, and hands the page on when the answer says the page it just asked for is
past the end. `onRows` and both of its readings are gone from all seven paged screens; `onPage`
stays, because a sentence still has to be keyed for wherever the person now is. The hand-on draws
nothing (drawing an empty page would paint it, and the sentence over it, for a frame before the
correction lands), returns a third answer rather than `true` or `false` (#159), and re-keys the
waiting sentence for the read it hands to — which is what the `finally`'s new `if (!handedOn)` is
for. Nothing in a handler decides anything about the page any more.

**A fixture whose candidate values collapse makes a faithful mutant invisible, and that is #206's
tenth reading of a survivor met *before* the sweep rather than in it.** The first draft of the
landing row stood the person on page 3 and left page 1 as the last page that still existed — so of
the three answers a reader of this code might give (*the last page the server names*, *one page
back*, *page one*), two were the same number, and a mutant swapping one for another would have
passed. The rebuilt fixture is four pages and nineteen rows left: the person is on 4, the answer is
2, one page back is 3. The cost of noticing it late would have been a survivor to explain; the cost
of noticing it early was ten lines of fixture.

**A settle point is chosen by how the row will fail.** Row 2 — *a page that filled up again moves
nobody* — first used `untilDrawn`, which waits for the pager to read out what *this* answer carried.
That is the right settle point on a screen that behaves, and a timeout on every screen that does
not: every way of getting this wrong **moves** the person, so the drawing the helper waits for never
happens at all, and the row dies at a timeout, which is what a mutant that stopped the application
prints too (#139). Polling the pager's own line fails instead with the page and the total the screen
is showing. The rule is #139 read one step earlier: not *is this assertion a wait* but *is the thing
I am waiting for the thing the defect removes*.

**The obvious other side of a comparison was a mutant that killed too much — and the boundary it was
wrong at was the one every fixture stands on.** `>` to `>=` reads as *hand on even when the page
asked for is exactly the last one*, and it killed all three rows at a `toContainText` inside a
fixture helper, which is a line no row of the sheet ever wrote: under it no screen can land on its
own last page, and landing on the last page is how every row here builds its situation. #97's
reading, with a place to look added — when a guard's boundary is *the last page*, *the first page*
or *the only page*, the fixtures are standing on it.

**Then the narrowed mutant measured the closure instead of the claim.** The choice the ticket took
away is the count of the list drawn, so the replacement grafted that count back on to the new
decision — written inside `load`, where it survived all three rows. `data` is not in that
`useCallback`'s dependency list: it closes over the render where the page changed, and that render's

code under test. The site is decided by where the code being reproduced did its deciding (#193), and
that is the handler — drawn in JSX, closing over the render it was drawn in (#208), where the count
really is live. There it kills row 2 alone, **with the same values row 2 showed against `HEAD`**:
carried to page 2 of 3 while the page held twenty-two rows.

**A fix that deletes a reading deletes the mutants that could have expressed it.** The old rule
cannot be restored anywhere but the handler, because the ref it read no longer exists and no single
edit can declare a ref and its three writers. That is the same shape as #210's four withdrawals read
from the other end: there a closed way in left mutants with nothing to kill, here a deleted reading
leaves a defect with nothing to write it with.

**And two small ones, both found by instruments rather than by reading.** A `|` inside a code span
still ends a table cell, so `answer.per_page || PAGE_SIZE` in a catalogue row made it *5 cells in a
3-column table* — the same family as #79's stray pipe, caught by `anchors.py` this time instead of
by a renderer. And row 1's first green run was a red: nineteen rows make page two hold **nine**, not

### Phase B's sweep — a retrying wait can move a press instead of failing, and twelve mutants went quiet

The fix re-aimed 41 mutants in 11 files, so they were swept one at a time, read against the row each
was written for (#152, #203). Thirty-nine still kill at their own rows. The two that stopped are the
two lessons, and neither of them is about this fix's code.

**Twelve of #140's thirteen survived 32 of 32, and the debt is #210's.** `140a`'s rows hold back a
read of page one, press a handler, then press ถัดไป to supersede that read; the mutant lets the
superseded read draw. #210 — landed the same morning — gave the six administration pagers
`disabled={busy}`, and `busy` is up for the whole window those rows hold the read in, because the
handler awaits the reload inside its own `writing`. `supersede` presses the control after
`await expect(next(page)).toBeEnabled()`, which is a **retrying wait and not an assertion**: it does
not fail, it postpones the press until after the held answer has landed and drawn. The race the rows
were built on stops happening, and they pass with the mutant applied exactly as they pass without
it — green for the wrong reason (#171), which is why no instrument said anything: the anchors are
exact, the code is untouched, nothing is red. The confirmation is which mutant still kills:
`offeringssavestalewins`, whose row is the one #210 gave a busy-free superseding control. **#210's
census asked which rows have `busy` up at the moment the superseding control is pressed and answered
one; the question that decides is which rows *wait* for that control**, because a retrying wait moves
the press rather than failing the row. The repair belongs to the rows, not to the mutants, which
still reproduce a real defect — so it is a ticket, and the twelve stay where they are meanwhile.

**And a guard a key already covers one layer along cannot be put at risk where it stands.**
`202:enrolmentremovesaysanyway` removed the `onScreen.current === sent` half of the enrolment
removal's own sentence, which before #209 was said by the handler. Since #209 the handler says
nothing: it hands the sentence over keyed on `readOf(sectionId, onPage.current)`, and the read that
draws says it only when the key matches — so after a jump to another Section the key refuses it
whatever that half does, and the mutant survived 10 of 10. The mistake is still writable, one layer
along at the key comparison, which is where `205:saysanyread` lives: measured, it kills both of
`202a`'s negatives, so the negative row keeps its ⚙ with a new citation. The **positive** row had
been propped up by the withdrawn mutant and by nothing else (`205:clearsoutside` survives that file),
which is the shape of a mark that outlives its proof — so it got a mutant of its own the same day,
keyed for a page nobody will read, #206's mistake written at this site. A withdrawal is only
finished when every row that cited it has been read again.

### The clean suite's one red, and a kill count that was right for the wrong reason

The full browser suite, run once at the end as the ticket asks, came back **828 passed, 1
failed, 45.4 minutes**. The red was `152a`'s page-2 row, which asserts that the read a refused
removal makes asks for `page=1` — and it got `2`. That is the correct answer under the owner's
option ก: the removal no longer decides anything about the page, it re-reads the page the person
is standing on, and `load` hands them on only when the answer says that page has gone. The row
had been asserting the mechanism the ticket moved to the server, with a comment beside it saying
exactly that (*"which is what says the handler took the moving branch"*), so the re-aim was to
the new page number, with the row's own #152 claim — no frame says it removed, one refusal at the
end — untouched.

What makes it worth a story is **where the evidence had already been printed.** The re-aim sweep
of the day before ran 41 mutants and recorded `152:enrolmentremovalanyway` as *kills 2, passes
19*. Its two reds were its own intended row and this one, which was red at `HEAD` whatever the
mutant did. The count was right; one half of it was not a kill. The sweep's own output named both
rows, and what I read was the number — #52's *read the names beside the count* met from the other
side, where the count looks like the sheet rather than like a leak. And no instrument could have
said so: the anchors were exact, the mutated code untouched, and a sweep cannot see the row your
own fix breaks (#83, #96, #107) — only the clean suite can, which is why the ticket's closing
criteria run it. Re-measured after the re-aim, the figure is *kills 2, passes 19* again, and this
time both reds are the mutant's; `152:enrolmentmovedremovalanyway` is *kills 1, passes 20* at the
same assertion, as its record said.

So a sweep's **kill** has a twelfth reading, beside #49's flaky bystander: a red that is a row
your own change broke. It looks like every other red, it inflates the count by one, and the
mutant's coverage of that row stays unmeasured until the row is fixed and the mutant run again.

## #223 — the twelve rows that were nineteen, and the two with nowhere left to press

#223 was written by #209's own closing sweep: thirteen mutants of
`mutation/140-superseded-handler-reload.py` re-aimed, twelve of them surviving `140a` 32 of 32,
and the mechanism already diagnosed in that record — #210 had given six administration pagers
`disabled={busy}` the same morning, `busy` is held from a save, a removal or a refused read until
the reload it awaits answers, and `140a`'s `supersede` presses ถัดไป behind
`await expect(next(page)).toBeEnabled()`. A retrying wait is not an assertion: it moved the press
to after the held answer had been drawn, so the race the row exists to build never happened and
the row passed with the mutant applied and without it (#209's rule, met here as the thing to
repair).

So the diagnosis was right, and every number attached to it was a number about **thirteen
mutants**.

**A ticket written from another ticket's closing sweep inherits that sweep's population.** #209
swept the mutants its own fix had re-aimed, which is the right scope for #209 and not a statement
about the file. The file holds thirty-one. Re-swept whole, before anything was changed:
**fifteen** survived, not twelve; five of the rest belong to screens #210 never touched (`users`
×3, `students` ×2 — the live pagers, which is #221's question); and **eleven were still killing**,
through three different ways in that the ticket's one sentence had no room for — the four MASTER
screens' import rows and `enrolmentreloadstalewins` because `ImportPanel` keeps its own flag, the
four refusal mutants because `144a`'s filter rows press the same handlers (a file #209's one-file
sweep never ran), `offeringssavestalewins` because #210 had already moved that row to the
ปีการศึกษา box, and `offeringsbackstalewins` because `onBack` lets `busy` down before it reloads.
The ticket's option 2 — *withdraw the mutants of the rows that cannot be re-aimed* — was therefore
answered **no** with a number: every one of the thirty-one claims still had a live way in
somewhere.

**What makes a re-aim possible is written in the flag's own comment, not in the JSX.** The
sentence over `writing` in `Departments.js` says `ImportPanel` holds its own flag and touches
neither half of `busy`. That one line is what turned twelve impossible rows into twelve
one-import-line rows: the row walks onto page two first, holds page two's reads, presses the
handler, and then imports a single line — `onImported` calls `setPage(1)` when the screen is not
on page one, which builds a new `load` exactly as the pager did (#83 again; #140's own rule that a
control is a way in only if it feeds what the request asks for). The four screens with no import
panel took the other two shapes: `Rubrics` and `Offerings` supersede with a filter that is a
dependency of `load` and is not disabled, and `SubjectStudents`, which has neither, supersedes
with #141b's **section jump** — `load` is keyed on `sectionId` as well as `page`, so one move of
the history list to another Section of the same route shape replaces the loader without replacing
the document.

**The repair was nineteen rows and two nets, not twelve rows.** Twelve through the import panel,
four through a filter, two through the jump — and a nineteenth nobody had counted: `Offerings`'
*เปิดรายวิชา* row, which #210 moved to the year box in code on 19 October and left described on
its sheet as pressing ถัดไป. A re-aim that does not reach the sheet leaves the sheet telling a
later reader to press a control the row has not pressed for a day (#130, one layer along: the
prose expires like the number, and this one expired inside the diff that caused it).

**Two rows had nowhere left to press, and their mutants did not go with them.** The refused
*แก้ไข* of `Rubrics` and the refused *ตอนเรียนและผู้สอน* of `Offerings` reach the same situation
only through the pager: the screens have no import panel, and their filters are the way in of a
*different* claim, which `144a` already holds in rows of its own. Both became nets that read the
**mechanism** — ถัดไป is disabled for the whole window — with the condition that would make the
claim measurable again written in the ☐ beside it (#47, #203, #141). But #210's rule that *a row
left as a net takes its mutants with it* does not hold here: `rubricsrefusalstalewins` still kills
one row of `144a` and `offeringsrefusalstalewins` still kills three, so neither is withdrawn. The
net and the mutant part company exactly when a second file's rows press the same handler — which
is also why reading the re-sweep against the total would have said nothing: both mutants kill the
same number of rows as before, and the row that stopped being proved is in another file.

**The re-sweep, 20 October 2569.** All thirty-one, one at a time, code restored between, each
against its own screen's rows in `140a` and `144a` — 19.5 minutes, every one red at the row it was
written for, bar the two refusal mutants whose rows are now nets and which died at their filter
rows instead. The clean `140a` was **32 of 32** (2.8 minutes) before any of it, which is what says
the nineteen re-aimed rows and the two nets pass on good code; the sweep is what says they fail on
broken code. Neither question is answered by the other (#107, #68).

One instrument finding on the way in: the first reading of the stage-2 log counted every
`[chromium] › …` line as a failure, because the `line` reporter prints one per row, pass or fail.
The counts came from the reporter's own `N passed` / `N failed` summary after that — a count read
off the wrong lines is #187's shape, met in my own driver rather than in a ticket.

**What the two review axes found after it was committed.** Four things, and three of them are
rules this file already carries, met somewhere new.

The spec file's own docstring partitioned its rows as eighteen re-aimed, two nets and eleven still

The ticket's third question — *does any other caller defer a press the same way* — was asked

Of the nine sheets, the dated 18 ก.ย. records on **two** describe their mutant as killing *its own

And the retrying wait is **still in `supersede`** for the eleven rows whose screens leave the

## #225 — the wait that came out, and the five rows that were three

#223 left the retrying wait in `supersede` for the eleven rows whose screens still leave the
pager live, wrote the prediction into the docstring, dated it, and filed the deferral as a ticket
because a deferral in prose is a decision nobody can find. The fix is one shape in three places:
read `isDisabled()` once and assert it, instead of `await expect(...).toBeEnabled()`.

**The census I published was evidence about the control, not about the species.** #223's third
question had been counted by the **pager**: four press sites in the suite, only `supersede`'s
behind a retrying wait, so *empty*. Counted by the **mechanism** — a retrying enable-wait in front
of a press that has to land inside the held window — it is **three**, and all three are in the
same file: `supersede`'s default press and the two **filter** presses, which `moveTo.press` runs
after `reloadSent` exactly as it runs the pager's. The day a filter is given `disabled={busy}`,
which is what #210 did to the pagers, five rows would defer their press and pass in silence. That
is #174 met in my own instrument, one layer up from where it was written: the population was not
*presses of a pager*, it was *presses inside a held window*. The nine other files that write
`toBeEnabled` hold none of the species — their waits are claims that a control comes **back** when
the answer lands, where retrying is the whole point, or premises read with nothing out, where a
dead control hangs and the row dies red at the timeout rather than passing. `ontoPageTwo` and
`pagerIsDeadWhileTheReloadIsOut`'s own premise are that second kind and keep their waits, which is
the same reading as #50/#214's *who else removes this*: ask what the wait can be satisfied by.

**And the ticket's number for what the fix buys was wrong, measured.** #225 said five rows: three
on ข้อมูลผู้ใช้งาน and two on ข้อมูลนักศึกษา, the two screens whose `<Pager>` is handed no `busy`
although the screen holds one (#221's question). The measurement is four cells — two mutants that
are #221's proposal **made to run** (#48), each with the wait in and with it out:

| | with the wait in | with the read in |
|---|---|---|
| `140:usersbusypager` (three rows) | 3 passed | **2 red**, 1 passed |
| `140:studentsbusypager` (two rows) | 2 passed | **1 red**, 1 passed |

Five of five pass blind with the wait in, which is the defect, and **three** go red with it out.
The two that still pass are the **import** rows: `ImportPanel` keeps its own flag and never raises
the screen's, so a `<Pager>` handed a `busy` the import does not put up is live through the import
anyway — the same three-ways-in reading that gave #223 eleven survivors instead of one, met from
the other side. So the eleven rows that press ถัดไป are three that #221 would blind, seven imports
that no mutant here can blind at all, and `onBack`, which lets `busy` down before it reloads.

The wrong five had been published in four places by then: both docstring paragraphs, the mutation
file's own block, the ticket body and a comment on #221 pointing the number at the owner. The two
docstrings and the mutation block are corrected; the **ticket body is left standing**, being a
record of what was claimed on the day it was written (#54), and #221 gets a second comment rather
than an edited one, for the same reason. What a ticket's closing comment is for is the refutation.

**The re-sweep, 20 October 2569.** Eighteen mutants, one at a time, code restored between, each
against its own screen's rows in `140a`: the eleven that still killed after #210, #225's own two,
and the five whose rows press a **filter**, because a change to how a row presses is a change to
what the row measures (#107, #68) and those five presses changed too. Every one red at the row it
was written for; `140a` with the read in and no mutant applied was **32 of 32**
on 20 October 2569 (2.7 minutes), run before the sweep - a different measurement
from #223's baseline of the same shape the day before, and the one #225's closing
condition asks for. `enrolmentreloadstalewins` kills
**two** rows, เพิ่มนักศึกษา and การนำเข้า, and that is right rather than a bystander: the file's own
docstring says those two call one guard, so one mutant is two reachability claims and not one claim
counted twice (#191). What was wrong there was the *written for* label in my sweep driver, which
named one of the two — a driver's own table is a hand-kept figure like any other (#119).

## #143 — three ways in that all reproduced, and a fix with nothing to guard

#139 decided on 1 October 2026 that a section write's banner is **not** guarded against the person
moving: the sentence is about a write they ordered and not about the panel they are now looking at.
#143 asked the half #139 left — whether a sentence that lands over *another Offering's* panel is
readable at all — and wrote its own sequence down as *read from the code, not measured*.

**Measured first, the ticket's diagnosis was right: all three ways in reproduce.** A probe on the
browser seam, 21 October 2569, before any row was written — an accepted เพิ่มตอนเรียน, a refused
one and a ลบตอนเรียน, each said over the seeded Offering's panel while the work was on this file's
own subject. That is worth writing down because the index's long list under *a ticket's diagnosis*
is twelve ways one was **wrong**; here it was right, and the measurement still changed the ticket,
because what it bought was three things the ticket did not know.

**The first: a way in can need another ticket's escape hatch pressed before it is a way in at
all.** Since #217 the confirmation box traps focus and covers the screen until the write answers,
so กลับไปหน้ารายการ is under the cover. The probe's first version simply clicked it — and
Playwright waited for the cover to lift, which *is* the answer landing, and `onBack`'s
`setNotice(null)` then wiped the sentence. It read as *the removal is already silent*, which would
have closed a third of the ticket as not-a-defect. The press that makes it a way in is ยกเลิก,
which puts the box away while the write it confirmed is still in flight: #217's own rule — *ask
what they can still do before writing those rows off* — met from the measuring side rather than
the pricing side. A probe that waits for a cover to lift is timing the cover.

**The second: the guard that is there answers a different question, and the census cannot see it.**
`confirmRemoval`'s sentence sits behind `showing.current === sent`, which #146 documented as *the
last thing that opened on this screen* — it says whether anything has opened since, never which
panel. `sentences-after-a-move.js` reads the site as `enclosed (ref)` and reports green, because
the instrument finds a guard **by the ref** and does not ask what that ref can tell apart. That is
#208's species exactly, one file along — not *the instrument cannot find it* but *it found it and
counted it as enough* — and it is filed as [#226](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/226) rather than fixed, the owner's answer
having made the sentence readable wherever it lands. In the tracker and not in prose, because a
deferral nobody can find is a decision nobody can find (#119, #89, #125), with the condition that
would make it a real defect written on it: a reversal of #139/#143's decision, after which
`showing` could not guard the sentence and the census would still be green.

**The third: one of the ticket's three options was already the repository's convention, which
turns another into #152's question.** `ActivityScores.js` has named the activity its sentence is
about since 12 October 2569. So *keep it as it is* did not mean *change nothing*; it meant **keep
two behaviours, three sentences to one**, and the owner's question was which behaviour the system
should have. #152's rule is written about a ticket's *as today* option being a claim that today is
one thing, on one screen's nine-to-ten split; this is the same reading across screens, and the
cheapest way to find it is to grep the sibling sentences before writing the owner's options down.

### A sentence that cannot be read is not a sentence that is wrong

The owner chose the third option, and the fix is then **wording with nothing to guard**. `onSection`
is re-created every render, so the `viewing` one invocation closed over is the panel the press was
made on for as long as it runs, however far the person has moved — the sentence was about the right
Offering all along and simply never said which. Every rule this repo has about these refs (#201,
#185, #207, #211) is about a closure being **stale**; this is the one case where a frozen closure is
exactly what makes the value right.

Two consequences. The call-site name `const offering = viewing` is a label and not a guard, and the
comment says so, because the next reader will otherwise take it for one. And the rows' negative
assertion — *the sentence does not name the Offering on the screen* — is a **net**: the only mutant
that would put it at risk substitutes `viewing` back for `offering`, which is the same program, so
it is an equivalent mutant and not a claim the harness can fail. That is #47's sixth reading from
the other side — there the situation could not be built at the seam, here it cannot be built at all
— and what is owed is the condition that would make it readable again, written beside it: somebody
making that line read a live value, a ref or state the handler reads when the answer lands.

### The rows, the mutants, and a filename that aged a closed sheet's citations

`143a` holds a row per way in, each with the write's answer held back three seconds by
`support/late-answer.js` as #139's rows do, and each reading the banner once at a settle point
rather than through a retrying wait, which would die at the timeout instead of dying with the words
it found (#209). All three were run against the **unfixed** code first and were red at
*names the Offering it is about*, having passed the assertions above it — the window really opened
and the sentence really was drawn — so none of them is a row that measures nothing (#203).

Four mutants. Three are the declined options made to run (#48), one per way in: `bareadd`,
`barerefusal` and `bareremoval` each kill their own row and leave the other two standing, one red
and two passed. The fourth, `nameonly`, drops the term and keeps the subject, and kills **all
three** at *names that Offering's academic year* — it lives in the code the three ways in share, so
it cannot tell the rows apart, and that is what it proves: each row's claim is that its own way in
reaches that line (#191). The term is the half that is load-bearing today, because `01076105` is
opened in two terms; the หลักสูตร is left out of the sentence because no subject is placed in more
than one, which is a condition with a date on it and a written expiry (#113, #81) rather than a
property of the key.

**And the new spec's filename aged a closed sheet's citations.** `143a-a-sentence-that-names-its-offering.spec.js`
contains `43a`, so `npx playwright test 43a` in `mutation/43-program-level-all-students.py` and
two `` `43a:NNN` `` citations in `e2e/README.md` became two-file names the moment the file landed.
`anchors.py` printed all four before anything was committed, and the repair is the one #51 made
when `151a` landed: narrow the citation, not the filename, since every `1NNa` contains `NNa` and
the ticket number is not negotiable. Second time for this species, which is why it is a sentence
here and not a new line in the index.

## #153 — the accepted price that was wider than the page that accepted it

A `question` ticket, and the owner's answer was the cheapest of the four options put to them: **leave
the behaviour as it stands, and have the price measured.** So the ticket cost no line of production
code and seven rows at the HTTP seam, which is the shape #48 describes from the other side — a
criterion answered *no* needs a row as much as one answered *yes* — except that here what is answered
*no* is a whole ticket, and the row is what keeps the answer from being a sentence nobody can check.

**The ticket said it was not measurable, and its own next paragraph said how to measure it.** *Not
measured in a row: both seams run a single browser context, so neither can hold two sessions of one
account at once* — and then, four lines later, *`backend/test/shell.test.js` can, by signing two
cookies and sending them in turn*. Two sessions of one account is `signInAs` twice: there is no
browser at that seam at all, only cookies, and nothing stops a row holding two. The whole measurement
was a probe of five rows that passed first time, which makes this #141's rule met again — a ticket's
reason for being untestable is a claim like its numbers — with the aggravation that the claim was
refuted inside the ticket. What was true was the clause nobody had reason to doubt: there is no
`newContext` anywhere in `e2e/`, so the browser half is still unmeasured, and the jar is where *last
write wins* actually happens.

**Measuring it widened the price, which is the finding.** ADR-0006 §What it costs had it as *the
second machine is signed out when its half hour runs out*. What the probe found is that the second
machine is not stuck at all: switching grant there writes a cookie **whatever the counter said**,
because the switch bumps the counter and stamps the value it has just written — so the person has a
way back. And the moment they take it, the *first* machine is the one that cannot renew. Two devices
take it in turns, and only the one that switched last can renew. That is a different sentence to
price a fix against, and it was invisible from the code: the mechanism is in `routes/me.js`, the
symptom is in `session.js`, and nothing in either file says that the two of them make the cost
symmetrical. It is #225's rule read from the other end — there the count of what a fix *buys* was a
claim to measure; here it is the count of what *not* fixing costs, and the instrument is the same,
the situation built with the defect in.

**The reach is the heartbeat, which is what makes the price's own wording true.** *However hard the
person is working on it* is only true if the request their typing produces is refused too, and
`POST /api/me/activity` is a request like any other: it reaches the same comparison and is refused
the same way (#99, ADR-0005 — the half hour counts from the last token *issued*, and none is being
issued). The row needed its control beside it, because a heartbeat that never renewed anything at
all would make the claim pass without the counter having refused a thing — #83's species, a row that
passes before and after the thing it is about.

**The ticket's supporting citation was a decision nobody had made.** Option 2 was priced as *a store
of session state the JWT was deliberately chosen to replace (ADR-0002)*, which made it read as an
amendment to a founding decision. ADR-0002 is about authorisation being derived server-side from the
database; it says nothing about session storage, and it already licenses exactly this kind of claim
in the token as a *pointer, not an authority* — `acting`, and since #51 `acting_epoch`. Grepping the
corpus for `stateless`, `session store` and `sessions table` returns **nothing**: the JWT was never
chosen over anything, it is **inherited** from the delivered student code, as `session.js`'s own
docstring says of `generateToken`. Re-derived from the mount points, option 2 is one migration, one
table and the three places a token is minted — sign-in, the switch, the renewal — and it amends
ADR-0006 alone, which is the page that says it is the one to reopen. This is #54's rule one layer
up: there the invented identifiers were table and column names, here it is the *decision* a cost line
cites, and because a cost line is what decides which option gets built (#77), a citation that inflates
one option's price is a thumb on the scale for the others.

**And the measurement found the fourth option** (#128's shape again). Nothing in the system stores the
selection — there is no `acting_role_id` column anywhere, the hat lives in the cookie alone — which
is why a renewal cannot simply re-stamp the account's current hat. Store it (two columns, no table)
and a mismatched renewal can stamp the newest selection instead of writing nothing: every device
renews, and *last write wins* stops being harmful because every renewal writes the newest value. It
closes #51 by a different mechanism, and its price is **behaviour rather than code** — the hat becomes
the account's rather than the browser's, so nobody can wear two hats on two machines. That is an
owner's question, which is why it is written into ADR-0006 for whoever prices this next rather than
built.

**The mutant for the declined option already existed.** Option 3 was *counter per token rather than
per account*, which made to run (#48) is a comparison of the token's number against itself — that is
`51:noguard`, the mutant that is already the code before #51. It kills four of the seven new rows,
and so does `51:nobump`; `51:neverrenew` kills the two controls and the last row, `51:bumpafterissue`
the last row alone, and `51:switchkeepsold` the recovery row. Six of the seven therefore have a
killer; the one that does not is the row saying the stale device is still *answered*, for the same
reason its #51 sibling has none — it is the behaviour #51 had to leave alone. Six mutants nobody
edited had their figures expire, the anchors exact and the code untouched, because the file gained
rows they can reach (#48, #202): re-swept at a baseline of 57, the HTTP counts went 2→6, 2→6, 4→7,
4→5 and 2→3, and `missingiszero`, which reaches none of the new rows, stayed at one. The browser
figures did not move and were not re-run: the diff is one test file, which no spec in `e2e/` imports.

**And the last row was killed by two of them while measuring nothing at all**, which is why the
second sweep is the one those figures come from. As first written it aged the cookie *sign-in*
issued rather than the cookie the switch issued — a token carrying the counter from before the bump,
which cannot renew whatever the second device does — so the claim the row exists for, *only the
device that switched last can renew*, was never at risk. `51:nobump` and `51:noguard` killed it
anyway: they make everything renew, and the row's assertion is that nothing was written. It read
exactly like a proved row, with the right mutants cited beside it. That is #116's fourth reading of
a sheet met again — a row that cites the right mutant and never states its claim, the only one of
the four that leaves the sheet looking modest — and it was found by `/code-review` rather than by a
sweep, because **no sweep can see it**: the mutant dies at an assertion that is true for a reason
the row did not arrange. What repaired it is a read *before* the second device switches, asserting
that this cookie renewed while it was the one that had switched last; and that read is what bought
`neverrenew` and `bumpafterissue` as killers. Tightening the recovery row from *a cookie was
written* to *exactly one cookie was written* bought `nobump` and `noguard` there as well, the
mutants that remove the comparison making the switch renew too. Repairing one vacuous row and one
loose count added four kills, which is the measure of how loose they were.

## #156 — the override that never landed, and the option nobody had priced

A `question` ticket raised by #105 on its way past, under `docs/06` §Out of Scope — *the UI is
reproduced as-is; any proposal to change it is raised as a question, not implemented.* #105 had made
the shell draw the icon each menu entry declares, a 20px box where a 4px dot had been, and the width
came out of the label: two more labels fell to two lines. The ticket put three answers to the owner —
leave it, tighten the gap, shorten the labels — with a table of numbers beside them.

**Every number in the table had to be measured again, and two of them were wrong in different
ways.**

The population first. The ticket counted 28 sub-items across the three role menus that had any;
today there are **32 across four**, because #49 gave the external assessor a menu on 16 October by
copying the programme manager's fourth group whole, and the longest label in the system came with
it. So *7 of 28* was a figure about the day it was written, which is the catalogue's first rule met
again — a ticket's *What is wrong* is a claim from the day it was written — but with the twist that
nothing in it was ever wrong: the sentence aged by a fix landing somewhere else, in a file the
ticket does not name, five weeks after it was filed. Re-measured, today's menus wrap **8 of 32**.

**Then the override.** The probe applied each candidate as an inline style over the live layout
rather than by editing the component — one page load per variant, so nothing accumulated — and
reported that tightening the gap to 8px changed nothing at all: `gap8` came back byte for byte
identical to `head`, same 194px, same eight labels. The first reading of that is that the ticket was
wrong about its own option. It was not. `link.style.setProperty('column-gap', '8px', 'important')`
had not landed, and the proof is in the probe's own output, where the variant called `gap8` printed
`gap=12` beside its name. The fix for the measurement was to stop measuring that way: `gap-3` was
edited to `gap-2` in the component, the probe run against the real tree, and the number came back
**198px and seven labels** — the direction the ticket claimed, at numbers one step along from the
ones it wrote, because its *7 instead of 6* had been measured when the menu was 28 items wide.

So an in-page override is a claim like any other, and the cheapest check on it is the property
itself: a variant that reports the value it was supposed to change has measured nothing, and it
reports it in the same shape as a real result — a row of numbers under a name. Nothing is red,
nothing times out, and the inert variant looks like a candidate that buys nothing, which is exactly
the answer somebody would act on. What settles it is the thing the probe's own docstring promised
and had not yet done: one candidate reproduced by editing the code, and compared.

**The option that was chosen is not one of the three.** All three in the ticket are priced by what
is on the screen. What none of them asks is which of the numbers in that drawing the delivered
system fixed and which the rebuild chose for itself —
`DEEP-QA-FRONTEND/src/components/SidebarItem.js` drew its 4px dot with `gap-3`, so **the 12px gap is
a delivered value and the 20px box is a number #105 picked**, sized to the label's 24px line so the
row height would not move. Shrinking the box to 16px gives back 4px of the 16 and buys the same one
label the gap change buys — at no divergence from the delivered UI at all, where tightening the gap
is a change to something the students shipped. That asymmetry is #45 one layer up (a number copied
from a sibling screen is a decision, not an inheritance) and it is invisible to a ticket that prices
its options by their effect: the two cheap options cost the same 4px and buy the same label, and
everything that distinguishes them is in a file the ticket never opens. The owner took it, and the
second item on the ticket — the mark no longer changing colour under the pointer, because
`text-primary` and `hover:text-primary` unfold to the same token — was answered *leave it*, which
makes the top-level row's behaviour the rule rather than a gap in this one.

**No mutant, and that is the whole of what #156 owes the suite.** `105a` asks whether the shell
reads each entry's own config — no entry drawing nothing, two entries not drawing the same thing —
and a box's size is not that question. Size is appearance, appearance is hand-walked here, and so
the deliverable is three ◐ rows: the menu row of sheets 30, 31 and 32, each of which was walked at
20px on 23 September and now has a drawing nobody has looked at. That is #105's own rule read the
other way — a row can gain a walkable half the day a ticket lands — except that here the ticket
that re-opened them is the one answering the question they were opened by.

**And the probe was deleted one measurement too early.** It had answered the question, so it went,
by #207's rule that a probe is an instrument: built, run, deleted. But a fix made from a probe's
numbers is owed a reading *after* it lands, and the instrument for that reading is the probe, so it
had to be written again from scratch to confirm the 198px and the seven labels in the tree as
committed. The rule is the same one, with its moment moved: delete the probe when the fix has been
measured, not when the question has been answered.

## #163 — the half that could not be measured, one layer down

#163 was opened out of the 24 September walk of sheets 11 and 12: a `disabled` button does not take
focus, so the `title` that says *why* it cannot be pressed has no way to be shown to anybody not
using a mouse. The measurement was clean and had a control — from *แก้ไข* on the signed-in
administrator's own row, one `Tab` landed on the next row's *แก้ไข*, skipping the *ระงับ* button
whole, while the same button on `cross01`, where it is not `disabled`, took the focus normally. It
was a question and not a task, because the fix changes behaviour rather than appearance
(`docs/06` §Out of Scope), and the ticket said so itself.

**And the ticket wrote down what it did not know, which is what made it answerable.** Its own last
section said the screen-reader half was unmeasured, that `disabled` keeping the keyboard away did
not kill it because browse mode sweeps content without regard to focus, that the walking machine
had no Thai voice, and — the sentence that mattered — that **if that half came back "heard", the
price of the ticket changes**, because the harmed group would then be keyboard users who are not
running a screen reader rather than both groups together. The ticket had priced its own
measurement in advance.

**The half needed a human ear; the layer under it needed no voice at all.** *Does anybody hear it*
cannot be asked without NVDA and a Thai voice. *Is the sentence in the accessibility tree, on a
node the browser does not mark ignored* can be asked of Chrome directly, and it decides the same
price. A throwaway Playwright probe pointed CDP at each button — a marker attribute on the element
the locator found, then `DOM.describeNode`, `Accessibility.getPartialAXTree` and
`Accessibility.getFullAXTree`, matched by `backendDOMNodeId` — and read the node Chrome itself
computes. Both dead buttons are in the full tree with `ignored: false` and role `button`; the
`title` arrives as the accessible **description**, 25 characters at `Users.js` equal to
`REFUSALS.selfStatus` and 26 at `GrantsPanel.js` equal to `REFUSALS.selfRevoke`; `nameFrom` lists
`contents` and `attribute` on the dead nodes against `contents` alone on the control, the attribute
being superseded, so the name is the button's own text and the title is a description rather than
being swallowed into it; and neither dead node carries a `focusable` property at all, where the
enabled control carries `focusable: true` and no description. That last pair is the tree confirming
the ticket's `Tab` measurement from the inside, with its own control.

So the reason does reach assistive technology, attached to a node the browser does not mark
ignored, and what is left of the unmeasured half is not about this code: it is whether a given
reader is configured to speak object descriptions. The owner left the behaviour alone on 21 October
2569 and the ticket closed as answered, with sheet 11's row staying ◐ — the human half is still
blocked by the voice, and a tree is not an ear.

**The two prices the ticket had not counted were both in the harness.** Seven mutants live on the
lines the WAI-ARIA route would edit: `84:alwaysenabled`, `84:everyrowisdead`, `84:titledrifts`,
`130:alwaysenabled`, `130:everyrowisdead`, `130:titledrifts` and `130:selfrowhidesthebutton`. Four
of them quote the two `disabled={…}` lines exactly, and two of those four would stop meaning what
their sheets say they mean — once the guard is in the handler, making the attribute wrong is no
longer making the button live — so they are rewrites and not re-aims (#203), and a sweep has to
follow (#107, #68). Second, every `disabled:` Tailwind variant stops applying the moment the
attribute goes (`disabled:text-gray-400`, `disabled:cursor-not-allowed`,
`disabled:hover:bg-transparent`, `disabled:opacity-40`), so the appearance the owner approved on 24
September — sheet 11's row *ปุ่มที่กดไม่ได้ ดูออกไหมว่ากดไม่ได้* and sheet 12's hover row, both ☑ —
would have to be rebuilt on `aria-disabled:` variants and walked again. The ticket's four-item cost
list named the rows and the walks and stopped at the seam it could see.

A third thing the ticket's list missed is smaller and sharper: `GrantsPanel` is
`disabled={busy || isSelf}`, and the `busy` half carries no title. A handler guard there has to
answer two reasons, not one, and the `busy` one belongs to #142.

**Its supporting identifiers had aged the usual way** (#54). Both line numbers had moved, 404–412 →
532 and 214–222 → 255; `title=` was 47 lines rather than 46; "`84a` rows 1 and 2" are both named
`row 3` in the file, after the sheet row they belong to; `12:291` is now `12:336`; and `12:63`,
offered as the second place this ticket's unmeasured half was recorded, was right at the ticket's
own commit — `git show 5af5903` puts the *#111 ครึ่งที่สอง* row on that line — and has only moved
since, to `12:68`. What that row records is the same blocker, a missing Thai voice, for a different
claim, which is why the line added to it says so rather than ticking it. The species held: HTML
`title` on a `disabled` control is still exactly two sites, the other 45 being component props
named `title` or `<th>` headers.

**The fourth option was cheap and was declined anyway.** Keeping `disabled` and putting the
sentence somewhere on the screen that depends on neither hover nor focus changes no behaviour,
re-aims no mutant, rewrites no assertion and needs no handler guard; it costs a hand-walk and a
permanent sentence on one row. It was worth putting in front of the owner beside the ARIA route,
and the measurement is what made leaving it alone defensible rather than merely cheaper.

**And nothing was owed a row, which is worth saying because the decision rests on a measurement.**
The property the answer leans on is that the refusal reaches the tree as a description — but the
step the repo controls is the `title` attribute, and `84a` and `12a` already assert it is
`REFUSALS.selfStatus` and `REFUSALS.selfRevoke` themselves. The attribute-to-description mapping is
Chrome's, not ours. There is no gap between what was measured and what is held, so there is no
ticket to open for one.

## #166 — the criterion with no caller, and the answer that was already in the spec

A `question` ticket, opened 27 September 2569 out of #47's own closing sweep. Criterion 5 of #47 —
*delete an account and the photo file must be gone from the disk, not only the row* — has no
caller, because the rebuild suspends accounts and never deletes them, and the third conjunct of
criterion 8 waits on the same absence. The ticket offered two: **(ก)** the day a delete route is
built, its ticket calls `removePhoto` per `user_image` row before the row goes and carries a
backend row that reads the file back off the disk; or **(ข)** if it is confirmed that accounts are
never deleted, strike criterion 5 and half of 8 out formally and rewrite sheet 47's ☐ row to say
so. Under `docs/06` §Out of Scope that choice is the owner's.

**Every claim in it measured true.** `backend/routes/users.js` has seven routes — a list, an import
template, one by id, a create, an update, a status change and an import — and **none of them
deletes**. `backend/lib/userPhoto.removePhoto` exists, is called by the replace path, and its own
header said the delete-account route must call it — a sentence that expired the day the criterion
was struck, in the file nobody thought they were changing (#130): the review found it, and it was
dated and redirected to `0004` as part of this change. So the criterion had no caller, exactly as
written, and this is one of the ones whose *What is wrong* was still true on the day it was read.

**What decided the question was not on the ticket: the answer was already in the spec.** `docs/06`
user story 19 reads *create, edit and deactivate user accounts*, and stories 29 and 40 write the
same doctrine for a Program and a Program Subject — *deactivated rather than deleted*. The missing
route is therefore a **decision already written down**, not an omission, which changes what the two
options are: (ก) is not a gap waiting to be filled on some later ticket, it is a change to user
story 19. The owner's question stops being *decide this* and becomes *confirm what you decided*,
which is a cheaper question and a different one. This is #86's rule with the other witness: there
