the **delivered UI** answered the owner's question about a missing control before the owner did;
here the **spec's own user story** answers it, and the two can point opposite ways on one absence.

**They do here, which is why the confirmation was still worth having.** The delivered system *had*
the control: `UserTable.js` draws a trash button per row behind a confirmation box, it calls
`DELETE /api/user/delete/:user_id`, and `userModel.deleteUser` really does delete the `users` row
after two business guards — sweeping `course_sections_teacher` by hand on the way, never touching
`user_image`, and never unlinking a file. So the rebuild's missing route is a **divergence that was
chosen**, and #47's *the day a delete route exists* was not hypothetical but a control the rebuild
had declined to reproduce. An absence can be a decision in the spec and a divergence from the
delivered code at the same time, and both halves belong in the owner's question.

**Striking a criterion would have lost its requirement with it — unless the requirement is written
where the mechanism that makes it true lives.** The owner took that option, which is neither of the
ticket's two: strike criterion 5 and the third half of 8, and move the requirement into
`db/migrations/0004_user_profile_image.sql`, beside the `ON DELETE CASCADE` on
`user_image.user_id`. That is the right address for it twice over. The migration chose CASCADE
against `0001`'s general `RESTRICT` **citing the inherited `deleteUser`**, so it is already the
file that anybody writing a deletion path has to read; and CASCADE makes the requirement true of
**every path that deletes a `users` row** — a future route, an administration script, a hand at a
`psql` prompt — rather than of a route, which is all the closed ticket could have bound. A struck
criterion's requirement goes to the mechanism, not to the ticket that is being closed over it.

**And the price it is written against is smaller than the migration said.** `0004`'s own comment
had it that an orphaned file is *still served*: true of the delivered system, which served the
photos through an unguarded `express.static`. Since #47 the rebuild has **no static mount at all**
and `GET /me/photo` reads `user_image` for `req.auth.userId` only, so an orphan here is reachable
through **no route**. What it costs is disk, and a photograph of a person whose account is gone —
retention, not exposure. The sentence was right the day it was written and was expired by another
ticket's fix, which is #130 in a migration comment instead of a sheet: it was dated rather than
deleted.

**The requirement is also bounded, which is what makes one comment enough.** Photos are the only
file-bearing table that cascades from `users`: `activity_evidence.uploaded_by` is
`ON DELETE SET NULL`, so deleting an account leaves the evidence rows and their files alone, and
`course_sections_teacher.user_id` is `ON DELETE RESTRICT` here — a future delete route would be
**refused** for a teacher who has teaching load, where the delivered code swept that table clean
first. So the sweep the requirement asks for is one call about one table, not a doctrine.

**What changed on the sheets.** Sheet 47 row 5 keeps **☐** and keeps its place in the table:
the row is the record of what #47 asked for, not a queue, and there is no fifth mark to invent
(#97, #66) — what it gained is the dated sentence saying it was struck and where its requirement
now lives. Row 8's third conjunct is struck through in the criterion cell itself, which leaves two
conjuncts that both have rows in that table, so the row goes **◐ → ☑** and the walk queue is one
shorter. The answered question moved out of `## คำถามที่ยังไม่ได้ตอบ` into its own dated
section, on #48's pattern. On sheet 11 the sentence the ticket cites — *there is no `DELETE`, so
that account can only be suspended* — sits inside a **dated record** of #124's measurement, so it
was not rewritten: it got a dated line beside it saying that the absence reads as a confirmed
decision today and where the file-deletion requirement went (#54).

No production code, no row and no mutant: the ticket asked a question, and what the answer changed
was three documents and a migration comment.

## #169 — the box that outlived its close, and the condition the driver was hiding

A `question` ticket, opened 28 September 2569 out of what #47 and #167 left behind. Both of those
closed by fixing a box's **state** — every dialog now clears its own on the way out — and neither
touched the **presence of the node**: a box closed in a tab that is getting no frames is not
removed from the document. Under `docs/06` §Out of Scope that was the owner's to decide, because
every way the ticket could see to fix it changed an animation people watch. The ticket also named
its own precondition: both of its options waited on two measurements nobody had taken — the
change-password box's own numbers, and whether the lingering node reaches a person at all.

**The first finding was about the instrument, not about the box.** The record said the suite could
not put the claim at risk because stopping `requestAnimationFrame` from inside the page does not
reproduce it, the frame loop having bound its own reference at import. That is true and it is half
the reason. The other half is that **the driver removes the situation**: a Playwright page with
another tab in front still reports `visibilityState: "visible"` and counts 60 frames in a second,
`Page.setWebLifecycleState: frozen` is undone at once — 61 frames while it was supposed to be
frozen — and launching with `--disable-backgrounding-occluded-windows`,
`--disable-renderer-backgrounding` and `--disable-background-timer-throttling` removed changes
none of it. So the instrument was built outside the seam: a Chrome of its own, driven over raw
CDP, where a backgrounded tab is `hidden` with **0 frames in a second**. The condition reproduced
on the first run.

**Both measurements came back wider than the price the ticket had accepted** (#153). The ticket's
option (ก) priced the harm as an invisible node lingering in a tab nobody is looking at. What is
there is not faded at all: with no frames the tween never starts, so the box sits at
`opacity: 1`, `pointer-events: auto`, `checkVisibility()` true, outside any `aria-hidden` or
`inert` — still in the document at 0.5, 1 and 3 seconds. Every control in it takes focus: two in
the photo box, **eight** in the change-password box, its three password fields among them. The
accessibility tree holds the subtree whole — 23 nodes for the photo box and 35 for the password
box, with the heading, the three textboxes and both buttons still named and not ignored. And the
return is not a quiet cleanup: the tween starts on the first frame the tab is given, so the box the
person already closed is **drawn again at full opacity** and fades out in front of them, the last
frame still drawing it at 194–196ms. The change-password box — measurement 1, never taken before —
matched the photo box on every number.

**And the way in is not a race with the person's own hand** (#179). A cancel needs a press and a
press needs the tab in front, which leaves only the ~180ms between the click and the end of the
fade. But both boxes close themselves *after* an awaited request — the photo box through `onSaved`,
the change-password box through `closeChangePassword` — so pressing save and switching away while
the request is out lands the close in a tab that already has no frames. Measured: same numbers,
with nothing racing anybody.

**The measurement changed the option list before it changed the answer** (#128, #204). All three of
the ticket's ways in option (ข) moved something people see, and the fourth — retire the node on the
browser's own timeline instead of framer-motion's — died in the same hour it was thought of:
neither `transitionend` nor `animationend` fires in a frameless tab. What does still run is
`setTimeout`, throttled to about 1Hz (200ms arrived at 1000ms), and React's own scheduler, which is
why the close commits at all in a tab with no frames. That is the opening: when the flag goes false
while `document.hidden`, the child is dropped on the next commit with no `AnimatePresence` around
it to hold it, and a `visibilitychange` listener covers the other half — a box closed while the tab
is in front and the tab backgrounded inside the fade. **Nothing changes for anybody who is looking
at the screen**, which is the option the ticket said did not exist. The owner took it.

**Run on both sides, because nothing else could ever say so** (#203). Before: present at 0.5, 1 and
3 seconds on all three ways in. After: gone by 0.5 seconds on all three, and the per-frame sampler
sees it on **no frame at all** after the return. The visible case was measured at `HEAD` and on the
fix, which is the half that says the fix costs the person nothing: 12 frames still drawing the box
either way, the last at 186ms at `HEAD` and 192ms on the fix, opacity coming down both times, node
gone at the end both times.

**What holds the new behaviour is nothing in either suite, and that is written down rather than
left to be discovered.** `DialogPresence.js` says so in its own header (renamed to
`RetiringPresence.js` by #227 on 25 October 2569, which generalised the wrapper; the head comment
and this reason moved with it), and the probe is committed
at `e2e/probes/169-presence-without-frames.js` instead of being deleted with the measurement
(#207), because it is the only thing that can read this behaviour again — the seam that would
normally hold it is the seam that cannot build the condition. A claim no seam can put at risk is
still measurable; what is owed is the instrument, outside the seam, run on both sides and kept.

**And the fix's own first version failed the half that made the option allowed.** The owner's
answer was *drop it when nobody can see it*, which is only an answer while nothing changes for
somebody who can. The listener on `visibilitychange` was written with no dependencies, so it ran
behind an **open** box too: a tab sent away while the box was up put the flag down, nothing put it
back, and the close minutes later - in front of the person, tab in focus - dropped the node with no
fade at all. Three measurements had already passed, because all three closed the box in a
backgrounded tab or never left the tab at all; the sequence that catches it leaves and comes back
**while the box is open**. Keyed on the box being on its way out, the same sequence reads 13 frames
ending at ~195ms; with the first version it reads **0**. So the guard on a retirement change is not
*does the thing still go away* but *does it still go away at the same speed in front of somebody*,
and that reading belongs in the probe rather than in anybody's head - it was added as a fourth mode
and run on both versions (#203).

**And a probe is read at the moment its input is dirtiest** (#186's rule, one instrument along).
The first run of that fourth mode after restoring the file reported **1 frame**, which reads
exactly like the defect it was written to catch. Nothing was wrong with the code: the dev server was
recompiling the file that had just been written, and the page under measurement reloaded inside the
run. Re-running with nothing compiling gave 12. A probe that drives a hot-reloading dev server has
a precondition no assertion in it can state, and the cheapest way to meet it is to let the compile
finish before the measurement starts.

**Scope, and what was deferred into the tracker rather than into prose** (#119). The two navbar
modals are the ones with a raceless way in, and they are the two that changed. The five other
`AnimatePresence` sites — the user menu, `RoleDropdown`, `SidebarItem`'s submenu and `Login`'s two
— are retired by a press or by a navigation, which needs a tab in front, so only the ~180ms race
reaches them; that is a ticket, not a silence in this one. On the way past: sheet 10's census of
28 September counted **five files** using `AnimatePresence`, and four do. `ProfilePhotoDialog.js`
only names it in a comment, which is #111 in one word — a grep is evidence for the pattern you
typed.

## #177 — the year that was checked for shape, and the helper that was its mirror image

A `question` ticket, opened 30 September 2569. `programs.revision_year` holds the Buddhist-era
year a curriculum was revised in, as text, and `readProgram` checked it with `/^\d{4}$/` and
nothing else. So `1234` and `9999` were stored, and so was `2024` — the common-era year for what
somebody means as 2567 — and the three screens that print the value printed the wrong label. A
guard that is strict about a format cannot see a mistake about meaning (#124), which is #125's
whole ticket one column along, with the arithmetic running the other way.

Everything in the ticket's diagnosis measured true, which is worth writing down because it is the
rarer outcome (#66's catalogue). The guard was still the line it quoted, the three readers were
display-only, and the generic sentence *ข้อมูลหลักสูตรไม่ครบถ้วนหรือไม่ถูกต้อง* was what a wrong
year got. Two things it did not say were found by measuring around it.

**The helper the ticket named as the obvious home is the exact mirror image of what the column
needs.** The cost line offered `lib/year.js` and then dismissed it as *unsuitable*, which reads
like a judgement about style. Run, it is a refutation: `yearRefusal(2565)` — the correct value,
the one this column exists to hold — **refuses** it and offers ค.ศ. 2022, while `yearRefusal(2024)`
returns `null`. Its range is 1900–2200 *of the common era*. A helper named for a type is a promise
about that type (#107), and here the promise is kept and useless: the file is right about dates and
this column is not a date. So `backend/lib/revisionYear.js` is its own file, and what the two share
is the **shape** of the answer — inside the range accepted, the other reading offered when it lands
inside, the range named otherwise — and not one line of the range itself. A cost line is a claim
about the shape its author pictured (#77); this one named the right shape and the wrong file, and
only running the function says which.

**No bound in this server's validation is derived from the clock.** The ticket's second question
was whether the ceiling should be a constant or derived from today, and the argument for today is
good: a Program can be revised for a year that has not arrived, so the plausible ceiling is *a few
years ahead*. A ceiling of *a few years from now* would have been the first bound in the system
that moved with the day — #52's *anything written for timing must not be able to decide
anything*, met in the product rather than in a fixture (#199's species). That measurement went to
the owner as part of the question rather than as a recommendation dressed up as a fact, and the
answer on 22 October 2569 was **both links of the guard, with a constant ceiling** — 2500 to 2600,
which is how `lib/year.js` chose 2200.

**And the first wording of that sentence was wrong, which a grep found and a census did not.**
What went into four files first was *nothing in this server's validation reads the clock*, off a
census whose only hits were comments mentioning `Date.now()` in `evidence.js` and `userPhoto.js`.
`auth/accounts.js`'s `validityRefusal` reads it on both ways in — `today = BANGKOK.format(new
Date())` — and a grep for `new Date()` says so in a second. **A grep is evidence for the pattern
you typed** (#111, #124), and the pattern here was one spelling of two. What is true is narrower,
and it is the sentence the owner's answer actually rests on: the one guard that reads the clock
reads it to compare *somebody's stored window* against today, not to pick a bound of its own, so a
ceiling computed from today would be the first bound that moved. The correction reached five
files, because a claim written in prose expires like a number and the copy you will miss is in the
file you did not think you were changing (#130).

**The new gate goes second, and that is what keeps a closed ticket's walked row true.** `25` has no
year in it to do arithmetic with, so the shape gate is asked first and answers it exactly as it
always did. Sheet 15's row *ปีหลักสูตรต้องเป็นสี่หลัก* records that generic sentence from a curl
walk in August 2569, and it still reads as it did — the order of two gates decides which sentence
the caller gets (#60), and here the order was chosen so that no walked row expired. The row gained
a sentence saying four digits is no longer enough; its result did not change.

The sentence itself is a function in `REFUSALS`, like #125's, so the two route sites that looked the
refusal up as a key had to read `sentenceOf` instead. The import needed nothing: `lib/importer.js`
has read a `message` before a `reason` since #26, so the CSV path got the sentence for free — which
is a thing to measure rather than to assert, and `formsentenceisakey` and `editsentenceisakey` are
one mutant per site because three paths out of one reader fail one at a time or they were never
three.

**A browser row exists here for a reason no HTTP test can state.** The field carries
`pattern="\d{4}"` inside a form with no `noValidate`, which is why the *shape* refusal is the
browser's sentence and not the server's (#88) — sheet 15's own row says so in its own words,
*เบราว์เซอร์ทักที่ช่อง*. `2024` satisfies that pattern, so the claim `177a` holds is that **the
request leaves the page at all**, and then that what the person reads is the sentence naming the
year. Its second row reads the form back: a refusal that names a way out is a claim that the way out
is reachable from where it is read (#178), and typing 2567 instead is worth nothing if the save
threw away what was typed.

**And one of the guard's two links cannot be mutated apart from the other.** `edgesoftherangearerefused`
and `ceilingisnotread` hold the ceiling, at its edge and whole. The floor has no equivalent: the
value the era sentence exists for, 2024, lies *below* the floor, so a mutant that stops reading the
floor stops refusing 2024 as well and dies at the era row — a duplicate of `theyearisonlyshaped`
rather than a second claim. The floor is proved whole by that mutant, at its edge by the first, and
apart from its sentence by `alwaysoffersthebuddhistreading`, and the file says which of #101's three
the missing mutant is: structurally unreachable, not a gap. #97's *one mutant per link* is a rule
about what to try, and #101's three answers are what to write down when one of them turns out to be
the same mutant twice.

## #180 — the status field in three shapes, and the label that read its own options

A `question` ticket, opened 1 October 2569. Five forms carry a status field. Three of them —
`DepartmentForm`, `ProgramForm`, `SubjectForm` — drew a checkbox reading *เปิดใช้งาน*; two —
`ProgramSubjectForm`, `PloForm` — drew a two-option `select` reading *ใช้งานอยู่ / ปิดใช้งาน*,
which is the wording all five tables' own badges use. So three screens wrote one state in two
vocabularies on one screen. And ภาควิชา was the only one of the five that offered the field at
**creation**, its route the only one of the five that read `is_active` out of a POST body.

**The delivered code answered the question that comes before the owner's.** Under `docs/06`
§Out of Scope an option that moves a delivered number is a divergence and one that moves a number
the rebuild chose is not (#156), so the first measurement was not of the five forms but of
`DEEP-QA-FRONTEND`: it has no status control on any screen and reads `is_active` nowhere. All five
fields are the rebuild's own, and the shape question was the owner's to answer with nothing in the
way. The departments route was the other half of the same measurement and came out differently:
`departmentModel.js` in the delivered backend writes `is_active` on create, so that read was
**inherited** rather than chosen — an inherited mechanism is not a decision (#77), which is what
made taking it out a correction rather than a divergence.

The owner answered on 22 October 2569: a two-option `select` on all five, in the badge's words;
the shape and the words first, with the hint paragraph and the `disabled={busy}` that the other two
forms carry left to #228; and the field off the ภาควิชา create form. The deferral went into the
tracker the same hour, because a deferral written into prose and not into the tracker is a decision
nobody can find (#119).

**The ticket's opinion was right for a reason that was wrong.** It recorded, from 1 October, that
*the shape question is the one real finding left over from #178* — and #178's premise had been that
no status control existed on any screen, which that day's measurement had already refuted. A
conclusion right for the wrong reason expires on the wrong day (#141), so the opinion was re-derived
from the five forms rather than inherited: it survived, which is worth writing down because the
ticket's own paragraph could not be cited for it.

### Four rows priced, nine rows measured, and the sheet's own prediction refuted

The ticket's cost line said four e2e rows would expire, in `16a` and `18a`. True on 1 October.
#181 landed after it and brought five more rows that press this control through two helpers, so the
figure is **nine rows at nine sites** — four pressing it directly as an **instrument** (#171) and
five of `181a` through `statusBox`. A ticket's cost line is a claim about the shape its author
pictured (#77), and this one had been overtaken by another ticket rather than being wrong when
written.

Sheet `14`'s §#181 had gone further and predicted the price in advance: *if the answer is yes, the
one line that changes is `statusBox` in `e2e/support/` for each screen*. It is one line **in that
file**; it is nine sites in the suite, and one of them was not a status reader at all. A sheet's
prediction about what a future fix will cost is a claim like its numbers (#52), and the one place
it was recorded is the place a later ticket reads it as settled.

No mutant needed re-aiming, which is the rarer outcome when a fix reaches three components: #181's
four are anchored on the `is_active: draft.is_active` line of each submit payload, which this change
does not touch. `python mutation/anchors.py` says the anchors still apply; only a sweep says they
still prove what their sheets credit them with (#107, #68), and the full suite at the end is where
that was read.

### A wrapping label carries its control's own text

The first move was the obvious one: `statusBox` became
`getByLabel('สถานะ', { exact: true })`. Six rows went red with **not found** — on a screen that was
drawing the field correctly.

`Field` in all three forms wraps the control inside the `<label>`:
`<label><span>{label}</span>{children}</label>`. A wrapping label's **text content** is everything
inside it, the `<option>`s included, so the label's text is `สถานะใช้งานอยู่ปิดใช้งาน` and matching
on `สถานะ` exactly matches nothing. The **accessible name** is the label's own words, `สถานะ`, which
is a different string computed by a different rule. The failing run said so itself: its snapshot
printed `combobox "สถานะ"`, which is the second time this repo has learned to read the saved
snapshot before the waiting stack (#160). Every reader became
`getByRole('combobox', { name: 'สถานะ' })`.

**And one unfiltered locator broke.** `departmentPicker` in `e2e/support/subjects-screen.js` was a
bare `getByRole('combobox')`, unique only because that form had no second `select`. Adding the
status field made it a strict-mode violation — a locator can be unique only by accident of the thing
you are about to remove, or to add (#93). The repair is the name, and the census that found it was
every `getByRole('combobox'` and `getByRole('checkbox'` in `e2e/` (#111, #122); this was the only
site, which is a measured number and not an estimate.

### The marks, including two that went backwards

Sheet `16`'s rows for this field had been hand-walked through the checkbox. *ข้อมูลเดิมยังอ่านได้*
became ◐: its first half (name, credits, department, description still there) was walked and is
still true, while the half that reads the status control was walked through a control that no longer
exists. *เปิดกลับมาได้* went back to ☐, the whole row being that one press. *ฟอร์ม เพิ่ม
ไม่มีช่องสถานะ* stayed ☑, because its claim is the **absence**, which did not change — only the word
*checkbox* in its wording expired, and that is dated rather than deleted (#54).

Neither of the two that went backwards is earned by `16a` pressing the control, because `16a` row 97
and `18a` row 10 press it to arrange a situation for another screen. An instrument is not an
assertion (#171), which is also why there is no swapped-options mutant for `SubjectForm`: it would
go red on those rows and the kill would be credited to rows that never said anything about the
form's words.

Each sheet gained one ☐ row for the shape and the wording, because that is the half the browser
seam cannot answer (`CLAUDE.md` §Two test seams). The walk queue grows by five.

### The mutants, and the two rows that could not be written

`statusatcreation` is the diagnosed code restored (#115): the route reading `is_active` out of a
creation's body. It kills **one** backend subtest and nothing else — no row in eleven tickets had
ever sent the field to a creation, which is exactly why the behaviour was invisible until a ticket
went looking for it.

`createformshowsstatus` draws the field at creation again and kills `180a` at the count. That row
reads the **same locator** back as present on the edit form one line later, because a row that only
ever counted zero would pass on a screen that never drew the control at all (#171's rule from the
counting side, and #164's *count the controls as well as reading them*).

`departmentoptionsswapped` and `programoptionsswapped` swap the two options' values, one mutant per
form, because the two forms hold two copies of one opinion and there is nothing shared for a single
mutant to stand in the middle of (#97). The department one kills **three** rows, not the two
predicted: the third is `16a` row 97, whose instrument closes department `01` through this very
form. A fix that changes a control is a change to every row that presses it, including the rows that
press it to arrange something (#199), and the prediction written before the sweep was corrected from
the sweep rather than the other way round.

`180a` survives both swaps, which is the #193 split doing its work from the other side: `181a`
asserts its precondition **by `value`** and presses **by the visible word**, so a swapped-options
mutant lands on the badge the row is for instead of dying one line above it on the precondition.

Two rows could not be written. There is no browser row for *a department is created open*: the
form's `EMPTY` has `is_active` true, so a screen with the field back still creates an open
department, and the row would pass against the unfixed code and measure nothing (#203). That claim
lives at the HTTP seam, where the body can say `false` and the answer must still say open. And there
is no mutant for the รายวิชา form, for the instrument reason above.

### What the review changed

Four findings of six survived checking, which is the usual rate.

**The sheet credited a row to a mutant that never read most of it.** The backend
subtest asserts the answer's `is_active`, then the column in the table, then that
an edit still switches one off; `statusatcreation` dies at the first, so
everything below that line was credited and unread (#88). The row's own comment
had already written the mutant that was missing — *a route that inserted false
and reported true* — so `reportsopenbutinsertsclosed` is that sentence made to
run (#115 from the other side) and it dies at `:673`, the read of the table,
rather than at `:664`. Its third assertion is left without one on purpose: it is
criterion 3's claim, held by `181a`, and it is in this row to make the two above
it about the **creation** rather than about the column.

**A count of another ticket's mutants was wrong in three places.** The prose said
`181-the-status-switch.py` holds four; it holds **six**, the other two being in
`backend/auth/authorise.js`. A ticket that states how many places something
touches has published a claim a one-minute grep can check (#55, #96, #107), and
this one had been read off the four that happened to matter rather than off the
file. The same paragraph's re-aim claim was narrower than the change for the same
reason: `SubjectForm.js` is edited here too and belongs to `16-subjects.py` and
`18-program-subjects.py`. Those anchors are exact, which `anchors.py` says for
the whole catalogue at once — but it was the wrong sentence standing on the right
measurement.

**Four inline reads of one control, across two files, with the helpers already
there.** `16a`'s two are on the ภาควิชา screen, whose `statusField` this ticket
had just written; `18a`'s two are on the รายวิชา form, whose helper had none. An
instrument a second file needs is shared, because no row's claim lives in it
(#171). Moving a press behind a helper is the same press, and what says so is
re-running `departmentoptionsswapped` rather than reasoning about it (#107, #68):
the same three rows, the same bystander.

**And one finding was declined.** The sweep table in
`mutation/181-the-status-switch.py` cites `181a` by line number, and this change
moved those lines by six. But the line above the table says *the line numbers are
of the spec file as it was at the last sweep*, and the table is dated: a dated
record is not a citation (#54, #173). What a dated record owes is the note, and
it already carried it.


## #182 — the prop nothing could make a caller pass, and the instrument that was red in the right place for the wrong reason

#179 gave `ImportPanel` a prop, `target`, saying what the report in the panel is
about, and wrote in its own docstring that nothing enforces it: an eleventh
caller that forgot it would get `undefined` on both sides of every comparison in
the panel, which is the silent behaviour from before the ticket. **A prop is not
an argument.** `isCurrent` is passed in a call, so forgetting it throws;
`target=` missing from JSX is `undefined` and the screen draws. So whatever makes
a prop required is an instrument or nothing at all, and #179 could not write the
instrument: `frontend/` has no component test harness, `prop-types` is not a
dependency, and the five censuses then in the tree read a screen's `await`s, its
labels and its refs and had never read a prop that JSX passes. The gap went into
the docstring and into `34-activity-marks.md` rather than being hidden (#123),
and #182 was its queue.

**The ticket's four options came with a column saying which were provable, and
that column is a claim like its numbers** (#141). The first option — `prop-types`
with CRA's console warning — was priced **ไม่**, because *nothing reads the dev
server's console and a warning makes nothing red*. The first half is a fact about
today's suite; the second is a claim about what a row can do, which is a different
thing. A probe measured it, and was deleted after (#207): `e2e` runs **CRA's dev
server**, not a build, so a `console.error` emitted while a component renders
reaches `page.on('console')` — eight times in one screen open, through React's
double render. The console is reachable; what is not available is a *global* net
over it, because 2 of the 12 messages on one screen open are `Failed to load
resource: 401` from signing in. A net matching the message would work.

**And measuring that produced an option the ticket had not listed** (#128, #204):
if the console is readable, the panel can say the sentence itself — three lines of
plain JavaScript, no dependency — which buys exactly what `prop-types` buys and
costs less, with a **narrow** mutant: removing `target=` from one real screen
makes the warning appear and kills only the row that reads for it, the screen
still drawing. That is the asymmetry the ticket's second option does not have: a
`throw` in the panel is proved only by a mutant that takes the whole screen down,
which is not the shape a mutant has to have (#97). So the measurement left the
owner four live options rather than the two the table implied, and the
dominated one was the ticket's own first.

**The owner chose the census**, and the ticket's own condition on that choice was
the interesting part: the rule had to be about *a prop the component declares it
must have* rather than about the name `ImportPanel`, or it is a rule for one
component wearing the clothes of a general instrument — `mutation/README.md`'s
word for that is a list, not a catalogue (#126). So the component declares, in
code rather than in a comment:

    export const REQUIRED_PROPS = ['target']

a named export beside the default one, which is a spelling this tree already
writes (`RadarChart.js` exports `MAX_AXES`) and a syntax the parser reads, which a
`//` between two tags is not (#93). The census's population is every file that
writes one. **A declaration is then a claim to check against its own subject**:
a name the component never destructures is a declaration that proves nothing, and
`required-props.js` reports it.

**Breaking real sites found two defects in the census that its own twenty-one
fixtures were silent about** (#141, and #124 — before trusting a new assertion,
break the thing it is about). Eight readings, on `Departments.js` and on the
panel itself, restored each time:

- `{...rest}` in place of `target=` was reported as **is given no `target`** — a
  sentence the instrument cannot say, because what the object holds was decided
  in another file. The spread has to be asked about *first*: it removes the
  attribute, so asking *what is missing* first reads a call it cannot read as one
  it had read.
- A declaration with a typo in it — `['taget']` — was reported once at the
  declaration and then **ten more times, once per caller**, and those ten reports
  name the wrong fix: add `taget=` to ten screens. A name the component does not
  take apart is now dropped from what callers are measured against.

Both were **red in the right place**. The exit code was 1 either way, the file and
the line were right either way, and what was wrong was the sentence and the blast
radius — which is the part a count never shows and a fixture written from the
rule rather than from the tree cannot reach. The other six readings were the ones
a fixture can hold, and they are rows in `required-props.test.js` now: the missing
prop, a spread beside a prop that is passed, a marker with a reason and a ticket,
a marker without a ticket, a marker written as `//` between two tags, and a
declaration that is not a literal array.

The gap paragraph in `ImportPanel`'s docstring is rewritten rather than deleted,
because half of it is still true and dated: there is still no component harness
and still no `prop-types`. What changed is the last sentence.

**And the review found the instrument red in the right place and wrong about
what to do twice more, in its own code this time.** The summary line printed
`problems 0` **before** the loop that turns an unparsable code file into a
problem, so the day a `.jsx` lands the script would have printed `problems 0`,
then listed a problem, then exited 1 — `label-codes.js` pushes first and logs
after, and this one had the two the other way round. And the soundness filter,
the repair for the typo declaration above, was written inside `main()`, where no
fixture can ask it: the rows holding it asked about `destructures` instead, which
is one question short of the claim. It moved into `declaration()`, which now
answers `sound` and `unsound`, and three fixtures ask it directly —
`npm run census:test` 112 → **115**. The other three findings were #123's rule
again: a second-pass parse failure swallowed by a bare `catch { continue }`, the
`not code` count the three newest siblings print missing, and a blind-spot list
that said nothing about `export { REQUIRED_PROPS }`, a re-export, or a second
declaration in one file silently winning.

## #192 — the claim that was written in three places and held in one

`Mainpage.js` asked *is this segment all digits* with the same `/^\d+$/` written
out three times, one per crumb resolver: `teacherSectionCrumb` (#116),
`labelledIdCrumb`'s `numeric` (#185) and `wordCrumbLabel` (#189). #189 raised it
rather than merging it, because two of the three copies predated that ticket, and
the question cited #97 — *two places holding one opinion is a claim neither of
them can be shown to hold.* The ticket offered three options: consolidate and
move the mutants to the call sites, priced as *re-anchoring two sheets' mutants
and re-sweeping*; keep three and write the reason; or consolidate without moving
the mutants, which the ticket itself named as the trap.

**The cost line was refuted before anything was built**, which matters because
that is the one claim a ticket makes about the *fix* and so the one that decides
which option gets built (#77). Reading every file's `MUTANTS` in `mutation/` with
seven needles: **no mutant was anchored on any of the three lines.** The only file
that quotes a #192 site at all is #185's, and it quotes
`wordCrumbLabel(decodedNames, index)` — the **call**, not the expression inside.
So option 1's price was **zero re-aims**, not two sheets' worth, and the sweep it
owed was the one any new mutant owes.

**Then the question underneath the ticket's question: how many rows held the
claim?** The copies are what a grep counts; what the rows hold is what breaking
each copy separately measures. Widening one copy at a time so every segment reads
as an id, against `116a 185a 188a 10a` (baseline 22 passed):

| copy | widened | what went red |
|---|---|---|
| `teacherSectionCrumb` | 22 passed | **nothing** |
| `labelledIdCrumb` | 22 passed | **nothing** |
| `wordCrumbLabel` | 1 failed / 21 passed | `185a` row 1 |

One of three, and not because the situation is unreachable: `:sectionId` matches
any segment, `rubrics/:rubricId/criteria` matches a word, and
`courseOutcomes/:cloId/criteria` matches a word at the fifth segment. What no spec
did was *type* such an address — a grep of `e2e/` found five, all `:id` inside a
comment. **Untested, not structurally unreachable** (#102, #107), which is the
sentence a merge would have made unwritable.

**So the answer to *should these be merged* was an order, not a yes or a no**, and
it was the owner's: write the rows first, merge second. While the three copies
still stand, each row holds its own copy, and that is the only arrangement in
which #97's three claims are ever separately proved. Merge first and the three
become one claim with nobody able to say whether two of its three ways in reach
it. **In that order the merge buys proof rather than costing it** — the opposite
of what the ticket priced, and the opposite of #68's warning about one hook behind
fifteen screens, because there the merge removed rows that existed and here it
followed rows written for the purpose.

**The two rows assert the request and not the drawing**, because on a word at an
id's position the crumb reads the word either way: with the guard because nothing
was asked, and without it because the answer is a 404 and a refusal is left to say
nothing — #116's fourth reading, where a row cites the right mutant and never
states its claim. The drawing cannot tell the two apart; the absence of
`GET /api/teaching/sections/1a` can. The matcher had to be the resolver's **own
exact pathname**: the screen under each address asks for its own data under the
same prefix, so a prefix matcher would have answered *the shell asked* about the
screen's own request (#218). Measured rather than assumed — of the seventeen
screens under that id only `TeacherSection`, the index, fetches the Section for
itself, and `RubricCriteria` reads `/api/rubrics/:id/criteria` and never the
rubric. The fixture is `1a` rather than `abc` because a fixture is built where two
implementations **disagree**, not where one is missing (#117): `parseInt('1a')` is
`1`, which is the shape a consolidated helper is most likely to be written as.
Each row was run against the three unwidened copies first — both green, which is
what says a row measures nothing (#203) — and then against each copy widened in
turn: row 1 red only under the first, row 2 red only under the second.

**The merged helper took no bound, and that is a claim about what the caller
means.** `backend/lib/fields.js`'s `integerId` refuses anything above
`INT4_MAX`, and the obvious reading of a consolidation is that the frontend
should match it. It should not: a digits-only segment too big for the column is
still **what a person meant as a key**, so asking is right, the server answers
*not found* on its own, and the crumb drawing that segment literally says nothing
untrue. *A guard that greps the same is not the same guard — read what it does
with its `null`* (#107), here with the two guards' **callers** rather than their
bodies.

**The mutants went to the three call sites**, which is what keeps the extraction
free (#104): `isIdSegment` became a premise, like an attribute a locator is built
on, and each caller's *use* of it stayed a claim. Aiming them at the helper is
what would have turned three claims into one — a choice, not a consequence of the
merge. After the merge each kill is a **reachability** claim for that way in
(#191). Two of the three are the same shape, weakening one call site to `/^\d/`;
the third is not, and that is a measurement rather than a style: every id in the
addresses `185a` walks is all digits, so `/^\d/` is skipped on both sides there
and kills nothing. Only *no guard at all* reaches that call site's claim (#96).
The full suite, one run per mutant, because the mutants live in the shell all 837
rows share: `sectionsegmentloose` **1 failed / 836 passed**, `deepersegmentloose`
**1 failed / 836 passed**, each dying on its own row's `not.toContain` and taking
no bystander with it.

**And the sheet's own record of all this was already there to be aged.** #189's
paragraph names the three copies at `:39 :64 :101`, and it is a dated record, so
it stays and the new section says which of its sentences read differently today
(#54). Two of them do: the expression is no longer in three places, and *no mutant
can tell them apart* is no longer true of the first two copies. The third number
was already wrong when written — the copy was at `:111` — which is why the new
rows and the new section cite the code by **name** and not by line (#173).

## #196 — the two rules that pointed opposite ways, and the file that had already chosen

The ticket was a `question`, and it asked it well. The pipe that injects into the
`/api/plo-mapping` answer — fetch the real one, rewrite a field of the body, fulfil
with the rewritten body — was written out twice, in `117a` for a long รายวิชา name
and in `20a` for a curriculum with twenty outcomes, and what was duplicated was the
pipe and not what either row injects. Then it quoted `CLAUDE.md` against itself:
*an instrument is not an assertion — a fixture a second file needs is shared,
because no row's claim lives in it* (#171), so the merge is free; and *a ticket that
offers to de-duplicate is answered with what the merge costs the proof* (#68), so
the price is a closed ticket's spec reopened. **Both sentences are about this case,
and they point opposite ways.**

**What settled it was neither sentence but a file.** `e2e/support/late-answer.js`
already holds a shared route instrument for the same endpoint, and it already
carries a section headed *Why it is here rather than in a spec* — the same question
asked of the same screen, answered in writing, with the shape of the answer in the
code: the pipe is shared, and the precondition that the pipe fired stays in each
row (#51), which is what `wentThroughTheWindow` is. A rule that is met again is a
sentence in this ticket's story and not a second line in the index; a rule that was
**already applied to this very endpoint** is not even that — it is a decision, and
the work was to find it before writing the owner a question nobody needed to answer.

**The price was then measurable rather than arguable, and it was zero.** #68 says to
price the merge against the proof, so the question is which mutants are anchored in
the two files being changed. None are, and the census says so with a number: of the
**369 `FILES` entries** across `mutation/*.py` on 23 October 2569, **none** names
anything under `e2e/`, and exactly **one** names a test file at all —
`backend/test/auth.test.js`, whose `fromusesdbclock` and `untilusesdbclock` edit that
file's own SQL (#187). So *every entry is production code* is false while the
conclusion holds, which is the premise shape that expires on the wrong day (#141):
the right sentence is the dated census, not the law about the seam, **and it has to
be dated because a support file has held a mutant before** — `mutation/README.md`
records `e2e/support/auth.js` in `66`'s `FILES`, where it no longer is. What would
expire the figure is a leaf that takes a path under `e2e/`. Against that, moving a
route handler out of two spec files re-aims nothing, which is the difference between
extracting test code and extracting the shared string of #104, where the mutants had
to move to the call sites to keep the extraction free.

**The measurement that mattered was not the mutants, though.** Both rows were green
before the merge and green after, which proves nothing at all: a `page.route` that
is never installed reads perfectly. So the pipe was deliberately broken — one
`return route.fallback();` at the top of `withInjectedGrid` — and the run came back
**2 failed / 20 passed**, exactly those two rows, each dying on its own
*the injection landed* read. That is the row-level answer to the ticket's first
acceptance criterion, and it is the one *22 passed* cannot give. The probe was
deleted once the fix was measured (#207), being an instrument and no sheet's claim.

The three mutants that hold the two rows were then re-run over `117a 20a` together,
one at a time and never two harnesses at once, because `117` and `20` share
`frontend/src/components/ploMapping/exportPdf.js` (#125): `117:notwrappedgrid`
**1 failed / 21 passed** at row 8, `117:bycharacter` **2 failed / 20 passed** at rows
2 and 8, `20:narrowpage` **1 failed / 21 passed** at the twenty-outcome row, and a
clean control of **22 passed**. Each kills its own rows and no more, which is the
ticket's second criterion. The sheets' own kill tables were counted against one file
each and stay as the dated records they are (#54), with a note saying what was
re-measured and that the 388 in #20's borrowed-mutant paragraph was not.

## #197 — the reason for not deciding, and the fourth row the question did not contain

The ticket was an owner's question, and it gave two reasons for being one rather than
a task. Three ⚙ rows of `38-learning-detail-heatmap.md` assert colour; the colour was
hand-walked twice, in ☑ rows two lines below them; no row mentions the other. Fill in
a cross-reference, or leave it? The reasons not to decide alone were that **editing
those cells moves the sheet's line numbers under the tickets that cite them**, naming
#141, and that if the answer is *fill* it is a question about all 161 such rows and
not about the three somebody happened to walk past.

**A ticket's reason for not deciding itself is a claim like its numbers, and the first
one was false.** #141's table is *sheet → component file → line*, and the line beside
this sheet's name is `frontend/src/pages/LearningDetails.js:79` — a line in the
component, not in the sheet. `grep -rn "38-learning-detail-heatmap.md:"` over the
repository returns nothing but the three sentences that quote the command itself, in
this sheet, in the handoff and here: **no citation of this sheet by line number
exists**, so
the edit the reason was protecting against costs nothing. The rule the reason
invoked is real (*a citation by line number ages the day anything above it grows*),
and what it licenses is the one-minute grep, not the conclusion. Half of an owner's
question was therefore not the owner's: the reason for asking it had expired, or had
never been true.

**The second reason was the right species and the wrong grain.** 161 is #194's
figure for every ⚙ row naming any of fourteen drawn properties; this ticket's three
rows assert **colour**, which is one of the fourteen. Re-running #194's selection
through `mutation/anchors.py`'s own traversal (#194: a counter that disagrees with the
instrument the figures came from is the counter's bug) gave 188 word-hits, of which
**27 already carried an annotation** and 161 did not, and of those **47 named a
colour**. Forty-seven rows is a hand read, and the hand read is what the question
needed: it found what #194 found at 65, that nearly all of them **mention** colour
rather than claim it — a *แถบเขียว* used as the address of a sentence, `15-programs.md`
writing on its own face that it keeps colour in a row of its own *so this row does not
claim it*, `40-clo-assessment-report.md` claiming the verdict is a **word** and not
only a red cell, which is the opposite of an appearance claim, and ten #149 rows
already annotated with *the wording and the position of that line are not claimed*.

**And two sheets had already written the annotation the owner was being asked for.**
`16-subjects.md` and `18-program-subjects.md` both claim a field *is grey*, and both
say in the cell that the greyness is what the browser draws **from** the `disabled`
attribute, so the seam asserts the cause. The answer to *should we write this down*
was already in the corpus in the house's own words, which is #86's shape read for a
wording instead of for a control: the question had a precedent before it had an owner.

**The hand read also returned a finding the question did not contain.**
`24-teacher-dashboard.md`'s criterion 2 claims *a white box, not a red band*, is
marked ⚙, and says itself that `24a` row 2 asserts the sentence names the term —
which the spec confirms: its two assertions on the screen are that `getByText` and a
`toHaveCount(0)` over the section cards, and neither touches the colour. And unlike this sheet's three rows, **nothing walked it
either**: that sheet's walk record says *every row that is not ⚙ was walked*, which
puts a ⚙ row outside the walk by construction. The same species, one step worse: here
the walk happened and the cross-reference was missing, there the walk never happened.
That is a walk-queue finding rather than a documentation one, so it went to the owner
as its own question and became [#229](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/229),
`ready-for-human` because the claim is *does a person read this as an explanation and
not as an error*, which is answered by an eye. **A population re-derived to price a
question answers the question and surveys its neighbours in the same pass** (#223 from
the other side), and what the neighbours return need not be the same kind of thing the
ticket was about.

What was changed is four cells and nothing else. The three on this sheet now name the
rows below them with their dates, say which half each spec actually asserts — row 2
pins the five **tokens** in order, row 3 reads only the `!` and the label and never
the redness — and the third of them says it does not claim colour at all, its claim
being the label's text, with the half a person would add being *whether anybody hears
it*, which it never claimed (#163). The fourth, on `24`, says the colour half is
asserted by nobody and walked by nobody, and points at #229. No mark moved, which is
what the ticket asked for; the figures it published did move, and they are dated
rather than corrected: ☑ 499 · ⚙ 731 · ◐ 23 · ☐ 14 was 8–21 October's, and on 23
October `anchors.py` prints `marks 1417`, which the census reusing its traversal
splits ☑ 517 · ⚙ 847 · ◐ 26 · ☐ 27 —
the tree grew, and a survey of the store has a date on it (#50, #85, #172).

## #198 — the re-read that was a remount, and the rule that came back out of the structure

#155 settled *re-read when the address does not move, and only then*. The way it was
built was a key on the shell's `<Outlet />`, and #198 asked what else a remount takes
with it. The ticket offered three options: accept it, put the acting grant into each
panel's load dependencies, or lift the typed draft above the outlet.

**The ticket's own count of what is at stake was wrong in two places, and the
population was not six.** It wrote that all six landings hold an add form of their
own. Four do; `/teacher/teacherDashboard` has neither a filter nor a form, which its
own docstring says on purpose, and `/main/programLevelByIntake` has no form, holding
instead a drill-down and two pickers. And the shape the whole ticket needs — two
grants of one role code at different scopes, because `landingPath` is keyed on
`role_id` alone — cannot exist for `FULL_ADMIN` at all: `user_roles`' primary key is
`(user_id, role_id, scope_id)` and that role's scope is the literal string
`'FULL_ADMIN'`, so a second grant is the same row. `FACULTY_ADMIN` needs a second
faculty, which the seed does not have. Five landings are reachable and one of those
needs SQL.

**The delivered UI answered the Out-of-Scope question before the owner could.**
`DEEP-QA-FRONTEND/src/components/RoleDropdown.js` calls `window.location.reload()` on
every switch, so what was delivered threw away the page, the filter and the draft on
*every* switch and not only on the one that stays put. Option 1 is therefore narrower
than the delivered behaviour rather than equal to it, and every option in the ticket
moves a number the **rebuild** chose in #155, not one the student's code chose — none
of them is a divergence (#156). That is what made all four options allowed, and the
fourth is the one the measurement produced: hand the generation *down* and let each
landing name it as a dependency of its own read.

**Option 2 as the ticket wrote it is red, and one row said so in forty seconds.**
Putting the acting grant into `ProgramSubjects`' load dependencies fails `155a` row 2
— the screen a moving switch is leaving asks `/api/program-subjects` again on its way
out, under a hat that may not be able to read it. The probe for option 4 passed both
`155a` rows and a draft-survival row written against `HEAD`, where it fails with
`element(s) not found`: at `HEAD` the dialog is not wrong, it is gone. Both probes were
deleted once they had answered (#207).

**What landed is three sites, not two.** `RoleDropdown` says the switch stayed put,
the shell hands the number down through `context/ScreenGeneration.js`, and each landing
reads it in its `load`'s dependency list. The number is read nowhere in any load's
body, which is honest and which `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` calls an unnecessary
dependency: the tree is otherwise warning-free, so each of the six carries the repo's
own idiom, a disable line with the reason written above it. `useCohortPickers` reads
it too, for the list of curricula an account may report on — the intakes do not,
because they belong to a curriculum and not to a grant.

**A row can be blocked from reading its second claim by the screen it is standing
on.** The first draft of `198a` row 1 asserted the draft survived *and* that the table
had become the new grant's rows. The table is not in the document while the add form
is open — the dialog replaces the list rather than sitting over it — so the poll read
`[]` for fifteen seconds on a screen that was behaving. Two claims that cannot be
observed in the same state are two rows: the drawing stays `155a` row 1's claim, and
this row pairs the draft with the **request**, which is observable with the form open.

**A fix that moves a rule from one structural point into each caller gives back the
census question the earlier ticket closed by construction.** #155's sheet says in so
many words that the ticket's instruction to let a census choose the screen was made
moot, because one key on one outlet covered every panel structurally. After #198 the
rule is six identical lines, and nothing asks whether the seventh landing has it. That
is [#230](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/230), opened the same day, and it
is the price of the owner's answer rather than a defect in it.

**And when the mechanism moves, a mutant's kill moves with it.** `nokey` quoted
`<Outlet key={screenEpoch} />`, which no longer exists; it was re-aimed at the
dependency it has become — the same claim, that the second site is necessary, not a
different mistake (#203) — and renamed `noscreendep`, because a mutant's name is part
of what the sheet claims about it. `alwaysreread` is the sharper case: it still
reproduces the declined option faithfully, but `155a` row 2 leaves
`/main/course-in-program`, which is nobody's landing and now reads the generation
never, so that row no longer dies under it. The kill moved to `198a` row 2, which
leaves the committee's own landing, and `155a` row 2's claim **for screens that are not
landings** became structurally unreachable rather than unproved (#179): no mutant can
make a screen re-read a generation it does not read. The situation of both rows is
still held by `81:staysput`, re-swept the same day, which kills them both.

**Narrowing a remount to a re-fetch owes every read the mount made, and the one it
misses is the read somebody wrote *fetched once* above.** A remount re-read everything
the screen asks for on mount; a dependency re-reads one list. `Rubrics` asks for two —
its own rows, and the curricula this grant may place a rubric in — and the second was
fetched once under a comment that said itself it was a property of the grant, which was
true exactly while a new grant meant a new mount. The review of 23 October 2569 found
it: after the fix the sentence saying which curricula the form may choose from was the
old hat's until a reload, which is #155's defect read **backwards** — the rows changed
scope and the control over them did not. The dependency was added because of the row
that caught it, and that row was run against the unfixed code first, where it died at
its claim and not at its precondition (#203). `Programs` holds the same pair for
departments and got the same dependency the same hour; which screen *proves* a rule
many screens hold is still the census's answer and not the subject's (#68, #171) — so
#230 now carries two questions rather than one: does a new landing read the generation,
**and** does a landing's second read read it.

## #215 — the endpoint that answered a different question, and the audience that said so

#90 gave the scope picker the kind word — *ภาควิชา · วิศวกรรมคอมพิวเตอร์ (05)* — and closed with a debt
it had measured itself: three more places draw a scope for somebody to **read**, and all
three say only the code. The owner answered on 23 October 2569 that the two
administration screens take the picker's wording letter for letter, with no change to the
server, and that the third is a question of its own.

**An endpoint that answers *what may be offered* is not one that answers *what this value
is*, and the gap shows as an audience.** `GET /api/users/grantable` is the only answer in
the system carrying a scope's name and kind, so all four sites that want the words want
it. The two that could have it were the two already holding it for their own pickers:
`GrantsPanel` draws the table above its picker and `Users` draws the role column on the
screen that opens that panel, so the fix was a lookup in a list already on the screen, no
new request and nothing added to the server. `RoleDropdown` could not be fixed that way at
all, and the reason is not that it lacks a call — it is that its readers are the people the
endpoint refuses. The hat picker is drawn for everybody with two roles; `grantable` is for
administrators. Asking it from there would answer 403 for a teacher, which is the shape
#218 names from the other side: a matcher two questions share cannot be narrowed for one of
them. So the third site is not a smaller version of the first two. It needs `/api/me` to
carry what it draws, which is a server change and a ticket of its own — #231, with the
reason and the date written on `10-application-shell.md` beside a ☐ row rather than left in
this prose (#119, #125).

**The wording moved into a module and the proof did not move with it.** `scopeLabel` had
lived inside `GrantPicker`; three screens now share it, so it went into
`frontend/src/components/users/scopeLabel.js` — and every one of #90's five mutants was
re-aimed there and re-swept, because the file a mutant edits changed name even though the
code it edits did not. That re-aim cost the proof nothing exactly because the mutants stay
where they are: the shared function is the **premise** of all four rows and each screen's
*use* of it is still that screen's own claim (#104). What the re-sweep then showed is the
other half of #202: `nokind` and `swapsthewords` now kill two rows more than their sheet
credited them with, not because anybody edited them but because a spec gained rows they can
reach. No instrument says so — the anchor is exact and the code untouched — only running
them again.

**The sweep is what said to split a row, and it said so by killing it at the wrong
assertion.** Row 3 began as one row holding both halves of the fallback: the accounts
column keeps the bare code, and so does the panel cell, with the picker's own options read
beside it to prove *why*. `dashwhenunknown` — the dash this ticket declined, made to run
(#48) — died at the first of those, so the panel's claim sat under a red line and was
proved by nothing (#88). The split is #198's shape rather than a tidying: the editor
**replaces** the accounts table, so the two readings cannot be taken in one state. Row 4
then needed `grantable`'s options waited for by what the answer carries, because
`openEditor` waits for the panel's own read and the picker's second call has not drawn yet
when it returns (#132).

**And one mutant's row list was decided by the fixture's arithmetic.** `anyscopewilldo`
takes the first scope in the list instead of the matching one, and it kills row 1 at its
**second** assertion: the first scope a 05 administrator may offer *is* department 05, so
the faithful copy of half the defect makes the row's first claim true (#206). Rows 1 and 2
were run against the unfixed code before their mutants were written and died at their
claims; rows 3 and 4 passed there — what both of them claim is the bare code, which is
what the two screens already drew — so those two were bought for free and it is
`dashwhenunknown`, not a red, that makes them measure anything (#203).

**And two of the four rows were killed at the row they were looking for rather than at the
cell they were reading, which the review found and only a re-sweep could have.** Rows 1 and
4 read the panel's scope cell through `grantCell`, which finds a grant by its role **and**
its scope code — so on those rows the code was both the locator and the claim, and every
mutant that rewrote the cell left the row unfindable: the red was a timeout and the
assertion under it was never read, which is #139's wait in place of an assertion and the
half of #213 that says to be wrong on the side the row reads and right on the side it
presses. Here no mutant can be wrong on one side only, because one function writes both,
so the repair is the **reader**: find the row by the role alone, assert that the role gives
one row (#51), and read the column by its header (#173). Row 3 came out of the same reading
with a settle point it had been missing — `grantable` draws nothing of its own on the
accounts list, so before it lands every scope reads as a bare code and the row would have
passed on a screen that never asked (#132); the fence is another account's row, which puts
`userscode` and #90's two mutants on row 3 as well, dying at the precondition rather than
at the claim. The third sweep then shows every claim dying at its own line.

**And the clean suite's one red was not this ticket's, which five runs said and three did
not.** The full browser suite ended 843 passed and one failed: `198a` row 1, the row #198
closed the day before, asserting that a form typed and not saved survives a switch of hats
that stays put. The row reproduced on its own, it went green with `HEAD`'s
`useGrantable.js` put back, it went red again with mine, and it went red with the
dependency taken out and only the hook call left — three reproductions against a control,
pointing at a file that is not in `Rubrics`'s import graph at all. The probe built from the
row itself then refused to go green on **either** side, which is the tell: a red is not a
measurement until the same read has been seen green (#171). `--repeat-each=5` at `HEAD`
answered ✘ ✓ ✓ ✘ ✘, and the row's own copy in a second file failed beside the original in
one invocation. So the row is red about three times in five whatever is in the tree, and
what the first three runs measured was the coincidence #150 names in as many words. The
mechanism is a real defect and it is not intermittent: `RubricForm` resets its draft in an
effect whose dependency list holds `onlyOne`, derived from `programs.filter(...)` and so a
new identity every time the second read #198 added sets `programs` — the form is thrown
away by its own effect, and the row is green only when it reads before that answer lands
(#152's seventh reading). It is [#232](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/232), with
the sheet's own cell dated beside the ⚙ it still carries, because the mark is that
ticket's to move.

## #232 — the form its own effect threw away, and the owner's question that was already void

[#232](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/232) is the defect
[#198](https://github.com/khthana/Deep-QA/issues/198) was opened to prevent, read backwards and
landed by #198 itself. #198 narrowed a re-read from a remount to a re-fetch so that a form typed
and not saved survives a switch of hats which stays put; its own review then added the screen's
generation to the dependency list of `Rubrics`'s **second** read, the curricula this account may
place a rubric in. That read sets `programs`. `RubricForm` computes `onlyOne` from
`programs.filter(...)` and had it in the dependency list of an effect that reset the whole draft —
a new array identity every time the answer lands, so the form was thrown away by its own effect
the moment the thing #198 narrowed the remount to keep was re-read.

**The row was red about three runs in five, and the screen was wrong on every one of them.** The
assertion was a retrying `toHaveValue` read from the press onwards, so it passed whenever it won
the race with the answer; the sampler built from the row read the field ten frames at 300ms and
forty frames at 500ms and saw `n=1 v=""` in every single frame. What was intermittent was the
**read**, not the thing read (#164), which is #152's seventh reading of a survivor met in a row
rather than in a mutant. The repair is the row: ask for the response before the press, then settle
on what the answer *carries* — the new scope's `option` appearing in the picker (#132) — and read
the field on the far side of that, where the claim lives on one side of a known event instead of
racing it. That settle point is row 1's precondition and row 3's claim, asserted where it is used
(#51).

**The owner's question the ticket wrote down was void by the time it was written.** Item 3 asked
whether an open, half-typed form should show the new hat's curriculum or the old one's. Row 3 of
`198a`, landed hours earlier the same day, had already decided that the pool is the new grant's;
and a `program_id` outside the pool is one the server refuses, authority being derived from the
database (ADR-0002) — and on the add form no `option` draws it either, the old hat's curricula
being absent from the new answer altogether. So *keep the old curriculum* does not name a state
the person could see — it names an empty select that cannot be saved. One consistent rule was left:
keep every typed field, keep `program_id` while it is still in reach, re-pick when it is not. The
question was answered by measuring what each option would actually put on the screen, not by
asking. **An option the system cannot carry to the end is not an option**, and the half of the
question that looked like a preference had already been settled by a sibling row.

**The fix is two halves, so it is two mutants, and one of them is bought for free.** `value` — state
in the screen above — is the only thing that resets the draft; the pool is written as a *value*, a
string of ids, and a second effect re-picks only when the field names something no longer in it,
reading the live state through a functional updater rather than through a closure (#201). Row 4 was
written for the second half and its **first** assertion passed against the unfixed code, because
wiping the form re-picks the curriculum anyway (#203): a control bought for free. What measures the
fix is its second assertion, and what tells the two apart is `keepsthecurriculum`, the ticket's own
option 1 made to run (#48) — the form survives, the curriculum never moves, row 4 dies at its first
assertion and **row 1 passes**. Beside it `arrayidentity` is the diagnosed code made to run (#115),
killing row 1 and row 4's second assertion. Both needed more edits than the claim: a mutant that
leaves `starting` or `pool` with no reader turns `no-unused-vars` into a failed compile under
`CI=true`, which is a mutant that stops the application rather than one that fails a row (#101).
The ticket's own wording for the second half — *auto-fill the curriculum only while nobody has
touched the field* — is not what landed: a touched flag would keep a value the switch has just taken
out of reach, which is a form the person cannot save, so what landed is the membership test and the
divergence is written on the sheet with its date.

**The `if (editing) return` branch was written up as having no mutant, and the review measured that
the same day.** The reasoning was that an existing rubric's curriculum came from the list this
account reaches, so it is always in the pool and the *in the pool* test does not move the field
either — the situation that separates the two conditions cannot be built at this seam. But
`reachablePrograms` says of itself that *Retired ones come too*, and the pool is `usable`, which
filters the retired ones out. A rubric filed in a retired curriculum therefore holds a `program_id`
the pool does not contain, which is exactly that situation, and a row can build it: switch a
curriculum off through the faculty administrator's route, open the editor, put it back in `finally`.
**A claim called structurally unreachable is the third of #102's three answers read as the second**,
and what tells them apart is the file that defines the pool's own population — the reasoning named
`programs` and the code reads `usable`. Row 5 holds the branch, `movesanexistingrubric` kills it,
and the first draft of the sheet is the kind of overclaim that reads as modest (#116).

## #216 — the code that was not a code, and the audience of one

#90 gave the scope picker the kind word and the stored code in brackets —
*ภาควิชา · วิศวกรรมคอมพิวเตอร์ (05)*, *คณะวิศวกรรมศาสตร์ (ENG)* — and one entry in that
field read *ทั้งมหาวิทยาลัย (FULL_ADMIN)*. `FULL_ADMIN` is not a code anybody in this
organisation says. It is the sentinel `CONTEXT.md` §Scope chose in place of a null so that
`user_roles.scope_id` could stay `NOT NULL`. The owner answered on 24 October 2569 that
the brackets go with it, which was option 1 of the three the ticket offered.

**A value the schema chose is not a value anybody says.** The field teaches *brackets hold
this thing's code*, so the day it prints the stored value for every entry it publishes the
one entry whose stored value exists only to keep a column non-null. Nothing was wrong in
the data and nothing was wrong in the picker's rule: what was wrong is that a storage
decision had become wording. And because it is wording, who may change it is settled by
who chose it (#156) — which is the next measurement, not an argument.

**The delivered screen answered that one before the owner did.** `AddRoleDialog.js` drew
its entries as `{scope_id} - {nameTH} - {year}` and `user_rolesController.getScope` never
returned an entry for `FULL_ADMIN` at all, so the delivered system never showed the
sentinel as a scope. There is no delivered number or word being diverged from here: the
string is the rebuild's own, start to finish, which makes the ticket an owner's question
rather than a regression (#86, #166). Had the control been there and dropped, the wording
would have been decided already.

**#215 had widened the population, and the ticket was written before it.** The ticket was
opened on 17 October 2569, when the picker was the only site; #215 landed on 23 October and
gave two more screens the same words. On the day the question was asked the picker and the
held-roles table read `ทั้งมหาวิทยาลัย (FULL_ADMIN)` and the accounts list read
`ผู้ดูแลระบบกลาง (ทั้งมหาวิทยาลัย (FULL_ADMIN))` — brackets inside brackets, which no row had
ever read, and which is the third site's own version of the defect. A ticket's claim is
dated by the day it was written (#66); here the population was.

**And the audience is one person, which is #215's rule met from the other side.** The
fallback `scopeNamed` keeps for a code it cannot name — the one rows 3 and 4 of §#215 are
about — cannot be reached for this scope at all, and the clause that does it is not about
scope alone. `backend/routes/users.js` filters the accounts list with
`COALESCE(SENIORITY, 99) >= $2` beside `OWN_SCOPE = ANY($1)`, both built from the
expressions `backend/auth/administration.js` defines - its own single-account read numbers
the same clause `$3`. Seniority is the half that excludes **every** holder of a grant
confined to nothing, whatever their place; the account actually measured, `admin01`, is
outside the scope half too, having neither a department nor a programme, which `OWN_SCOPE`'s
own comment calls the intended answer. Either way a faculty or a department administrator
searching for it is shown **0 rows**. Whoever may read that grant is offered it, and so has
its name. That measurement came out of a probe that failed: the first version granted
`FULL_ADMIN` through the screen and then signed in as a `05` administrator to read the row,
which timed out and left a grant behind in `deep_core_e2e`. Rewriting the arrangement below
the seam with SQL and a `finally` (#181) did not fix it, because the row was not slow — the
account was gone from the list. The failing probe was the measurement.

**The ticket's cost line was a claim like its numbers, and it was the wrong way round
(#77).** It said row 4 of `90a` — *the grant confined to nothing is left as it was* — would
have to change. Both of that row's assertions (there is exactly one such entry; it carries
no kind word) are **true on both sides of option 1**, so nothing had to change: what was
owed was a new assertion, one new mutant, and one re-aim. Option 3, *keep it as it is*, was
not free either, for the same reason in reverse: a decision taken needs the declined option
made to run (#48). The price is read off the mount points, not off the ticket.

**Three claims in one row, and the third one needed its own mutant.** The new assertion
reads the whole string with `toBe` rather than the absence of a substring, because what is
owed is one sentence and a code could come back in any shape — which is also why the
declined option 2, Thai words inside the brackets, needs no mutant of its own: anything
back inside the brackets fails both rows. It sits **below** the two older assertions, so
`namestheunconfined` still dies at the second and the third would be proved by nothing
(#88) if it had no killer of its own. It has two: `216:bracketsthesentinel`, the pre-ticket
code made to run (#115), which dies at the third line with the two above it passing; and
`90:nokind`, which the fix re-aimed to three edits and which reaches the third claim
honestly, because the code before #90 bracketed every scope's code, the sentinel included.
A re-aimed mutant's kill is read against the row it is *for* and not against the total
(#203): `nokind` went from killing three rows of one file to killing eight of two.

## #219 — the census that had to run, and the shape that was already gone

#219 was a `question` with three parts, all of them about test code: merge `pressPager` and
`stepBack` into `support/pager.js` (shape one), make every confirm-box `ยกเลิก` press use the
scoped, detachment-waiting `dismiss` (shape two), give form `ยกเลิก` presses a form-scoped
helper or leave them (shape three). The owner answered on 24 October 2569: shape one **void**,
shape two **`118a` only**, shape three **left, with what would break it written down**.

**Where one name is on two controls, which one a row presses is a runtime property.** `ยกเลิก`
is the word on the confirm box's button and on every form's. 37 of the 45 sites that name it
build their locator on a bare `page`, and nothing in the text of those files says which of the
two is on the screen at that moment — the answer is a property of the run. So the ticket's
first closing criterion, *classify every press by instrument and not by reading*, could not be
met by a census of the source at all. It took three instruments: one that holds the
**population** by parsing (`e2e/probes/219-cancel-sites.js`), one that patches
`Locator.prototype.click` inside the worker and asks the element itself
(`219-cancel-presses.js`), `el.closest('.max-w-sm')` against `el.closest('form')`, and one that
**joins** them (`219-join.js`), because without it the per-site table would have been a hand
pairing — a reading, which is the thing the criterion refuses. Over a full
run of 849 rows it recorded **108 presses, 48 on the box and 60 on a form, with no `neither`
and no `both`** — the two selectors separate every press in the suite. Attributed back to the
sites: 20 the box's, 25 a form's. The ticket's own hand reading, which it dated and called a
claim, had said 7 and 13.

**A red ends a runtime census, and it reads exactly like a suite that stopped pressing**
(#208's tell one layer along). Playwright tears the worker down after a failing test and the
next one starts unpatched, with nothing to install the patch again. The second measuring run
recorded **12** presses against the first's 108, over a single red at `142a` — and no
instrument says so, because the file it writes is simply shorter. The count is the tell, not
the exit code. The repair was to make the probe cheap enough not to cause the red: the stack is
captured before the first `await` but **formatted** after the press, because some of these rows
are racing a write and the formatting is the expensive half.

**A stack cannot cross an `await`, so the question *which row is pressing* is asked of the
runner.** 56 of one run's 108 presses came back with no `e2e/` frame at all, and the nine
`remove*` helpers reported only themselves: an `async` function's stack holds its synchronous
callers and loses everything across a tick. `test.info()` is answered by the worker and is the
same answer wherever it is asked from, which closed the gap to zero. Joining the two
instruments then went by frame, by test title, and by file; the last site to resolve,
`142a:302`, sits inside a title written as a template, which matches the runtime titles by the
literal halves of that template in order and never by equality. **And a press log is dated against
