the tree it was taken from**: the frame reader keys on `file:line`, so re-running the join against
#219's own log now reports `? 1` for `confirm-dialog.js:77`, which the log names at `:74` because
the fix grew three lines of docblock above it — a citation by line number ages the day anything
above it grows (#173), and here the instrument saying so is the right answer rather than a failure.

**And the census counted itself** (#173). Its own `CANCEL` comparisons — the mechanism it
classifies other sites *with* — are call expressions whose arguments hold the word, so its
first run returned 47 sites where the suite has 45. It leaves itself out by `__filename`, which
is identity: a list of names would have been a thing a new file makes lie (#126).

**Shape one was void, and not because it was wrong when it was written.** `96f076b` (#210)
deleted all fifteen lines that named `pressPager`, `stepBack` and `awayAndBack` on 19 October
2569 — **the day after the ticket was filed** — and added none; the three specs now call `next`,
`previous`, `untilDrawn` and `toLastPage` from `pager.js`, which is what the ticket asked for.
A ticket's *what is wrong* is a claim from the day it was written (#66), and this is a species
the catalogue did not have: not aged, not generalised, not never true, but **already carried
out by a later ticket**, leaving the ticket's subject absent from the tree. What stands in its
place is a different triple — `askToRemove` in `206a`, `207a` and `208a`, where 207a's body is
208a's plus one `dismiss(page)` line — which went out as #236 rather than being carried in prose
here (#119, #125). Shape one's own reopen condition is on the sheet, because a shape closed as void
still owes one: the day a spec writes its own pager stepper again instead of calling `pager.js`.

**Shape two's own figures had aged in the other direction.** The shared `dismiss` was imported
by five files when #217 wrote the paragraph saying so, seven when #219 counted, and eight once
`118a` came over: a claim written in prose expires like a number (#130), and the fix to the
prose is dated rather than rewritten. `118a` was the one site worth moving, and the reason is
not that its copy was unscoped but **where its calls sit**: rows 3 and 4 dismiss the box and
then open a second confirmation in their `finally`, which is the one place in the suite where
not waiting for the first box to leave has a race to lose. That reason lasted eight hours:
#235 took those second confirmations out the same evening, which leaves the move right for the
other half of its reason — the scope — and is why the comment in `118a` is dated rather than
deleted (#54, and #235's story below).

**The other ten box presses are instruments of their own screens, not copies racing the shared
one.** Nine live in `support/*-screen.js` inside `remove*(page, …, { confirm = true })`, where
the `confirm: false` path *is* the dismissal, and each has exactly one caller taking that path
— nine callers, nine single presses in the runtime table. Merging them would not delete a copy;
it would move the press one layer down and make the shared helper's wait a premise of every
caller it already has (#81), which is a price no row asked for. The condition that would
reopen it is written beside the answer: the day one of those helpers is called with a form open
as well, or a screen draws its confirmation with something other than `.max-w-sm`.

**Leaving shape three was an answer with a measurement under it.** The non-ambiguity of 25
unscoped form presses is accidental (#93) — box and form are never on the screen together in
those rows — and the measurement is that **no press of the 108 answered `both`**. What would
break it is a screen that draws a confirmation over an open form, or two forms on one screen,
which `146a` nearly has already. The lucky half of this accident is that a click is strict: the
day a row resolves two `ยกเลิก` buttons it fails, rather than pressing the wrong one quietly.

**The re-sweep's kill counts were right and its durations were the finding.** Criterion 3 asked
for the mutants of the files that changed; only `118a` changed, and only
`mutation/118-thai-line-breaks.py` runs it. All three mutants reproduced their documented kills
exactly — 2, 2 and 1, at the documented rows. What moved was time: a clean run takes 26.2
seconds and `nobreakwords` took 2.4 minutes, because rows 3 and 4 die at a **timeout** and not
at an assertion. Their body throws before reaching `dismiss`, the box stays, and the `finally`
presses *ลบ* underneath its cover until the test times out; and a throwing `finally` replaces
the body's error (#181), so the report names `rubrics-screen.js` and the `lines drawn:` message
the row wrote for a person to read appears nowhere. A kill count cannot tell a row that died at
its claim from a row that died at a timeout — **the duration can** (#146). It is not #219's
defect: `dismiss` is the last statement of the `try` and the clean run passes five rows in 26.2
seconds, so it dates to the day the file was written, 24 September 2569. It went out as #235
rather than being fixed here (#119, #125).

**The answer to a de-duplication question can be one copy.** #192's answer was *rows first,
merge second*; #196's was *merge, and the price is a census with a date on it*; this one's is
*move the single site where the duplication can cost something, and write down why the others
are not copies*. What made that answerable was pricing each shape separately, which the ticket
itself demanded — `dismiss` is shared because no row's claim lives in getting out of a box
(#171), and that reason has to be asked of each shape rather than of the three at once.

## #235 — the cleanup the row's own failure had locked out

The ticket was #219's own by-catch, filed rather than written into prose (#119, #125) and not
#219's defect: `dismiss` was already the last statement of the `try`, and the clean run passed
five rows in 26.2 seconds. It dated to the day `118a` was written, 24 September 2569, and what
made it visible a month later was a sweep's **durations** rather than its kill count (#146).

**A teardown through the screen is reached through whatever state the row's failure left.** Rows
3 and 4 made a rubric, read the confirmation dialog it drew, and tidied up by pressing *ลบ* a
second time and confirming it. That works on every passing run and on no failing one: the body
throws at its claim *before* `dismiss`, so the first box is still over the table, and the second
press retries into `<div class="fixed inset-0 z-[9998] …">` until the file runs out of time. The
teardown's obstacle was built by the only event that makes a teardown interesting. This is a
third way a cleanup speaks over the claim, beside #181's two: no mutant is needed, and a genuine
regression caught by a clean suite would have been reported the same way.

**And the report is a claim to measure, not to reason about.** The kill count was right — 2, 2
and 1, the rows the sheet names — while what came out named `support/rubrics-screen.js:123` and
a timeout. The cheap instrument is where the report's own code frame points: Playwright prints the
source around the dying assertion, so `grep -c 'lines drawn'` over the saved output counts the
frames that stopped at the rows' own claim rather than counting any sentence the run wrote. It
answered **0** before the fix, which is the whole defect in one number, and **4** and **2** after
it, for the two mutants. A sweep has two halves to check, the number and the sentence, and only
the first has an instrument built for it.

**The fix was the repo's own answer, found by asking for it.** #181's story had already settled
this shape in `155a`: the restore goes below the seam over HTTP, it asserts nothing, it records
its own trouble in a module-level variable, and a last `afterAll` throws if anything was recorded
— last, so that it fails the file without speaking over a row. What it is *not* there for is to
catch a leftover: `hold()` takes out whatever rows appeared when it releases, so the suite's own
`leftovers` report would stay clean with this file's housekeeping broken, which is why the
refusal has to be carried by hand. `rubrics-screen.js` gained a `clearRubric` that answers with
the response rather than asserting on it, which is what makes *whether a refused teardown fails
the file* the caller's decision and not the helper's.

The ticket's second option — close the box as the first statement of the `finally` — was declined
with a date: it is still a teardown through the code under test, so the day the failure is in
*opening* the box, `dismiss` is the call that times out and the ticket comes back. An instrument
is not an assertion (#171), and a teardown is an instrument. **Its third option was not a rival
to the first and was taken as well**: a ticket can write its options as a list to choose from
while two of them answer different questions — *where does the teardown go* and *who speaks when
the teardown itself is refused* — and here the second is what keeps the first from being silent,
because a helper that asserts nothing refuses in silence by design.

**What the fix falsified was a sentence eight hours old.** #219 had just written into `118a` that
the shared `dismiss` mattered there because rows 3 and 4 open a second confirmation in their
`finally` — the one place in the suite where not waiting has a race to lose. Those second
confirmations are what this ticket removed. The comment was rewritten with both dates rather
than deleted, the move staying right for the other half of its reason, and #219's story in this
file got a clause instead of an edit, because a story is a record of a day (#54).

The sweep's own numbers moved the way the mechanism predicts and no further: the two mutants that
kill rows 3 and 4 came down to twenty-five and twenty-four seconds, where the timeout used to be,
and the clean run and `notglued` came down a little because the housekeeping stopped pressing two
buttons. What they fell *from* is two figures with two provenances, which is worth saying rather
than averaging: the 3.0 minutes for `nobreakwords` is the one this ticket measured on the unfixed
code, and #219's own sweep table reads 2.4 for that same mutant and 1.4 for `nowrapinstead`, which
nothing re-measured here. A duration is a sample (#102, #146), so the claim this story makes is
the direction and the floor, not the difference.

## #220 — the sentence that closed the way in, and the mount point nobody had counted

A tracker rather than a defect. #141 closed with fifteen of its sixteen sites proved and one left:
`GrantsPanel`, which carries three claims — `load`'s flag and the answers of `add` and `remove`.
What a tracker owes each visit is not a fix but the measurement that could expire it, and this
visit two of the ticket's own sentences moved.

**A ticket's line numbers are a claim with a date, and two readings minutes apart say whose line
it was.** The ticket's table, written on 19 October 2569, gave `:84` `:128` `:168`. The census run
before anything was touched gave `:85` `:129` `:169`, and the one run after this ticket added a
seven-line comment to `load` gave `:92` `:136` `:176`. Eight lines, of which exactly one belonged
to somebody else's work in the six days between — and only the first of those two readings can
say so. That is why the ticket's own first criterion is *measure with `--guarded`, not by reading
the paragraph above*: a hand-kept number in a file that grows every ticket is already wrong
(#130), including when the file is the ticket.

**An *unreachable* that rests on a prop is a claim about every place the component is mounted.**
The sentence that has closed this way in since #133 describes one screen's JSX: the form replaces
the table, so a second account can only be opened once this panel has come down. That is a reason
about a screen, and the thing it holds up is a claim about a component — every mount point is a
place where a prop could change without an unmount. Measured on 25 October 2569: `GrantsPanel` is
imported and drawn in exactly one file, and `listGrants`, `grantRole` and `revokeGrant` are
imported nowhere else in `src/`. So the reason covers the population and not only the screen it
was written on, which nobody had established in the three months the three sites have been
waiting. It is #68's rule — *a guard written for one caller is a claim about every caller* — in
the direction of the way in rather than of the guard, and it cuts both ways: the day anything
draws this panel beside a list, three claims become reachable and nothing in the suite would say
so (#131). *One mount point* is a dated claim like the line numbers, and the census that found it
is a grep for `import`, blind to a dynamic import, a re-export or a wrapper that passes the prop
on — the shape `required-props.js` writes down about itself (#182).

The rest was the ticket's own list, measured rather than re-read (criterion 3): `setEditing` still
has four sites in `Users.js` and the two reachable while the form is open both write `null`;
`users` is still mounted without an `:id`; and `141c` ran 4 of 4 in 57.9 seconds with row 4 — the
net that counts the controls while the panel is open — green. All three sites therefore end as
**ยังไม่ได้ทดสอบ** with 8 January 2570 as the date to measure again, which is what the ticket
allows and what *ไม่ต้องมี* is not. No mark moved, and what holds that sentence up is that the
diff touches no criteria row at all.

**An instrument that cannot run is not a measurement, and the reason can be the machine rather
than the code.** Three attempts at `141c` died with `Process from config.webServer exited early.`
and nothing above it, which reads as a crash in the backend. It was the port: 3400 ran the whole
suite on 24 October, and the morning after a reboot it was inside Hyper-V's `3324-3423`. Inside an
excluded range the bind does not raise — `server.js` printed `Server running on
http://localhost:3400`, printed its environment banner, and ended on its own with status 0 about
300ms later, which is a second symptom beside the `EACCES` one `e2e/support/env.js` already
documented. Running `node server.js` by hand on that port and on 3600 is what told them apart, in
two commands. The comment now carries both; the twelve `mutation/` run blocks that hand-carry
`E2E_BACKEND_PORT=3400` are #237 rather than a sentence here, for #119's reason — twelve and
not the thirteen a grep for the variable name returns, because the thirteenth writes `3110` and
still runs today. A census by the mechanism counts the value, not the variable (#174).

## #221 — the two screens that were not one question, and the control beside the one being closed

A `question` ticket that forbids its own implementation: #210's second owner's question is
unanswered, and the ticket says in its own words that the answer to that one is the answer here
too. So what was owed was the measurement, and the measurement moved the question twice.

**A ticket that pairs two screens has paired them by the mechanism it could count.** #221's table
held `Students.js` and `Users.js` in one cell, because what could be counted from the code was
identical: each holds a `busy` flag, each passes it to other components, neither passes it to its
`<Pager>`. Nine arms on the screen said they are on opposite sides. `Users.js` says the sentence
in all six of its sequences — one behaviour, no fork, the state #210 measured on the six
administration screens. `Students.js` says it 210 frames of 229 when nobody presses and **0 of
360** when somebody does: #199's two-way split, alive. The mechanism is one line each.
`Students.save` hands the sentence over keyed on `readOf(1, program)` and `load` says it only when
`waiting.current.of === key`, so the read of page two does not match and the `finally` then clears
the ref — which is #205's own clearing, now **inside** `if (isCurrent())` and correct, so the 0 of
360 is the key mismatch alone and not #205's defect walked into again; `Users.save` keys nothing but `showing.current`,
which holds *what is open on the screen* rather than the list's coordinates, and reads `load`'s
`return true` as *it drew* when it only says *nothing refused the read* (#202). So the ticket's one
question is two: `Users.js` asks #210's question word for word, and `Students.js` asks a different
one, because there the clock picks what the person reads (#52, #199) and that is a defect rather
than a preference. It is #122's rule — *a ticket that generalises across screens has usually
generalised the symptom* — met where the generalisation was in the owner's question itself.

**An option that disables one control is priced by every other control that changes what the read
is of.** The option in front of the owner is #210's: give `<Pager>` the flag. Two arms moved the
screen's **filter** instead of its pager, inside the same held window: `Students.js` went silent
again, 0 of 356 frames, and `Users.js` said the sentence again, 212 of 360. The filter rebuilds the
same `load` — it calls `setPage(1)` and then sets its own value, so the key changes while the page
does not — and **no screen's filter is `disabled={busy}`**, including the ปีการศึกษา input on
`Offerings.js`, a screen
whose pager has carried the flag since #210. That last one is not a reading of the JSX: `140a`'s
*ยกเลิกการเปิด* row has used that filter as its way in since #223. So `busy={busy}` closes a
control and narrows a window; it does not close one. Nothing about #210's own record becomes
false — there the fork was already gone and there is nothing for a clock to pick — but the sentence
*the way in is closed* was never the sentence, and on `Students.js` it would be wrong. This is #217
read from inside the mechanism: the price of closing a way in is measurable only once you know what
the person can still do, and here the answer moves the price rather than ending it (#153).

**A census of a control counts reads as presses unless it is told the difference.** Criterion 4
asked for a census by the **press** and not by the claim (#199, #217). `pager.js` writes
`const next = page => page.getByRole('button', { name: 'ถัดไป' })`, which makes `next`
and `previous` locators, so `expect(previous(page)).toBeDisabled()` is a read of the control, and
the first draft of the instrument counted it — which pulled in `208a`'s first row, whose only
mention of the pager is that assertion. The population is 48 blocks under `e2e/tests` that press a
pager, 11 of them on these two screens, and **3** that `busy={busy}` would actually re-aim:
`140a`'s *บันทึก* and *ระงับ* on `Users.js` and *บันทึก* on `Students.js`. The ticket had already
reached 3 from the other side on 20 ตุลาคม 2569, with `140:usersbusypager` and
`140:studentsbusypager` — the ticket's own proposal made to run (#48) — so two instruments agree,
which is worth more than either. The eight that are not re-aimed are not re-aimed for four
different reasons, and that is what a census by the claim cannot see: two press with no write out
at all, two press in a `beforeEach` before the write starts, two press while a **read** is held
rather than a write, and two go through `ImportPanel`, which keeps its own flag and never raises
the screen's: both screens raise the flag at exactly three sites — `setBusy(true)` in `Users.save`,
in `Users.confirmSwitch` and in `Students.save` — and a grep for `setBusy(` answers **six**, the
other three being the `setBusy(false)` in each one's `finally`. The count that matters is the one
by the call's own argument, which is the species of #174: a census is evidence about the property
it counted.

**An instrument that finds a block by its first delimiter has made a claim about the syntax between
them, and the tell is a count of zero rather than an error.** Brace-matching a `test(` block from
its first `{` closes on the destructured `{ page }` of
`test('...', async ({ page }) => {`, which made every block two words long and every press
invisible: the run printed `0` and exited `0`. The count is the tell, not the exit code (#208).
The repair matches the `test(` from its own paren. Two more readings of the same species were
repaired on the way: a helper's declaration reads exactly like a call to itself, so taking a file's
preamble whole attributed every row of `140a` to every screen one of its helpers opens; and an
indented `beforeEach` belongs to its own `describe`, so taking them all gave every row of `57a` the
screen the first `describe` opens.

The first window — press the pager while the write is still out — is not buildable at `บันทึก` on
either screen, and not by a person either: the form and the table are the two halves of one
ternary, so while the save is out there is no list and no pager in the document. Reading that is
where the probe's own first run was wrong, and it is #85 and #111 from the other end. A bare count
of `ถัดไป` answers **1** on `Users.js`, because `HistoryPanel` is drawn in the branch the form
occupies and has a `<Pager>` of its own — one of the two callers #221's own table calls *safe by
construction*. The reading is three numbers instead of one, and they say `1 · 1 · 2` on `Users.js`
and `0 · 0 · 0` on `Students.js`: everything left on the screen belongs to the history panel. The
window is buildable at **สถานะ**, where `ConfirmDialog` covers the list rather than replacing it,
and both of #199's sequences were measured there.

## #222 — the owner's answer that reached seven of eleven, and the person who needed nobody's help

#222 is a question ticket: should `backend/lib/paging.js` put a ceiling on `page`, refuse past the
end, or keep today's behaviour and write the reason at the file with a date on it? Nothing in it is
a task, so what there was to do was measure its claims before writing the owner's question down.
Three were true - `Math.max(1, ...)` floors `page` with no ceiling anywhere near it, eleven route
files call `pageOf`, and nothing at `paging.js` writes a word about a page past the end.

The claim that decided all three options was the one about why it does not hurt yet: *every
paginated screen corrects the server on the client since #209*. That is a reason with a date on it
(#81), and the first census I ran to check it was blind - it counted the spelling `Math.ceil`, which
is evidence about the property it counted and not about the claim I wanted (#174, #208). Re-run by
the mechanism - `lastPage`, `handedOn`, `HANDED_ON`, `answer.page >` - and narrowed to the eleven
mount points of `<Pager>`, it says **seven**. The four without the rule are `Students.js`,
`Users.js`, `components/users/HistoryPanel.js` and `components/groups/GroupHistory.js`: the same
four #221's caller table had named a day earlier, found again without reading it.

Why #209 stopped at seven is not a mistake of #209's. Its population was the screens with a
page-stepping delete handler, because a page-stepping delete handler was the thing it was fixing, and
a census whose population is *the things that carry X* cannot find the thing that carries no X
(#141); a ticket written from another ticket's sweep inherits that sweep's population (#223). What
is new here is the half one layer along: **the owner's answer reached that population too.** The
owner chose option ก for the departments screen and gave a reason - *"the person who manages the
departments page is probably the only one"* - which is still true of that screen and was never a
sentence about any other.

So the probe asked the screen rather than reasoning about it. `Users.js` is the only one of the four
with a write that shortens the list it is drawing: the *active* status filter plus ระงับ. Signed in
as the system administrator, filtering to active gives `ทั้งหมด 13` over two pages with three rows on
the last; suspending those three one at a time, waiting for each reload, walks the pager line from
`ทั้งหมด 12 รายการ · หน้า 2 จาก 2` to `ทั้งหมด 11 รายการ · หน้า 2 จาก 2` to
**`ทั้งหมด 10 รายการ · หน้า 2 จาก 1`**, with
*ไม่พบผู้ใช้งานตามเงื่อนไขที่เลือก* in the table on a page the screen is standing on. One person, one
filter, one press at a time: no second actor, no race, nothing held. A reload does take it away, the
page number being `useState(1)` rather than part of the URL - which is a way out the person has, and
#153 says to ask what they can do about it, because the recovery may move the price rather than end
it. What is left of the price is that the screen tells them the filter found nobody while the filter
found ten.

The probe's own first prediction was wrong, and for a reason this file already holds one species of:
it counted the drawn rows and expected 0, but the empty state **is** a row (#164). The repair is to
read what the table holds rather than how many rows it has. It is kept rather than deleted (#169),
because nothing else can read this answer again, and its docblock says what it cannot say (#123) -
above all that it says nothing about the other three mount points, where no press shortens the
screen's own list and a second actor is a different question.

Re-pricing the three options then moved two of them. Option 3's paragraph was costed at one
paragraph, but the paragraph would have to say something: *the client corrects it everywhere* is a
sentence the code makes false at four of eleven mount points, and a marker outlives the gap it
documents, which turns it into an exemption (#141). Option 2 proposes refusing, in a file whose own
docblock has already decided the other way - *"A page number is navigation, not data"*, so `page=abc`
gets the first page rather than a refusal - which is the species of a ticket that proposes to change
the file that already decided against it (#102). Option 1 changes what closed tickets recorded, and
the hunt for those is by value and not by name (#145): `หน้า N จาก M` with `N > M` finds three
`หน้า 3 จาก 2` and one `หน้า 4 จาก 2`, all in §#209 of the departments sheet, and the same hunt
collides with a `หน้า 2 จาก 2` on the user-accounts sheet which is not past the end at all - a false
positive of hunting by value, and the walked row the probe's own writes would have expired had
`hold()` not put the three accounts back. That restoration is measured rather than assumed: the
probe's second run arrived at `ทั้งหมด 13` exactly as the first did.

And the measurement produced a fourth option the ticket does not list: extend #209's rule to the
four remaining mount points. It changes no API contract, touches no sheet's record, applies a
decision the owner has already taken to a population that day's census could not see (#196), and is
the only one of the four that takes what the probe measured off the screen. It does not answer #222
- the server still answers a page that does not exist - which is exactly why it belongs in a ticket
of its own (#119) rather than in the owner's question: #239, filed as a `bug` and not a `question`,
because one person alone reaching it is not a preference anybody chose.

What the hunt by value also found is that the repository had already answered this species once. Two
of the three `หน้า 1 จาก 0` in the tree are a row and a mutant: `57a-pager.spec.js` row 9 holds *an
empty list reads `หน้า 1 จาก 1`, not `จาก 0`*, calling `จาก 0` "a page count that says the page the
reader is on does not exist", and `57:nofloor` removes `Pager.js`'s floor of one so that the row can
die. That is the same sentence as `หน้า 2 จาก 1` read from the other end: the claim is held where the
page **count** would say the reader's page does not exist, and held by nothing where the page the
reader is **on** exceeds the count. An answer the repo has already given to the same species is a
decision rather than a precedent to weigh (#196), which is what makes the fourth option a question
about the reach of a rule already chosen rather than a new question for the owner.

Today's contract, meanwhile, is held at one route of eleven: `backend/test/history.test.js` has the
only row in the backend suite that asks for a page past the end. If the owner picks option 1 or 2,
the mutant of the rejected option (#48) has exactly one place to stand, and the other ten routes
hold nothing at all - a number that belongs in the question rather than in the fix.

## #224 — the two behaviours an invisible number was choosing between

#224 is a question ticket out of #209's two-axis review: since #209 `load` re-keys a waiting
sentence only when `waiting.current.of === key`, and its `finally` clears one only when the read did
not hand the page on, so a sentence belonging to some *other* read is neither re-keyed nor cleared.
Before #209 the `finally` cleared it every time. The ticket's own first step is the one that decided
the answer: **measure whether the situation can be reached before deciding what is right** (#141),
by the mechanism rather than by the buttons' names (#174, #139).

The census found the way in one press past #209's own. Eighteen sites on the paged screens give a
sentence to a read — thirteen keyed on `readOf(onPage.current, …)` and five on the read of page one —
and all eighteen hold `writing`, so with the six administration pagers carrying `busy` since #210
the pager cannot move the page *while* a sentence is being handed over. What it can do is move it
**after a hand-on**: a read that hands on has drawn nothing, so `data` still carries the total of the
page before, `Pager` computes its page count from that total, and ถัดไป is live and offers a page the
list no longer has. One person, one removal, a second actor who shortened the list — no race, and no
second defect.

That census's first version said *ten*, counting screens and sites in one column, which is the
species of a census being evidence about the property it counted (#174) — and the thing that caught
it was a one-line grep, because a count published in a sheet is a claim a grep can check (#55, #96).
The behavioural conclusion did not turn on the number; the next paragraph is what turned it.

**The ticket's harm is unreachable, and the reason is the half of the clause nobody had read.** On a
read that *draws*, the `finally` clears the waiting sentence whatever its key. Every hand-on is
followed by exactly one drawing read — the read of the page it handed to — so a stranded sentence is
thrown away there, and no later read of the keyed page can arrive first. The sentence therefore
never turns up late over a fresher list, which is what the ticket said it would do.

But that same line is why the answer is not *the clause is right* either. The two rows are one
situation with one number moved: when the hand-on lands **on** the keyed page the sentence is said,
and when it lands anywhere else the sentence is dropped and nobody hears it. One person doing the
same thing twice gets the sentence once and silence the other time, and what differs is how far a
second actor shortened the list — an invisible number choosing between two defensible behaviours,
which is a defect rather than a preference (#199), and the shape of #152's *an "as today" option is
a claim that today is one thing*. So which single behaviour the person should get is the owner's
question, and both of the ticket's options are now the mutant of a row: option 1 made to run kills
row 1, option 2 made to run kills row 2 (#48).

Two things about where a mutant goes. The ticket's prose points at `if (!handedOn) waiting.current =
null`, and option 1 written there killed `224a` **and** `209a` row 3 — a mutant that kills too much
(#97), because by the time the `finally` runs the re-key has already changed `waiting.current.of`, so
a sentence re-keyed *successfully* reads at that point as one whose key does not match. The site is
chosen by which line has to go red, not by which line the ticket discusses (#193). And the two new
rows expired four mutants nobody had edited: re-swept, `209:stepsbackinstead` kills `224a` row 2,
`209:handsontopageone` kills both, `209:clearedonthehandon` kills row 1 — a spec that gains a row a
mutant can reach expires its count with the anchor still exact and nothing to report it (#202, #48).

The last of it is an instrument. Row 1's first draft waited for ถัดไป with a retrying
`toBeEnabled()` — in front of a press that has to land inside a held window, which is exactly the
wait #225 took out of `140a`: it moves the press instead of failing the row. Both rows now read
`isDisabled()` once. The review that found it quoted my own docblock citing #209 as the reason to
assert the precondition, which is true, and the instrument I had reached for was the one #209 and
#225 had removed.

## #226 — the guard it found, and the question that guard could not answer

`sentences-after-a-move.js` asks whether a success sentence said after an `await` is enclosed by
something asking whether the screen is still the one that asked, and it counted a site as answered
when a `.current` comparison enclosed it. #143 had found the hole from the other side: on
`Offerings` the removal's sentence sits inside `showing.current === sent`, and `showing` means *the
last thing that opened on this screen* (#146), which cannot tell one Offering's panel from another's
because neither of them opens anything. The census reported that site green, and it was right about
the question it asked — but anybody reading `(ref)` as *this site knows where the person went* read
a stronger claim than the instrument had made. That is #208's blind spot one layer along: not *it
cannot find the guard* but *it found one and counted it as enough*.

The ticket asked for a measurement rather than a fix, and named two possible criteria for a split:
read what the ref is **written with**, which it called a reading an instrument does with difficulty,
or keep a hand-written list with a reason per site. The measurement answered the question of which:
the first is forty lines. A value that carries no position at all is a fresh `{}`, `[]`, `null`, or
a name bound to one of those, and a ref written only with those can answer *has anything opened
since* and nothing else. So `opened` is every write being one of those, `position` is a write that
carries a value — `onScreen.current = load`, a loader rebuilt on its own dependencies and so
changing the moment the question changes — `mixed` is both, and `unwritten` is nothing in the file
writing it. The hand list was refused for the reason this file has never held one: a tool that skips
things by name lies the day a file is added (#126).

What the tree said on 25 October 2569: of 22 sites counted `enclosed (ref)`, **19 read `showing`**
and **3 read `onScreen`**. `useRef(load)` had to count as a write for the second three to read
`position`, which is also what stops a ref born with a value and never reassigned from reading
`unwritten`.

Then the second layer, because the label says what the ref *can* tell apart and not whether the
screen has a move it cannot see. That is read off the loader's own dependency list, a dependency the
screen sets itself being a control on that screen: 15 of the 19 are on screens whose loader is keyed
on route parameters alone, where moving away is a route change that takes the screen down, and **4
are not** — `Offerings.js:567`, `Plos.js:354`, `Users.js:293` and `:386`, where a pager or a filter
rebuilds the loader and writes nothing the guard reads. Three of those four were already somebody's
question: `Offerings` was answered on 21 October 2569 (#143 — the sentence names its Offering), and
`Users` is #238's first question. `Plos.js:354` was nobody's, and reading the handler says why: the
confirmation box closes before the reload is awaited, so the curriculum filter is on the screen and
not disabled while the read is out. That paragraph is read from the code and not measured in the
browser, so it went into the sheet and a ticket of its own rather than into this change.

The three questions the instrument still cannot reach are now written in its docblock, with the
date and the figures: whether the screen has a move the ref cannot see, whether that move is
reachable while the write is out (a question about `disabled` and about what a dialog covers, which
only the browser answers), and whether the sentence *should* be silent after a move, which is the
owner's. A tool that cannot say what it did not look at is the species of the hand-kept numbers it
replaces (#123, #126, #132).

Two smaller things. The instrument's own seven new fixtures pass either way (#141), so the run that
decided was breaking two real sites: `Plos.js`'s open-the-editor write made to carry the curriculum
moved the report to `mixed 1 .. opened 18 .. position 3`, and `StudentGroups`'s `onScreen.current =
load` made `{}` moved it to `mixed 1 .. opened 19 .. position 2` — `mixed` and not `opened`, because
`useRef(load)` is the write that is still carrying a value. And the first green run was not the
first run: turning `namesHoldingTheQuestion` from a `Set` into a `Map`, so the refs inside a named
comparison could be followed, broke `ref by name` — `for (const name of named)` over a Map hands
over pairs. An existing fixture said so in the same second, which is the whole reason the file has
one per shape.

And then the review of this very change found the rule loose in the other direction, both axes
finding it without seeing each other. `isSentinel` listed `{}`, `[]` and `null`, so a ref born empty
in any other shape — `useRef()`, `useRef(false)`, `useRef(0)`, `useRef('')`, `useRef(new Map())` —
read as a value and took a label stronger than the truth. That is this ticket's own species reversed:
not *it cannot find the guard* but *it found one and said it knows where the person went*. #174 had
the line already — a rule that is too loose fails the other way, and only breaking a real site shows
it — and the shape that would have arrived silently is the commonest idiom React has.

What settled it was the same instrument read on both sides, which cost one temporary copy of the
script with the old three-type body: `Plos.js`'s `useRef(null)`, read by three of the 22 sites, put
into each of the four shapes. The unrepaired instrument answered `mixed 1 .. opened 18 .. position 3`
for `useRef(false)`, `useRef()` and `useRef(new Map())` alike; the repaired one holds `opened 19 ..
position 3` for all three and still answers `mixed` for `useRef(1)`, which is the control that says
the repair did not become *accept anything*. `mixed` rather than `position` on that site because
`showing.current = {}` writes it elsewhere too, so the per-ref label and the merged one are not the
same sentence — worth saying, because the review's wording was right about the mechanism and one
step strong about this site.

The tree's figures did not move, before or after. That is what makes it a latent gap rather than a
wrong number, and it is also why the fixtures and that table are the whole proof: a report that
reads the same either way proves nothing (#141). Two of the review's remaining findings were
writing-down rather than fixing — a ref born through `React.useRef` or an aliased import reads as
`unwritten`, and the name-to-value map is read over the whole file rather than per function, which
can only understate — and both went into the docblock's list beside the three that were already
there. The ladder in `tellsApart`, which had stated its ordering in prose and implemented it in
three branches, became a `STRENGTH` array read with `indexOf`.

## #241 — the window with nothing in the way, and the instrument the ticket named

#226's closing paragraph read `Plos.js:354` out of the code and said so: the confirmation box closes
with `setRemoving(null)` **before** the reload is awaited, so the curriculum filter is on the screen
and not disabled while the read is out, and neither clause of
`if (reloaded && showing.current === sent)` can see a move — `reloaded` is `load`'s `return true`,
which its own comment says means *the read was not refused* and never *it drew* (#152, #203), and
`showing` is *the last thing that opened on this screen* (#146), which a filter does not write. That
is a claim from the day it was written (#66, #111), and what the ticket asked for first was the
measurement.

Six sequences at the browser seam, on `dept.admin.05@kmitl.ac.th`, who reaches `0501` and `0503`,
each arm carrying its prediction as an assertion (#205) because the sampler is built from the
sentence's own text and a wording change would print `0 of n` and exit 0 — the probe's answer
inverted with nothing saying so (#208, #171). The control said the sentence 211 frames of 225 over
`0501`'s own 51 rows. The filter moved while the DELETE was held said it 222 of 360, and moved while
the *reload* was held 213 of 347, both over `0503`'s four. Three runs, the same answers to within a
few frames.

**The paragraph read from the code was right, and the measurement confirmed it rather than refuting
it** — the rarer side of #66. And what the measurement adds is not in the code reading: of the two
windows this handler has, the second one needs **nobody's help and nothing dismissed**. While the
DELETE is out the box is still up, under a cover that eats a click (#199) and, since #217, a focus
trap, so the filter is reached by pressing ยกเลิก first, which is the way a person has. While the
*reload* is out the box has closed itself: 0 covers, 0 confirm buttons, filter not disabled. So the
argument that nobody can reach the window — the argument the file's own `onScreen` docblock makes
about the box being up, in the sentence *"the dialog behind ลบ leaves it drawn"* — is dated by
**where in the handler the close runs**, not by the box existing (#220).

Those first arms, though, cannot answer the ticket's second ask, and that is the lesson. All four of
them press **inside** a held window, so between them they say what happens when a press lands in the
window and nothing about whether that is what decided the outcome. #52's defect and #199's are a
system holding *two* behaviours with an invisible clock choosing, and the thing that tells that apart
from one behaviour reached two ways is **the same press outside the window**. So each control was
measured on both sides and the four cells read as a grid (#148, #149): a fifth arm moved the filter
after the sentence had landed with nothing held at all, and a sixth pressed
เพิ่มผลการเรียนรู้ there.

Both columns agreed. The filter's cells are the same sentence over the same new curriculum, standing
in one banner, because **nothing takes the notice away when the filter moves**: `setNotice(null)` is
called by the controls that write the ref and by nothing else. The `เพิ่มผลการเรียนรู้` cells differ
only in *when* — never said inside the window because the guard works, said and then taken away by
the person's own press outside it — and leave the person with the same screen either way. One
behaviour, no clock choosing, so the ticket's second ask is answered: the owner's question of #238's
first kind, asked now for three screens instead of two, and not #52's defect.

**Whether a system holds one behaviour or two is decided by the same press outside the window, not
by more presses inside it.** Four arms inside a window look thorough and are one cell of a grid. And
the fifth arm did something else to the ticket: if the sentence stands with nothing held, the
sequence needs no window, no second actor and no particular moment — only that somebody moves the
filter after pressing ลบ. The ticket's own wording, *in the window*, named a window where the
population of ways in is *any time afterwards* (#179 met again). What the two windows decide is the
`เพิ่มผลการเรียนรู้` column, not the filter's.

The last two arms also read something the sampler cannot: whether the banner is still **standing**
after the press. The fifth reads it once, at a settle point, because nothing in that arm calls
`setNotice(null)` and a retrying read there would be an assertion that cannot fail (#50); the sixth
retries, because there the code under test is itself the remover, which is #214's exception to that
rule. Both halves of one rule, in one file, ten lines apart.

The other finding is the instrument. The ticket named `e2e/support/late-answer.js`, and that file's
own docblock says what it is for: the window between an **answer** and its **drawing**, 400ms, by
wrapping `fetch` inside the document — and says `page.route` cannot do it, a fulfilled route being
answered all at once. What this ticket needs is the inverse: the answer itself held for seconds
while the person acts, which is a held `route.continue` and exactly the shape #221's probe already
uses. **A ticket's named instrument is a claim like its numbers, and the instrument's own docblock
is where it is checked** — #133 and #145 one species along, from a file list that is somebody
else's grep to a tool that is somebody else's measurement. Reading it cost a minute; believing it
would have cost the measurement.

Two probes now hold that held-route shape and it stays in both, because they identify the held
request by different things — #221 by the method, this one by the `program_id` in the query, which
is what identifies the request on a screen whose every read has the same path (#160, #185). That
is the price of not merging, priced as a census with a date on it rather than argued as a law about
the seam (#196); the day a third file needs it is the day it is shared (#171).

Two details the arms had to get right, and both are old rules. The held route goes on **before** the
press, not when the DELETE's response event fires: the handler runs on that same event, so the
reload can leave before the route is in place — a flag paired with a later event is not identity
(#168). And the moved arm does not use `filterTo`, whose `waitForList` matches any `/api/plos` GET
including the held one, so it waits on `0503`'s own answer instead: a matcher two questions share
cannot be narrowed for one of them (#218).
## #227 — the five sites, the one way in, and the exit that was reversed

#169 had asked whether a box that was closed leaves the document in a tab that is being given no
frames, measured that it does not, and had the owner answer, on 21 October 2569, that it must.
#227 asked the same question of the other five places in `frontend/src/` that still mount
`AnimatePresence` themselves, and it asked for the measurement **first**: per site, is there a
close that can land in a frameless tab *without racing the person's own hand*. Only then the fix,
and only at the sites with such a way in.

The census that decides is by mechanism — **who writes the state the presence is keyed on** — and
not by what the screen draws. Four of the five are written by presses and nothing else: the user
menu's `isOpen`, `RoleDropdown`'s `open` (whose `choose` lowers it *before* awaiting
`switchRole`, so no answer can ever close it), `SidebarItem`'s `openMenu`, and `Login.js`'s
`errorMessage`, cleared by a keystroke or by the next submit. The fifth is `Login.js`'s
`mode="wait"` swap, and `LoadLogin` comes down in a `finally` after an awaited request: press,
switch tabs, and the close lands with nobody watching. One of five, which is the narrower way in
the ticket's own title had predicted.

**The harm at that one site is not the harm #169 fixed, and it is worse.** With `mode="wait"` the
child being held is the one on its way **out**, so the one waiting to come in never mounts at all.
Measured on 25 October 2569: the spinner was still in the document 500ms and 2500ms after the 401
had landed, at `opacity: 1`, `pointer-events: auto`, its *กำลังเข้าสู่ระบบ* still in the
accessibility tree — and the form and the refusal were **not in the document at all**. #169's boxes
left something extra on the screen; this one left the screen unable to say the thing the person was
waiting for. A sentence they are owed and cannot be given is a different species from a node nobody
can see (#153), and it is why this site was fixed and the other four were not.

The four that were not each carry the price on themselves, in numbers rather than in the words
*node ที่มองไม่เห็น* which #169 disproved: present at 0.5, 1 and 3 seconds, at `opacity: 1`,
`pointer-events: auto`, 0/3/1/2 controls still focusable, 4/19/6/11 nodes in the accessibility
tree, and a window to be hit that is the fade itself — 198, 198, 183 and 318ms, the last of them
longer because the exit tweens `height` too. The instrument reached those windows at 6 to 13ms,
which is the speed of an instrument and not of a hand.

**The fix is a generation counter, not a flag, and that is what `mode="wait"` costs.** #169's
wrapper stopped rendering `AnimatePresence` while a flag was up; with a swap there is always a
child to draw, so what goes in is a counter used as the presence's `key`: mounting a new
`AnimatePresence` takes whatever the old one was holding with it, and whatever is to be drawn now
mounts in the new one. The prop that names what is being drawn is `at`, and it is required
(`REQUIRED_PROPS`, #182) because a caller that forgets it gets a wrapper that silently never
retires anything. `mode="wait"` is passed through rather than dropped, which is what kept this a
task: the ticket said that a fix needing a change to what a watching person sees becomes the
owner's question, and the watching measurement did not move (106 of 157 frames ending at 1764ms
against 1765 before; 37 of 157 at 617 against 40 at 665). The wrapper is no longer a dialog's, so
it is `RetiringPresence` now, and the rename was part of the ticket.

**And the first version failed #169's fourth mode again, by a route #169 did not have.** That mode
— away and back while the thing is still open, then close it in front of the person — exists
because the owner's answer is only an answer if somebody looking at the screen sees no difference.
#169's first version failed it with a listener that had no dependency. This one failed it with a
flag that was raised correctly and could never come down: under `mode="wait"`, when the answer
arrives faster than the 180ms the form takes to leave, the form's exit is **reversed**, and a
reversed exit never fires `onExitComplete`. Measured with nothing emulated, the answer landed at
79ms, so the spinner was never drawn at all — the ordinary case, not a corner. The flag therefore
stayed up for ever, and the next time the tab went away the whole sign-in screen was remounted
under somebody who had closed nothing: **0 of 44 frames** drawing the refusal they were watching,
where the measurement wants 13. So: **a flag that says something may still be on its way out has
to come down where the removal is reversed, and not only where it completes** — which means it
cannot be a boolean. It holds the `at` whose child may still be leaving, and it is cleared when
`at` comes back to that value. After the change, 13 of 44 ending at 195ms, which is what the
unfixed code read.

**That failure was reported as a disappearance, and it was a replacement.** The instrument marks
the node it is about with an attribute and then reads the mark per frame — so a remount, which
makes a new node without the mark, reads exactly like a node dropped with no fade:
`stillOpenOnReturn: 0`, `framesStillDrawingIt: 0`, `opacityCameDown: false`. **A reader built on a mark cannot tell a node
that was removed from one that was replaced.** Here it did not matter, because both answers are
bad for the same reason and the mechanism was findable by reading the code the mark could not see;
on a ticket where only one of the two is a defect it would decide the answer, and the repair is to
count the unmarked siblings as well as the marked one (#164's blind sampler, one species along).

One more reading, this one about the numbers rather than the mechanism. The on-return figures for
the four untouched sites **flipped between two runs of the same code**: in the first the role
dropdown was gone in one frame and the submenu faded for 308ms; in the second, exactly the other
way round. A tween resumed after a pause of seconds either jumps to its end or runs itself out, and
which one happens is a property of the resumed tween and not of the site. So the reasons on those
four sites carry both readings, not the one this session happened to get — the measured number, and
all of it (#102, #52).

**There is no row and no mutant**, and that is written in the wrapper's own head comment as #169
wrote it there: the condition cannot be built at either seam, which is the whole reason the probe
exists. Nor does bringing three call sites under one wrapper cost the proof anything, because
nothing was proving them in the first place (#68, #171).

## #228 — the answer that was priced before it was built

#180 had asked, and the owner had answered on 22 October 2569, that all five forms carry the same
two-option `select` for a record's status. #228 is what that answer left behind: three of the five —
`DepartmentForm.js`, `ProgramForm.js`, `SubjectForm.js` — had neither a sentence under the field nor
any sign that a save was in flight, where `ProgramSubjectForm.js` and `PloForm.js` had both. Two
halves, and the ticket was right that both were the owner's: the **wording** of a sentence that does
not exist yet, and the **behaviour** of the controls while a save is out.

Three of the ticket's claims were measured first. The one about the delivered tree held, and it is
what made every option allowed rather than a change to a delivered screen: `is_active` appears **0
times** in `DEEP-QA-FRONTEND`, so all five of these fields are the rebuild's own and none of them is
a number somebody else chose (#156). The other two were wrong. *One line per file* was a count of
the files and not of the sites: `busy` reached the *บันทึก* button and nothing else in all three, so
matching the upper two forms was **21 lines at 21 sites** — the same species the sheet had already
recorded against #180's own prediction two days before (#52). And the owner had **one** sentence to
settle rather than three: the programme's and the subject's follow the pattern of the two forms that
already carried a hint — `PloForm.js:265` and `ProgramSubjectForm.js:176`, the only two with that
tail before this change — with the noun changed, and both of those screens already say the same fact
at the moment of the refusal (`Programs.js:322`, `Subjects.js:313`). The department's comes from
`REFUSALS.departmentInUse`, and no pattern fitted it, because a department with anything pointing at it is **refused**, where a programme, a
subject, a mapping, an outcome and a rubric are closed for you by `lib/removal`'s
`deleteOrDeactivate` — so a sentence copied from `PloForm.js` would have been wrong on exactly the
screen the ticket was filed from, and it is the only control that performs the sentence the server
already says (#178).

**The owner's first answer was sent back, and that is this ticket's rule.** The answer was `busy` on
every control, as the upper two forms have always had it. What priced it was a census of the
**press** rather than of the claim (#199, #221): **19 rows in two closed tickets arrange their
situation by pressing *ยกเลิก* while a save is out on these three screens** — `142a`'s
`cancelDuringSave` marks exactly these three, and `146a`'s `saveAndCancel` is the whole
administration block's arrangement, six rows for ภาควิชา, five for หลักสูตร, five for รายวิชา.
Three of the 19 go one further and type into a **second** form while the first write is still out,
which `busy` on the fields alone would have broken too, `busy` being the page's flag and not the
form's. #146's whole subject is that window: a person may move on while a save is out.

#152 says to run the closed tickets' suites against the cheapest reading of a decision and, if one
breaks, to implement the decision the other way up so both hold. Here the price was not in how the
diff is written but in **what the person can still do** — abandon a form whose write has not landed,
and start another — so it went back to the owner rather than into whichever implementation kept the
suites green. The second answer, the same day, was the form's own flag: `sending`, raised in
`submit` and lowered in `.finally`, on every **field**, with *ยกเลิก* holding nothing at all. What
that leaves unguarded is written on the three sheets in plain words rather than left to be
discovered: *ยกเลิก* is still pressable while the save is out, which is what #142 and #146 measured
and is not a gap this ticket left.

The locator question was measured rather than reasoned about (#121). The hint goes **inside** the
`<label>`, where the other four forms put theirs, so it lands in the control's accessible name:
measured on 26 October 2569 against `PloForm.js`'s own hinted box, `{ exact: true }` finds 0 and the
form the three screen helpers actually use — a string `name` with no `exact`, which Playwright
matches as a substring — finds 1. `getByRole('combobox', { name: 'สถานะ' })` therefore kept working
in all three helpers with no re-aim, and the probe was deleted once that number was written into the
sheet and into `DepartmentForm.js`'s head comment (#207). A census of the words the sentences add,
one query per word (#93, #116), found no loose locator they collide with.

Nine mutants, three per file, because each screen's row reads three claims in order and a row
reports the **first** assertion that dies, so a claim written under another is proved by nothing
without a mutant of its own (#88). Per file: the status field left live, which is the code the
ticket diagnosed (#115); the Thai-name box left live; and that box reading `busy` instead of
`sending`, which is the declined option made to run (#48) and the only thing that can tell the
form's flag from the page's. All nine came back fail 1 pass 2 at the assertion the table predicted
before the sweep, read by the dying assertion's name and not by the count (#201). There is **no
mutant for *ยกเลิก***: the one that would prove it is `disabled={busy}` on that button, which would
kill 19 rows in two other files, and a mutant has to be able to fail one row and leave the rest
standing (#97). That claim is therefore a check that the price above is still unpaid, not a claim of
this ticket's own — and what it buys is that the three rows reach the fourth claim at all.

One thing expired that nothing in this ticket touched. A test-file argument is matched as a
substring, so the day `228a-the-form-that-sent-the-save.spec.js` landed, `npx playwright test 28a`
began running two files and `28a:224` in `docs/acceptance/41-continuous-improvement-plan.md` named
two specs (#154, #158). `python mutation/anchors.py` is what said so, in the same breath as the
missing `mutation/README.md` row — three sentences written full-length by a file that was never
about them.

## #230 — the population that was derived, and the instrument proved by moving it

#155's defect was a screen left drawing one scope's rows under a picker that had already changed
hat, and it was closed with a key on the `<Outlet />` in `Mainpage.js`: one structural point, every
screen under it covered by construction — which is why #155's own instruction to let a census choose
the screen was recorded as having *lapsed*. #198 asked what a remount took with it, measured the
answer — the page, the filter, and a form typed and not saved — and the owner chose, on 23 October
2569, the re-read without the remount. The rule moved out of the outlet and into the dependency list
of each landing's own `load`, and the census question came back with it. That is the price of the
narrower mechanism and not a defect in it, which is how `docs/acceptance/10-application-shell.md`
records it, and #230 is the ticket opened in the same breath (#119).

**The ticket's own table of the reads was out of date on the day it was written.** It lists six
landings and, inside the sixth, `components/results/CohortPickers.js` — seven **files**. The tree had
eight: `components/users/useGrantable.js` gained the dependency in #215's commit `d7ebf84`, the same
23 October (#66, and #223 — a ticket written from another ticket's day inherits that day's
population). Counted as **reads** rather than as files it had ten, because `Programs.js:234` and
`Rubrics.js:242` are the second reads #198 itself added — which the ticket's comment names and its
table does not count. The eighth read is the one that made the ticket's own comment right about there being
**two** questions rather than one, because it is a read question 1 cannot see: it is not in a
landing's file at all.

So the census asks two questions over two populations:

1. **Does each landing read the number in its own reads?** The population is derived, not listed
   (#123): `components/SidebarItem/menus.js` says which menu a role gets and `landingPath` says the
   role lands on its first entry, so the landings are a property of the menus and move when they do;
   `routes/AppRoutes.js` turns the path into a component and the component's own import turns it into
   a file. Nothing in the script holds the name `Users.js`.
2. **Does a landing's second read ask too?** `Rubrics` and `Programs` each ask for two different
   lists — their own rows, and the curricula or departments this grant reaches — and the same kind of
   read lives one hop out, in `useGrantable.js` and `CohortPickers.js`. The population is every
   module a landing **reaches** by import, and the calls asked about are the ones an api module has
   declared grant-scoped: `export const GRANT_SCOPED = ['listGrantable']`, #182's shape, a
   declaration the subject makes in code and that the census checks against what the module exports,
   rather than a list of names in the script. Eleven functions in ten api modules declare it. What
   makes a read one of those is measurable rather than a feeling: it takes **no argument** saying
   which rows it means, so there is no prop a landing could hand down to move it, where a row list
   the screen filters (`listUsers`, `listPrograms`) takes `params` and moves with the landing's own
   dependency list. Nine of the eleven are consulted by nothing today, two being all a landing
   reaches: that is the net for the next landing, and declaring only what is reached would make the
   declaration a property of today's import graph instead of a property of the module.

**Question 2 is narrow on purpose, and that is the #141 half of this ticket.** *Every api read in
every component a landing reaches* would be the rule too loose: a panel's read is usually keyed on a
prop the landing hands it, and the landing's own dependency list is what moves that prop. What has
no prop to move is a list the **server** scopes to the acting grant. The same question decided why
only landings are the population at all: the number is raised by `onStayedPut` in `Mainpage.js`,
which fires when a switch lands where the router already is, so a screen that is nobody's landing is
carried away by any switch that moves and never sees the number change.

**Question 1 is deliberately loose, which is the other half of the same choice.** It asks about
*every* api read in a landing's own file and not only the grant-scoped ones, because a landing's
`load` is what the number is for and the screens are six; a read in a landing that is legitimately
keyed on something else says so with the marker. Outside the landings, where the files are a hundred
and forty, a rule that wide is the one too loose — which is the sentence the script's own docblock
owed a future author, and did not carry until the review asked for it.

Nine reads are measured in question 1 and two more in question 2, eleven in all, and one is exempt. `loadDrill` in `pages/ProgramLevelByIntake.js` reads
`getOutcomeContributions` and names no generation, correctly: the `load` above it closes the
drill-down on every read, so a panel can only be open for the generation that is drawn. The reason
was already written in that code; what the ticket added was the marker that makes the instrument
read it — `// screen-generation: <why> (#NNN)`, the escape `label-codes.js` and `required-props.js`
already carry, because a rule with no way to say *this one is deliberate* is a rule people route
around by deleting it.

**The proof is four real sites broken, and the fourth is the one worth keeping.** A landing's
dependency list emptied (`Departments.js`), a landing's call to the hook replaced by the constant
`0` (`TeacherDashboard.js`), and a second read's list emptied one hop out (`useGrantable.js`) each
put the census red on the right line and green again when restored — three breakages inside the
population. The fourth moved the **population**: `FULL_ADMIN`'s first menu entry was pointed at
`/main/subjects`, and the census named `pages/Subjects.js`, a file nobody had touched, as a landing
that never reads the number. No fixture can hold that row, because what it measures is that the
population is derived rather than listed — which is the one claim the script's own twenty-three
fixtures cannot make about themselves (#141, #124).

What it cannot measure is on the script's own face rather than in a count: a read written as
anything but `useCallback` or `useEffect`, a dependency forwarded through a prop, an api function
reached through a binding a grep for the call misses too (#133), a menu whose first entry is
computed, and `firstEntry`'s rule restated here — a restatement is a second place the rule can be
wrong (#96), and what holds the real rule is `66a` rows 1–2, which read the landing off the sidebar
rather than off a constant.

## #233 — the four forms, the row read in the wrong order, and the marker the instrument could not read

#232 found one form being cleared by its own effect: `onlyOne`, computed from an answer **by
identity**, sitting in the dependency list of an effect that wrote the whole draft again, so every
re-read of the pool threw away what somebody had typed — the one thing #198 narrowed its mechanism
to keep. `grep -rln onlyOne frontend/src/components` found seven files; four of them wrote the draft
the same way. #233 is those four, and it asked four things: `Programs.js` first because that is the
way in a person meets today, the other three fixed with #232's shape but not copied whole (#83),
dated reasons beside the two forms that are exempt (#141), and a census that asks the question of
the code (#174).

**The two ways in are not the same way in, and only one of them has a screen.** The second read of
a pool happens where the screen names the generation in its own read's dependency list (#198), and
of these four screens exactly one does — `Programs.js`, measured against `useScreenGeneration`
across `frontend/src/pages` on 26 October 2569, where `Plos.js`, `ProgramSubjects.js` and
`Subjects.js` all close the pool read with `}, [report])`. So the hat-switch way in exists on
`/main/programs` and nowhere else, which is why the ticket said to do that one first. The other
three have a way in that needs no second grant and no switch at all: the pool is read once per
mount, and that answer alone moves `onlyOne` from `null` to an object once, so anybody who opens the
form and types before the answer arrives loses what they typed. That one is not a race to wait for
but a window to open, with `e2e/support/late-answer.js` (#170) — and the window had to be measured
rather than guessed: at 3 seconds the hold had already elapsed before the add form was open, and the
rows only went red at their own claims once it was 15.

**A precondition read above the claim takes the mutant's red, and the claim is never read.** This is
#88 one layer along. Row 2 holds the half of the fix that leaves an existing programme alone
(`if (editing) return`), and it was written the way a row about a retired department wants to be
written: first the precondition that the retired option is still drawn, then the claim that the
field still says which department the programme is in. `movesanexistingprogramme` then died at the
**precondition** — because the option is drawn only while the field holds it, so a mutant that
clears the field takes the option with it. The kill count was right, the mutant was credited, and
the row's own claim sat under the red line unread. The repair is the order, not the assertion: the
claim first, the picker's count second. #88 says a claim written below another claim is proved by
nothing; what this adds is that a *precondition* is another claim for that purpose, and that the
ones derived from the claim are exactly the ones to read afterwards.

**Row 2 passes against the unfixed code, which is what its mutant is for.** All five rows were run
against `HEAD` before the mutants were written (#203): four failed at their own claims, and row 2
passed, because the code before the fix already wrote the whole draft from `value`, which carries
that programme's own department with it. `if (editing) return` is a **new** clause rather than
something the old code got wrong, so the only thing that can measure it is the mutant. Its three
other copies — `PloForm`, `ProgramSubjectForm`, `SubjectForm` — have no row at all, which is
*untested* and not *structurally unreachable* (#102's three answers), and that went to the tracker
as #244 rather than staying a paragraph in the mutation file (#119, #125).

**An instrument that reads a marker has to read it in the shape people write markers.** The census
#233 asked for lets a form off with a written reason, in the family's usual syntax —
`// form-identity: <why> (#NNN)` — and the two exempt forms carry one, because a reason only a
person can read is a paragraph the instrument cannot count. Both of them were then rejected by the
census as *markers naming no ticket*. Babel hands back **one comment per `//` line**, and the ticket
number was two lines down from the word `form-identity:`, so the first version of the script read a
marker whose reason was the first line of a paragraph. That is #93 from the other side: there, a
marker written in a syntax the instrument does not read ended up drawn on the screen; here, a marker
written in the shape every reason in this repo is written in was invisible to the instrument built
to read it. The fix is to join consecutive comments into the paragraph they are, and the rows that
hold it are the two fixtures that put the ticket number on a line of its own.

**The census asks what state a person types into, which is readable, rather than what a form is,
which is not.** `setDraft` is a name and a list of names lies the day a file arrives (#126), so the
population is derived in three questions: which `useState` has its value handed to a controlled
`value=` or `checked=` anywhere in the file; which effects call that state's own setter and have a
dependency list; and what each dependency's initialiser is compared by — `primitive`, `reference`,
or `unclassified` for a prop, a hook's return or a name after a dot. `usable[0]` and `.find(…)` are
`reference` because an element of a fresh answer is a fresh object; `.map(…).join(' ')` is
`primitive`, which is exactly what #232's fix turned the pool into. A `reference` dependency is green
only behind an updater with a branch that returns what it was given, or behind a marker. On 26
October 2569: `typed-into states 65 · by value 28 · guarded 0 · marked 2 · unclassified 32`.

**Its proof is the ticket's own mutant, applied to the tree** (#141, #124): with
`233:programmearrayidentity` in place the census goes red at `components/programs/ProgramForm.js`
and green again on `restore`, which is the diagnosed code read at a real site rather than in a
fixture. And the count has a hole worth saying out loud: **`guarded 0`** — a fix that keeps the
identity dependency and guards the write would be green, and all five forms of #232 and #233 took
the other road and are `by value`, so that branch is held by the script's own fixtures and by
nothing in `src/`. `unclassified` is the wide blind spot, `useMemo` inside it: `recorded` in
`ActivityScores.js` is rebuilt whenever its own dependencies move, which is this family's mechanism
wearing a hook, and nothing here can say whether it reaches a field.

**A fixture undone through the seam is not a fixture removed.** The full run reported `user_roles: +1 deptadm05/DEPT_ADMIN/01` although `233a`'s `afterAll` had revoked that grant and been answered 200. The revoke route is `UPDATE user_roles SET is_active = false`, on purpose: the grant stops being honoured and the record that it existed stays. `155a` and `198a` make the same kind of fixture and have never appeared in that report, because the key they ask for is one the seed already holds, so a soft revoke puts it back as it was; this one asked for a key nothing held, and no call through the seam can ever take that row out again. So the cleanup has two halves - the revoke above the seam, which is the behaviour, and a `DELETE ... AND NOT is_active` below it, which is the row - and what says the second half landed is running the file alone and reading the report again (#132). What is left is the `acting_epoch` a hat switch writes, which is the leftover two earlier tickets accepted for `multi01` for the same reason: nothing but the switch writes it and no seam puts it back.

**A mutation file's own table is a claim like a ticket's numbers.** This one said
`movesanexistingprogramme` kills at an assertion it does not kill, and gave two of the six mutants
an edit count the harness does not report. The sweep is what corrected both, and the paragraph under
the table now records the reordering of row 2 — because the next person to read that table will read
it instead of running it. The same sweep covered the re-aim of `18:noautoprogram`, whose line this
fix moved out of the effect and into `starting`: a re-aim is faithful when it preserves the mistake
rather than the line (#203), and it still kills `18a` row 1.

## #237 — the twelve that were thirty-three, and the instrument figure that had already expired

#220 lost three runs to a port: `E2E_BACKEND_PORT=3400`, written into the *วิธีรัน* block of
mutation files on a day it worked, and inside Hyper-V's reserved range `3324-3423` the morning
somebody read it. The ticket's own first sentence said twelve files, listed them, and said the
twelve were by value rather than by variable name — one more file names `E2E_BACKEND_PORT` and was
still runnable that morning, because its number was outside the ranges of that particular boot.

**The ticket counted by the symptom, and the mechanism's population is two and a half times as
large.** A grep of the *values* on 26 October 2569 found five numbers across two variables —
`E2E_FRONTEND_PORT=5300` × 19, `=5310` × 14, `E2E_BACKEND_PORT=3400` × 12, `=3600` × 2 and
`=3110` × 1 — in 33 files of `mutation/`, which is 23 run blocks once the ten dated records and the
one fixture are taken out, and three more docblocks in `e2e/probes/` that this first grep never
reached. The twelve are
exactly the files holding the number that was reserved on the morning of the 25th: a census by the
value that hurt rather than by the value that can hurt (#174). It is also the ticket's own evidence
for its fix, read one step further: five numbers in two variables is a population that was never
consistent, so there was never one number to correct.

**The three-way split is what decides which of them are edited at all.** *Commands somebody will
type* are the 23 run blocks and the three probe docblocks, and they were edited. *Dated records* are
ten lines in `mutation/` — `52:102` `68:58` `83:54` `84:48` `89:80` `118:104` `129:48` `133:106`
`146:82` `149:64` — plus `docs/acceptance/11-user-accounts.md:492` and `:985` and every file in
`docs/handoff/`: they say what one measurement returned on one day and are not edited (#54).
*The rule* is the paragraph itself, in two copies. And there is a fourth kind the ticket did not
name: `mutation/anchors_test.py` writes a command down in order to have something for `anchors.py`
to read, which is the same reason `_store()` counts it out loud (#126) — a fixture, not a command.

**The cheap option is the one that removes the mechanism rather than the one that automates it.**
The prefix came off entirely; what replaced it is one line per place pointing at `e2e/README.md`
§Ports. The ticket's second option — a script in `e2e/package.json` that reads `excludedportrange`
itself — buys the same thing and costs a mechanism inside the running suite in order to fix
documentation, and it would still leave a number in front of anybody *reading* the file rather than
running it. The pointer needed the README to have something to name: the port paragraph had no
heading, so it got `### Ports`, which is what the twenty-six places cite.

**What that buys is not a command that works; it is a command with no number in it to go stale.**
The first draft of this record said the commands now run on the defaults with nothing to set,
having read `env.js` and found it returns 3100 and 5100. That is what the module returns, which is
not what the machine will bind: `netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp` on
26 October 2569 put **3100 inside `3024-3123`**, so a run that morning still needed
`E2E_BACKEND_PORT`. #118's own dated paragraph had said the same thing about 24 October and was
sitting two lines under the command being edited. A default is a value somebody chose; whether it
can be bound is a measurement of the day.

**The line between a command and a dated record is what the line says, not the heading it sits
under.** Seven files keep their port because the sentence holding it states a measurement — a row
count and a date, `(376 แถว) วัดเมื่อ 11 ก.ย. 2569` — and those are not edited (#54). All seven sit
under `## การกวาด`, beside sentences that say what to run and *are* commands, which is why a script
keyed on the heading would have got them wrong in both directions. The first pass edited all seven;
the spec review found them against this ticket's own census table, and they were restored from
`HEAD`.

**A pointer inserted into a command is a command that no longer runs.** One of the thirty blocks
wrote `cd e2e && \` and continued on the next line, and the pointer went in between, so the
continuation swallowed it: pasting the block would `cd` and then run the suite in the wrong
directory. A census that finds *the line carrying the value* cannot see that the line below it is
part of the same command, and nothing in the diff is red — the standards review read it. Eleven
more pointers had landed in Thai prose rather than in a command block, where a leading `#` is an
H1 and not a comment (#93, #233): seven of those were the records above, and the remaining four
were rewritten as prose.

**And the first census was evidence about the files it globbed.** It asked `mutation/*.py` and so
could not see `e2e/probes/221`, `222` and `241`, whose *How to run it* docblocks carried the same
prefix — commands somebody types, by `CLAUDE.md`'s own description of that directory. They also
each held a paragraph of the rule, which is #97 again; those are pointers now too. What the grep by
value could not have found at all is the root `CLAUDE.md`'s bare `ports 3100/5100`, which carries no
`E2E_*_PORT=` to match: a census is evidence about the property it counted (#174), and this one
counted an assignment.

**A pointer is only as good as the copy it points at, so the second copy went the other way.**
#220 had written the second symptom into `e2e/support/env.js` and not into the README, which is
#97's shape: two places holding one opinion, one of them already wrong. The README now carries both
symptoms — the frontend's `EACCES` reported by CRA as *Something is already running on port 5100*,
and the backend's bind that does not raise at all, printing its banner and ending with status 0 in
about 300ms, which Playwright reports as `Process from config.webServer exited early.` with no
