error above it — and `env.js` is reduced to a pointer with its reason and the date it stopped being
a summary.

**And the instrument figure the ticket told us to watch had expired before the ticket was read.**
Criterion 4 asked that `anchors.py`'s `commands` section still read `arguments 107`, as it had on
25 October 2569. It reads **110**, and it read 110 at `HEAD` too — measured by running the
instrument in a separate worktree at the commit, which is the only thing that settles an instrument
against a hand-kept figure (#141). What moved it was #233's own mutation file, three commands added
after the number was written down. This ticket's edit moved it by **zero**: `COMMAND` matches from
the words `playwright test` onward, so an environment prefix in front of `npx` was never inside
what it counts, and `UNTIL` stops at `#`, so the pointer line is not read either. A ticket's
expected instrument reading is a claim with a date like all its others — and the edit a criterion
warns you about can be invisible to the instrument it warns you with.

## #244 — the three copies, the account the way in came with, and the screen that made one of them unreachable

#233 put `if (editing) return` into four forms. It is the half that leaves a record which already
exists where it is, instead of letting the effect that picks a parent for a *new* record move it:
the reach endpoints answer with retired parents too, the form keeps those out of the pool it may
pick from, and a record filed under a retired parent therefore holds a value the pool does not
contain — the one shape that separates the effect's two conditions. One of the four was held by a
row (`233a` row 2, `233:movesanexistingprogramme`), and `RubricForm` had `198a` row 5 from #232.
The other three had nothing, and the ticket priced them at three rows and three mutants, one each,
each row retiring its own record's parent over HTTP and restoring in `finally` as `233a` row 2
does.

**Two of the three are rows. The third is a net, and the reason is the screen above the form.**

`starting` is `defaultProgram || onlyOne?.program_id || ''` on both `PloForm` and
`ProgramSubjectForm`, letter for letter, and `defaultProgram` is the parent screen's filter.
`pages/Plos.js` has one mount point, and its list is *per curriculum*: `load` returns without asking
while no curriculum is chosen, and the read is `listPlos({ program_id: program })`. So every outcome
the table can offer an แก้ไข for belongs to the curriculum the filter is on, which is exactly the
value `starting` holds — the two branches of the effect write the same `program_id`, and a faithful
copy of the defect is a mutant nothing can see (#206, with the screen's arithmetic in place of the
row's). `pages/ProgramSubjects.js` is the same shape with one difference: its filter starts at `''`
and its list is **not** per programme, so a pair filed in a retired curriculum is listed while
`starting` is the one curriculum still active. That difference is the whole of row 2, and the row
asserts it as its own precondition (#51).

That was measured and not argued (#141). `movesanexistingoutcome` was written, applied and run:
**twenty rows green** — row 3 of `244a` and all seventeen of `19a-plos.spec.js`, which is every row
that opens that form. Then the mutant came out, and the row was left holding the **mechanism**
rather than the absence, with the condition that would make the claim readable again written beside
it (#203's ninth reading): the day `PloForm` is mounted on a screen whose `defaultProgram` can
differ from the curriculum of the outcome being edited. One mount point is a dated claim like any
other (#220).

So **#102's three answers are answers about a copy, not about a line.** The same line in two forms
gets two different answers, and what decides is the **scope of the parent screen's list** — not the
form, not the number of mount points, and not anything a grep for the line can see. A ticket that
counts copies has counted copies; the price is per screen.

**And the way in the ticket borrowed came with the account of the row it was borrowed from.**

The ticket said the way in was *the same one `233a` row 2 already uses*, which is right about the
mechanism and silent about the reader. The first draft of all three rows signed in as the faculty
administrator, as that row does, and the run came back **403, 403 and a timeout**. The Subjects
screen is not the faculty administrator's, to read or to write — #61 decided that, and
`backend/routes/subjects.js` says `MAINTAINERS = ['DEPT_ADMIN']` with the reasoning above it — while
`/api/plos` and `/api/program-subjects` both admit `PROG_MANAGER` and `DEPT_ADMIN` only. `233a` row
2 stands on the Programmes screen, which is the one screen of the four that *is* the faculty
administrator's. The three rows now sign in as `deptadm05`, which reaches all three screens, and the
retirement is still made over HTTP with the faculty administrator's session, because the departments
and programmes routes are his (`198a` row 5 had already measured that a system administrator is
refused 403 there).

**And this ticket expired #237's number the same day #237 was written.** `e2e/README.md` §Ports said
*twenty-three run blocks in `mutation/`* and *a port typed into twenty-six places*; a mutation file
with a run block in it makes that twenty-four and twenty-seven. The pointer #237 built is doing its
job — nothing here had to learn a port number — and the sentence *around* the pointer is still a
hand-kept count in a directory that grows every ticket, which is the rule it was written to obey.
#237's own story keeps its figures, because a dated record is not a citation (#54).

Two accounts in one row is not a complication to apologise for: it is the shape of the situation.
The person who may switch a parent off and the person who maintains the records under it are
different people, which is why a record can be sitting under a retired parent at all.

**A last thing the rows inherited was an order — and only one of them inherited the claim it
ordered.** `SubjectForm`'s `offered` draws a retired department only when it is the value the field
holds, so a mutant that clears the field takes the option with it. Read the option count first and
that read takes the red, leaving the row's own claim under a red line with nobody reading it (#88).
`233a` row 2 had met this and written the order down; row 1 copies the order and the reason.

Row 2's twin assertion was not a twin. `ProgramSubjectForm` does not filter: it maps **every**
programme to an `<option>` and sets `disabled` on a retired one unless it is the value the field
holds, so the count is 1 with the guard and without it — a claim nothing could put at risk (#97),
bought for free at the end of a row whose first assertion was doing all the work, which is the shape
that makes this kind of assertion easy to write and easy to believe. What the guard decides on that
form is whether the person sees their own curriculum as a live choice rather than greyed out, which
is `disabled`. So the sentence above about the copies has one more layer in it: **the guard is
copied letter for letter and the drawing around it is not, so what is at risk is not either** — #83
read from the other side, where what the copy does not carry is not the proof but the way the screen
would show the defect.

And that repair could not be made where the old assertion stood. A `disabled` read written under
row 2's value read is a claim below a claim: the mutant kills the line above it and nobody reads the
line below (#88). It is a row, so it was **appended** as row 4 rather than inserted after row 2,
which keeps every citation to rows 1–3 where it was (#97, #85). `movesanexistingpair` then kills two
rows, each at its own assertion — two reachability claims and not one claim counted twice (#191).

## #234 — the filter that was wider than the pool, and the owner's question a comment had already answered

Four screens draw a curriculum filter from `reachablePrograms`, which answers with retired curricula
too — the comment in `backend/lib/reach.js` says *Retired ones come too*, and that is the whole
reason somebody can read the rubrics, the pairs and the outcomes of a curriculum that has been
closed. The forms under those screens pick from `usable`, which filters the retired ones out,
because `programInReach` requires `is_active` and a value outside the pool is one the server refuses
(ADR-0002). Three of the four forms then started on the filter's value anyway:
`const starting = defaultProgram || onlyOne?.program_id || ''`. Filter by a closed curriculum, press
เพิ่ม, and the form opens already set to a value no save can carry, with its option drawn and
*enabled* — the clause #232 wrote for the record that is already filed in one. A form that reads as
complete, and a refusal at บันทึก.

**The ticket's second option was an owner's question until a comment in the product code answered
it.**

Option 1 was *pin `starting` to the pool*, a fix. Option 2 was *stop drawing retired curricula in
the filter*, which takes a capability away and is therefore `docs/06` §Out of Scope's question and
not mine. What settled it was not an argument but a file that had already chosen: `Plos.js:180-192`
lands the screen on the first curriculum **still running**, with the reason spelled out — *a retired
one is a poor thing to open on, and is landed on only when it is all there is*. That is this very
screen, deciding this very species, which makes it a decision rather than a precedent to weigh
(#196). What the decision had not covered is the curriculum a person picks **by hand** afterwards,
which is every row of this ticket. And the witness is new in kind: #196's earlier witnesses were
other tickets' files, while here the repo's earlier answer was a comment beside the code the fix
lands next to.

Option 2 also failed on its own terms. `GET /api/rubrics` filters by scope and serves the list of a
retired curriculum with a 200 — so the thing option 2 proposed to remove is a capability the server
still offers, which makes it a change to a user story rather than a change to a screen (#166).

And the two witnesses hold two different halves, which is what the review separated. `Plos.js`'s
comment decides **where a screen lands**, which is option 1's species exactly; it says nothing about
**what a filter lists**, which is the mechanism option 2 would change. So #196 carries option 1 and
#166 is what closes option 2. Reading one witness as the answer to both halves is reading an
analogy as a decision — the failure #196 was written to prevent, met from the inside.

**The census was by the mechanism, and it found four sites in two shapes.**

The ticket named three forms. Asking *which form starts on `defaultProgram` while its own pool is
narrower than the list the screen's filter is drawn from* found four — and the fourth does not look
like the other three on the screen. `RubricForm`, `PloForm` and `ProgramSubjectForm` draw the retired
option and leave it enabled while the field holds it, so the person sees a form that is ready. The
`OfferingForm` picker is drawn from `usable` alone, so the retired value is one **no option can show
at all**: the field read as the curriculum still running while the draft held the closed one, and
`listOfferableSubjects` was called for a curriculum the server refuses. #174's rule gave the
population; #244's — what the copy does not carry is not the proof but the way the screen would show
the defect — gave the shapes.

The fix lands at all four, because it is one line, and leaving a copy unfixed is what #244 was
opened to repair. The row for the fourth is at #245: it is *untested* and not *structurally
unreachable* (#102's three answers), because the Offerings screen is `PROG_MANAGER`'s alone and a
committee grant's scope is one curriculum, so no account in the seed sees that filter and the
situation needs a second grant made over HTTP as `198a`'s fixture does. A deferral written into
prose and not into the tracker is a decision nobody can find (#119).

**The clause had to choose a side of a marker.**

`OfferingForm` carries a `// form-identity:` marker, which `forms-cleared-by-identity.js` reads as
the comment **immediately above** the effect it exempts. The first draft put `const filtered`
between the two, and the census would have stopped seeing the marker. It says so out loud, which is
the whole point of the convention #233 settled — and the lesson for a fix is that a marker is part
of the code's shape: a line inserted near one has to pick a side, and the side is decided by what
the instrument reads rather than by what the code reads better.

**Rewriting a line is a change to every mutant anchored on it, and the anchor check is not the
proof.**

`anchors.py` came back with `problems 4` immediately: `18:noautoprogram`, `232:arrayidentity`,
`233:outcomearrayidentity` and `233:pairarrayidentity` all quoted the `starting` line this fix
rewrote. Each was re-aimed by preserving the **mistake** and not by finding the line (#203): the new
pool clause is left standing in every edit, so each mutant goes on reproducing its own ticket's
defect alone. A mutant that also undid #234's clause would be a mutant of two tickets and would
prove neither cleanly.

`232:arrayidentity`'s anchor had quoted the comment paragraph along with the line, and this fix
rewrote that paragraph — so the repair was to **shrink** the anchor to the bare line rather than
retype the prose, which is #121 and #123 enforced a ticket late rather than discovered.

Then all four were run again against the rows their own sheets name — `18a` row 1, `198a` rows 1 and
4, `233a` rows 4 and 5 — and all four still kill them. An anchor check tells you a mutant no longer
applies; only a sweep tells you it no longer proves anything (#107, #68).

**A new file name expired another file's command.** `mutation/34-activity-scores.py` documented
`npx playwright test 34a`, which was exact the day it was written; `234a` arriving made it match two
files, because a test-file argument is matched as a **substring** (#154, #158). `anchors.py` caught
it in the same run. The fix is `tests/34a`, which is the convention every file written since uses.

**The review found the mutant the rules already owed, and its first draft killed at a timeout.**

The first draft of this ticket declined option 2 and stopped. That breaks the repo's own rule: when
a ticket's proposal is declined, the mutant to write is that proposal made to run (#48), because
otherwise *a closed curriculum's rubrics are still listed* is asserted on a sheet and held by
nothing. `234:rubricfilterhidestheretired` is that option — aimed at `pages/Rubrics.js` and not at a
form, because what option 2 takes away is the **reading**. The screen that proves the rule is chosen
by the census and not by the subject (#68), which is why one of the three screens carries it.

Written and run, it killed row 1 inside `filterTo`'s `waitForList`, at the timeout rather than at a
claim (#139): the capability was being held as the row's **premise** — `filterTo` selecting the
closed curriculum — and a filter that no longer offers that option leaves `selectOption` with
nothing to pick. So row 1 gained one assertion, that the option is **offered**, read *above* the
filtering. The order is necessity and not taste, which is #233's rule from the other side: there a
precondition read above the claim was the mistake, because the mutant killed it first and the claim
below was never read; here the reading that follows from the claim is the filtering itself, so the
claim has to come first. Then the mutant dies at that claim with `Received: 0`.

And `rubricfollowstheretiredfilter` was run again afterwards, because a row that gains an assertion
expires the kill count of a mutant nobody edited, with the anchor still exact and the code it edits
untouched (#202). It still kills at its own claim and not at the new one above it.

**The review's other three findings were all about the new instrument.** `e2e/support/retiring.js`
was extracted at its second caller, and `onFailure` was **optional** in the first draft — a caller
that forgot it would drop a failed restore on the floor and leave a curriculum switched off for the
next file, with nothing red to say so (#89, #132). It is required now, and throws when absent, which
is safe because that line is the row's arrangement and not its `finally`. The restore itself only
guarded a non-200: a transport error threw out of `finally` and **replaced** the row's own error,
which is the failure #181 is about, so both paths go to `onFailure` now and the dispose is in
`finally`. And *one `switchOff` per context* went into the docblock, the restore being what closes
the context.

The last one is a name. Three forms use `filtered` for a **boolean**; `OfferingForm` needed the
curriculum code itself, and calling that `filtered` too is the thing a fifth copy misreads — so it
is `filteredProgram` there, with the asymmetry written beside it. No mutant held the line, which was
checked by grepping `mutation/` for both the anchors and the **replacement strings** (#140).

**Nothing new went into `CLAUDE.md`'s index.** Every rule this ticket leaned on was already
there — #196, #166, #174, #102, #119, #203, #107, #121, #154, #233's marker convention, and, from
the review, #48, #68, #139, #202, #89, #132, #181 and #140 — and a rule met again is a sentence in
this story, not a second line in a file that grows every ticket.

## #231 — the name that reached the record and not the button, and the half of the question that was mine

The role picker read `กรรมการหลักสูตร 0501`: the role's name and a bare code. #215 had written the debt
itself when it closed, because the two administration screens that draw a scope's name get it from
the list `GET /api/users/grantable` answers, and the readers of *this* label are the two roles that
endpoint refuses — #215's own rule from the other side, an endpoint that answers *what may be
offered* standing in for one that answers *what this value is*, with the gap showing as an audience.
So the picker could not be closed by that mechanism at all. The ticket offered three options: have
the server send name and kind, decline and write the reason, or the wording is the owner's.

**The three options were two questions, and only one of them was the owner's.**

Where a value is resolved on the server is mechanism; what the person reads is wording. Read as
alternatives, the three options either send the owner a question about plumbing or send me off to
pick words. So they were split: the wording went to the owner, and the mechanism was decided by
measurement. #204 is this rule's parent — a ticket that proposes one fix can be proposing two — met
one layer along, where the split is not between two fixes but between two answerers.

The mechanism half had a cost line to refute first. The ticket priced option 1 as *extra tables on
every request*, and `attachRoles` already runs that query on every request: resolving `scope_id` is
three `LEFT JOIN`s on a query that was being sent anyway, not a round trip. #77's rule — a ticket's
cost line is a claim about the shape its author pictured, not about the option — and it is the one
claim in a ticket that is about the *fix*, so it is what chooses which option gets built.

Then the question was where the names go, and the answer was not `/api/me`. `X-Deep-Grants` carries
the same grant set with **every** answer, so a grant given mid-session reaches the screen through
that header and never through `/api/me`. Putting the names in `/api/me` alone would draw a new grant
as a bare code in front of the person who had just been given it — which is row 3 of the new spec.
The names went into `allRoles`, which both channels read. The resolution walks `scopeChain`'s own
order, curriculum then department then faculty, because that is the order the server's guard already
walks; `is_active` is deliberately not asked of the scope tables, since a grant whose scope has been
retired is still a grant somebody holds and a label that vanishes is worse than one that still
reads; and `FULL_ADMIN`, a value the schema chose rather than one anybody says (#216), stays
unnamed.

The owner answered the wording on 27 October 2569: **name and code, no kind word** —
`กรรมการหลักสูตร วิศวกรรมคอมพิวเตอร์ (0501)` — because this label's role name already says which kind of
scope it is, unlike `scopeLabel` on the administration screens, where `หลักสูตร ·` is the only
thing that says it. The criterion row #215 had left behind said *the option says the kind of scope
in words*, which was #215 guessing at the answer while writing the debt down, so the criterion's own
wording changed with the mark.

**A value added to a record does not reach a screen that draws a pointer to it.**

With the server sending names, rows 1 and 2 of the new spec were still red while row 3 passed. That
is not the shape of a fix that does not work, so rather than argue with it I wrote a throwaway probe
spec that printed the sign-in body and the trigger's text side by side: the body carried
`scope_name` for every grant, and the button still read `กรรมการหลักสูตร 0501`. The trigger
draws `label(acting)`, and `acting` — in `shellState` and in the `X-Deep-Grants` header alike — is a
two-column **pointer**, `role_id` with `scope_id`, which is what the switch is keyed on. The name had
reached the record and not the thing drawing it.

The tell was the subset. Row 3 arrives at its claim through the menu, which is built from the list,
so it passed; rows 1 and 2 read the worn label, which is built from the pointer, so they failed.
Read without the probe, a fix that works for one row of three looks like a fix that half-works,
when it is a fix that landed somewhere else entirely. The repair is at the drawing —
`const worn = roles.find(isActing) ?? acting` — finding the record the pointer names, rather than
fattening the pointer so the server sends the name twice: two places holding one opinion is a claim
neither of them can be shown to hold (#97). The ticket never mentioned this half, and it is the half
that made the server fix invisible on the screen.

**The shared text cost the proof nothing, because the mutants went to the call sites.**

`withCode` in `components/users/scopeLabel.js` became an exported `scopeCoded`, since #231 is the
first caller that wants that half without the kind word, and `scopeLabel` calls it. #104: extracting
shared text costs the proof nothing if the mutants move to the call sites. So `nokind` (#90) and
`bracketsthesentinel` (#216) were re-aimed onto `scopeCoded` and onto the `scopeLabel = scopeCoded`
line rather than merged upward into one mutant, and each killed exactly the rows its own sheet
records — nine and three — with the new spec standing in both sweeps. `stalelabel` on this sheet was
re-aimed onto `{label(worn)}` and still kills `10a` row 3 at the same assertion. An anchor check says
a mutant no longer applies; only a sweep says it no longer proves anything (#107, #68), and a mutant
nobody re-aimed can stop killing the row it was written for without anything going red (#198).

On the spec side, the pinned label text became `committeeLabel(scopeId)` in `e2e/support/shell.js`,
which reads the names out of `db/seed` instead of retyping them (#118) and is an instrument rather
than any row's claim, so it is shared (#171). No `RegExp` anywhere, because `0503`'s name has
brackets in it.

**And the ticket's count of what it would change was wrong by a factor of four.** It said *four
places in two files*; the label was pinned on 17 lines in 5 spec files, and the ticket also named a
spec file that does not exist. A ticket that states how many places it changes has published a claim
a one-minute grep can check (#55, #96, #107), and a grep is evidence for the pattern you typed
rather than for the claim you wanted (#111, #124).

The three mutants of the new file are the three claims. `namelessresolver` is the diagnosed code made
to run (#115) and kills all three rows. `triggerreadsthepointer` is the half the ticket did not
report, and kills rows 1 and 2 while row 3 stands — which is what makes row 3 a claim of its own
rather than a copy of row 1. `kindwordinfront` is the owner's declined wording made to run (#48),
killing all three with
`Received: "กรรมการหลักสูตร หลักสูตร · วิศวกรรมคอมพิวเตอร์ (0501)"` — the only thing that turns *we chose
otherwise* from a sentence on a sheet into a claim the suite holds.

What the new spec cannot say is how the longer label **looks**, so sheet 10 gained a ☐ row beside the
⚙ one: the spec reads the label's characters, not the width of the button or whether the button is
still in the bar. The account to walk it with is `prog.manager.0503@`, whose scope has the longest
name in the seed and brackets inside it, so the drawn label ends with two bracketed groups.

**And the clean suite found two rows this change had broken, both of them lines the census could
not see.**

866 passed, 2 failed, and both reds were mine — which is what the clean run is for, since no sweep
can see the row your own fix breaks (#83, #96, #107). The census that found 17 pinned lines had
asked for the label's **text**, and neither of these two is written as text. `12a:431` built it from
two constants, ``new RegExp(`^${COMMITTEE} ${PROGRAM}`)``, so a grep for the words could not find it:
#111 and #124 one layer along, where what the pattern cannot find is not a different spelling but a
string that does not exist in the file at all.

`81a:146` is the better one. It passed the label into `new RegExp(label)`, and the label now ends in
`(0501)` — brackets, which a regular expression reads as a capture group, so the pattern requires
the code without them and fails against text that is character for character what it was given:

    Expected pattern: /กรรมการหลักสูตร วิศวกรรมคอมพิวเตอร์ (0501)/
    Received string:  "กรรมการหลักสูตร วิศวกรรมคอมพิวเตอร์ (0501)"

A value interpolated into a `RegExp` is a claim that the value holds no metacharacters, and the
failure it produces is the one that reads as no failure at all — the two lines in the report are
identical, so the eye goes looking for whitespace or a zero-width character rather than for the
brackets it can see. `e2e/support/shell.js` had this written down already, in the reason
`committeeLabel` is built without a `RegExp`; what it had not done was reach the caller that builds
its own. Both sites are plain-text `toHaveText` now, and the reason lives in `wearing`'s docblock,
which is where the mechanism is (#168).

**And the review found the name and the kind being resolved by two different precedences.**

Both axes landed on the same line. `scope_kind` is resolved by which row exists, which is
`scopeChain`'s walk; `scope_name` was a `COALESCE` over the three name columns, which is resolved by
which name is not null. `programs.program_name_th` and `departments.department_name_th` are both
nullable, so a programme with no Thai name and a department sharing its id would answer
`scope_kind: 'program'` with the **department's** words — one tier's name over another tier's
authority, which is exactly what the paragraph four lines above it calls worse than a bare code. The
docblock had written the failure down and the query produced it the other way round.

Two columns that describe one row are read off that row, both of them. The repair is one `CASE` on
the same three ids, so a tier with nothing to say answers `null` and the screen keeps the code,
which `scopeNamed` already has a rule for. It is cheap, it is strictly better, and nothing in the
suite held it: the collision row above builds two *named* rows, so neither resolver could fail it.

What the finding cost is a row and a mutant. The row builds its own tiers — a nameless programme
`0599`, a named department `0599`, a grant over it — rather than emptying a name the seed handed
out, because a suite that shares one database is a world every other file is handed too (#132), and
takes all three out below the seam (#134). `nameofanothertier` is that `COALESCE` made to run
(#115), and it is the only mutant in this file proved at the HTTP seam rather than in the browser.
`namelessresolver` was re-aimed onto the `CASE` that replaced its line, keeping the mistake and not
the line (#203).

It is also the second finding this ticket owes to a reader rather than to a run, and both were of
the same species: a claim the code made about itself that no row could fail. The first was the
ticket's own count of the places it would change; this one was a docblock's promise about what the
resolver could not do.

## #239 — the fourth mount point, the sentence that had to cross a hand-on, and the instrument that asks the next one

#209's owner answered on 19 October 2569 that the server says how many pages there are and a
person whose page has gone is handed to the last one that has not. That answer went into the
`load` of the seven screens #209's census could see. `<Pager>` had eleven mount points.

The ticket's numbers were measured before they were believed, by the mechanism rather than by a
spelling: seven files hold a comparison of the answer's page against a bound and move the pager's
own state to it, four do not, and eleven elements are mounted. Of the four, `Users.js` is the one
a single person reaches alone — the filter *ใช้งานอยู่* and the button *ระงับ* are a read and a
write of one list, so suspending the last page's only row leaves the person standing past the end,
reading *ไม่พบผู้ใช้งานตามเงื่อนไขที่เลือก* over a filter that has just found ten people. No second
actor, no race, nothing held. That is not a new rule to decide but a decision already taken,
applied to a population the census of the day could not see.

### The shape the seven screens use does not fit a screen whose callers listen

`Departments.js` §`HANDED_ON` had written down, on 20 October 2569, that no caller on those six
screens reads what `load` answers, and that the day one did the shape would have to change. On
`Users.js` both writers read it: `save` and `confirmSwitch` ask whether the reload drew before
saying what they did. So the third answer could not be a bare *I handed on*. A caller that hears
only that keys its sentence to the read it sent, which is the read that has just been superseded —
the sentence is then held for a page nobody will ask for again, and nothing says it.

The answer carries the read it handed to, and the caller files its sentence under that read. The
target travels in the **answer** and not in a ref, for the reason #207 and #211 both found from
their own side: a ref is read a turn later, by which time the hand-on has rewritten it, so a ref
can answer *is this still the page I was sent from* and cannot hand the caller the thing it has to
pick. Every rule in this family is about what a value is **of**.

### The row had to hold a window, because nothing clears a notice

The first draft of the sentence row read the finished screen: the handed page arrives, the sentence
is on it, green. It was green against the unfixed code too. Nothing on this screen clears a notice,
so a sentence said on the truthy answer is still on the screen when the handed page lands — the end
state is identical under both behaviours, and the mutant written for that claim would have survived
for free. What tells them apart is *when*. The row now holds the handed read at the route and reads
the negative inside that window, at a named settle point: the held request having reached the route.
In that window the correct screen says nothing, because the sentence is a key in a ref; the only
thing that can put it there is the code the row is about.

The first draft also failed in the #233 way: it polled for the landing *above* its own claim, so the
mutant killed the precondition and the claim under the red line was never read. The row is ordered
by what the mutant takes away.

Run against the unfixed code first (#203), row one went red at its own poll with `shown` 2 against
`pages` 1 — `หน้า 2 จาก 1`, the ticket's diagnosis measured rather than believed. The two sentence
rows went red there too, but at the gate's timeout rather than at their claim, the handed read never
happening at all; that is a kill at a wait (#139), which is why the sentence claims are measured by
their own two mutants and not by the unfixed run.

### A sentence line that became three lines, and the seven anchors that quoted it

`python mutation/anchors.py`, run while the work was being finished, reported seven mutants of five
closed tickets with no match: #140's two, #202's one, #203's two, #208's one and #86's. All seven
had quoted the handler block whole, and the fix turned its sentence line into three. The anchor
check says a mutant still applies; only a sweep says it still proves anything, so all seven were
re-aimed and all seven were re-swept. Each still kills exactly the row it was written for.

Two of the re-aims were not mechanical. #202's claim is the comparison `showing.current === sent`,
and the fix writes that comparison **twice** in the handler, so the faithful mutant is wrong in both
places: a re-aim is faithful when it preserves the mistake, not when it finds one line. And #203's
two mutants are built from `SAVE_READS`/`SAVE_ANYWAY`, which has a byte-identical twin in the same
file, `PLOS_REMOVAL_READS`, belonging to a screen this fix does not touch — so the restatement went
into the named constant and not into every block that looks like it (#202's tenth reading, a shared
constant edited to move one mutant moving others in files the ticket never opened).

The fix then moved its own comments above the block, so that what those anchors quote is contiguous
code with no comment inside it. An anchor is built from the code a mutant breaks, never from the
comment beside it, and a comment inserted into the middle of a quoted block makes every anchor over
it depend on prose.

### The instrument that asks the next mount point

#198 had already written down the price of moving a rule from one structural point into each caller:
the census question comes back, and nothing asks whether the next landing carries it. That price was
paid here. `frontend/scripts/pager-last-page.js` asks by the mechanism — which files mount `<Pager>`
and what each hands `onPage`, and whether the file holds an `if` comparing something's `.page` with
`>` against a bound whose body hands that same setter the same bound. Nothing about `Math.ceil`,
`total`, `lastPage` or `HANDED_ON`: a screen that computes the bound another way and moves the person
is green, and a screen that writes all four names and moves nobody is not. Its first run read
`corrected 8 · marked 3 · unclassified 0 · problems 0`, the eight being #209's seven plus this
screen — the same population the ticket's hand census found, which is evidence that the instrument
reads the mechanism and not a memory of it.

Its own fixtures pass whether or not it can see anything, so it was proved by breaking a real site
and by moving the population: `Departments.js` made to hand the person to page one instead of the
last page went red, and a `<Pager>` planted in `pages/Plos.js` made it name a file nobody had
touched. The second of those is the half a fixture cannot hold — an instrument whose population is
derived is proved by moving the population, not only by breaking a member of it.

The three mount points with no rule carry a dated marker instead, each in its own words, because
nothing a person can press on those screens makes the list it is drawing shorter: `Students.js` has
only *เพิ่มนักศึกษา* and the import, both of which can only add rows, and its program filter calls
`setPage(1)` in the same handler that changes the filter; the two history panels write nothing and
have no filter. A marker is a claim like a ticket's numbers, and the day one of those screens gains
a write that takes a row out of what the pager asked for the marker is an exemption with nothing to
say so — which is written inside the marker, since the census asks whether a guard is there and
cannot ask whether the screen has the move.

### The probe was dated, not deleted

`e2e/probes/222-the-page-past-the-end.spec.js` measured the defect on 25 October 2569 and its
predictions are now false. It stays, because it is the only thing that reads this sequence as a
person walks it, with a first paragraph saying what landed and when; its table is the record of a
measurement and not a prediction about today. #222 itself is untouched: the ceiling at
`backend/lib/paging.js`, which would reach all eleven callers, is still the owner's question, and
closing a ticket does not answer one.

## #236 — the two differences that were one difference and one convention, and the record a serial run had written short

#219 asked on 24 October 2569 whether `pressPager`, `stepBack` and `awayAndBack`, written out in
three spec files, should be merged. #210 had deleted all three the day after that ticket was
written, so the question was closed void — and what stood in that place instead was
`askToRemove`, the same three files, letter for letter apart from two things. The ticket named
them: the dismissal of the box, and what `gate` is told to do with the answer. Its own cost line
was the sweep of five mutation files.

### The ticket's two differences, measured

The repo had already answered the species. #219's own second shape merged `dismiss` because no
row's claim lives in the leaving of a box (#171), and #196 says a rule already applied to this very
screen is a decision rather than a precedent to weigh. So the question was not *may this be
merged* but *which of the two differences is the instrument's and which is the row's* — and that
is read off the files, not argued.

There is no `expect` anywhere in the three copies. Every claim the five calling rows make is read
after the hold is opened or beside it. So the asking is an arrangement, and `removeDepartment`,
already in `e2e/support/departments-screen.js`, is a different instrument rather than the same one:
it asserts `status() === 200` and waits for the list, which is a claim it holds itself.

The first of the two differences then dissolved. `dismiss` was not a property of three
implementations: **three of the five rows already wrote it at their own call site**, `207a` had
folded it inside, and the fifth never dismisses at all — so after the merge four of the five do. Moving that one line out to its one caller leaves the shared asking with no
wait of its own, which is exactly what #81 is about — a wait put in a shared helper stops being
one row's claim and becomes every caller's premise. The option nobody had listed was to take the
convention the majority of the call sites already used.

The second difference is real and is the row's: it is `gate`'s own fourth argument, so it is passed
through under `gate`'s own name rather than renamed. `206a`'s inverted `{ writes = false }`, which
had to be read twice to see which way round it went, is gone; the file holds `ANSWERED_HERE` for
the two rows that answer at the route, and the row that lets the write through passes nothing. The
long dated #209 note that explained why that one row is the exception went to **that row's call
site**, because it is a fact about one row's fixture and not about the instrument (#124).

### The merge is read by breaking it, not by the rows staying green

Three green files prove that nothing fell over. What has to be measured is that each row's way in
really goes through the shared instrument (#196, #203, #207). Removing the confirm press from the
helper turned **all five calling rows red** — three in the combined run and the other two run
one at a time, because `mode: 'serial'` skips what follows a red (#67). The `Users.js` row of `208a`
stayed green, correctly: it does not ask to remove a department.

### The record of a serial run is short by the rows it skipped

The ticket's price was six mutants, not seven: `207:refnevermoves` is `SUPERSEDED`, a withdrawn
record the harness refuses to apply, so the file the ticket counted has nothing live in it. A
ticket's cost line is a claim like its numbers (#77), and this one was measurable before it was
paid.

Reading the six per row rather than against a total (#203) found something that was not about this
ticket at all. `206:sentenceofthepagetheyleft` killed `206a` row 1 **and row 3**, where the sweep
record of 19 October 2569 lists only the first row. The probe that dates it is #103's and #207's:
stash the merge out of the tree with the mutant still applied, run that row by its title — red
there too, so the kill is pre-existing. The reason the record is short is `serial` again: row 1 died
first, rows 2 and 3 were skipped and never run alone, and row 3 had arrived on 14 October 2569,
five days before that sweep. **A sweep record written off a `serial` run names the rows that ran,
and reads exactly like a list of the rows the mutant kills.** The old table was not edited, being
the record of what was measured that day; a dated paragraph beside it says what a run today returns
(#54).

## #245 — the fourth copy's row, and the fixture the ticket prescribed that could not build the situation

#234's fix landed in four forms on 27 October 2569 and its spec file held three rows. The fourth
copy, `components/offerings/OfferingForm.js`, had no row and no mutant, which made it *untested*
rather than *structurally unreachable* (#102's three answers) — and the deferral was written in the
tracker rather than in a paragraph, which is what #119 is about. #245 was that ticket.

It also prescribed its own fixture, in a sentence both the spec file's `§what this file does not
measure` and the mutation file's header had copied: *reaching that form needs a second committee
grant made over HTTP as `198a`'s fixture does, on top of the retirement*. The screen is
`PROG_MANAGER`'s alone and a committee grant's scope is one curriculum, so no account the seed
holds ever sees the screen's curriculum **filter** at all — `programs.length > 1` is never true,
the field is drawn as a `<span>`, and #234's situation cannot be arranged.

### The prescribed fixture builds nothing

A probe measured it before a row was written. `GET /api/offerings/programs` is answered from
`reachablePrograms(pool, req.auth.acting.scope_id)` — **the one grant being worn**, not the union
of what the person holds. So a second committee grant at a second curriculum is a second shell
showing one curriculum, the filter is still not drawn, and the fixture the ticket named would have
produced a row that passes against the unfixed code: nothing to measure, bought for free (#203).

What draws the filter is a `PROG_MANAGER` grant whose **scope is a department**. `assignable`
permits it — it asks that the role be no more senior than the administrator's and that the scope
exist, be live and be in reach, and it does not ask that the scope's kind match the role — so the
probe got `201` and then two curricula back. And nothing has to be pressed to wear it: `allRoles`
orders `BY r.priority ASC, ur.scope_id ASC`, both grants are `PROG_MANAGER`, so `05` sorts before
`0501` and `actingFrom` wears the department grant by default. It is a state an administrator can
put somebody in through the real screens, which is what separates it from a state only the seam can
build (#47).

So **a ticket's prescribed fixture is a claim like its numbers**, and it is #141's rule read from
the other side. #141 says a ticket's reason for being *untestable* is a claim: measure whether the
situation can be built. This is a ticket that said the situation *can* be built and named the way —
and the way it named was one that cannot build it, while another, which the ticket did not know
about, can. The two failures are not symmetric in what they cost: #141's wrong reason leaves a
situation unmeasured, and this one leaves a row that is green for nothing.

### The defect's shape there, and the direction the row had to reverse

The three sibling forms draw the retired option and leave it **enabled** while the field holds it,
so the person reads a form that looks complete and is refused at บันทึก. `OfferingForm` draws its
picker from `usable` alone, so a retired curriculum there is a value **no option can show**: before
the fix the field read out the name of a curriculum still running while the draft held the closed
one, and `listOfferableSubjects` was called with a curriculum the server refuses. Two claims and
not one (#66), ordered as the mutant leads (#88): the request first, the drawing that follows from
it second.

The row closes the **other** curriculum than its three siblings do. `db/seed.js` files its one
`program_subjects` row under `0501`, so `0501` is the only curriculum whose subject picker can hold
anything; closing `0503` instead lets the second claim read a subject that is there, rather than an
empty picker, which is drawn identically whether the form asked about the right curriculum or was
refused for asking about the wrong one (#164). The waiter is matched by the **request** and never by
the answer's value, so the row fails at its own `expect` instead of at a timeout (#116).

### What the mutant could not borrow

`offeringfollowstheretiredfilter` is written with its own text rather than the `POOL_CLAUSE` the
three siblings share: the fourth copy is one expression where they are two, and it holds a
**curriculum code** where they hold a boolean — which is the rename #234's review had already asked
for. The name stays referenced by the effect and by its dependency list, so `CI=true` still
compiles (#101). It kills row 4 alone, at the row's first claim, `Received: "0503"`.

And the four existing mutants were re-swept although nothing touched them: **a spec file that gains
a row a mutant can reach expires that mutant's count with nothing to report it** — the anchor is
still exact and the code it edits untouched, so only running it again speaks (#202). All four still
kill their own row alone; what moved is the number that passed, two to three, which is the
population and not the measurement. Row 4 stands under all four, which is what four copies should do
(#83).

## #238 — the owner's rule on two more screens, and the bystander assertion it turned negative

#238 was a `question` ticket, not a fix. It carried the second of #210's two questions, which #221
had measured in full on 25 October 2569 and could not answer: when a write's sentence and the read
that draws its result come apart, **who says the sentence, and over which list**. #221's own
nine-arm table is what made the question answerable: `Users.js` says *บันทึกข้อมูลเรียบร้อยแล้ว*
in all six of its sequences, including over the rows of a page the saved account was never on,
while `Students.js` says nothing at all once the person has moved, because #205 had keyed its
sentence to the read that would draw it. #241 then measured `Plos.js` on 25 October 2569 and put it
on the `Users.js` side with a sequence neither of the other two has: there the sentence stands over
another curriculum's outcomes with **no window held at all**.

The owner answered on 28 October 2569: rule **ก** — *the sentence is bound to the read it talks
about* — and, to the second question, *do all of it in this ticket*. So the work was #205's
mechanism written into `Users.js` and `Plos.js`, and nothing at all in `Students.js`, which already
was the answer. That absence is the answer to a question, and the acceptance sheets say so rather
than leaving the screen unmentioned.

### The mechanism is two halves, and only one of them was new code

The caller hands the sentence over **before** the read, keyed to the list the write is about
(`waiting.current = { of: readOf(page, filters), said }`), and `load` says it only when
`waiting.current.of === key`, clearing the ref in `finally` inside `isCurrent()` unless it handed
the page on. On `Users.js` the first half already existed on one of the two paths: #239 had landed
that morning and built the keyed hand-on for the case where the write takes the person's page away.
What #238 changed is that the keyed path became the **only** path — the `reloaded` branch that said
the sentence whatever the person had done meanwhile is gone.

That matters for the mutants more than for the code. The caller half's mistake — *say it yourself
after the read* — is exactly what `239:savesaysitovertheoldpage`,
`239:switchsaysitovertheoldpage`, `203:plossaveanyway` and `203:plosremovalanyway` restore, and all
four were re-aimed the same day. So `mutation/238-…py` writes no mutant for it: a mutant that
quietly becomes a twin of another leaves its own assertion as unrun as it was before (#201). Its
four mutants hold the **second** half, the key, two per screen: one that drops the comparison and
says the pending sentence over any read that draws, and one that removes the sentence altogether,
which asks what holds the positive row.

### A bystander assertion, not a bystander row

`211a` row 1 ended by reading *ลบผลการเรียนรู้เรียบร้อยแล้ว* over the list, and after the fix that
sentence is not said: the row moves the filter inside the window, which is the whole point of
#211's row, so the key no longer matches and nothing says it. The row went red.

This is #86 one layer in. #86 says a fix that puts a dialog in front of a control re-dates every
other ticket's **prose** about how that control is reached; here an owner's rule about *who speaks*
re-dates another ticket's **assertion**, and no instrument reports it — `anchors.py` is about
mutants, the census is about the code, and the row simply fails. The repair is not to delete the
row: its claim is `handlerReads`, which is untouched. The last assertion turns negative —
`expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveCount(0)` with the sentence quoted in the comment beside
it — and the positive claim travels to #238's own rows, which is where the behaviour now lives.
The constant that held the wording went with it, because a constant nothing reads is a claim
nobody checks.

### Sixteen re-aims, and a sweep that measured nothing

The fix rewrote the sentence line of four handlers across two screens into three lines each, which
re-aimed sixteen mutants in eight closed tickets' files. `python mutation/anchors.py` says they
still apply; only a sweep says they still prove anything (#107, #68), so all sixteen were run
against their own spec files, each read against the row it was written *for* and not against a
total (#203).

The first attempt at that sweep is the lesson. A PowerShell loop applied each mutant, ran
Playwright, restored, and exited 0 with a tidy log — twenty blocks, each one `saved 2 files`,
`applied <mutant>`, `restored`. What it did not contain was a single line of test output: `& npx`
inside the loop produced nothing that reached the log, so twenty mutants had been applied and taken
out again with no suite ever run. Exit code 0, a log that reads like a record, and nothing measured.
**The count is the tell, not the exit code** (#208) — here the count was of the lines the runner
prints, which is the same question asked of a sweep rather than of a census. The repair was to run
each one through `cmd /c "npx playwright test … >> log 2>&1"`, and the control that proved the
repair was the clean run of `238a` itself.

### What the rows had to be told about frames and pages

Two smaller things cost a reading each. `238a` row 1 first failed because `teacher.one@kmitl.ac.th`
is on the second page of the account list: the row searched for nothing and read a table the
account was not in. The repair is a search in `beforeEach`, which also makes the three accounts the
row's own arrival assertion (#129).

The negative rows then failed with `frames sampled … Received: 1`. A sentence that is never said
cannot be waited for, so the row has to **watch** rather than wait, and a sampler needs frames to
sample: `WATCHING_MS = 1_500` is there so the sampler has something to count, and the comment beside
it says what #52 requires — the wait decides nothing, because `neverSaid` asserts the frame count
and would be red if the window were empty.

### The census the fix was measured against

`frontend/scripts/sentences-after-a-move.js` reads `success sentences 24 · after an await 24 ·
enclosed 19 (opened 16 · position 3) · marked 5` after the fix, where before it read
`opened 19 · position 3`. The orphaned `// sentence-after-a-move:` marker in `Plos.save` came out:
the gap it documented was closed by this ticket, and a marker that outlives its gap is an exemption
(#93, #141). The five sites that keep their markers are earlier decisions, each dated at its own
site — `Offerings.js` is the owner's answer of 1 October 2026 that the sentence belongs to the
command the person gave and not to the panel they are now looking at (#143), which is **another
question**, not this one (#196).

### What the review found, and what each finding turned out to be

Two reviewers read the change. Three of their five findings held, and the two that did not held
something else.

The standards axis saw that the comment beside the hand-over said *the shape the seven
administration screens carry* while those screens key on the live ref — `readOf(onPage.current)` —
and this one keys on the render's own `readOf(page, filters)`. That difference is real, and the
conclusion drawn from it — that the seven screens therefore hold the defect this ticket just
fixed — is not: each of them hands `<Pager>` `busy={busy}`, and `components/Pager.js` turns that
into `disabled` on both buttons, so the page cannot move while a write is out and the live ref is
the render's value there. `Users.js` does not hand it over, which is #210's **first** question,
still open, and that is exactly why the render's coordinates are the only reading of the list this
save was about (#207). So the finding bought a correction to the prose and not to the code (#130),
and the prose now says which reader each screen uses and what decides it. **A reviewer's finding
can be right about the difference and wrong about its consequence** — #205's rule for a
reviewer's name met one layer along, where what settles it is a third file neither screen
mentions.

The same axis found `// Whether it drew, for a handler that has a sentence to say - #203` left
standing above `return true` on both screens, and it was right: `load(() => current)` inside the
effect is the only caller left, and it discards the answer, so `true`, `false` and `HANDED_ON` are
**structurally unreachable** here rather than untested — the second of #102's three answers, and
the comment now says so. The shape stays because it is the ten administration screens' own and
because `SubjectStudents.js`'s `reload` really does compare the answer with `HANDED_ON`.

The spec axis found the thing worth a ticket. `PloForm` closes its หลักสูตร field with
`disabled={busy || editing}`, so on **add** it is open and `draft.program_id` need not be the
curriculum the table is on — a shape `parentPool` was built for on purpose. `load` asks
`listPlos({ program_id: program })`, so after a save into another curriculum the key matches, the
read lands, and *บันทึกข้อมูลเรียบร้อยแล้ว* stands over a list that does not hold the row just
saved. It is not a regression — the sentence stood over that same list before this ticket, said
unconditionally — and **the owner's rule cannot answer it, because the read the sentence talks
about is never ordered**: the screen does not read the other curriculum, so keying on
`draft.program_id` to the letter would leave a successful save silent. That is a state the system
can carry, so it is a question and not a void one (#232), and it is the owner's: four options, each
with its price, and no row presses the sequence today, so whichever answer comes back owes one
(#48 for *keep it as today*).

Both of those questions are tickets rather than paragraphs (#119), which is the finding the spec
axis made about this very sheet: §#238 of the `19` sheet had written *this has to become a ticket*
about #241's reversed fourth arm, and no such ticket existed when the reviewer looked. Both were
opened on 28 October 2026, the hour this ticket closed: #246 for the sentence over a form just
opened, #247 for the save into a curriculum the table is not on.

## #242 — the four screens the owner's reason was silent about, and the eight reasons that named the day

#228 asked whether a form's controls should be disabled while its save is out. The owner answered on
26 October 2569: yes, with **the form's own flag**, and *ยกเลิก* holding no flag at all. That answer
landed on three screens — departments, programs, subjects — and the reason the owner gave is a
sentence about those three. A census by **mechanism** rather than by screen name (#174) — what flag
does each field read — gives four more forms whose fields read `busy`, the page's flag, where
`const busy = writing || reading` is written letter for letter the same in all four parents. That
population is #242, and it is the same shape as #141, #223 and #222: an owner's answer reaches the
population the ticket's census had.

### The first order was to measure, and it decided what kind of ticket this is

The ticket's own first item is #141's rule applied to itself: build the way in at the e2e seam
before arguing about it. The eight rows the file then held, run against the unfixed code on 28 October 2569, came
back **red eight of eight**, each dying at the assertion it is named for. (This sheet and
four acceptance sheets first said *red eight of nine*, corrected on 29 October 2569: the
ninth row, the PLO screen's refusal row, was written afterwards and never read against the
unfixed code — `242:ploreported` is what measures it, which is a mutant's job and not a
before-run's (#115). The wrong wording implied a row that was green against the unfixed
code, which would be a row measuring nothing (#203), and there was none. Before the eight
there was a four-row draft, one row per screen, red four of four.) So this is a defect people meet
today and not a second owner's question: the shape was settled on 26 October, and what was left was
the population. The window is one HTTP round trip — `save`'s `finally` releases `writing`
**after** the `await` of the list re-read — so the sequence is *saved → form closes → press
เพิ่ม… → the new form is drawn with every field disabled* until that read lands. No clock
chooses (#199) and no second actor is needed.

That run also redesigned the rows. The first draft read *ยกเลิก* in the middle of row 1, and all
four first rows died there against the unfixed code — which means the step the ticket actually
asked about, *can the form opened afterwards still be typed into*, **was never read at all**,
because a row reports the first assertion that dies (#88). The claim moved to row 2, and it is
**read as a claim before it is pressed**, because pressing a disabled control dies at the timeout
rather than at the row's claim (#139). This is #203's rule paying for itself: running a new row
against the unfixed code is what says which claim the row holds, hours before a sweep would.

### Item 4 was a name read as a claim

The ticket said `ProgramSubjectForm.js` holds an `<input>` with no flag either way, and asked for it
in the same fix. The form has six controls. The five that can hold a flag held `busy` in full, and
all five became `sending`; the sixth is the field that draws the chosen subject code, `disabled
readOnly` with no condition at all, so nobody could type into it before the save or after it. The
diagnosis read a **name** — a `disabled` with no condition — as a **claim** — holds no flag —
and the measured number is the one that gets reported (#102, #48). The refutation goes in the
closing comment as well as on the sheet, because the ticket's number was pointed at somebody else
(#54, #225).

### The eight reasons that named their own expiry condition

The real find is in the four parent screens. #202 had left eight written reasons there, two per
screen, saying that the `showing.current === sent` guard around `save`'s drawing was a sentence no
row and no mutant could reach (#97) **because** *ยกเลิก* was disabled by `busy` — and each of them
wrote down the condition that would end that: *the day ยกเลิก stops being disabled, this point needs
the three lines `confirmRemoval` already has*. #242 is that day, and it is the fix itself that fires
the condition.

So the fix is not one change but a pair, and the second half was prescribed by a comment written
seventeen days earlier: `setEditing(null)`, the sentence hand-over and `report(error)` all go under
`if (showing.current === sent)` in all four screens. **A dated reason that names its own expiry
condition and its own remedy is a work item, not only a record** — #54's *date it, do not delete it*
paying back, and the reason it pays back is that the remedy was written beside the condition. Had
those eight comments only said *unreachable today*, the four forms would have been freed and four
screens would have been left saying *บันทึกข้อมูลเรียบร้อยแล้ว* over a form the person had meanwhile
replaced, with nothing to say so.

In `Plos.js` the hand-over is written as a block rather than as `confirmRemoval`'s one-liner, on
purpose: four closed tickets' mutants quote that neighbourhood, and a guard copied in the sibling's
exact spelling makes a one-line anchor find two sites (#202). The key answers *which curriculum this
sentence is about* and cannot answer *was this form replaced*, the curriculum being the same on both
sides of a *ยกเลิก* (#205, #207) — which is why the guard is a second clause beside #238's key and
not a narrowing of it.

### The price the ticket asked to be censused, and the kill count it expired

Item 3 asked for a fresh census of the **presses** of #142 and #146 on these four screens, and for
the answer to go back to the owner if the price changed. It did not change: `142a`'s
`cancelDuringSave` arm is a marker for screens where the form's *ยกเลิก* can be pressed while a save
is out, and it now marks **seven** screens instead of three. `146a` deliberately does not take the
four, because its question on these screens **is** `242a`'s row 2, and both docblocks say so.

What nothing reported is that the same arms expire the kill counts of `mutation/142-…py`. The
anchors are exact and the code those mutants edit is untouched; the spec simply gained rows they can
reach, so only re-running them speaks (#202, #107, #68). Two of the twelve were re-swept before the
run was stopped, and one of them says it out loud: `142:pairscurrentletsgo` now kills **two** rows,
its own and the fourth arm that has just arrived on that screen, which is one defect two rows reach
and not two claims (#191).

That re-sweep is also a reminder with a date on it. It was stopped by the system for low memory
after ten of twenty mutants, with `142:pairsletgowhileasked` left applied in the tree: restore, read
`git status`, clear the ports — and do not restart it unasked.

### What the instruments said afterwards

`frontend/scripts/sentences-after-a-move.js` reads `enclosed 20 (opened 17 · position 3) ·
marked 4`, where before the fix it read `enclosed 19 (opened 16 · position 3) · marked 5`:
`RubricCriteria.js` traded its `// sentence-after-a-move:` marker for the guard that marker's own
expiry condition named, which is the census reading the same event the comments did. The other nine
censuses are `problems 0`, `python mutation/anchors.py` is `problems 0` in six sections, and the
backend suite is 850 pass, 0 fail.

All twenty-one of this file's mutants are swept, eleven on 28 October and ten on 29 October 2569,
each killing the row it was written for at the assertion the table named before the sweep (#201).
The four `pagewide` mutants — the page's flag restored at the **declaration**, which is where it has
to go, the field the killing assertion reads belonging to the form opened afterwards — each kill
**two** rows, for #191's reason. There is no mutant for *ยกเลิก*: it would kill other files' rows,
which breaks the rule that a mutant must fail one row and leave the rest standing (#97), so that
claim is a net saying the price has not been paid.

## #243 — the two buttons that held nothing, and the order the ticket prescribed that could not order anything

#228's owner answer of 26 October 2569 reached three screens; #242 took it to four more, found by
mechanism (#174). #243 is the rest: 61 fields in 15 forms holding no flag at all while their own
save is out — the population the owner's reason was silent about, the same shape as #141, #223 and
#222 one step further out. Its first item says, in so many words, **do not land #228's shape on 61
fields at once**: prioritise first, by a question the ticket's own census did not ask — *which
screens leave the form open after a refused save* — measuring the new population's window rather
than inheriting #228's (#223).

### The ticket's order was a claim like its numbers, and the measurement handed over another one

That question was measured before anything was built, and it ordered nothing: the answer is **every
screen**. All eleven parents write `setEditing(null)` **inside** the `try`, after the `await`, so a
refusal skips it and the form stays open with values nobody sent. The window is everywhere, which
makes the ticket's prescribed discriminator true and useless — #241's rule, one species along: a
ticket's named instrument can be the inverse of the one it needs, and a ticket's named *ordering*
can be a property the whole population shares.

What did order it was the sentence #228 wrote to **excuse** its own defect: *the save button of all
five screens is `disabled={busy}` already, so moving a field while the save is out does not send
twice.* That is a claim about each screen (#133), and a census of the submit buttons on 29 October
2569 answers it: of 27, **25 hold the page's flag and two hold nothing at all** — `components/Navbar.js`
and `components/LoginForm.js`, which are exactly the two files the ticket's item 3 had singled out
for a dated reason. The excuse is false on precisely two members of its own population, and those
two are where the defect is a defect rather than a divergence. **So the thing that prioritised 61
fields was not a property of the fields. It was the earlier ticket's self-exemption, read as a
claim and measured.**

### Two members of one population, and opposite answers

`Navbar.js`'s change-password dialog stays on a refusal, and nothing stopped a second press. Row 2
of `243a`, run against the unfixed code before any mutant was written (#203), reads `Expected: 1`
and `Received: 2` — a second request, carrying the **old** password that the first request had just
replaced, so the person is told their current password is wrong, over a change that had already
succeeded. That is the measurement that makes #243 a defect and not only the divergence #228 named,
and it is what bought this screen its place ahead of fifteen other files.

`LoginForm.js` is in the same population by mechanism and gets the opposite answer. `pages/Login.js`
draws the whole form inside `<RetiringPresence at={LoadLogin ? 'loading' : 'content'} mode="wait">`,
and `LoadLogin` is raised before the POST and let go in its `finally`: while the sign-in is out
there is no field to type into and no button to press again. That is #203's ninth reading one layer
along — a screen that answers by replacing itself leaves the defect unreachable for the person, not
merely unproved — so the file gets a reason with a date and an expiry condition (#141), not a flag.
And the reason is a claim about frames, so it is read rather than argued (#169): row 3 holds the
sign-in open and asserts `toHaveCount(0)`. Its mutant is **the accepted reason made to run**
(`loginformstays` pins `at` to `'content'`), which is #48 the other way up — #115's rule reaching a
reason rather than a diagnosis.

### A comment read as the attribute it describes

The first census of the population reported `LoginForm.js`'s submit button as **flagged**, because
the line above it is `// disabled={loading}` — the inherited markup's own intention, left as it was
found. The instrument was reading attributes out of text it had not stripped comments from, so a
sentence *about* a flag counted as the flag. #93 is this trap from the other side, where a `//`
written between two JSX tags is drawn on the screen; here a comment inside JSX props was read as
code. The instrument that read it that way was the throwaway script in `_local/`, which read
attributes out of raw text and was repaired with three lines of stripping; the committed census,
`frontend/scripts/save-window-fields.js`, never had the defect, because it parses the file with
`@babel/parser` and strips nothing, so there a comment cannot be read as an attribute at all.
The finding is that the number the unrepaired reading produced was wrong in the safe-looking
direction, and only the hand reading of the two named files caught it — which
is what item 3 of the ticket was for.

My own comment on the ticket carried a wrong sentence for the same species one layer along: *the
population of fields holding the page's flag is now empty*, from a script that classified by a
**hand-typed list** of flag names with no `loading` in it (#208 — the count is the tell, not the
exit code). Two `<select>`s hold one, and both are read flags raised in a fetch effect and never in
`submit`, so the conclusion about #228's shape stood while its reason did not (#141). The correction
went where the wrong number had been pointed at somebody else (#225): a comment on #243, and a
comment on the ticket whose table it shortens.

### The price of the shape is not uniform, which is why the rest is a separate ticket

Item 2 says: wherever the shape lands, census that screen's *ยกเลิก* **press** first (#199, #221).
By mechanism — rows that hold a request open and then press or fill before releasing it — the suite
has **126 such presses in 20 spec files, 29 of them fills**. For this dialog the answer is **zero**:
five call sites in three spec files all go through one helper, `submitPasswordChange`, which fills
all three fields and *then* presses, so no row types or presses while the save is out and the fix
cost no re-aims. One site in the remaining population is not free — `142a:sectionNumber(page).fill('92')` fills
`SectionsPanel.js`'s field inside a held window — so the work left over is uneven and goes screen by
screen. That is what #249 is, and the ticket's own first item is what produced it.

### The bystanders that gained a row

`Navbar.js` and `pages/Login.js` are read by mutants of ten other files — 21 in all. Nothing was
re-aimed, the fix adding lines rather than rewriting any, and `anchors.py` was clean. The question a
clean anchor check cannot answer is whether the **new** spec's rows are rows those mutants can now
reach (#48, #202), so all 21 were run against `243a` alone: twenty leave its three rows green, and
`10-application-shell:ejectonrefusal` — `if (err.expired)` → `if (true)` — kills row 2, ejecting the
person on the refusal that row arranges itself. That is one more reachability claim for row 2 (#191):
a refused password change leaves the person on the screen. Nothing reports such a gain; the anchor
is exact, the code it edits untouched, and only running it says so.

### The instrument, and the ticket it landed with

Item 4 left it open whether to write a census at all. `frontend/scripts/save-window-fields.js` asks
two questions over the files holding `type="submit"` — does the submit button hold a `disabled`, and
does every field — and its first run is a red gate over a population no ticket has yet fixed:
`forms 27 · flagged 72 · always 1 · marked 3 · bare 57 · problems 0`. So it lands **unwired**, with #249 as the
ticket for the gap, which is #200's shape exactly; wiring it green-by-marker would have taught the
reader to ignore all nine of its siblings.

Both proofs item 4 asked for were run (#230). Breaking a real site: `228/deptstatuslive` leaves
`DepartmentForm.js`'s status field live and `bare` rises to 58, the report naming the line. Moving
the population: flipping that file's `type="submit"` to `type="button"` takes `forms` from 27 to 26
and `flagged` from 72 to 67, and the file leaves the report altogether — which is what shows the
instrument following its own rule rather than a list of names, since its own fixtures pass either
way (#141).

And the first of its six printed limits was measured on a real site the same day, which is #226's
rule met in my own instrument: *it has found a guard and not asked what the guard is for.*
`offerings/OfferingForm.js:182` reads `flagged` while the flag it holds is a read flag that is down
by the time anybody can press save. So `bare 57` is a **lower bound**, and the ticket that inherits
it says so on its face.
